Sports.title: Melbourne boxer's career in turmoil after Australian Idol star exposes his vile private messages - as Anthony Mundine vows to 'teach him a lesson'
Sports.content:
Melbourne boxer Tommy Pedis has been dumped from Victoria's boxing team days before the national championships after sending vile messages to Australian Idol contestant Majeda Beatty.

Beatty went public on Monday with screenshots and a video she said the Craigieburn boxer had sent her directly.

In the video, Pedis used a racist slur, called Indigenous Australians 'petrol sniffers' and told them to 'leave our country'.

Beatty, who competed on Australian Idol in 2025, said the experience had been 'incredibly upsetting, confronting and honestly exhausting'.

'I've been riddled with anxiety today. It's one thing to experience racism, but it's another to have someone deliberately direct it towards you, continue to antagonise you and make you feel as though you're powerless to do anything about it,' she said.

'I never intended to spend my day having to defend my existence, my identity or my people. I'm proud to be Aboriginal, proud of my heritage and proud of the communities I come from. I will not be intimidated into silence or made to feel ashamed of who I am.

'Racism isn't banter, it isn't a joke and it certainly isn't something we should have to tolerate. Boxing is a sport that brings people together from all walks of life, and there should be absolutely no room for racism within it.'

Pedis claimed his remarks had been 'meant to be a joke' and acknowledged that his language was racist, saying he took full responsibility.

Melbourne boxer Tommy Pedis as been booted off the state team just days before the national championships after racist remarks he directed at a former Australian Idol contestant emerged online

He later issued an apology for the vile messages after Majeda outed him online

Majeda publicly exposed him on social media for making the vile comments

'I understand that people are disappointed and angry at me. I don't blame them,' he said.

'I can see my action, what I've done was wrong, it has hurt certain people, and in future I would not do that again.

'My comments were completely unacceptable, and I take full responsibility for what I said.

'There is no excuse for my behaviour, and I deeply regret the hurt and offence I have caused.'

On Tuesday, the VABL and ANABA suspended Pedis from all their events with immediate effect and until further notice, and dropped him from Team Victoria for the national championships.

Former world boxing champion Anthony Mundine challenged Pedis to get in the ring with him.

'This is the s*** I fought against my whole life,' Mundine said.

'Get in touch with me brah, and I'm going to teach you a lesson.

'I don't want to be a bully, but you need to be put in line.'

Sports.title: Huge crowd gathers for funeral of Irish boxer Lee Reeves after he passed away following knockout in the ring and three-month coma
Sports.content:
Huge crowds have gathered today for the funeral of Irish boxer Lee Reeves who died this week.

The 31-year-old died in hospital on Monday after being placed in a medically induced coma following a fight in August.

After being knocked down twice in the 10th round, the Irish southpaw was carried from the ring on a stretcher following his defeat to fellow countryman Gary Cully and taken to hospital.

His promoters, Queensberry, later revealed he was in a 'critical but stable' condition before undergoing surgery.

Reeves was then placed in an induced coma, where he remained until his death three months later, surrounded by his family.

Along with being a professional boxer, Reeves was a serving member of the 12th Infantry Battalion out of Sarsfield Barracks, an ambassador for Limerick Treaty Suicide Prevention and a model.

A large crowd gathered at the Church of Our Lady, Queen of Peace for the funeral mass in Roxboro, Limerick, on Friday, with thousands also tuning in to a livestream of the service.

Dreams by The Cranberries played in the church as the coffin carrying Reeves' body, draped in the Irish tricolour, was carried inside.

Irish boxer Lee Reeves died on Monday after spending three months in a medically-induced coma

Family members accompanied the hearse carrying the coffin of boxer Lee Reeves arriving at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, for his funeral with full military honours on Friday

Members of the Irish Defence Forces carry the coffin of boxer Reeves out of Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

It had been brought to the church on an adapted gun carriage, as part of the military honours for the service.

His Defence Forces cap was also placed on the coffin.

Reeves' boxing gloves and belt, his Bible, and a pizza box were among items placed at the altar to represent his interests including his love of his religion – along with photographs of the Limerick-born boxer.

The mass heard tributes from some of his four sisters: Louise, Shannon, Jodie and Jessie, who described him as 'one of the greatest men on this earth' and 'an inspiration to everyone he met'.

Jodie told the funeral mass that Reeves was a family man who 'did everything' for his sisters.

'He was my mother's whole life, and she was his. He dedicated every fight to her, and no doubt made her proud.

'She was his number one supporter from day one.

'You were a father to us all, and that even includes Dad.'

She added: 'Nothing is going to be the same without you around, but I promise you'll never be forgotten.'

Jodie, also reading a tribute from Reeves' father, said: 'You had a heart and a presence that touched so many lives.'

Continuing that tribute, she added: 'God knows how much we will miss you, and how much of a piece of our hearts will go with you. Rest easy, son.'

Reeves had been carried out of the ring on a stretcher after his defeat to his countryman Gary Cully and taken to hospital (Source: Instagram/Lee Reeves)

A car is pictured following the funeral cortege of Reeves as it leaves Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, after his funeral mass on Friday

Wreaths and tributes are seen on display before the funeral of boxer Lee Reeves at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick,on Friday

Shannon said: 'I will miss you every day that I'm on this earth.'

She added: 'You never deserved this, brother, but it's not the end.

'Your story will live on, and your legacy will live on.'

Outside, a large screen and several framed photographs depicted images of Reeves and his loved ones as well as his boxing gloves.

The images carried captions such as 'brother', 'son', 'nephew', 'uncle' and 'pride of Limerick'.

Attendees included Mayor of Limerick John Horan as well as Defence Forces colleagues including the General Officer Commanding 1 Brigade, Brigadier General Caimin Keogh and Officer Commanding 12th Infantry Battalion, Lieutenant Colonel Ian Harrington.

Reeves was placed in a medically-induced coma and had emergency surgery after a junior welterweight fight in Dublin on August 1.

He had won 16 of his 18 bouts after turning professional in 2018, with several of his fights in Canada and Colombia.

The hearse is pictured carrying the coffin of boxer Lee Reeves arriving at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, for his funeral with full military honours, on Friday

Family members stand behind as soldiers from the Irish Defence Forces place the coffin of boxer and serving soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

Reeves' August clash with final opponent Gary Cully saw the 31-year-old knocked down twice in the 10th round

He was also a contestant on BBC reality show, Survivor, in 2023.

Defence Forces head chaplain Fr Paschal Hanrahan said Reeves showed physical courage in the boxing ring but also moral, courage and integrity in his mental health advocacy.

'We hold in our prayers today his colleagues serving overseas at this time with the 128th Infantry Battalion in Unifil, along with their chaplain Fr Piotr, who I know are gathered at this very moment in prayer for Lee.

'With all the agility and dexterity of a professional boxer, Lee moves seamlessly from being a model to being a role model in the Defence Forces.

'And those who served with him in Sarsfield Barracks saw our Defence Forces values in the way that he lived.'

He added: 'They saw his respect in the way he treated people, his loyalty in the way he stood by his comrades, and his selflessness in the time he gave to those who needed encouragement.'

Reeves, who was nicknamed 'El Champo', had won 16 of his 18 professional bouts since turning professional in 2018, and had been challenging Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic light-welterweight title.

He had been knocked down twice in the 10th round against Cully before being taken out of the ring, and in his tribute message for his opponent, Cully admitted that he was still in shock at how their match had ended.

Members of the Irish Defence Forces walked in procession alongside the coffin of boxer and soldier Reeves on an adapted gun carriage at Our Lady Queen Of Peace Church, Limerick, on Friday

'I still remember the stadium days when I used to watch Lee in the nationals, the weight above me, and (I would) always be impressed by his fights and his flashy gear,' Cully wrote.

'What a character and a gent. It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Sports.title: 'It's amazing that Scotland now has TWO world champions'... Meet the Kilmarnock kid who idolises Prince Naseem Hamed and is part of the Scottish boxing boom with Willy Hutchinson
Sports.content:
'It's amazing that Scotland now has TWO world champions'... Meet the Kilmarnock kid who idolises Prince Naseem Hamed and is part of the Scottish boxing boom with Willy Hutchinson

Only last month, the mutterings were about where Scottish boxing goes from here, three years after Tartan Tornado Josh Taylor was toppled and with doubts mounting about the health of the sport’s grass roots.

Three weeks on, seemingly from nowhere, the nation has not one but two new world champions.

Willy Hutchinson claimed the WBC light heavyweight belt in a tussle with Joshua Buatsi earlier this month in the full glare of the television cameras. But slipping beneath the radar were the achievements of Aaron Sarwar, who was anointed the under-19 world flyweight champion in Montenegro on October 27.

Both men sobbed in the ring and fell to their knees as the simple raising of a referee’s hand detonated identical emotional explosions in them – sudden vindication of years of grinding roadwork, gruelling gymwork and grafting ringwork.

With beautiful symmetry, the only other Scot to have won a world amateur title was Hutchinson himself, in Russia in 2016. Now his ascent to the top of the pro game has lit the path for Sarwar to follow. And if there are still mutterings, they are that this kid from Kilmarnock could be the real deal.

Compared with big-ticket bouts, youth boxing’s short contests can appear cagey and sterile – but it’s hard to peel your eyes off Sarwar’s compelling repertoire of shots, defence, switches and occasional showboating.

Kilmarnock fighter Aaron Sarwar with his trophy for winning the Under-19 world championship

Those who know him best say his most remarkable asset is an iron psyche that, even at such a tender age, has created a machine-like drive to reach whatever peak is placed in front of him.

Having become a world junior karate champion and double black belt by the age of 11, the ring became his home during the Covid-19 pandemic as he looked for a fresh challenge.

Speaking to Daily Mail Sport, Sarwar insists he has already set off on a mission for another Montenegro moment.

He said: ‘People ask me about that feeling. It’s indescribable. I wish I could go back and relive that ten, 15 seconds of getting my hand raised because I don’t think anything will come close to it again.

‘But I’ll be chasing it. I want to make my mum and dad proud again. I watch [the video of] it every day. I get goosebumps every time.

‘I’d spoken to Willy before, but we met at a boxing show this week and had a good chat about what’s next for us.

Sarwar admits he still struggles to describe the euphoria he felt on being crowned the winner

‘It’s amazing that in the space of two weeks, Scotland’s got two new world champions. It’s crazy.’

Sarwar turned to boxing when lockdown meant karate was reduced to online seminars. He stumbled across a basic gym with punchbags behind the shop from where he’d buy lunch on school breaks – and from there he joined the local club.

The 18-year-old was back to his roots this week at the Northwest ABC in Onthank, the estate made infamous by the BBC Scotland fly-on-the-wall documentary The Scheme.

Hitting our screens in 2010, the series won a Bafta award but also stood accused of creating a ‘poverty safari’ for the chattering classes and creating dubious celebrities out of light-fingered drug addict Marvin Baird and his dog Bullet.

Northwest ABC was feted and funded for being a beacon among the anti-social behaviour, even receiving a personal visit from Justice Secretary Kenny MacAskill. Now Graeme Marshall’s committed coaching team has helped create a new poster boy for The Scheme.

Down at the club, they are proud of their prodigy, but the mood is more about hope than hype. They remorselessly tease Sarwar about his fussy fringe and point out, to rein in expectations, that he’s still so young he’s yet to even fight without a headguard.

Sarwar bumped into his fellow world title holder Willy Hutchinson during a boxing show

But Marshall – who Sarwar refers to as akin to a second father – is in no doubt about their boy’s freakish potential.

He said: ‘When he asked to come to the club after lockdown, it was Aaron himself who called up, which was unusual for a 12-year-old.

‘We knew straight away there was a talent there — he’s fast and strong and dedicated. After a few months, we entered him for the Scottish championships. It was his first fight, but he went and won the tournament.

‘Second season, he won the GB championships. I took him all over to fight. In Sweden, he stopped the Swedish champion, and when you see him beating Irish boys in Ireland, you know you’re dealing with something special.

‘He’ll turn professional at some point; it’s every young boy’s dream. And there’s no reason why he can’t go on and match what Willy Hutchinson’s done and become a world champion.’

The calls have started coming from managers testing the water about going pro – as Hutchinson did immediately after winning amateur gold – and McBookie are already offering odds of 8/1 that he goes right to the top.

Hutchinson brought Scottish boxing out of the doldrums with his defeat of Joshua Buatsi

But, for now at least, Sarwar – who ditched his engineering college course to concentrate on the sport – remains focused on fighting for Scotland at the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India.

He said: ‘I’ve got all the time in the world. I’ve opened myself a lot of doors now. I’ll speak to my coaches and mum and dad about what they think is best for me. But I know what I can achieve off the back of this now.

‘For karate, I was dedicated and hard-working but I didn’t have that same passion. Boxing, it’s all I do. I’ve left all my education to box full time. It’s all my eggs in one basket so there’s no choice, I have to do it. It’s boxing or nothing.’

Sarwar names his inspiration as Prince Naseem Hamed, the flamboyant featherweight world champion from the 1990s, for ‘his style, his flashiness, his power’. He added: ‘I’ve got that flashy side too, but if they get serious, I’ll stand toe to toe. I can box, I can fight, I can do it all.’

Despite training solely with Boxing Scotland now, Sarwar can’t keep away from his home club. He added: ‘I try to carry myself well all the time and inspire the young ones to come to the gym and train that bit harder, and it’s good to be around the coaches all the time.

Sarwar is in no rush to turn professional and is eyeing the 2030 Commonwealth Games in India

‘The support they’ve given me over the years has been second to none, I can’t thank them enough. There’ll be no way I can ever repay them the sacrifices they’ve made [for me].’

Meanwhile, in the ring at the Northwest, a small boy’s fists are a deadly blur, thwacking the pads held out by his coach with awesome efficiency. To misquote Muhammad Ali, he has the legs of a sparrow but the sting of a bee.

Aidan Sarwar – 12 years old – is already part of the Scotland set-up.

It was a Glasgow music hall crowd that first memorably coined the heckle, ‘Oh no, there’s two of them’ when English comedian Bernie Winters joined his brother Mike on stage. Boxers across the land may soon empathise.

Sports.title: Sainz proposes intriguing DRS solution for F1 2030
Sports.content:
With F1 close to signing off on the overarching tenets of its 2030 return to V8 power units, some of its leading drivers have fleshed out ideas of how to make those into a compelling product.

F1 is set to move to all-new turbo V8 engines in 2030, with a smaller electric unit of up to 200kW and sustainable fuel. That should make engines simpler, cheaper and lighter, and therefore reduce the reliance on energy from the battery compared to today's oft-criticised formula.

By signing off the V8 move at the next FIA World Motor Sport Council gathering in Shanghai on 12 December, F1 and the FIA are giving themselves time to properly flesh out the chassis and aerodynamic regulations that should work in unison with the V8 power units to produce a better on-track show.

Last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix has given the series some food for thought about what it really wants from its next rules cycle. At the Las Vegas street circuit, F1 delivered an absorbing spectacle featuring a record 35 lead changes, aided by a combination of the powerful slipstreaming effect and the boost mode from the power unit, which led to so-called yo-yo racing as the lead car often ended up a sitting duck on the straight.

While there was debate on whether that's the kind of show F1 wants to see more of, or whether Vegas was too artificial for its own good, it further highlighted the importance of developing a combination of power unit parameters and aerodynamic overtaking aids that can be fine-tuned on a race-to-race basis to deliver a solid spectacle without making overtaking too trivial either.

It prompted Williams driver and Grand Prix Drivers' Association director Carlos Sainz to come up with an intriguing idea on how to tune a DRS-like overtaking system for 2030, suggesting a straightline boost that aids chasing drivers coming right out of the corners. That would offset the loss of cornering speed from following a car in its dirty air.

"I think for 2030 I have an idea of where I would like it to be," Sainz explained. "I think the delta on speed should come more at the beginning of the straight when you are trying to get the slipstream rather than at the end of the straight when the overtaking and the delta speed is too high. It would also leave more overtaking down to driver skill rather than simply sailing past the car in front.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"The power on the overtake mode, push to pass, DRS, whatever you want to call it, should happen exiting the corner, so that you have an extra power boost, let's say, to catch up what you are losing in the corner [due to dirty air] but the boost shouldn't then help you to finish the overtake. I think the boost should help you manage to get back into the very close slipstream and then use the draft and the rest of the braking point to make your own move."

Rather than a straightline boost that kicks in when cars are already approaching terminal velocity, it would also avoid creating a dangerous top speed deficit, which Sainz said is actually discouraging drivers from defending their position.

"The weird overtaking that happened also a bit with DRS is when you get delta top speeds of 30 km/h and you arrive so quick that even when you are in front you are too scared to defend and cut him off, because the delta speed is so high," Sainz added. "So that is my idea of how I would like it to be and go racing with. Similar to a DRS and overtake mode that when you get into a certain distance you get that advantage, because you earn it through speed and through having to suffer the dirty air and manage to get yourself into a certain opportunity to get that advantage."

The current thinking is for the KERS unit of F1's next power units to make 100kW of electric energy available in standard mode, with an additional 100kW of boost mode accessed in a way that has yet to be fully defined and a total harvest of 200kW.

The next generation of engines will no longer require active aerodynamics, but the FIA hasn't ruled out pairing that push-to-pash system with a return of the DRS overtaking device on the rear wing.

While Las Vegas showed how crucial the role of slipstreaming can be with this year's Straight Mode, four-time world champion Max Verstappen is wondering if cars can be made draggy enough so that DRS is no longer necessary.

"You can still come up with a formula where maybe a car is just super draggy in a straight line, so you don't need to rely so much on DRS," Verstappen suggested. "A push-to-pass system for me is fine, but it needs to be a much easier engine. Every time I do a show run, for example in an RB7 or whatever, it's just so nice to drive because the throttle responds, everything is just easy, it drives off nice, the car is not shaking about, it has no lag, stuff like that. It's just a lot nicer to drive than what we have currently.

"I know it needs to be some kind of hybrid element, probably turbocharger, because otherwise you are not even allowed to drive at some tracks anymore because it's too loud. That is fine, as long as it's not overruling the natural driving element, which of course at the moment is happening."

Sports.title: Honda can't find an issue after Fernando Alonso's intriguing "broken engine" radio message
Sports.content:
On his final lap of the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix, Fernando Alonso called it a day. The two-time world champion locked up at the end of the long straight before telling the team over the radio: “Box, box, broken engine.”

In the media pen afterwards, the Spaniard reiterated that something was wrong with the power unit in his Aston Martin: “The engine was down from the beginning of the race, I think. We saw already in qualifying that the engine was down and I think it was down the whole race as well.

“So I was losing a lot of time on the straights, not only to the rest of the field but also to Lance. I think in the last two laps the engine completely gave up.”

In the days that followed, engine supplier Honda examined all the data, but remarkably, chief engineer Shintaro Orihara revealed in Qatar that no problem had been identified.

“After the weekend, we have checked all the data that we have now and also in the maintenance we have checked the engine physically. At this moment, we haven't found any issue on the engine from the data and also from the maintenance check, but again, we will check on Friday to see how the engine works at this track,” Orihara told media including Autosport on Thursday.

The latter is not only to see how the power unit performs at the Lusail International Circuit – a completely different type of track – but also to obtain more feedback from Alonso himself to determine whether this particular unit is still fit for use or whether an engine change is needed.

“Yes, we carefully analysed his comments and we also respected his comments,” Orihara continued. “That's why we checked all the data and why we checked the engine condition. From the data, at this moment, we haven't seen any issue, but as I mentioned, we will check again on Friday to get some feedback from Fernando.”

Shintaro Orihara, Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer of Honda Racing Corporation Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

Orihara added that it was difficult for the drivers to feel exactly what was happening in Las Vegas, precisely because the circuit was extremely power-sensitive and energy-poor.

“In Las Vegas, it was difficult to analyse how engine performance affected car speed, because there was a lot of torque effect and also different energy management across the two cars. Our metrics say that the power itself is okay, but we should probably check carefully at this track again.”

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack underlined the complexity of the situation and explained that the poor feeling Alonso experienced – which led him to believe there was a power unit problem – could also be related to MGU-K deployment and difficulties in that area.

“I think we need to be careful because the MGU-K part is so much higher. And that means that as soon as you have a small variation in MGU-K [deployment], it could be felt like a problem with the internal combustion engine. And you have different MGU-K power in different places. So very often, it's much more difficult for drivers to judge than it used to be in the past, and I think some of it is coming from there.”

Although some of the confusion may indeed stem from uncertainty surrounding MGU-K deployment, Orihara acknowledged that another part of it could simply come from sheer frustration. Both Alonso and Lance Stroll stressed that they were losing two seconds per lap purely due to a lack of power, meaning that, according to Orihara, Alonso's retirement could also be related to that frustration.

“Please ask Fernando. From the data viewpoint, we haven't seen any issue, but probably this year our engine performance is not enough to give satisfaction or confidence to the driver and then probably they feel some, how to say, feeling that the engine performance is not great.”

Stroll once again expressed that frustration during media day in Qatar, stating that under these circumstances the Aston Martin drivers cannot even put up a fight, particularly at a circuit such as Las Vegas.

“We know the areas we're going to work on with the car, and what we have to improve on the chassis side, but going to races like Vegas and missing like two seconds with just the engine, there's really not much we can do. We just need a lot more power, and hopefully we get that next year.”

Stroll is optimistic that Aston Martin will make progress on the chassis side for 2027, but immediately pointed out that such progress will be worth little unless the power unit improves considerably.

“Everyone at Silverstone is pushing flat out to hit our targets. And then, like I said, the engine, it doesn't matter how good of a chassis you have, if you're missing two seconds of power on the long straights. I mean, then it's going to be almost impossible to compete. That's where we are, so we really hope we get a lot more power next year.”

Sports.title: F1 drivers go through quizzical exercise in stewarding debate
Sports.content:
Few matters of day-to-day business in a Formula 1 weekend divide opinion as deeply as stewarding decisions, particularly their consistency. A vocal minority of drivers tend to dominate this debate while others pointedly avoid getting involved.

The FIA leaned into this in its annual summit with the drivers, deploying the online quiz platform Kahoot! to solicit a broad spectrum of opinion. It's understood this took the form of multiple-choice questions about various incidents from throughout the year and the penalties applied to them.

While some readers may decry ‘gamification' in this way as trivialising an important subject, the fresh approach to the meeting attracted some drivers, including Lewis Hamilton, who usually don't attend on the grounds that they feel little of use eventuates from it. Enabling the drivers to play on their phones boosted engagement from a demographic with a notoriously short attention span – especially since many were tired and still jet-lagged from Las Vegas.

It also had a ‘flattening' effect in that everybody could make themselves heard, whereas in a traditional meeting format some drivers would sit quietly and fulminate while the more vocal ones monopolised the floor.

"I didn't go last year but I'm going to go tonight," said Lewis Hamilton ahead of the meeting.

"Ultimately, just because I want to help them, help the racing be better – and the ruling system I'm sure we can improve."

Hamilton attended Qatar meeting, having turned his back on it last year Photo by: Getty Images

Historically, this annual forum has been important in that it shapes the continuously evolving ‘driving standards guidelines' which the FIA usually updates, along with the associated penalty tariffs, over the winter. This is the drivers' opportunity to discuss what has and hasn't worked in the current guidelines.

Although consistency of stewards' decisions is a perennial topic, and one which the FIA hopes to address by appointing a permanent panel of professional stewards, the recent run of triple-headers has put several incidents in the spotlight. The draconian nature of some sanctions have been called into question, along with the process of handing a position back if it has been gained by going off the track.

Hamilton has been involved in two of those recent cases. Firstly in Mexico, where his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc gained the lead by short-cutting Turn 5 while attacking Hamilton on the opening lap, then took the time penalty rather than handing the position back. That penalty, usually 10s, was mitigated down to 5s because the stewards deemed that Hamilton also overcommitted to the corner and ran wide.

In that instance alone there are a lot of questions to unpack. Are the guidelines governing when a driver is entitled to ‘racing room' fit for purpose? Under what circumstances should a driver give the position back? How can the system be improved to prevent drivers minimising the downside of a penalty by consolidating track position before taking it?

The most recent incident came last weekend in Las Vegas, when Leclerc launched an opportunistic move up the inside at Turn 7 and rode partly over the kerb, tapping Hamilton into a spin. For this he was penalised 10s as well as being given a furious dressing-down by team principal Frederic Vasseur.

This affair highlighted what remains a grey area in the driving guidelines despite several refinements since the topic first came up in the 2024 season. While the guidelines attempt to establish a threshold around the relative positions of the cars for when a driver is entitled to ‘racing room', there is a caveat concerning whether the attacking driver is in control of their car or not. Relative position can be objectively measured but the question of control is open to interpretation, and therefore subjective.

When drivers are operating at the limit, this facet takes on a high degree of significance.

Russell was penalised for leaving the track and gaining an advantage on the opening lap of the US GP Photo by: Getty Images

Speaking ahead of the meeting, Alex Albon laid out his thoughts on the recent crop of incidents.

"I'm jet-lagged, I don't really want it to happen tonight," he said.

"It's just a general understanding of what we're racing with. I feel like there's a few incidents that stand out to me: George [Russell] in Austin [for leaving the track and gaining an advantage on the opening lap], Oscar [Piastri] in Mexico against Lindblad.

"I'd even honestly say the Charles incident itself in Mexico, the five seconds – which I think a lot of drivers would say it should be a fundamental position change that's instructed by the FIA. And then for me there's still question marks around… I looked at the Charles and Lewis crash [in Las Vegas]. Maybe I'm the only one in that I thought, I don't think there was anything wrong with what Charles did.

"And I think the rules are still a bit, it's one of those weird ones, where if you release the brake more and then make contact, is that better? A lot of those really grey areas for me, where I'm like, I don't like this. Certain positions, it's so dominating over, the further you can get in front of a car before contact or whatever, determines you're more in control."

The 'anonymised' format naturally discouraged ‘groupthink', so there was broader consensus in some instances than others. Interestingly, the timing of the meeting – on Thursday evening in Qatar – meant it split the usual round of media engagements. Two drivers, Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli, spoke after the gathering, and one was more loquacious than the other.

"It's just a general discussion that we have with the stewards, we don't need to go into detail here about it," said Verstappen.

"They will make their minds up about what we said about certain incidents and then we'll see what we can change maybe for next year potentially.

"I think we all agree that compared to maybe two years ago this is better. I think we can also all say that in some scenarios I think we can still change maybe certain penalties a little bit. I think that's always going to be like that, work in progress and things maybe need to change a little bit, but that's something that we'll keep on discussing with them."

Hardly a melodious endorsement of the new meeting format, but this has to be viewed in the context of stewards' consistency having been a topic of ongoing debate for much of Verstappen's long F1 experience. Equally, many of the tweaks to the driving standards guidelines have been applied as a result of him having been seen to have expertly ‘gamed' the system, such as in the 2024 championship run-in.

On-track incidents between Verstappen and Norris late in 2024, such as here in the US GP, triggered changes in guidelines of when a driver is entitled to 'racing room' Photo by: Getty Images

Antonelli took a somewhat less jaundiced view of the meeting's outcome.

"It was good for, especially the stewards, to see how we see certain scenarios and to give them our point of view," he said.

"And also the good thing is that most of us in the room were all aligned on the episodes we saw – it was good for the stewards to see. And as well to talk about guidelines, which they don't really need to change.

"It's just seeing, understanding our point of view, and understanding that in some scenarios it would just need to be [declared] a racing incident and no penalty. Some scenarios are so borderline that it's so hard to establish who is at fault, and instead of giving a penalty it should just be a racing incident."

It's understood the meeting also involved inviting the drivers to set their phones aside briefly and discuss other contentious topics, including the where and when of handing back a position which has been gained by running off-track. The preference is for drivers to be instructed to hand the position back straight away in these circumstances, rather than sticking it out and potentially using clear air to bolster track position and mitigate – or even negate – the impact of any penalty.

But even this isn't necessarily straightforward. In Mexico, for instance, Verstappen overtook Hamilton as the two Ferraris had their dispute, so Leclerc couldn't yield to his team-mate without handing Verstappen the lead. And in any case, race control had already made it clear ahead of the event that drivers gaining position by short-cutting the track at Turns 1-3 and 4-5 had to move over straight away, which Leclerc did not.

Thus we can anticipate more contentious outcomes next year. And what, then, will the FIA do to enliven the Qatar drivers' summit? Host a game of Spin The Bottle?

Sports.title: How Rosberg beat Hamilton – and his demons – to clinch F1 world title
Sports.content:
“My superpower was preparation.”

This may not make for a fascinating storyline but perfectly encapsulates how Nico Rosberg surpassed Lewis Hamilton on his way the 2016 Formula 1 world title.

You won’t often hear drivers downplay their natural ability, but 10 years on from his triumph with Mercedes, Rosberg was very open about it in the latest Beyond The Grid podcast. He couldn’t match Hamilton’s talent – “Lewis is the GOAT,” he candidly admitted – so he had to dig deep in every other field to come out on top.

“It’s just extracting 110% of my potential,” Rosberg explained. “That’s what it’s about. And that means every single area that there is – and there are many: there’s food, there’s sleep, there’s working with the engineers, there’s car development, there’s media, there’s fitness, there’s body weight.”

So the German’s work with a psychologist was crucial, as what he describes as a “demon” kept creeping in. “In preparation for 2016, two hours of mental training every two days,” he detailed. “It was harder than the physical training.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“It’s loads of things: meditation, repetition, visualisation, techniques to remain present when you feel emotions of fear coming, when you’re terrified to mess up and have the world laughing at you because you’re leading the race and you mess up the starts.”

This helped Rosberg not only out on track but also when addressing the media, as he attempted to assuage the immense pressure on his shoulders.

“It’s a whole game you have to play, because the media is so powerful,” he pointed out. “It’s such a key part of sporting performance, because you guys get to us, because we have to stand in front of you every single race weekend, throughout the whole weekend, and we cannot say ‘no comment’. I have to engage. When you [journalists] tell me, ‘Are you the new Rubens Barrichello?’, the always-number-two? Boom! That hurts.

“You guys repeat things, and you start to believe them at some point. So it’s a game you really need to master. So with my psychologist, very important for me in my championship year was also, never, ever, ever use the word ‘championship’, in any media conversation. Because you [as a journalist] would always say, ‘You’re the favourite for the championship, right, Nico?’ – [so] just deviate.”

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

There were reasons to believe Rosberg was ideally positioned for a more sustained title bid. After claiming the runner-up spot in 2014 and 2015 and also being outscored by Hamilton in 2013, his campaign began in ideal fashion with four consecutive victories – marking seven straight wins from the end of the previous season – despite Toto Wolff swapping the engineers’ and mechanics’ squads around, which had been a shock to the German.

“Every race matters,” Rosberg said of his strong end to the 2015 campaign. “And it was my chance, because of course he was now I-don’t-know-how-many-times world champion – and you just lose an inkling of motivation then. It’s normal, because the races don’t count for anything anymore. And he was up against me, who was as motivated as ever in my life because it was just, ‘I don’t want to lose anymore’ – it sucks.

“And so I won the last three, and it naturally just puts a dent in the confidence. It’s the way it is in sport. And you carry that into the long winter. Now he knows, yes, he’s champion, but I won the last three really driving amazingly.”

Read Also:

Hamilton did fight back after Rosberg’s perfect score of 100 points in the opening four grands prix, clinching six wins in seven races from Monaco to Hockenheim. Going into the Malaysian GP, the Briton was just eight points down on his team-mate, but his engine failed as he led the race by 23 seconds – with Rosberg fourth, more than a minute adrift, after being spun around by Sebastian Vettel at the start.

Rosberg inherited third, meaning Hamilton’s retirement induced a 28-point swing: instead of leading the standings by five points, the reigning champion now was 23 points behind.

This was ideal for Rosberg, but started mentally crumbling under the weight of pressure as the title favourite – though he did win the following race in Suzuka. Meanwhile a terrible start dropped Hamilton to eighth on lap one, and he could only recover to third amid robust defence from runner-up Max Verstappen.

“Japan already, I don’t even know how I still managed to drive so well, because if I think about my qualifying lap, I am terrified,” said Rosberg, who snatched pole position away from his team-mate by 0.013s. “I am like shaking, my hands are shaking in the race car – and I’m still able to put her on pole, which I don’t even know how that’s possible.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

“Because I’m the big favourite now, my dream is within reach! It’s mine! I just need to bring it home every time, that’s enough. I’m just, like, ‘Don’t mess it up’. It’s scary. Am I ever going to get another opportunity? I don’t know, I’ve got the greatest of all time in the car next to me. You never know.”

The Japanese result meant Rosberg now was 33 points up on Hamilton, so he could afford to finish second in every of the four remaining races – but this did not make him feel any lighter.

“Just terrified, absolutely terrified, because this is my chance,” he said of his mindset going into the title decider. “And all the last races before – it’s not that easy to be second, because you have Max with the Red Bull, [Daniel] Ricciardo, the Ferraris, they’re close. Especially when you’ve got the demon in your head, then it really is not easy to be second.

“Max was all over me all the time. In Mexico, bumping into me in Turn 1, knocking me off the track, lunging me later in the middle of the race. This guy was the highest-risk driver at the time, because he’s the young, crazy Max, you know.

“Brazil, he’s all over me again in the wet, which was treacherous conditions. It was massive survival mode out there to not spin and crash like most others were, and then Max is hammering it round the outside of me, Turn 3, without even seeing that he’s there, so I jump in my car when I suddenly see him. It was not a walk in the park.”

Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes, Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Adam Pretty / Getty Images

Rosberg was supposed to be joined by family and friends at the Abu Dhabi finale, but as his anxiety skyrocketed, he explained he initially asked them to stay away as he wanted the weekend to be “business as usual”, though it hardly was.

“Last race weekend, I was just terrified, completely terrified – from the beginning to the end, it’s just so bad,” he said. “And the whole world looking at you – you walk in, you see the eyes, like everybody trying to see, ‘How nervous is he?’. It’s just unbelievable.”

The stress took a toll on the Mercedes driver, who was struggling to sleep any more than two hours a night, despite help from a sleep doctor and meditation techniques.

“Terrible,” he commented. “The heart racing, all night long, adrenaline pumping. And when you do two hours, it’s a spiral, because you think, ‘I’ve got to drive with two hours of sleep’ – so it just gets worse and worse, the demon just goes nuts and you sleep even less.”

And when Rosberg was awake, eating was not any easier. “I couldn’t even eat properly anymore, I was so scared,” he confessed.

“The only thing that would go down is my childhood memory food, which was Frosties. I hadn’t eaten Frosties in 20 years, because it’s not really healthy, it’s not very good. It’s the only thing that my brain would tell me, ‘Yes, this will go down’. I tried pasta, wouldn’t go down – it literally would not go in. So that’s what I was living on, Frosties, which is not really good either, because that’s not a very solid food to let you perform for a whole weekend.”

As a consequence, Rosberg wasn’t exactly in the ideal shape to compete, as his free practice out-laps showed: “Nauseous, in the car, because I’m living on Frosties. Nauseous! Can you believe that?. I’ve never had nausea in a race car in my life. And then the demon tells you, ‘You can’t drive a race car if you’re nauseous’. It went away, fortunately – I don’t know how.

“It’s just my preparation and my natural talent that carried me through the weekend, somehow. Even mentally not being there at all, I was still able to do decent, and really well. This is incredible. To this day, I don’t know how it’s possible.”

Hamilton outpaced Rosberg in all three practice sessions and took pole by 0.303s over his team-mate. The order was unchanged at the start, and the Briton kept the pack bunched up in the hope that his rival might drop out of the podium positions – which was necessary for Hamilton to have a shot at the title.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

Both drivers pitted very early, on laps seven and eight. Rosberg’s stop, however, was longer than planned as his mechanics avoided an unsafe release, and he emerged right behind Verstappen, who was yet to pit after spinning on lap one. It took 12 laps for him to find a way past the Red Bull.

“Horrible. Horrible,” Rosberg commented. “Understandably, [Hamilton] has to do something, so he tries something and it was working.

“He put me behind Max Verstappen with that strategy. I should never have been behind Max Verstappen, and suddenly I’m behind Max Verstappen – the worst guy to be behind. It was Mad Max at the time, it was a 50/50 chance of a crash, if you ever tried to pass him or whatever.

“Probably the most extreme moment in my whole career is when [race engineer] Tony Ross comes on the radio and says, ‘Nico, your championship is at risk. You need to now pass Max Verstappen in the next two laps.’ What? You don’t pass Max Verstappen, like it’s not something you do.

“I’m forever thankful to Max, because he played it fairly, left the space.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

“I came out of that and my foot starts shaking so much from fear and adrenaline that I am uncontrollable on the throttle pedal. I’ll never have that in my life again, I’ll never experience that, I’ve never had it before. The whole foot is jumping, because of Max. So now I cannot push the throttle properly anymore. My demon starts off again, ‘Okay, it’s done, you cannot drive anymore because you cannot control the throttle pedal anymore’.

“I get lucky, because the next is a long straight. I push my whole leg down into the cockpit from my buttocks onwards, so that allowed me at least to get the full throttle. And then, for some reason, somehow the foot again found a little bit of control, so then my brain said, ‘Okay, yes, it’s coming, this should be okay’. So I was able to drive again. It’s nuts, it’s completely nuts.

“And all the mental training I did helped zero in that moment. Zero. All my techniques, zero point zero. It was just red mist. But I’m sure the preparation did, because I probably would have been that 1% more out of control if I hadn’t prepared myself the way that I had.”

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes, Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Rosberg swiftly caught Hamilton, who desperately intensified his backing-up tactics in the final laps – to no avail, with the German leading Vettel and Verstappen under the chequered flag to clinch his maiden world title.

“The first [feeling] is relief,” he said. “Relief that it’s over and it’s done, and you did it. And then it just goes ecstatic, it just goes nuts, the feeling. It’s the most extreme feeling, apart from the birth of your child and getting married, maybe. A little bit comparable, but different. Anyway, it’s the most extreme, ridiculous feeling.”

Five days later, Rosberg announced his retirement from Formula 1.

Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images Nico Rosberg, Mercedes Photo by: Peter J Fox / Getty Images

Sports.title: Verstappen to work with new race engineer Tom Hart again at Qatar GP
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen will be without his regular right-hand man Gianpiero Lambiase this weekend at the Lusail International Circuit. Red Bull had already opted for a rotation system for the latter part of this Formula 1 season, primarily to allow Tom Hart to settle into the role ahead of his expected permanent appointment while Lambiase is still with the team.

The initial plan was for Lambiase to cover the final two grands prix of the season as Verstappen's race engineer, besides his duties as Red Bull’s head of racing, but he will be absent in Qatar due to personal circumstances. The team told Autosport that Lambiase is expected to return in Abu Dhabi, provided his personal circumstances allow.

Lambiase is expected to be placed on gardening leave in 2027 ahead of his move to McLaren. While Red Bull has yet to formally announce it, this makes it very likely that Hart will become Verstappen's permanent race engineer as early as the start of the 2027 season.

Hart, who has worked for Red Bull since 2013, was on his way to Williams until Verstappen internally expressed his preference for Hart as Lambiase's replacement. Red Bull subsequently managed to reverse Hart's planned move to the Grove-based team, where he was due to become Alexander Albon's race engineer.

Hart’s first races working with the four-time world champion have presented several challenges. In Austin, there were technical problems with the radio connection, while in Brazil Verstappen repeatedly complained about a strange feeling in the RB22 after his opening stint. A particularly chaotic race unfolded in Las Vegas, although communication between Verstappen and Hart already appeared to be considerably better.

Verstappen has spoken positively about Hart, who he says has made a “good impression” despite those challenges.

How Verstappen has adapted to F1’s energy management demands

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

In Las Vegas, Verstappen was praised for "outsmarting" Mercedes, as Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies put it. Although the Dutchman is still not a fan of the current regulations, he demonstrated his understanding of energy management in his battle with George Russell, whom he repeatedly repassed.

Verstappen’s performance underlined the progress Red Bull has made with its DM01 power unit on energy-poor circuits, but also the extent to which Verstappen played with the tools at his disposal – something that also appeared to represent a step forward compared with the season opener in Melbourne.

“I think we all got better at it, drivers and teams, in understanding the energy management, but that's normal when it's a new regulation,” Verstappen said when asked by Autosport in Qatar which steps he has taken behind the scenes.

“When you look at the first race weekend, I think if we go back, you would do things differently. It would also be bad if you go back and you wouldn't know what to do differently, so it's just normal progression, I would say.”

While Verstappen felt the layout in Las Vegas suited the RB22 well, he expects Qatar to present a different challenge. The Lusail International Circuit is dominated by high-speed corners, an area in which Verstappen says Red Bull has not always been particularly competitive this year.

However, following Red Bull's successful upgrade in Baku, team-mate Isack Hadjar believes the team should now be competitive everywhere.

Sports.title: Hamilton convinced Ferrari will "figure it out" following Leclerc skirmish
Sports.content:
Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton says he is confident that he and team-mate Charles Leclerc will "figure it out" following their latest on-track skirmish at last week's Las Vegas Grand Prix.

A fortnight on from a costly on-track incident fighting for the lead in Mexico, which drew the ire of team boss Fred Vasseur, history repeated itself when Leclerc was found responsible for contact with Hamilton on the streets of Las Vegas, robbing both drivers of a solid result.

The clash prompted more anger from Vasseur and fresh talks over how he will get his two number one drivers in line. "It's unacceptable," Vasseur fumed after the race. "It's a lack of respect for the team, for the sponsors, the same speech as after Mexico. I think we had a clear discussion in Sao Paulo. Today it wasn't professional."

Speaking in Doha on Thursday ahead of the Qatar Grand Prix, Leclerc said he was "very much thinking about trying to find a solution together with the team in order to make sure that we maximise the team points and that episodes like last week don't happen again" - stopping short of offering any suggestions.

Hamilton also struck a conciliatory tone and said he was still convinced that the pair could co-exist in harmony at the team as joint number one drivers.

"I do, I do. We're going to figure it out," Hamilton said. "We're team-mates at the end of the day, and I think we always learn from these experiences, whilst maybe it doesn't necessarily look like it. But there will be learnings that we take from this difficult period.

"I still believe in everything we're building and working towards in the background. We came here with the goal of taking Ferrari back to the top."

He added: "You learn really through the hardest times. And these are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Chares and I. But think these are the moments that you really learn and grow closer together through conversation and communicating and having those sit-downs."

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Manuel Eletto

Hamilton revealed he and Leclerc have gone through every corner and every incident between the pair this year, which also included a clash at Monza. But the seven-time world champion also acknowledged every incident is different and dynamic, so it's not as simple as imposing strict racing rules. Instead, he suggested that he and Leclerc have to use their instinct while keeping the team's interests in the back of their minds.

"You can never cover everything, because every scenario is different," Hamilton explained. "But you can definitely go through every single race, corner by corner, and discuss things, which Charles and I have.

"But there's always going to be something new that you maybe haven't foreseen. You also have to use your instinct, and at the core you always have to have the team.

"Speaking for myself, when I'm driving, when I'm attacking, whoever it is on track, I'm always thinking: 'OK, how is this going to impact everybody behind me, team-wise?' So, I really do try to be as responsible as I can, and make the best decision when I am attacking, I think."

Sports.title: Leclerc furious with integrity being questioned after Hamilton clashes
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc was left furious by those ‘questioning his integrity and love for Ferrari’ after yet another clash with Formula 1 team-mate Lewis Hamilton - having urged to find a “solution”.

The Ferrari pair have been at loggerheads several times during the second half of the 2026 F1 campaign, clashing at Monza, Zandvoort and Mexico before their latest spat in Las Vegas.

Last weekend Leclerc attempted to overtake Hamilton for sixth down the inside of Turn 7, but copped a 10-second penalty for causing a spin - leaving team boss Fred Vasseur furious.

The Frenchman said on team radio during the cooldown lap: “Charles, I want to see you at the end of the race, before anything else.”

Now a week later in Qatar, Leclerc has accepted responsibility for the “unacceptable” clash but refuted any theory that he is attempting to establish dominance as Ferrari’s number one driver.

“I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract,” said Leclerc, who signed a “multi-year” renewal in June. “It's never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

“So no, I don't. I think the only thing that I don't like seeing is people questioning my integrity to the team, my love for the team. I've been in Ferrari since 2019.

“I think there's nothing clearer than the love I have for the team and I'll do absolutely everything in order to bring Ferrari back to the top.

“Then, of course, mistakes happen along the way and always will. We just have to minimise them and particularly between team-mates.

“But yeah, I think it's more the question mark of that that I have seen going around that hurts me more than anything else.

“The rest is a lot of noise and it's not the most enjoyable time, but it's part of the game and I have to accept that.”

Leclerc then insisted that the relationship between him and the seven-time world champion is still “very good”, claiming much of the talk has been heightened due to the nature of driving for Ferrari.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Bryn Lennon / Formula 1 via Getty Images

So the team is striving to find a solution with several internal discussions, which started in the aftermath of the Mexico incident amid Hamilton criticising Leclerc’s “do or die” attitude to racing.

“At least one more year together, we've got to do the best for the team,” said Leclerc, with Hamilton’s current contract expiring at the end of 2027.

“So, I think I've been very much thinking about trying to find a solution together with the team in order to make sure that we maximise the team points and that episodes like last week don't happen again.

“That is my main priority. We're just really very much focused on trying to find a solution that works and particularly because I really believe we are in a good momentum.

“If next year we are to be in a position of fighting for the championship, it's even more important to find the right solution for both of us to bring Ferrari back to the top.”

Leclerc eventually finished 10th in Vegas with Hamilton three spots higher, leaving Ferrari still second in the championship ahead of the final two rounds: Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Sports.title: Russell stands by Verstappen comments at Las Vegas GP - despite "amusing" reaction
Sports.content:
Two years after their last major spat around this time of the year, George Russell and Max Verstappen clashed again last week in Las Vegas after an impeding incident in free practice. It infuriated the Briton, with Verstappen ruining the Mercedes driver's lap by passing him into the last corner - an unwritten rule that the Dutchman doesn't tend to mind breaking.

Russell responded by sending his car up the inside, pushing Verstappen off.

The end result was a needless, though moderately entertaining spat at this quiet time of the season, reprise of Verstappen's and Russell's off-track rivalry.

"He does this week in week out with many drivers and everybody accepts it, and I'm not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they're bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody's got to stand up to that guy," Russell said.

So, when Russell sent his Mercedes into the wall while trying to pass team-mate Kimi Antonelli, right behind leader Verstappen, the four-time world champion couldn't hide his glee post-race. "He speaks a lot next to the track," he said. "And honestly, for me, it doesn't really matter because he's so far below my level that it doesn't really make any sense for me anyway, to try and challenge that. So, it doesn't bother me. And today, karma is a bitch."

A few days on, tempers have cooled and while Russell may not win too many mind games against the steely Dutchman, he stands by what he said.

"I found some of the comments post-race quite amusing, but at the end of the day, he drove an incredible race and won it, so he can afford to say what he wants, really," Russell mused when grilled on the topic.

"At the end of the day, I guess I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn't.

"How I responded on track would have been the same if it was any driver, because if you're going into the last corner, preparing for your lap, if somebody does overtake you into that corner, your next lap is screwed.

"So you either have a decision just to try and retake the position and start your lap like normal or just accept you're going to lose that next lap because you're too close to the car in front."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Lars Baron / LAT Images via Getty Images

'My risk dial is too great'

Russell could have responded on-track instead, by winning the race as he and Verstappen battled lap after lap as part of an oval-like overtaking bonanza. But having fallen behind Antonelli, Russell took too big a risk trying to overtake the world champion on the dirty inside of Turn 4 and veered into the wall.

The Briton admitted he is so eager for a big result at the end of the season that he's probably taking too many risks to try and get one more morale-boosting win after what has been a brutal campaign.

"Obviously, my mistake in Vegas came when I was trying to overtake my team-mate," he said. "I think the truth is my risk dial is probably a bit too great at the moment because I'm just kind of wanting to go for these big results and get some highlights on the board towards the end of the season.

"If that was race one of the season, there's no way I would have gone for that move with two laps remaining. But with two races to go in the season, I kind of wanted to go for it.

"It wasn't out of any frustration. It was just willing to risk more to get a victory. Was it a mistake in hindsight? Yes. But as I mentioned, I could have been conservative and I'm confident I would have finished third or second. And I probably would have been frustrated with myself that I didn't go for the move."

Reflecting on his latest spat with Verstappen, Russell suggested he had been too open with the media in saying what he thinks, which he says is his "biggest takeaway" from the whole episode.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Jim Watson / AFP via Getty Images

"Maybe I have been guilty of being just too open and honest," he added. "I feel with all of the media and the journalists I have a good relationship with and you sometimes forget that you're not talking to one person.

"I'm talking to millions of people on the television, so I think that good relationship has actually probably hindered me a little bit. And that's, I guess, life lessons in this world we live in.

"The competition is on track and that's where I want to have the battles. I respect Max immensely for his driving talents and everything he's achieved on track. And that's that, really.

"I'm not looking to have poor relationships with people. That's just not really the type of person I am."

Sports.title: Spotlight: Why the best thing about Las Vegas for Antonelli is its F1 track | Brief
Sports.content:
The temptations of Las Vegas had no effect on Formula 1’s new world champion.

“The thing I like the most here is the track, because I’m not allowed to do anything else other than drive around,” he told GQ. “Because I’m not 21…”

Antonelli demonstrated his skill on the circuit by setting the fastest lap time in qualifying, though he had to start sixth after a power unit penalty.

Sports.title: Russell says he’s learned some in media will be “cheeky” with his quotes | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell says he has learned to be more aware his words may not be used in the manner he intends to when speaking to the media.

The Mercedes driver had the latest in a series of public spats with rival Max Verstappen in Las Vegas last weekend. He admitted it was “all avoidable at the end of the day.”

“It’s all a bit unnecessary,” said Russell. “It’s not something I’m looking to continue now. I’m not looking to have poor relationships with people. That’s just not really the type of person I am.

“I think there are lessons just to be taken away from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media, because I feel that I’m having more of an open conversation with you guys, as opposed to remembering there’s a camera in front. Right now, there are more people in this room than there are cameras, and I feel like I’m talking to you, but I’m not actually talking to you.

“Indeed, to remind myself that I’m talking to the camera that’s broadcasting to millions of people. That’s the biggest takeaway.”

Russell said he knows from experience his words may not be taken as he intends and named two people he had dealt with in the paddock who had been “a little bit cheeky” with their representation of events.

“I remember in Abu Dhabi a few years ago when I was having an open conversation with [Sky F1 reporter] Ted Kravitz and [former F1 TV presenter] Will Buxton about the whole situation, and I said, ‘Just ask me the question on camera rather than having the conversation off camera.’ So, they asked me the question on camera, and then they go away and spin the truth into something slightly different.

“You kind of think that’s a little bit cheeky, because it is the truth, but it’s not how it was in reality. As I said, that’s just a learning for me personally.”

Sports.title: Leclerc denies claim he has a ‘number one’ clause in his Ferrari contract | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc has denied he has a clause in his contract guaranteeing him number one status at Ferrari.

The claim was made in a report following the Las Vegas Grand Prix and has been widely shared on social media. Leclerc stated he did not have such a clause in his current contract.

“I normally never disclose what I have in my contract but I think this one is an important one to speak about,” he said. “I absolutely have zero clause that says that in my contract.

“It’s never something that I was interested in and never something that I personally wanted. So, no, I don’t.”

The claim was made by Rebecca Clancy, who spent 10 years as Formula 1 correspondent for The Times before joining Motorsport Network. She now contributes to the BBC’s F1 coverage.

“Certain drivers, like Charles Leclerc, they want that number one status, they have had it written into their contracts as well,” she said. “Whether or not the team would miss it or not is a different thing, but they get it written into their contract.

“Max Verstappen is another one, he is obviously the number one driver. He couldn’t care less either.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Leclerc joined Ferrari in 2019 and last extended his contract to drive for the team in June.

He was penalised for colliding with his team mate Lewis Hamilton at the last round in Jeddah. Despite the criticism he faced over the incident – his second penalty for an incident involving his team mate in two rounds – Leclerc said he is committed to putting Ferrari back on top.

“The only thing that I don’t like seeing is people questioning my integrity to the team, my love for the team,” he said. “I’ve been at Ferrari since 2019. I think there’s nothing clearer than the love I have for the team, and I will do absolutely everything in order to bring Ferrari back to the top.

“Of course, mistakes happen along the way and always will. We just try to minimise them, and particularly between team-mates.”

He said claims he isn’t committed to the team “hurt me more than anything else” but “the rest is a lot of noise.”

“It’s not the most enjoyable time, but it’s part of the game and I have to accept that,” he added.

Sports.title: “We need to find another solution” to Ferrari driver clashes, admits Leclerc | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc accepts Ferrari needs to improve how its drivers interact on-track following his latest clash with his team mate in Las Vegas.

The stewards penalised Leclerc for knocking Lewis Hamilton into a spin during the race. It was the second time in three rounds the Ferrari drivers have badly disadvantaged each other.

However Leclerc was reluctant to reveal what has been discussed between the pair and Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur.

“I’m not going to disclose that,” said Leclerc. “I’m not allowed to anyway, so I cannot go into the detail of that.”

The trio held discussions after they tangled in the Mexican Grand Prix, opening the door for Max Verstappen to beat them to victory. However Leclerc said it was clear this had failed to solve the problem.

“We are speaking about a solution to that. Lewis and I already talked. I think our off-track relationship is really strong but at the same time it happened again in Las Vegas and before that moment there were other moments as well. And so for that, we need to find another solution. That’s all I can say.”

He admitted the Las Vegas incident was “unacceptable” for Ferrari.

“As a team, we cannot afford clashes between team mates. I think that is very clear for everyone.

“For the clash in particular of Las Vegas, as I said, I took responsibility. I think there’s just tension around that we just need to dissipate and make sure that we look at more positive days in the future. That’s all I’m looking for.

Sports.title: Hadjar says unfortunate timing caused his front wing to “explode” in Las Vegas | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar says Red Bull are reinforcing the design of their car’s front wing after his failed during the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver believes his failure occured as he switched his wings to the closed position while approaching turn five. This coincided with him running over a bump.

“I think it’s just unfortunate timing,” Hadjar explained. “I think the moment I was closing SM {Straight Mode], the moment of the bump, I think just everything timed it perfectly so the front wing couldn’t take it.

“The team has been working on that for the weekend, reinforcing it. We should have enough for that not to happen, so it’s still going under investigation.

“But collapsing by itself is definitely extremely not what I want here, for sure. They are working hard on it.

“I really believe if I had closed that system two-tenths earlier it would not have happened. I just think everything aligned so it would explode at that time, which is just very unfortunate.”

The Red Bull driver was running in second place when the Safety Car was deployed in Las Vegas, prior to his front wing failure. He believes he is getting closer to winning a race.

“Of course that’s the closest I’ve been in my whole season, my whole career. It feels very nice to be up there.

“But I believe that now Max [Verstappen] has won four races in that second half, it just shows how good the car is behaving.

“On my side, if I just keep doing what I’m doing, I just believe it’s going to happen. I’m still pushing very hard, I have two more races.

“I’m not playing for anything now in the championship, so I can take some risks, try new things and just have a lot of fun and be out there and fight with the big boys.”

Sports.title: Russell “amused” by Verstappen’s comments in Las Vegas: “I stand by what I said” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell was “amused” by Max Verstappen saying he is “so far below my level” following their clash at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

The pair tangled in practice earlier in the weekend. The stewards gave Verstappen a formal warning for the collision and Russell remarked afterwards: “somebody’s got to stand up to that guy.”

Verstappen won the race while Russell fell to ninth place after skidding off the track while trying to pass his team mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli. Afterwards Verstappen said it was “honestly fantastic” to see Russell retire from the race. “Karma is a bitch,” he added.

Russell made light of Verstappen’s response. “It was quite amusing, I found, some of the comments post-race,” he said. “But at the end of the day he drove an incredible race and won it so he can afford to say what he wants really and from my side, moving on.”

The Mercedes driver said he hadn’t changed his view that Verstappen tries to intimidate his rivals on the track. “I stand by what I said after practice,” he said.

“But he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn’t, and I’m sure he had a bit of a laugh about that, and that was reasonably amusing. So from my side, just new race weekend, try and focus on the driving, and move on.”

Nonetheless Russell said he does not want a “war of words” and indicated he may choose his words more carefully in the future when speaking to broadcasters and journalists.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“I maybe have been guilty of being just too open and honest when I speak with you [media] guys. I feel with all of the media and the journalists I have a good relationship.

“You sometimes forget that you’re not talking to one person. We’re having a conversation now and you forget that, actually, I’m not really talking to you, I’m talking to millions of people on the television.

“So I think that good relationship has actually probably hindered me a little bit, and that’s, I guess, life lessons in this world we live. But the competition is on-track, and that’s where I want to have the battles, that’s why I want to have the fights. I respect Max immensely for his driving talent and everything he’s achieved on track, and that’s that.”

However he made it clear he isn’t interested in improving his relationship with Verstappen. “I don’t think it’s important to have a good relationship or no relationship in that regard to be honest,” he said. “We’re all fighting for race wins.”

Having lost the drivers’ championship to his team mate, Russell said he was prepared to take more risks to win the final rounds of the season. “Obviously my mistake in Vegas came when I was trying to overtake my team mate.

“I think the truth is my risk dial is probably bit too great at the moment because I’m just kind of wanting to go for these big results and get some highlights on the board towards the end of the season. If that was race one of the season there’s no way I would have gone for that move with two laps remaining, but with two races to go in the season, I kind of wanted to go through.

“But I think the majority of us respect one another out there and we have hard and good battles. Even the race with Max until that point was good and fair, it was very strategic, it was difficult.

“I didn’t really want to overtake into the last corner and lose the Overtake Mode. But we were so fast down the straight and slower everywhere else it was challenging to know what the right approach was to try and win that race.”
