Turkiye’s Anadolu Agency reported that the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel opposition.

In the 26th minute, the game was temporarily suspended when clashes broke out between Georgian police and Besiktas supporters. Turkish media outlets reported that police entered the stands and used pepper spray against Turkish fans.



According to reports, the police involvement came after a fan displayed a Palestinian flag and banner.

Turkiye’s TRT World reported that police surrounded the fan and used pepper spray, adding that video later showed a Besiktas fan being carried out on a stretcher and others being injured during the intervention.

What have Turkiye and Georgia said?

Omer Celik, spokesperson and deputy chairman of Turkiye’s ruling AK party, posted on X that the “intervention and violence” against the Besiktas fans who unfurled a ‘FREEDOM FOR PALESTINE’ banner and held a Palestine flag was “unacceptable”.

“Besiktas fans spoke on behalf of the alliance of humanity and became the voice of humanity. We strongly condemn the Israeli team’s provocations on the pitch. We extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to our fans who were injured in the incidents and taken to hospital. We are closely monitoring the condition of our citizens,” Celik said.

But Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters that UEFA officials confiscated the fans’ Palestine flags and Georgian state authorities played no role in the confiscation.

Tamazashvili said that 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured.

“While marching from European Square towards Batumi Arena, some of the fans of the football club ‘Besiktas’ stood out by their aggressive actions,” the ministry said in a statement.

“They violated the public order by making indecent shouting and shooting of various objects, disobeyed the legal demands of the police, resisted law enforcement and physically confronted them.”

Police took appropriate measures to curb the violence, de-escalate incidents and ensure public safety, including the use of what it called “special means”, the ministry added.

It denied that the use of force was related to the display of pro-Palestine banners and flags.

“We categorically deny this information and emphasise that violent actions by fans and physical confrontation with law enforcers prior to the display of flags and banners have just begun while marching towards the stadium.”

How have Besiktas and other Turkish clubs responded?

Besiktas said it condemned the use of “disproportionate force”.

“We have initiated formal inquiries with our Consulate General in Batumi and with UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security personnel against our supporters; we will continue to monitor the situation closely until every single one of our supporters has returned home safely,” read a club statement.



In a post on X congratulating the Besiktas victory, the Turkish Football Federation said it would “closely monitor the unacceptable behaviour directed at our club, Besiktas and our supporters in Batumi tonight, and that we will take action with the relevant authorities to ensure that these incidents are fully investigated and the necessary steps are taken.”

Other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, also condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.

Why was Georgia hosting a match between Israeli and Turkish teams?

Since the onset of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, Turkish clubs have not hosted Israeli opposition at home because of security concerns, with matches played in neutral territories instead.

Turkish-Israeli relations have taken a downturn since the war began, with Turkish authorities taking a hard line against the military policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the occupied Palestinian territories.

However, Georgia and Israel have good relations with close ties maintained amid the war.

Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was in the capital Tbilisi for a diplomatic visit last year.

What’s Europe’s track record when dealing with pro-Palestine fans?

Not great.

Last year, English club Aston Villa hosted a Europa League game against Maccabi Tel Aviv, but security concerns prompted West Midlands Police to recommend the banning of Israeli fans from the game.

The decision was taken following violence after a match in Amsterdam between Maccabi and Dutch side Ajax. Police intervened against protesters and Israeli media framed the clashes as a “violent, anti-Semitic pogrom”.

In 2024, another match between Ajax and Maccabi Tel Aviv led to clashes between fans of the Israeli team and pro-Palestine protesters, as Maccabi fans burned Palestinian flags and attacked homes displaying them.

World.title: Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
World.content:
Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.

The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons.

For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions.

Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman, promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel.

This, despite the fact that Lieberman himself became chair of the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee thanks to those same votes. That contradiction was pointed out by Mohamed Majadli, the chief editor of AlNas Radio in Israel and an analyst on the country’s Channel 12.

In such a limited space for political manoeuvres, Eisenkot embarked on forming a coalition, holding talks with his partners, while also trying to open channels of communication with ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly the United Torah Judaism party. At the same time, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett led efforts to form a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party and succeeded in convincing Eisenkot’s Yashar party to open formal talks with Likud.



The prospect of reneging on the change bloc’s central promise to oust Netanyahu looms large over these talks. Bennett and others are advocating for that outcome in light of the lack of a clear Zionist majority against Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

Meanwhile, leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, has publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu and has called out Bennett for his efforts to reach it. The Yashar-Likud talks are complex and overshadowed by, among other issues, accusations between the two sides.

Netanyahu accuses the change bloc of working to undermine Israel by working with Arab-led parties, which he has referred to as “the enemy”. Eisenkot has gone on the record saying that Netanyahu endangers the security of Israel and is willing to ignite war for his personal gain.

From Likud’s perspective, a unity government would require a rotation agreement on the premiership. That means that rather than getting rid of Netanyahu, Eisenkot would have to agree to Netanyahu staying on as prime minister for two years, or agreeing to serve second in the rotation.

This scenario gained traction after judges presiding over Netanyahu corruption trials recommended dropping the most serious charge of bribery, as well as reconsidering the charges or reaching a plea bargain in the others. This development has strengthened Netanyahu’s negotiating position and prompted him to call for an end to the political boycott against him.

Against this backdrop, Eisenkot is manoeuvring through dangerous political waters. If he fails to form a government, voters may be forced to return to the polls again while Netanyahu remains at the helm. This scenario could translate into a loss of support for the change bloc and hand Netanyahu a renewed mandate, while simultaneously ending the political careers of some leaders such as Eisenkot.

If Eisenkot chooses unity with Netanyahu over the promises he made to his voters, he will lose credibility among supporters. Additionally, Eisenkot could be outmanoeuvred by Netanyahu.

Many point to the coalition agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020, which included a rotating premiership. The government collapsed before Benny Gantz assumed his position and his political career never recovered.

In political terms, forming a unity government with Netanyahu would represent a reversal of election promises on fundamental issues such as transparency, judicial reform, and the influence of religion on the state, because unlike the change bloc, Netanyahu’s allies are already embedded in the state bureaucracy and able to entrench these policies.



More strategically, it reflects the knee-jerk reaction of Israel’s body politic to Palestinian citizens of Israel. This is what leading sociologist and researcher Honaida Ghanem calls Israel’s structural problem: its inability to reconcile that part of Israel’s political and leadership crisis is that in today’s Israel, anti-Arab sentiment is one of the few policies most Jewish Israelis can agree on, while they no longer agree on the nature of the state, the influence of religion over the state, or many other fundamental issues of identity and governance.

The prospect of a unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu remains possible, though not likely, primarily because of the personal and political risks such an unholy political marriage would entail for the change bloc leaders.

World.title: Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UN
World.content:
El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.

Hunger ‌is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six ⁠months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme climate events, two United Nations agencies said in a new report.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen ⁠faced the gravest threats of famine, driven by violence, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather, including the El Nino phenomenon.

Listings in the report, released twice a year through the Global Network Against Food Crises, have risen from 13 hotspots in June, with ⁠Chad, Uganda and parts of both Southern Africa and Central America added, while Lebanon was removed.

Armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, the report said, as soaring food, energy ⁠and transport costs were eroding people’s ability to feed themselves.

El Nino, which is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots: Southern Africa, the Central American Dry Corridor and northeastern Uganda.

Covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was affecting efforts to avert catastrophe.

In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1bn to $2bn.



“While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote the FAO and WFP.

While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks – including risk of famine – re-emerged within a few years.”

In Sudan, famine remains a risk ⁠in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, as fighting disrupts food production, markets and aid deliveries.

The agencies also identified famine risks in parts of Somalia and South ‌Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation.

Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Gaza were also classified as areas of very great concern.

Gaza was ‌downgraded ‌from the highest level of concern after small improvements in food security following the October 2025 “ceasefire”. But agencies warned that conditions remained fragile in Gaza, while in the occupied West Bank, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen.

World.title: England’s Overton takes 5-12 as Australia bowled out for record low in T20
World.content:
Australia are bowled out for 108 as Jamie Overton claims career-best figures in England’s seven-wicket win in Brisbane.

Share England’s Overton takes 5-12 as Australia bowled out for record low in T20 on social media

Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as England thrashed Australia by seven wickets in the third T20 international in Brisbane on Friday.

Overton’s figures were the best by an Englishman against Australia in T20s as the home side were bundled out for 108, their lowest score on Australian soil.

“I thought Jamie Overton was outstanding tonight,” England captain Harry Brook said.

“He’s worked hard and put in some extra graft at training.

“He simplified his game and reaped the rewards tonight – he had it on a string and it felt like we could change the field and make them make a mistake.”

Brook won the toss and sent Australia in to bat, and off-spinner Liam Dawson struck early when he had Australian skipper Mitch Marsh caught at mid-on.

Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper attacked during the powerplay, taking the score to 55 after five overs.

Harper raced to 26 off 14 balls before Dawson grabbed his second when the Australian wicketkeeper got a top edge to Overton at mid-on.

Overton then swung into action with the ball, claiming the next five wickets as Australia slumped from 65-2 to 92-7 and then collapsed to 108 all out when Sam Curran clean-bowled Billy Stanlake.

Aneurin Donald, who smashed 85 off 32 on the Gold Coast on Tuesday, got the run chase off to a spectacular start, belting 31 from just 11 balls.

But a rain delay seemed to help the Australians, as Brook holed out for nine after play resumed, before Donald fell for 32, leaving England 49-3.

Another rain break threatened to stop England’s momentum again, but Jordan Cox blasted 33 in quick time to give the visitors an easy win and go ahead in the five-game series 2-1.



Marsh conceded that Australia were outplayed by a better team.

“No excuses, we’ve got to be better,” he said.

“We’ve all played Big Bash games here (at the Gabba).

“You have to give yourself the chance to cash in at the back end (of the innings), but we didn’t get near that tonight.”

The two teams head to Sydney for the fourth game on Sunday night.

World.title: Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan?
World.content:
US president’s new tariff regime targets China hardest, just weeks before Trump and Xi meet again at the G20 in Miami.

Share Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan? on social media

In February 2025, US President Donald Trump marked his return to office by kick-starting a trade war with China.

New tariffs, amid accusations that China was failing to prevent the flow of drugs into the United States, set the stage for an escalating economic confrontation between the world’s two largest economies, which stands to reshape global trade.

While Trump’s new trade tariffs regime hit allies and rivals alike, China took the fight head-on.

Washington first put a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods, citing fentanyl and immigration concerns, and Beijing responded by curbing exports of five rare earth metals key to defence, clean energy and tech products.

Then it came to a showdown with Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April, including 34 percent for Chinese products. A tit-for-tat exercise ensued as headline US tariffs on China climbed to 145 percent, while US goods entering China were slapped with tariffs of 125 percent, alongside restrictions on rare earth exports.

The tariff war seesawed for much of that year before the two leaders sat at a table in October, on the sidelines of the 2025 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea, to call a truce.

The limited-time pause in hostilities paved the way for a diplomatic thaw.

Trump then travelled to Beijing last May for talks with Xi, who then visited Washington in September for the first time in more than a decade. Trump embraced the Chinese president when he arrived in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, earlier this month for this year’s APEC summit.



But then Trump returned to Washington and, in less than a week, his administration had announced a new tariff regime – its second attempt at reshaping its trade war after the Supreme Court declared his Liberation Day tariffs of April last year illegal.

“The practical purpose is simple: rebuild [the] tariff leverage the Supreme Court stripped away and force Beijing to the table before the next summit,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, the chief economist for Asia Pacific at investment bank Natixis.

‘Purpose changed somewhat’

This time, the Trump administration has announced plans to impose new tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods through unfair government subsidies, policies and suppressed wages.

China is subject to the highest rates – a new 20 percent levy that is still within the bounds of the trade truce that is set to expire in January. Washington has, however, threatened a 40 percent levy if trade talks break down.

Instead of the emergency powers it used the first time – and which the Supreme Court struck down – the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleging that targeted countries are making use of “structural excess capacity”. It has identified these 14 specific economies during an investigation it launched in March, but views China as the biggest offender, particularly in its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, a trade policy think tank in Singapore, said the “original intention” of the investigation “was to provide a more durable way to get back to the tariff levels” announced on Liberation Day.

“Over that time, I think the purpose changed somewhat,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Originally a means to apply tariffs, it seems clear that the White House wants a more sweeping use of Section 301, which allows a broad range of activities to be subject to possible negotiations and future punishment like tariffs,” she added.

Elms argued that Trump’s announcement coming in “now is rather interesting”, given he is due to meet with Xi next month, in Miami, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit. “This announcement adds another layer of possible tensions,” she said.

‘Right to retaliate’

Just before Trump landed in Shenzhen, where he was greeted by Xi on the tarmac, earlier this month, the Chinese leader had opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.



Xi also portrayed Beijing as a stable trade partner in contrast with the US, where Trump’s tariff war had already rattled global economic equations.

Responding to the latest round of tariffs this week, Beijing warned that it “reserves the right” to retaliate with steeper tariffs.

“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said, adding that Beijing “will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

Referring to the eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity” practices undertaken by Jamieson Greer, Trump’s trade representative, China said it was “a typical act of unilateralism that severely disrupts the international economic order and seriously violates WTO rules”.

Under the latest measures, Washington is seeking to take its economic confrontation with Beijing beyond bilateral trade, targeting the industrial policies of countries emerging as alternative manufacturing hubs but whose supply chains remain closely intertwined with China’s.

Hinrich Foundation’s Elms told Al Jazeera that while Beijing “is probably ok with a 20 percent tariff, they are undoubtedly less comfortable with the attempt to hold all other trade partners accountable to the US for engagement with China”.

‘China can blunt this’

Investment bank Natixis’s Herrero said that Trump’s latest tariffs “are less a grand strategy than a familiar negotiating ploy: keep the pressure on after a friendly photo-op”, referring to the meeting in Shenzhen.

“The stated rationale is Chinese overcapacity,” she said, adding that, however, the aim is to “rebuild tariff leverage” and “force Beijing to the table before the next summit”.

Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore (NUS), said the new measures are a substitute for the struck-down reciprocal tariffs, with “the same kind of inherent reasons or motivations”.

Bo argued that the US government “needs to raise money to keep its many activities going, including the war on Iran”. Furthermore, “it cannot rely on the bond market due to high interest rates – and consumer inflation already hit them hard in midterm election results”.

“Tariff money is one of the easiest ways to finance itself, rather than asking for more from Congress,” Bo told Al Jazeera.

Despite nearly a decade of the ongoing trade tensions between the US and China, Beijing’s global goods trade surplus reached a record $1.19 trillion last year, underscoring the scale of its export dominance. By comparison, the US ran a $1.24 trillion goods trade deficit over the same period.

“Nothing has changed substantially over the years,” he said, adding that “no new tariff will be effective to reduce the Chinese overcapacity at all, or in a significant way.”



Bo said he believes both China and the US are “working hard on the trade negotiations to de-escalate or mitigate” before the two leaders meet again next month, where they want to discuss issues like AI, nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. “That’s a much bigger picture for them than a trade relationship,” Bo said.

For Beijing’s part, Herrero said that “China can still blunt” these new measures by the US.

“Rare earths remain its sharpest tool,” she added.

“The risk for Trump is the same as always: higher prices land on American consumers, and the wider trade system frays further,” Herrero said. “Whether that counts as a feature or a bug depends on how much pain Washington is willing to absorb.”

World.title: European football violence causes concern with far-right claim in UEFA game
World.content:
Claims of Nazi salutes at UEFA Europa League game in Marseille headline night of further violence in European football.

Share ‘Far-right has no place in stadium’ – Marseille woes headline violent night on social media

Violent clashes at two European football matches have stoked concerns about fan violence and prompted the leaders of France and Bulgaria to condemn behaviour that had “no place in civilized Europe”.

Images showed masked ⁠and bloodied fans wielding improvised weapons and metal pipes during a brawl at a UEFA Europa League match on Wednesday evening between Marseille and Levski Sofia, which the Bulgarian club said began when their fans were attacked by supporters of the French side.

A photographer working for the Reuters news agency ⁠said the clashes at the Stade Velodrome in Marseille had started after a supporter from the visitors’ stand made a Nazi salute.

Clashes also broke out at a Europa League match in the Georgian city of Batumi between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva, forcing the referee to suspend the match for 30 minutes.

European football’s governing body UEFA told Reuters its disciplinary body “would assess the match reports before considering any potential ‌next steps”.

What was the reaction to the Marseille and Levski Sofia game?

Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he and French President Emmanuel Macron spoke by phone and condemned the violence at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match, in which Marseille police said 11 Bulgarian fans were hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.

“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilized Europe,” Radev said on Facebook.

“I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”



Macron said he had condemned “with the utmost ⁠force” acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans, which he said had “no place in sport or in ⁠public space”, and told Radev they would not go unpunished.

A protest was planned in front of the French embassy in Sofia ⁠later on Friday.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said: “Violence, racial hatred and provocation have no place in our stadiums.”

Manuel Bompard, a French lawmaker for the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party in the Marseille department, commented on a video on social media appearing to show a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.

“Congrats to the Marseille fans who responded with an antifascist chant,” Bompard wrote on X. “The far-right has no place in our stadiums!”

Batons fly, flares lit in Marseille and Levski Sofia clash

Levski Sofia, which lost the match 1-0, said masked fans had attacked its supporters with batons and flares. Some had let off flares and tried to get through ⁠the barrier as security staff tried to hold them back.

Images showed fans attacking each other through a netted fence separating sections of the stadium.

Before Thursday’s match, French authorities had introduced a sevenfold reduction of ticket sales to Levski supporters and imposed additional restrictions on their movement to and ⁠around the stadium, aiming to curb risks of violence.

The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would request a ⁠thorough investigation. Marseille said it would conduct its own analysis and was working closely ⁠with law enforcement.

What happened in the Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva match?

The match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva had been moved from Istanbul for what UEFA said were safety and security reasons.

Clashes in the stands led referee Morten Krogh to suspend the match in the 26th minute, and it resumed after a 30-minute delay. Georgian police entered the stands, and television footage showed one ‌fan being carried out on a stretcher.

Turkish outlet NTV reported that police used pepper spray. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said a number of fans had been denied entry. Besiktas went on to win 2-1.

Turkish Football Federation chair Ibrahim Haciosmanoglu defended the ‌decision ‌to keep Israeli clubs out of Turkiye following Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023 after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

World.title: Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
World.content:
Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.

Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group.

The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz.

The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.

A local source said that a residential building was struck and that “most” of the victims were children, according to the media report.

Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, the report said. Three people remain missing beneath the rubble.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting the internationally-recognised Yemen government did not immediately comment.

The coalition said later on Friday that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region.

Humanitarian crisis

Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.

Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, as the United States’ war on Iran escalated hostilities and the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.

Some 13,343 people have been killed or injured since August, according to the World Health Organization, while the country is sliding into a humanitarian crisis.



The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme said on Friday that Yemen is among conflict hotspots that face severe food insecurity.

The Norwegian Refugee Council warned this week that the renewed fighting has displaced thousands and piled pressure onto dangerously underfunded aid efforts.

Aid from the US, Germany and others has shrunk considerably in recent years, the nongovernmental organisation noted, saying it has received only 12 percent of funding for emergency shelter support in Yemen so far this year.

“Fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices,” NRC Secretary-General Jan Egeland said, warning that families across Yemen are being pushed deeper into need.

“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here,” Egeland stated.

Calling for better humanitarian access and civilian protection, he demanded that “the powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality”.

World.title: Italians killed in Kuwait: Why is Iran denying responsibility?
World.content:
Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?

Two Italian technicians have been killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.

Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.

The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?

Here’s what we know:

What happened in Kuwait?

On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.

Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.

The men were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.

They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.

The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.



This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .

Iran said it last struck Kuwait on November 18 .

What have Kuwait and Italy said about the latest incident?

Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.

After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.

Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.

What has Iran said?

Iran has denied any involvement.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.

Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.

Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.

The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.

The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.

Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.

This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.



What do we know about who launched the drones?

Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.

“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”

He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”

Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.

As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.

Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.

“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.

Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.

“It’s bizarre to suggest the United States would coordinate this attack on Kuwait, an ally in the Gulf, just to stir up feelings,” he said.

Von Schirach noted that Italy has refused to join the US war on Iran and does not support it. “Italy isn’t on America’s side in this conflict,” he said. “So we shouldn’t take this seriously.”

Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said it was important to “separate Iranian-made from Iranian-launched and Iranian-ordered”.

Tajani described the drone as Iranian-built, of a type also used by Iran-backed militias. Seloom said that makes an Iraqi armed faction the leading alternative suspect. Such groups have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the war began.

He called Yemen’s Houthis “a distant second” and said Tehran’s own suspects, the US, Israel and Ukraine, “come with no evidence”.

“Only debris, radar tracks and a launch point can settle it,” he told Al Jazeera.

Have ‘false flags’ happened before?

Iran’s “false-flag” defence is not new.

Seloom said Tehran first used it in March over strikes on Turkiye, Cyprus and Azerbaijan. However, he said that The Soufan Center, a US-based security think tank, found that it failed to convince Baku.

Claims have run the other way, too. The best known was the reported arrest of Mossad agents plotting bombings in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which came to nothing, Seloom said, because neither of those governments stood behind it.



“Alleged often, verified never, as far as I can establish,” he said. “What this war has is deniable action. Hiding the author is common. Framing someone else has yet to be shown.”

In the case of Thursday’s attack, he said, Iran’s false-flag claim “stands without evidence so far”.

If it was Iran, why deny it?

Abdullah al-Shayji, a professor of political science at Kuwait University, said Iran’s narrative “doesn’t come close to being rational or acceptable”.

“Iran bombed us eight days ago, on the 18th of this month, and didn’t deny it,” he said. He said Iran had fired 925 missiles and drones at Kuwait since the start of the war, and more projectiles at Gulf states and Jordan than at Israel. “This doesn’t fool anyone,” he said.

Al-Shayji said the denial comes down to who was killed and where. “Italian technicians were killed, and not at a US base,” he said.

That undermines Iran’s longstanding argument that it hits only US military targets, he said, an argument he believes had already collapsed because the US has now evacuated 16 bases in the region.

“The justification Iran has always used, ‘we don’t target countries, we target US military bases’, no longer exists,” he said.

Seloom offered two possible explanations. “Either it did not order it, or it cannot afford to own it,” he said.

He noted that Iran’s army openly claimed a strike on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem airbase last week. “This one hit a Kuwaiti site and killed European civilians, which risks turning Europe and the Gulf hosts against it,” he said.

Kuwaiti officials who spoke to Al Jazeera’s Kuwait bureau on condition of anonymity noted that Iran had not sought a joint investigation after earlier deadly attacks on Kuwait, including the drone strike on the airport.

Some Kuwaiti analysts said the denial appeared to be prompted by the victims’ nationality rather than the attack itself, and Al Jazeera’s bureau chief, Saad al-Saidi, said the Iranian statements had caused resentment in Kuwait.

Von Schirach linked the denial to the pressure Iran is under at home. “All the media reports say the economic situation in Iran is extremely bad,” he said, pointing to protests over the rising cost of living.

“I’m not saying the regime will fall, but it is feeling the heat of pressure from the street,” he said. “Iran is in a very difficult position.”

Could this pull Europe into the war?

Not in a combat role, according to Seloom. “Europe’s reflex is pressure,” he said.

He pointed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who called for more pressure on Tehran, and to Rome, which lodged a complaint with Iran’s embassy while urging caution.

But Seloom said the deaths showed how far Europe is already involved. “The two men were maintaining a Gulf air defence system, so Europe is already in this war as a supplier, and its people are now exposed,” he said.

“Expect sanctions and more defensive support for the Gulf, not European strikes.”

What does this mean for diplomatic efforts to end the war?

The Italian deaths come at a sensitive moment. US President Donald Trump has said he will not consider returning to military action until early next year. That leaves mediators with a few weeks to find terms Washington will accept, chiefly a tangible Iranian concession on its nuclear programme.

Iran has so far stated that it will not discuss its nuclear programme until seven conditions, including the lifting of sanctions and a guaranteed end to US strikes, are met.

Seloom said the drone attack on Kuwait “narrows the track without closing it”. The indirect channel was still running on the day of the strike, he said, with proposals moving through Qatar and Pakistan, according to Araghchi’s own account.



But talks have already stalled and the public position of Qatar, one of the main mediators, is that continued attacks on Kuwait put diplomacy at risk, Seloom said.

He added that the strike strengthens the case for military force, just as the option of targeting Iran’s leadership is being discussed in Washington, according to NBC News. “Washington’s reaction matters more than Kuwait’s,” he said.

Al-Shayji said that whoever is responsible for the drone strikes on Kuwait, Iran’s attacks on Gulf states generally risk lasting damage. “Iran needs to understand that taking revenge on America this way creates enmity with a whole generation” in the Gulf, he said. He added that Kuwait is documenting every Iranian attack and will likely seek compensation.

Ahmadian said confidence building has to go both ways. “Iran didn’t start the war,” he said. “Both sides need to talk about reality, not deny it.”

World.title: Zelensky criticises 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.

"He's an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.

Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.

Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.

The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

He said talks were expected to resume in December.

On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".

But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions â on everything.

And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.

The Kremlin appears to be resisting.

World.title: Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.

Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.

Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.

Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.

More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.

One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.

Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.

Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.

On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.

The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. In Maryland, almost two million customers were asked by authorities to limit their water consumption to essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".

Parts of eastern states are under states of emergency, including New York. Organisers of New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have also postponed the iconic event to Saturday.

World.title: Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
World.content:
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.

Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.

The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.

The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.

Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace SÃ¡nchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.

The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.

If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.

Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.

Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.

Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

World.title: Italy's former police chief rejected mafia inquiry allegations before death
World.content:
Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.

His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.

In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.

The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.

But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.

In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.

The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."

World.title: Ex-media executive admits saying Australian child sex abuse survivor 'looking to be raped again'
World.content:
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.

She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.

"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."

The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".

"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'

He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".

"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.

Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.

Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".

"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.

"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.

"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.

"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line.

World.title: Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson launches last-ditch High Court appeal
World.content:
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.

Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole â saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".

She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.

Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.

She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.

She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.

Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.

World.title: Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
World.content:
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French President Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.

There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Uefa says it has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors "to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence" from the Marseille-Levski Sofia and Besiktas-Hapoel Be'er-Sheva games.

European football's governing body said it "strongly condemns the serious incidents of violence and disorder" at those ties.

It added: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.

"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety."

In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.

With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.

They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.

"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."

Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".

According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.

Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.

"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.

"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."

World.title: Millions of wives in South Asia unprotected from marital rape - study
World.content:
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.

"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."

The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.

In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.

Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.

There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.

But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be "excessively harsh".

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

"Those who oppose criminalising marital rape say it would undermine the family unit and break them apart. And family is very important in our countries," Silwal says.

"They say it will affect our religious and cultural values and worry that there would be false accusations against men."

Also a change in law, she says, may not necessarily mean justice for survivors.

Silwal points to Bhutan where marital rape is a criminal offence but it's treated as a petty misdemeanour and is punishable by one month to one year.

In Nepal, the punishment for rape is between six and 20 years, but it's only up to five years for a husband who rapes his wife.

World.title: Lagos cancels November environmental sanitation exercise over INEC mock accreditation
World.content:
The Lagos State Government has cancelled the November edition of its monthly environmental sanitation exercise scheduled for Saturday, 28 November, to avoid disrupting the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) nationwide mock accreditation exercise.

The exercise was initially scheduled to hold on the last Saturday of every month, with residents expected to clean their surroundings during the designated period.

In an earlier statement issued on Thursday, the Lagos State Ministry of the Environment had dismissed reports of a postponement, insisting that the November sanitation exercise would hold as scheduled between 6:30 a.m. and 8:30 a.m. on Saturday.

The ministry said the exercise would be monitored across the state, adding that First Lady Ibijoke Sanwo-Olu would lead some state officials during the exercise.

However, Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu directed its cancellation following INEC’s plan to conduct a nationwide mock accreditation and result-upload exercise between 8:30 a.m. and 2:30 p.m. on Saturday.

In a latest statement issued on Friday, Gaji Tajudeen, the Permanent Secretary, Office of Environmental Services, said the governor was keen to ensure that the sanitation exercise, which was scheduled to end at 8:30 a.m., did not interfere with the commencement of INEC’s exercise at the same time.

According to the statement signed by Kunle Adeshina, Director of Public Affairs at the Ministry of the Environment and Water Resources, the INEC exercise will take place in two polling units in each of Nigeria’s 8,838 registration areas.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The commission is conducting the mock exercise ahead of the 2027 general elections to test its election technologies and assess the readiness of its personnel and systems for the electoral process.

The monthly environmental sanitation exercise is part of the Lagos government’s efforts to promote environmental cleanliness and improve waste management across the state.

The state government urged residents to maintain clean surroundings regularly rather than wait for the last Saturday of each month to do so.

It also encouraged residents to continue observing proper waste disposal practices despite the cancellation of Saturday’s exercise.

World.title: FG roots for local biotech development
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has reaffirmed his administration’s commitment to strengthening Nigeria’s biosafety regulatory framework and promoting indigenous biotechnology development as part of efforts to advance food security, public health, and sustainable development.

Mr Tinubu said biotechnology offered significant opportunities to strengthen the country’s healthcare system, improve agricultural productivity and address emerging national security challenges.

The president, represented by the Minister of Science and Technology, Kingsley Udeh, stated this in an address delivered at Nigeria’s National Biosafety and Biotechnology Summit in Abuja on Thursday.

The summit was organised by the National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA) under the theme “Unlocking Nigeria’s Bioeconomy: Advancing Biosafety and Biosecurity for Scientific Innovation and Sustainable Development.”

The summit was organised amid lingering concerns over Nigeria’s recent adoption of several genetically modified crops/seeds, in an effort to achieve food security.

The debate over GMO adoption in Nigeria has remained highly polarised. Critics, including environmental activists and public health scientists, have raised concerns about the lack of publicly available, independent, long-term risk assessments and feeding trials for approved GMO products.

Other concerns include inadequate labelling of genetically modified products and the potential for patent restrictions on GM seeds, which could affect farmers’ access to and control over seeds.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Past PREMIUM TIMES coverage/investigations and editorials have questioned the composition of biosafety oversight bodies, short public comment windows, and limited public consultation before approvals.

In his remarks, the President said the theme aligned with his administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda, which recognises science, technology and innovation as essential drivers of national development and economic prosperity.

According to him, biotechnology can improve farming practices, develop climate-resilient crop varieties, enhance nutritional quality and address persistent agricultural challenges.

“Nevertheless, the application of biotechnology must be guided and supported by rigorous scientific assessment, transparency in processes and appropriate safeguards,” he said.

Mr Tinubu identified NBMA as central to ensuring the responsible application of modern biotechnology through its regulatory mandate to protect public health and the environment.

He maintained that biosafety regulation should not be seen as an impediment to innovation but as a foundation for responsible technological advancement and public confidence.

“Let me emphasise that biosafety regulation should not be viewed as an obstacle to innovation. Rather, it is an essential foundation for responsible innovation, public confidence and sustainable technological advancement,” he said.

The president said his administration would continue to encourage collaboration among research institutions, regulatory agencies, universities, industries and development partners to ensure that biotechnology applications were scientifically validated, properly assessed and responsibly deployed.

He also called for stronger public education and science communication to address misinformation, build public trust and enable Nigerians to make informed decisions about emerging technologies.

Calls for investment in indigenous research

Mr Tinubu urged the NBMA to deepen collaboration with relevant ministries, departments and agencies, particularly the Federal Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology, and research institutions to strengthen national biosafety capacity.

He said Nigeria must invest in modern technologies, skilled human resources, research infrastructure, technology transfer and indigenous innovation to translate scientific discoveries into tangible development outcomes.

The president also stressed the need for regulatory frameworks to remain responsive to scientific advancements and emerging biological technologies.

He said biotechnology could help achieve several Sustainable Development Goals, including zero hunger, good health and well-being, industry, innovation and infrastructure, and responsible consumption and production.

“Our ambition is not simply to adopt technologies developed elsewhere, but to build national capacity to research, develop, regulate and deploy technologies that respond to our unique developmental needs,” he said.

Tinubu highlights research and innovation fund

The president also highlighted the Federal Executive Council’s approval to establish the National Research and Innovation Development Fund, describing it as an important step toward strengthening Nigeria’s research and innovation ecosystem.

He said the proposed fund had been forwarded to the National Assembly for accelerated legislative consideration.

According to him, establishing and operationalising it would help advance Nigeria’s research and innovation capacity and strengthen the country’s technological sovereignty.

Mr Tinubu commended the NBMA and other stakeholders for their commitment to advancing the country’s biosafety and biotechnology agenda.

He urged participants at the summit to ensure its deliberations and recommendations translate into practical, sustainable actions.

“Together, we can build a more scientifically advanced, technologically competitive and environmentally sustainable Nigeria,” he said.

World.title: How Uzodimma wants to sit on two seats, By Azu Ishiekwene
World.content:
The court has reminded Uzodimma that political offices are not like underwear, to be changed casually. And his political enemies have their hands on the trigger. But for a man who has built his political career on Nigeria’s shifting judicial sands, Uzodimma hasn’t ruled out hope.

Some politicians climb the ladder. Some descend from it. And then there is Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, who appears determined to prove that a political ladder is also a revolving door – preferably one with his name engraved on both sides.

And why not? If you have politicians in your party who have their cake and eat it, coveting a bespoke revolving door is the least of your problems. In the run-up to the 2023 election, Ahmed Lawan, then the Senate President, contested the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential primaries without relinquishing his seat.

He lost the primaries, and also lost the APC Yobe North senatorial primary to Bashir Sheriff Machina, who was returned unopposed.

Yet in a judgment hinged on a technicality, a split Supreme Court overturned the ruling of the two lower courts, handing Lawan a ticket he had intentionally gambled away.

The Uzodimma Way

Uzodimma’s present case is slightly different. While his proposed senatorial bid raises a broader constitutional question about the transition from one elective office to another before the expiration of an existing mandate, Lawan’s dispute concerns the validity of a party nomination.

Yet, as a leading beneficiary of Nigeria’s baffling court system, Uzodimma can test the judicial waters not only by using remote lessons from the Lawan model but also by doing so with the audacity of one who knows where the judicial corpses are buried.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

His second and final governorship term expires in January 2028. Yet he has been chasing the APC ticket for Imo West Senatorial District ahead of the 2027 election, apparently unperturbed by the small detail that he cannot occupy Government House and the Red Chamber at the same time.

On 29 October, Justice Obiora Egwuatu of the Federal High Court, Abuja nullified Uzodimma’s nomination as the APC candidate for Imo West, ordered INEC to remove his name and restore former Governor Rochas Okorocha as the party’s candidate. The court also barred Uzodimma from presenting himself as the APC candidate for the election.

For a man whose political story has often seemed to bend reality in his favour, it must have felt less like a judicial ruling and more like a celestial audit.

In the Beginning…

If Uzodimma’s life were a book, it would have been titled The Fourth Shall Be the First, taken from the Supreme Court ruling of January 2020, which exhumed and counted excluded votes in the Imo governorship election in favour of the man who had finished fourth.

But Uzodinma did not merely survive that controversy. He built on it to win a second term in 2023 and now struts about with the confidence of a man who believes that destiny, once it has cleared security at the gate, does not need an appointment.

There is something almost poetic about it. Uzodimma became governor through a judicial decision. Now, in pursuit of a Senate ticket, he has encountered another judicial decision – this one removing him from a race he thought should ultimately land him within shooting range of Akpabio’s present position.

Second Missionary Journey

Imo West, also known as Orlu Zone, has become less a senatorial district than a political boarding house with a permanent waiting list. The seat has been passed around among familiar faces with the frequency of a family inheritance that nobody wants to relinquish fully.

Uzodimma held it from 2011 to 2019. After leaving Government House, Rochas Okorocha won it in 2019. Okorocha later lost it to Osita Izunaso, the current occupant. Now Okorocha wants it back, while Uzodimma, still governor, wants it back too.

In the last 10 years in Imo, the state’s performance record in public examinations has improved, as has investment in road infrastructure. Yet multidimensional poverty, at an average of 40.7 per cent, remains a major problem.

Only 8.5 per cent of the state’s residents have access to safe drinking water, and 30 per cent live more than 30 minutes from a health facility. Tiger Base, the state’s internal vigilante, has been mostly weaponised, and insecurity remains a major problem in the state.

Legacy Issues

These problems did not start with Uzodimma, but if he hasn’t paid enough attention, it may well be that he’s more familiar with the Presidential Villa in Abuja, where he has retained a BQ for most of the last four years, and from where he hopes to secure support for this ambition.

The constitutional argument is not as straightforward as critics sometimes suggest. Section 68(1)(f) of the Constitution says a senator shall vacate his seat if he becomes president, vice-president, governor, deputy governor or holds another executive office.

That may be legally defensible. Politically, however, it has the charm of a man applying for a new job while still holding the old one, informing the interview panel that he will decide later whether to resign.

Between Law and Rectitude

The question is not only whether the law permits it. It is whether Uzodimma, with more than a year left in office, should be spending his final months plotting a return to the Senate rather than completing the work for which Imo people elected him.

There is something almost poetic about it. Uzodimma became governor through a judicial decision. Now, in pursuit of a Senate ticket, he has encountered another judicial decision – this one removing him from a race he thought should ultimately land him within shooting range of Akpabio’s present position.

The spectacle is almost theatrical. A former governor wants the Senate seat. The incumbent governor wants the same Senate seat. The sitting senator presumably wonders whether he has accidentally wandered into someone else’s family reunion.

Eyeing the Bigger Prize

Reports suggest that Uzodimma’s Senate ambition is not simply about representing the Orlu Zone. It is also about a larger prize: the Senate presidency in the forthcoming 12th National Assembly.

But he must first win the party’s ticket to contest the election. From the court ruling to the sniper fire from the incumbent Senate President Godswill Akpabio, and now FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, a deadly foe who wants President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to add Imo to his hunting ground, the auguries for Uzodimma are serious.

The bypass between Douglas House and the Senate President’s office has never been more threatened.

Irony of Ironies

There is a special irony in Rochas Okorocha being the man the court restored. Okorocha is not just any rival. He is Uzodinma’s immediate predecessor in Government House, a former senator for the same district, and a man whose political appetite has never been mistaken for modesty.

Okorocha represented Imo West after his governorship ended, then lost the seat to Izunaso. Now he has gone to court to reclaim the APC ticket from the man who succeeded him as governor.

The spectacle is almost theatrical. A former governor wants the Senate seat. The incumbent governor wants the same Senate seat. The sitting senator presumably wonders whether he has accidentally wandered into someone else’s family reunion.

A governor’s final year should ordinarily be a period of reflection: completing projects, settling scores peacefully, preparing an orderly transition, and perhaps composing a farewell speech that does not sound like a campaign advert.

Exit Door

Instead, Uzodimma’s final year is as if he has looked at the exit door of Government House and decided that the most dignified way to leave is through the window – straight into the Senate.

Of course, in Nigerian politics, no court ruling is ever truly final until the appeals have been exhausted. But for now, the message is clear: a governorship does not automatically convert into a Senate ticket, no matter how loudly the convoy honks or the siren wails.

The court has reminded Uzodimma that political offices are not like underwear, to be changed casually. And his political enemies have their hands on the trigger. But for a man who has built his political career on Nigeria’s shifting judicial sands, Uzodimma hasn’t ruled out hope.

Azu Ishiekwene is Editor-In-Chief of LEADERSHIP and author of the book,Writing for Media and Monetising It.

World.title: Six Plateau residents sue Nigerian Army over alleged detention without trial
World.content:
Six residents of Plateau State have asked a high court in Jos to enforce their fundamental rights over their alleged detention by the Nigerian Army for nearly three months without trial.

The applicants, led by Peter Saleh, filed a fundamental rights enforcement suit against the Nigerian Army and other respondents, alleging that they had been detained since their arrest on 5 September without being charged with any offence.

The case came up before Justice S. P. Gang of the Plateau State High Court in Jos, but proceedings were adjourned until 9 December following a preliminary objection by the respondents.

Counsel to the Commander of the Nigerian Army’s 3 Division and the Commander of Operation Enduring Peace challenged the competence of the suit against two military officers, arguing that they are not juristic persons and cannot be sued.

The applicants’ counsel, Dankat Dalong, filed a counter-affidavit opposing the objection. However, counsel to the respondents, Buhari Shehu, requested an adjournment to enable him to respond to the counter-affidavit.

The six men were arrested in Mangun and Chakfem in Mangu Local Government Area for allegedly planning an attack on Mangun community.

Mr Dalong told the court that his clients had remained in military detention for nearly three months without trial and had been denied access to their lawyers, relatives and friends.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He further alleged that the military authorities had failed to comply with an order issued by a Chief Magistrate’s Court directing them to produce the detainees before it.

READ ALSO: Nigerian Army arrests suspected ammunition supplier in Kogi

The alleged non-compliance with the magistrate’s order and the continued detention of the applicants without trial formed part of the circumstances leading to the fundamental rights enforcement suit.

The applicants are asking the high court to intervene over what they consider violations of their constitutional rights, particularly their right to personal liberty and access to legal representation.

The Nigerian Army was represented by Usman Jariri, while Mr Shehu appeared for the General Officer Commanding, 3 Division, and the Commander of Operation Enduring Peace.

The court is expected to hear the respondents’ preliminary objection when the matter resumes on 9 December.

World.title: Beyond protocol purism: Why Nigerians in South Africa welcome an envoy who refuses to whisper, By Abiodun Abidoye
World.content:
…so many Nigerians across the diaspora, and commentators at home, have hailed the posting of Fani Kayode as a long overdue turning point, with admirers even arguing that his vocal defence of national dignity exemplifies the energy that the broader foreign policy leadership of Nigeria ought to project. When a major African nation rebuilds its presence in Pretoria after a four year vacuum, it needs an envoy who commands attention and challenges discrimination openly, not one content to blend into the diplomatic wallpaper..​

When big men rise, little men tremble.

​When a patriot who truly cares about the welfare and safety of his people comes on the scene, the cowards and traitors murmur.

​When light comes, darkness cries and inevitably flees.

​It is in this context that we need to see and acknowledge the phenomenal rise and triumphs that Ambassador Femi Fani Kayode has recorded since his sojourn in South Africa as the Nigerian High Commissioner.
