​He has shaken the table and made Nigerians hold up their heads with pride again in a nation in which they have been subjected to the sort of discrimination and indignities that can best be imagined.

​I view Professor Babafemi A Badejo, who recently wrote an unkind article, as one of those bitter men who simply cannot bear the fact that Ambassador Femi Fani-Kayode is succeeding where archaic souls and career diplomats have failed and who is likely fronting for a number of identifiable individuals who feel threatened by the meteoric rise of Nigeria’s most popular and loved Ambassador.

​In that essay, “Jankara diplomacy,” Mr Badejo invokes the bustling, informal commerce of the historic Jankara market in Lagos to caricature the newly accredited High Commissioner of Nigeria to South Africa. While the scholarly excursion from Kautilya to the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations makes for brisk reading, Badejo’s selective invocation of protocol overlooks repeated violations of diplomatic norms and human dignity directed against Nigeria and its citizens, to which only the High Commissioner has had the courage to respond.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

​First, the factual record in Pretoria contradicts the alarmist portrait of a mission teetering on the edge of expulsion. On 13 November, Fani Kayode presented his Letter of Credence to President Cyril Ramaphosa at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House as the first substantive High Commissioner of Nigeria to South Africa in four years. Even Professor Badejo concedes that the formal address of the envoy, delivered while in traditional Nigerian attire, was executed with panache, and appropriately recalled the historic sacrifices of Nigeria during the struggle against Apartheid.

Yet when the segment of Nigeria, delivered last among fifteen envoys, was cut off from the live broadcast while others were aired, Badejo treats the silence as a virtue, rather than question whether denying an accredited envoy equal sovereign courtesy violated the spirit of the Vienna Convention.

​Even more glaring is the selective amnesia surrounding the official provocations that followed. When a South African presidential spokesperson publicly branded the Nigerian High Commissioner a liar over whether President Ramaphosa had intervened, only to fall mute when video evidence surfaced, and even went so far as to accuse President Bola Tinubu of lying regarding Afrophobic attacks in South Africa, where were the purists preaching the Vienna Convention?

Similarly, when a Minister in the South African Presidency broadly labelled Nigerians as drug dealers, was that not an egregious breach of diplomatic comity and international norms?

Yet across the foreign policy establishment, only High Commissioner Fani Kayode stood up to defend the honour of Nigeria and its leadership.

​The same double standard applies to the safety and dignity of Nigerian nationals and diplomatic personnel on the ground. Under the Vienna Convention, a receiving state bears a solemn obligation to protect the dignity of a diplomatic mission and ensure peace and order around foreign nationals. When marching mobs descended on Sunnyside in Pretoria, a neighbourhood widely known as Little Lagos, taunting Nigerians to provoke a violent clash, while declaring that Nigerians must not be permitted into South Africa or allowed to marry and have relations with South African women, the silence of commentators like Mr Badejo was deafening.

Even when the High Commissioner himself was subjected to humiliating treatment by airport officials on a Friday, as he prepared to depart, an incident witnessed by over a hundred travellers, that forced him to reschedule his flight until Sunday when he finally departed, and which he chose with remarkable restraint not to weaponise publicly, there was no outrage from those now lecturing him on protocol.

​Far from causing a diplomatic rupture, the subsequent 17 November engagement between High Commissioner Fani Kayode and the Director General of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa, Zane Dangor, was constructive. Crucially, the High Commissioner used that very meeting to place the safety, treatment, and unresolved deaths of Nigerians in South Africa squarely on the bilateral agenda. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola has since affirmed that the matter is closed, and the subsequent consultative visit of Fani Kayode to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja, where he dismissed the social media rumours of a recall, underscored institutional alignment rather than isolation.

​More importantly, the defence of subtle diplomacy by Mr Badejo rings hollow when measured against the lived experience of Nigerians in South Africa over the past four years. From wherever he is based, Badejo cannot fully appreciate the extent of Nigeria phobia on the ground, making it imperative that the High Commissioner protects the dignity of Nigerians in practical, visible ways.

During the prolonged absence of a substantive High Commissioner in Pretoria, hundreds of Nigerians were reported killed, including the perpetration of high profile attacks and disputed deaths in custody that yielded little justice, while thousands more were repatriated amid recurring waves of Afrophobic hostility, scapegoating, and consular bottlenecks.

To ordinary Nigerians working, studying, and building businesses in Johannesburg, Pretoria, Cape Town, and Durban, years of timid, behind-the-scenes orthodoxy felt indistinguishable from official abandonment, doing nothing to deter prejudice against Nigerians or compel accountability from host authorities.

​That context explains why so many Nigerians across the diaspora, and commentators at home, have hailed the posting of Fani Kayode as a long overdue turning point, with admirers even arguing that his vocal defence of national dignity exemplifies the energy that the broader foreign policy leadership of Nigeria ought to project. When a major African nation rebuilds its presence in Pretoria after a four year vacuum, it needs an envoy who commands attention and challenges discrimination openly, not one content to blend into the diplomatic wallpaper.

​It is equally telling how quickly sections of the foreign policy establishment and entrenched diplomatic circles rush to weaponise the purism of protocol against an envoy whose public resonance disrupts comfortable bureaucratic inertia. Too often, criticism disguised as concern for diplomatic etiquette reflects institutional discomfort, as some career diplomats appear envious of the rapid impact of Ambassador Fani-Kayode and seem eager to undermine a visibly effective political appointee who refuses to treat quiet passivity as statecraft.

​Respect for the Vienna Convention and the unapologetic defence of Nigerian citizens are not competing imperatives.

The early tenure of High Commissioner Fani Kayode in Pretoria has paired an insistence on bilateral parity and public accountability with direct engagement through the Department of International Relations and Cooperation and consultations with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja.

Far from diminishing Pan-Africanism, confronting discrimination against Nigerians honestly, while strengthening bilateral channels offers a far more durable foundation for genuine brotherhood between Nigeria and South Africa.

Abiodun Abidoye is a South Africa-based Nigerian and the Publisher of Africa Online News. Email: [email protected]

World.title: Why I tapped young people to lead offices in Oyo – Makinde
World.content:
Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has said he appointed some young people who worked on his 2019 governorship campaign into his administration because of their competence, explaining that their contributions to his electoral victory convinced him they could serve in government.

Mr Makinde, who is seeking the presidency in the 2027 general election on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), said the young people, most of whom were in their 20s, helped manage his campaign’s situation room, where they analysed data and coordinated communication with supporters.

He made the remarks during a podcast interview with Chude Jideonwo on Wednesday, recalling how the group devised strategies to keep his campaign operation running despite what he described as attempts to interfere with its activities by the ruling government.

Asked whether appointing young people was a deliberate strategy to appeal to the youth, Mr Makinde said the decision was based on their ability rather than their age.

“No, no, no. It wasn’t about what people like to see. Basically, these folks were competent,” he said.

The governor explained that the young supporters had played significant roles in his campaign, including a decision in which they moved their situation room to a hotel close to the base of the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate, Adebayo Adelabu, during the 2019 election.

“They were all in their 20s. So right after winning, yes, I tapped some of them to come into government because the positions were there,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Among the young people he appointed were Seun Fakorede, whom he appointed in 2019 as the commissioner for Youth and Sports at the age of 27. He also appointed Temilolu Asamu as the Commissioner for Energy in 2019 at the age of 32.

The governor also supported the emergence of the Oyo State House of Assembly Speaker, Adebo Ogundoyin, who was first elected Speaker of the 9th Assembly unopposed on June 10, 2019, at age 32, making him the youngest person to occupy the position in the state’s history at the time. He was subsequently re-elected to lead the 10th Assembly in June 2023.

The appointments of the two commissioners, alongside the emergence of Mr Ogundoyin as Speaker, highlighted the presence of young people in key public offices in Oyo State during Mr Makinde’s administration.

Following the 2019 governorship election, Mr Makinde secured 515,621 votes to defeat Mr Adelabu, who polled 357,982 votes, ending the APC’s eight-year rule in Oyo State. He subsequently secured re-election in 2023, defeating the APC candidate, Teslim Folarin, to deny the opposition party a return to power in the state.

Mr Makinde said his emergence as governor did not follow the traditional political structure, adding that the people who worked with him had demonstrated their ability to deliver despite widespread doubts about his chances of winning the election.

He said many of them were graduates with bachelor’s and master’s degrees who were eager to take on public responsibilities.

“Most of the folks, they have actually been very outstanding. Bachelor’s, Masters, degree holders, and then eager and ready to take on a task, and that is what has reflected in the progress that we’ve been able to make in our state,” he said.

“If good people are not coming into that system, then you shouldn’t complain if bad people are the ones running the affairs,” he said.

Young appointments and subsequent departures

Mr Makinde’s account comes against the background of a series of resignations by political appointees from his administration in recent months, as the governor pursues his presidential ambition ahead of the 2027 elections.

Among the officials who have left is Segun Ogunwuyi, who resigned as chief of staff on 12 October after serving in the position for more than five years. He did not state a reason for his departure in his resignation letter.

His exit was followed by that of Tara Adefope, the former director-general of the state’s Due Process Office.

On 2 November, Ayobami Ojo, the commissioner for Budget and Economic Planning, also resigned. The Special Adviser on Budget and Economic Planning, Simeon Oyeleke, and Sunday Falana, a member of the Oyo State Independent Electoral Commission, also left their positions.

Mr Oyeleke reportedly said he was no longer comfortable with the working environment in the administration, while Mr Ojo and Mr Falana did not publicly give reasons for their decisions.

Four other appointees, including Joshua Afolabi, Rebecca Agbejimi, Noah Adeyanju and Suleiman Adegbola, had also resigned their appointments on 19 October.

The departures have occurred amid political realignments in Oyo State ahead of the 2027 elections and Mr Makinde’s presidential bid. However, the resignation letters of several of the officials did not link their decisions to the governor’s ambition.

World.title: Why I supported Tinubu in 2023, but now challenge him – Makinde
World.content:
Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde has explained why he supported President Bola Tinubu in the 2023 presidential election despite belonging to the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), saying the decision followed discussions over a proposed government of national unity.

Mr Makinde said he and other aggrieved PDP governors, known as the G5, initially approached the Labour Party presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and Mr Tinubu, who contested on the platform of the All Progressives Congress (APC), to discuss an inclusive government after the election.

He said the group eventually backed Mr Tinubu because they were more convinced by his response to their proposal.

The governor spoke in a podcast interview with Chude Jideonwo on Wednesday, where he also explained why he had withdrawn his support for the president ahead of the 2027 general election.

Mr Makinde said his disagreement with the PDP began after the party decided to leave its presidential ticket open, despite his efforts to secure the nomination for a southern candidate following eight years of President Muhammadu Buhari’s administration, which was led by a northerner.

“I was at the forefront of zoning the presidency to the South in the PDP, such that after eight years of President Buhari, who’s from the North, we can have a southern president,” he said.

However, the party eventually nominated former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, from the North-East, as its presidential candidate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Makinde said the G5 governors, who opposed their own party’s (PDP) presidential candidate, subsequently approached Atiku with concerns about the concentration of key positions in the party and its presidential campaign in the hands of northern politicians.

He cited Atiku’s emergence as the presidential candidate, Iyorchia Ayu’s position as PDP national chairman and the appointment of Aminu Tambuwal, then governor of Sokoto State, as director-general of the presidential campaign.

The group emerged from the PDP crisis after Mr Atiku’s victory in the party’s May 2022 presidential primary. Its members demanded Mr Ayu’s resignation, arguing that the party’s presidential candidate and national chairman should not both come from the North. The disagreement contributed to the governors’ decision to withhold support from Mr Atiku during the 2023 election.

The G5 comprised Mr Makinde, former Rivers State Governor Nyesom Wike, former Benue State Governor Samuel Ortom, former Abia State Governor Okezie Ikpeazu and former Enugu State Governor Ifeanyi Ugwuanyi.

According to Mr Makinde, the arrangement left the governors concerned about how the South would be represented in the campaign and a possible PDP-led government.

“So, what do we have to use to campaign for our own people in the South? So, we couldn’t have an alignment,” he said.

Why the G5 chose Tinubu – Makinde

Mr Makinde said the governors later considered other political options after futile efforts to resolve the PDP’s party’s campaign arrangements ahead of the 2023 election, arguing that their decision to break ranks with their party should be based on what would happen after the election, rather than merely on securing political advantage.

He said they approached Mr Obi and Mr Tinubu with a proposal for a government of national unity that would bring competent people from across the country into government, irrespective of their political affiliations.

“We approached Peter Obi. We approached the Asiwaju, and we said, ‘Look, beyond this election, it will be a government of national unity. First, nobody should be a slave in their own country, where you should have a Nigeria that will work for not just the privileged few, but everybody,’” he said.

Mr Makinde described the discussion with Mr Obi as good but said the group was not convinced that the Labour Party candidate would implement the proposal.

He said Mr Tinubu, on the other hand, accepted their recommendations, including the proposed government of national unity and national competence.

“So when we now approached the President an, and we brought this before him, he accepted the government of national unity, all of those things we have put together, national competence, and things like that,” he said.

The governor added that the decision to support Mr Tinubu was also a political risk because the G5 governors were breaking ranks with their party and needed to be confident that their choice would produce an outcome for the country.

Why I’m breaking with Tinubu

Mr Makinde said his support for Mr Tinubu was based on the expectation that the president would establish an inclusive government capable of addressing Nigeria’s economic and security challenges.

He alleged that the president failed to implement the signed agreement reached before the election, which he said was the basis for the G5’s support, noting that agreement had not produced the expected outcome.

“The president accepted it, but he did not implement it, which wasisat has led to where we are now,” he said.

He stated that the proposed government of national unity was intended to bring competent Nigerians from different parts of the country into government to address the country’s economic difficulties and insecurity.

He added that the agreement was not merely a verbal understanding, saying he had a signed copy.

“We signed an agreement. I have it. I have the signed copy. It’s not like somebody said to somebody who said we sat,” he said.

Mr Makinde said he expected the president to demonstrate the same commitment to a written development plan that he said guided his administration in Oyo State.

He recalled that before his first election in 2019, he presented a roadmap for the state’s development to voters and later assessed its implementation when he sought re-election in 2023.

He said he expected a similar level of commitment from the president to the agreement reached before the 2023 election.

The governor said his decision to contest against Mr Tinubu was not simply about replacing the president but correcting what he described as a mistake made in 2023.

“What I can do is to say, look, okay, this was a mistake in 2023. We need to correct it. Players will come and go, governments will come and go, individuals will come and go, but our country, our state will remain,” he said.

Mr Makinde, who is seeking the presidency under the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), said his proposed alternative would be based on a reset agenda.

He challenged Nigerians to assess the performance of the current administration, arguing that those satisfied with its record could continue supporting it, while those dissatisfied should consider a change.

“If things have worked so well for you, then stick with the present administration. But if it hasn’t worked well for you, let us do a reset,” he said.

World.title: Reno Omokri presents Letter of Credence to Mexico, formally assumes duty as ambassador
World.content:
Nigerian Ambassador to Mexico, Reno Omokri, has presented his Letter of Credence to the Mexican government, marking the official start of his diplomatic assignment in the country.

Mr Omokri presented his letter to Mexico’s Director General of Protocol, Jonathan Auerbach, on Thursday at the country’s Foreign Ministry in Mexico City, Mexico.

The ambassador disclosed this in a post shared on Friday through his X handle.

“To the Glory of God and the Federal Republic of Nigeria, Yesterday I Presented Copies of My Letters of Credence To The Chief of Protocol of the Government of the United Mexican States, His Excellency Ambassador Jonathan Chait Auerbach, At The Secretaría de Relaciones Exteriores (Mexican Foreign Ministry),” he said.

Mr Omokri also said he presented a replica of the Eben sword, a traditional ceremonial sword belonging to the Benin Kingdom and Itsekiri royal tradition of Warri.

This symbolic gesture is in “appreciation of Mexico’s return of a 900-year-old Ifẹ Bronze statue to Nigeria in February 2020.”

The Eben, a ceremonial royal sword, is a symbol of authority, prestige and traditional heritage in the Benin Kingdom. Its presentation to Mexico therefore carries cultural and diplomatic significance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Similarly, in a post on X, the Mexican Foreign Ministry also said, “Today at @SRE_mx, Director General of Protocol Jonathan Chait (@JchaitA) received Bemigho Reno Omokri (@renoomokri), Nigeria’s ambassador-designate to Mexico, for the presentation of copies of his Letters of Credence.”

Mr Omokri becomes the latest Nigerian ambassador to present his letter of credence to his host country, formally marking the resumption of duties.

Letters of credence are formal diplomatic documents issued by a country’s head of state to confirm the appointment of an ambassador or permanent representative.

They officially introduce the envoy to the receiving authority, in this case, the Mexican government, and certify that the individual is empowered to speak and act on behalf of their nation.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that President Bola Tinubu announced the new ambassador last year and approved their posting in March.

This came two years after he recalled the previous ambassadors, during which the country operated without top representatives abroad, relying on senior officials of its embassies.

READ ALSO: Ukraine denies expanding war with Russia after Libya attack

Since the postings were announced, several appointees have assumed duties.

PREMIUM TIMES also reports that Mr Omokri’s nomination triggered a heated exchange in the Senate during the ambassadorial screening last December.

The concern centred on his suitability for a diplomatic posting, given his controversial history and public profile.

Mr Omokri, a former aide to President Goodluck Jonathan, was among President Tinubu’s fiercest critics during the 2023 presidential election, repeatedly questioning his integrity and making allegations against him.

His subsequent shift in political allegiance and support for the Tinubu administration raised questions about the considerations behind his nomination.

World.title: FG launches scheme to give 600 Nigerian tailors ₦5m each – How to apply
World.content:
President Tinubu

The Federal Government has introduced a business support programme to empower 600 tailors across Nigeria, with each selected beneficiary expected to receive ₦5 million in grants and repayable business financing.

The initiative, known as the Business Incubation for Renewed Hope Tailors Programme, will run for five years and is being implemented through the Industrial Training Fund (ITF).

The programme is designed to help skilled artisans establish, strengthen and expand their tailoring businesses, while creating employment opportunities across the country.

The ITF announced the initiative during a pre-launch sensitisation exercise in Jos, Plateau State, where it disclosed that 150 tailors from the North-Central zone had been selected for the pilot phase.

The initiative is one of the exit pathways under the ITF’s Skill-Up Artisans Programme (SUPA), which seeks to improve the technical and business skills of Nigerian artisans.

Who is eligible for the programme?

The programme is open to both participants of the ITF’s Skill-Up Artisans Programme and tailors who received their training outside the scheme.

However, prospective beneficiaries must meet specific requirements to qualify.

How can interested tailors apply?

The ITF has not announced a separate nationwide application deadline or confirmed that a fresh application window for all 600 beneficiaries is currently open.

However, its general Business Incubation Programme guidelines provide for registration through the Fund’s area offices.

Interested artisans can visit the nearest ITF area office to obtain and complete the business incubation application form.

They can also visit the Fund’s official website, www.itf.gov.ng, for information about its programmes and application procedures.

Tailors who did not participate in SUPA must ensure they obtain the required ITF certification and licence to meet the eligibility conditions.

The ITF’s general business incubation guidelines also state that participation in the incubation programme is free.

Applicants should note that registering for SUPA or submitting an application for the general business incubation programme does not automatically guarantee selection for the Renewed Hope Tailors initiative.

Although 150 beneficiaries have already been selected from the North-Central zone, the ITF has yet to provide a detailed selection timetable for the remaining 450 places.

The Director-General of ITF, Dr Afiz Oluwatoyin Ogun, represented by the Director of Legal Services, Safiya Abubakar, said the initiative aligned with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope agenda, which seeks to upgrade the skills of Nigerian artisans to international standards.

According to her, the programme would provide selected tailors with a structured opportunity to develop their businesses from start-up level to maturity over five years.

She urged prospective beneficiaries to pay attention to the programme’s processes and requirements.

World.title: Nigeria’s future depends on mentally resilient youths — Mamora
World.content:
Olorunnimbe Mamora, former Speaker of the Lagos State House of Assembly.

Former minister urges graduates to embrace purpose, adaptability, continuous learning

By Adeola Badru

Former Minister of Health, Olorunnimbe Mamora, has said Nigeria’s future depends largely on the mental resilience, character development and sense of purpose of its youths, warning that academic qualifications alone are insufficient to prepare them for the challenges of the modern world.

Mamora said young Nigerians must develop the capacity to navigate economic uncertainties, technological disruptions and changing employment opportunities through adaptability, continuous learning and problem-solving skills.

He spoke while delivering the 18th Convocation Lecture of Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, titled, “Youths’ Mental Health and Purpose: Thriving in a Volatile World.”

The former minister challenged graduating students to look beyond the certificates they had earned and prepare for a world where success would increasingly depend on their ability to manage uncertainty, identify opportunities and remain relevant.

He described convocation as a transition into a new phase of life, requiring graduates to demonstrate resilience, discipline, adaptability and a clear sense of purpose.

Mamora identified the growing influence of social media, economic pressures and rapid technological advancement as emerging challenges to the mental wellbeing of young people.

While acknowledging that the internet had expanded access to information and opportunities, he noted that excessive engagement with digital platforms could contribute to loneliness, anxiety and unhealthy comparisons.

He urged graduates not to measure their achievements or personal worth against the lifestyles and apparent successes of others on social media.

“Do not allow social media platforms to become the mirror through which you measure your worth.

“Your value is not determined by the number of people who like your photograph. Stop comparing your backstage with somebody else’s stage,” he said.

On the changing employment landscape, particularly with the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Mamora said graduates must recognise that education should go beyond acquiring academic qualifications.

He stressed the importance of critical thinking, problem-solving, skills acquisition and continuous learning, noting that adaptability would be essential to remaining relevant in the evolving world of work.

Drawing inspiration from the life of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther, after whom the university was named, Mamora said the cleric’s journey from slavery to becoming a renowned missionary and scholar demonstrated the importance of determination and resilience in overcoming adversity.

He urged the graduates to draw inspiration from Crowther’s life and remain committed to their aspirations despite the challenges they might encounter.

The former minister also challenged young Nigerians to move beyond waiting for paid employment and begin identifying problems in their communities for which they could develop practical solutions.

He said youths should see themselves as contributors to national development, adding that innovation and enterprise could create opportunities for both personal advancement and collective progress.

Addressing substance abuse, Mamora cautioned young people against turning to drugs as a means of escaping life’s pressures.

He described substance dependence as a potential “cage or catastrophic bondage,” urging youths to adopt healthier ways of managing stress and emotional difficulties.

He recommended healthy relationships, regular exercise and adequate rest, while encouraging those experiencing mental health challenges to seek professional support when necessary.

Mamora said protecting mental health was essential to achieving personal goals and making meaningful contributions to society.

At the convocation ceremony, 87 individuals were awarded doctorate degrees in various disciplines.

The university also conferred honorary doctorate degrees on renowned Professor of African History, Toyin Falola, and finance expert, Kayode Falowo, in recognition of their contributions to society.

The ceremony was attended by the Chairman of the Board of Trustees, Chief Wole Olanipekun, SAN, GCON; the Chancellor, Chief Tunde Afolabi; the Chairman of the Governing Council, Dr Olutoyin Okeowo; and the Vice-Chancellor, Professor Ebunoluwa Oduwole.

Other dignitaries present included principal officers of the university, distinguished guests and parents of the graduating students.

World.title: Omo-Agege denies snubbing police invitation over Uduere killings
World.content:
Omo-Agege

Senator Ovie Omo-Agege has denied reports claiming he refused to honour an invitation from the Delta State Police Command over Monday’s attack on members of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, at Uduere.

In a statement on Friday by his Media Adviser, Sunny Areh, the former Deputy President of the Senate said he had seen the reports and described them as untrue.

“Senator Ovie Omo-Agege has seen the reports claiming he refused to honour an invitation from the Delta State Police Command over Monday’s attack on members of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, at Uduere.

“It isn’t true. You can’t turn down an invitation you never received,” he said.

According to the statement, no formal invitation has reached the Senator or his office.

“No letter has reached the Senator or his office, and no officer has come to him with one. He first learned of it the same way everyone else did, from the Command’s announcement in the media.”

Areh said the report that Omo-Agege refused to appear was based on a single unnamed source.

“The claim that he refused leans on a single unnamed source. The Senator hasn’t told the police, or anyone else, that he won’t appear.”

The statement also revisited the events at Uduere, insisting that Omo-Agege was the victim of the attack.

“It is worth remembering what happened at Uduere. Senator Omo-Agege was the target of an assassination attempt. Senior members of his campaign team were murdered, and others are still in hospital with serious injuries.

“He is the one who survived an attack on his life, and the one demanding that those responsible be found and prosecuted.”

Omo-Agege said he wants the case resolved and justice for the victims.

“He wants this case resolved, and he wants justice for the dead and the wounded. If the police serve a lawful invitation, he will honour it. He asks only that it be sent through his office so a date can be agreed.”

He faulted the manner in which the alleged invitation was made public.

“A summons announced in the press before it reaches the person named is not due process, and he won’t be tried in the media,” he said.

World.title: 2027: National Counter Terrorism Centre moves to foil attacks on INEC facilities, personnel
World.content:
..Laka warns against electoral violence, voter intimidation, destruction of infrastructure

By Kingsley Omonobi

The National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Office of the National Security Adviser, has said it is working with security agencies to prevent planned attacks on Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) offices, personnel and electoral infrastructure ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The National Coordinator of the Centre, Major General Adamu Laka, also said measures were being strengthened to protect voters and prevent emerging security threats from disrupting the electoral process.

Laka spoke at the National Flag-off/North Central Zone Town Hall Engagement on Preventing Electoral Violence and Strengthening Election Security in Nigeria.

He urged youths not to allow themselves to be used as instruments of political violence, describing them as critical stakeholders in the country’s democratic future.

“In this regard, I urge our young people not to allow themselves to be used as instruments of political violence. You are important stakeholders in Nigeria’s democratic future and your energy, creativity and influence should be directed towards promoting peace, tolerance and responsible civic participation,” he said.

He said the Centre was working towards preventing attacks on INEC offices and personnel, protecting voters and electoral infrastructure, countering fake news and inflammatory narratives, strengthening community-based early warning systems and ensuring timely responses to emerging security threats.

Describing elections as the heartbeat of democracy, Laka said their credibility depended not only on the conduct of voting and announcement of results but also on the peace, security and public confidence surrounding the entire electoral process.

“There is absolutely no gain in any loss of life or property as a result of this democratic process,” he said.

The NCTC coordinator identified misinformation and disinformation, hate speech, political intolerance, incitement, youth manipulation, political thuggery, vote buying, voter intimidation, voter suppression and destruction of public infrastructure as factors that could fuel electoral violence.

He said stakeholders must collectively address the threats and strengthen early warning and response mechanisms to identify potential dangers before they escalate into violence.

Laka also stressed the need to build public confidence in the electoral process and ensure that women, youths, persons with disabilities and internally displaced persons were not excluded from meaningful participation.

He maintained that preventing electoral violence was not the responsibility of security agencies alone but required the collective commitment of political actors, government institutions, traditional and religious leaders, civil society organisations, the media and community-based organisations.

The National Coordinator commended the Centre for Civil-Military Cooperation (CIMICO) for partnering with the NCTC to organise the nationwide campaign.

He said the NCTC would provide coordination and technical leadership, while CIMICO and other partners would support community-level engagement, awareness creation and trust-building initiatives.

He added that collaboration with INEC, the Nigeria Police Force, the National Orientation Agency, other security agencies and development partners would help extend the campaign to communities across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

“Our objective is clear: to ensure that the 2027 general elections are peaceful, credible, inclusive and secure, free from electoral violence and intimidation,” he said.

Laka called on political parties and their supporters to embrace issue-based campaigns, respect the rule of law and demonstrate political maturity, warning that the pursuit of political power should not undermine the lives, security and unity of Nigerians.

He said the success of the campaign would be measured not by the number of meetings held or speeches delivered but by its impact on communities, public awareness, the effectiveness of early warning and response mechanisms, and the ability of citizens to participate in elections without fear.

He urged stakeholders to translate the commitments made at the town hall into practical actions across their communities.

Earlier, Dr Adams Otakwu of the Centre for Civil-Military Cooperation said the nationwide programme was designed to ensure that discussions on electoral violence prevention translated into practical actions, institutional commitments and measurable results.

He said the engagements would be guided by five core pillars, including building a deeper understanding of the risks and consequences of electoral violence, clarifying the responsibilities of institutions and stakeholders, adopting a common methodology for the town hall meetings, ensuring follow-up on recommendations, and promoting continuity and sustainability.

According to him, the programme would involve open discussions, identification of local risk factors, consideration of early warning mechanisms, experience sharing and the development of practical recommendations.

Otakwu said the organisers would also monitor the implementation of resolutions to ensure that the outcomes of the engagements reached communities at the grassroots and across the country.

He stressed that election security should not be treated as the exclusive responsibility of security agencies, noting that citizens and other stakeholders also had important roles to play in preventing violence.

He added that electoral violence prevention was a continuous process that extended beyond election day.

“There has to be timely information exchange. There has to be community vigilance so that at every point that anything is sensed to be a trigger of electoral violence, we’ll be able to promptly report it to legitimate security institutions,” he said.

World.title: OK Movement withdraws support for Obi, Kwankwaso, NDC
World.content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA- THE OK Movement, a political support platform associated with the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential ticket of Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso, has withdrawn its support for the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC.

According to the group, its national leadership has formally been made to understand that the presidential candidate of the NDC,Obi, and the party he represents have decided to discontinue their political relationship with the OK Movement.

In a statement on Friday by the National Director General of OK Movement, Hon. John Ozyl Ughulu, he said Politics is a game of numbers, and numbers play a decisive role in determining electoral strength, political relevance and, ultimately, the outcome of elections.

Ughulu who disclised that the OK Movement will, in due course, announce its preferred political party and presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections, said they have already commenced engagements with other political parties and potential presidential candidates whose political vision, leadership capacity and ideological commitments align with our established principles and values.

The National Director-General of OK Movement who noted that the organisation remained focused on the task ahead and firmly believe that their organisational strength cuts across wards, local governments and states of the federation, adding, “Our grassroots presence, organisational reach and mobilisation capacity position the OK Movement as a formidable independent political force capable of influencing the outcome of the 2027 general elections and challenging the present administration.

“Our data are clear. Our structures speak for us. Our ideology defines us. The OK Movement remains independent in its identity, organisational structure and political decisions. No individual, political party or political interest owns this movement.

“The National Leadership of the OK Movement has formally been made to understand that the presidential candidate of the NDC, His Excellency Peter Obi, and the party he represents have decided to discontinue their political relationship with the OK Movement.

“While we consider this development regrettable, we respect the decision and sincerely appreciate His Excellency for the time, engagements and opportunities shared with our movement.

“Following this development, the National Leadership of the OK Movement has resolved to officially discontinue all campaign, mobilisation and operational support for the NDC Party, effective immediately.

“Consequently, all OK Movement political structures and operational engagements at the ward, local government and state levels are hereby withdrawn from the NDC’s campaign and mobilisation activities.

“We recognise that the NDC has a considerable social media following which, if properly organised and translated into meaningful grassroots political participation, could deliver significant electoral benefits. The responsibility for converting that support into electoral strength now rests with the party and its leadership.”

Ughulu further said, “The OK Movement believes that leadership must be defined by capacity, competence, integrity and the ability to resolve issues.

“A true leader must possess the wisdom, courage and emotional intelligence to manage disagreements, build bridges and unite people rather than encourage division or benefit from internal conflicts.

“Leadership must never be about personal interests, self-centred ambitions or the pursuit of supremacy. It must be about selflessness, honesty, accountability and the willingness to place collective interests above personal considerations.

“Nigeria desperately needs this quality of leadership at this critical moment in our national history.”

On their next political direction, the National Director General, said, “The OK Movement will, in due course, announce its preferred political party and presidential candidate for the 2027 general elections.

“We have already commenced engagements with other political parties and potential presidential candidates whose political vision, leadership capacity and ideological commitments align with our established principles and values.

“We remain focused on the task ahead and firmly believe that our organisational strength cuts across wards, local governments and states of the federation.

“Our grassroots presence, organisational reach and mobilisation capacity position the OK Movement as a formidable independent political force capable of influencing the outcome of the 2027 general elections and challenging the present administration.

“Our data are clear. Our structures speak for us. Our ideology defines us.

“The OK Movement remains independent in its identity, organisational structure and political decisions. No individual, political party or political interest owns this movement.”

Ughulu who noted that their fundamental principles remain no – negotiable, said, ” we remain committed to the fundamental principles of: Integrity, Fairness, Equity, Justice, Competence, Accountability and National Unity.

“These principles are not negotiable, nor will we compromise them for political convenience.

“We will not allow intimidation, manipulation, personal interests or anyone’s selfish political ambition to determine the political direction of our movement.

“The OK Movement is bigger than any individual. It was established on principles, built through collective sacrifice and remains committed to the Nigerian people and the ideals upon which it was founded.

“The National Leadership wishes to express its profound appreciation to every member, coordinator, volunteer and supporter of the OK Movement for their resilience, sacrifices and unwavering commitment.

“We understand that some members may have developed strong political and emotional attachments to the NDC Party and may feel disappointed by this development and the decision we have taken.

“We respect the personal convictions and political choices of every member. Anyone who chooses to maintain their relationship with the NDC or pursue a different political direction is entitled to do so without intimidation, hostility or resentment.

“However, we must distinguish between individual political choices and the collective institutional decisions of the OK Movement.

“We recognise the time, resources, energy and personal sacrifices invested in building this movement across the country. We assure every member that these sacrifices have not been in vain. They remain an important part of our collective journey towards building a better Nigeria.

“We therefore urge all coordinators and members to remain calm, disciplined and focused while awaiting further directives from the National Leadership.”

World.title: ADC waste plan will create 21,000 jobs in Lagos – Gbadamosi
World.content:
By Adegboyega Adeleye

African Democratic Congress (ADC) deputy governorship candidate Babatunde Olalere Gbadamosi has projected that the party’s waste management plan would create at least 21,000 jobs in Lagos, including 20,000 for waste collection crews.

Gbadamosi, who is running with ADC governorship candidate Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour, spoke at the Road to Election 2027 Lagos Deputy Governorship Debate on Nigeria Info FM on Friday, where he outlined proposals on employment, waste collection, housing and transportation.

Addressing unemployment, Gbadamosi said he did not know the state’s unemployment rate and disputed figures published by the Lagos government. He proposed a review of public sector salaries and said his plans for waste management, housing, transportation and education would create jobs for Lagosians.

“First of all, the truth is, I suppose the truth is, I really don’t know what the unemployment rate is. Whatever figures that are put out by the APC government of Lagos State are usually just false. They just manufacture figures, yank them out of their a**,” he said.

He said he and Rhodes-Vivour had agreed to “undertake a review, a wholesale review of public sector salaries, in order to bring them in line with our current economic realities.” He also cited plans for 20,000 jobs in waste-to-energy, 100,000 affordable housing units and 16,000 electric buses.

“We plan to bring 16,000 electric buses into Lagos State because we simply don’t have enough capacity to carry the 24 million people of Lagos State on the current transportation system,” he said, adding that the housing and transport plans would also provide work for young people.

On waste collection, Gbadamosi proposed providing each local government with at least 200 dumpsters. He estimated that 4,000 trucks, each with a five-person crew, would create 20,000 jobs.

“All right, we have 20 local governments. So 200 times 20, that’s 4000 trucks. 4000 trucks times five crew members, each. That’s already 20,000 jobs,” he said.

He estimated that recycling centres would create at least another 1,000 jobs, based on a minimum of 50 workers at each of 20 local government centres.

“That’s 50 jobs times 20 local governments. That’s already what 1000 extra jobs minimum,” he said, adding that the programme would be funded with “25% of Lagos State revenue that is being paid to Alpha Beta at the moment.”

Other major contenders at the debate included Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) deputy governorship candidate Moriam Tolani Animashaun and Social Democratic Party (SDP) deputy candidate Kayode Evelyn Aderiyike.

The debate was hosted by Kofi Bartels and Ireti Bakare-Yusuf.

World.title: PANDEF rejects 20% NCDMB fund deduction for research council
World.content:
…Warns against diversion of local content funds, urges NASS to review proposed legislation

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA – The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF), the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone, has rejected the proposed 20 per cent deduction from the Nigerian Content Development Fund to finance the proposed National Council on Research, Science, Technology and Innovation.

The forum warned that the move could undermine years of investment in indigenous industrial capacity and weaken the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB), which has been instrumental in promoting local expertise, skills acquisition, enterprise development and industrialisation.

PANDEF urged the National Assembly to review Section 19 of the proposed legislation establishing the council and reject the provision earmarking 20 per cent of the Nigerian Content Development Fund for its financing.

Addressing journalists in Abuja on Friday, PANDEF National Chairman, Ambassador Godknows Igali, acknowledged the Federal Government’s efforts to strengthen the country’s research, science, technology and innovation capacity but expressed concern over Part IV, Section 19(a) of the proposed Bill.

He described the proposed funding arrangement as inappropriate, counterproductive and fundamentally flawed, arguing that a new national institution should not be financed by weakening an existing statutory agency with clearly defined responsibilities and ongoing development commitments.

Igali said the NCDMB, which commenced operations in 2010, had a statutory mandate to promote the development, acquisition and application of indigenous capacity in Nigeria’s oil and gas industry.

He noted that the Nigerian Content Development Fund was already supporting strategic investments in the oil and gas sector and related areas, including agriculture, manufacturing and transportation.

According to him, diverting 20 per cent of the fund could disrupt existing commitments, constrain ongoing investments and slow the progress recorded in local content development.

“The Nigerian Content Development Fund is not an idle pool of resources awaiting allocation. It is an active development instrument that is already financing and supporting several strategic investments in the oil and gas industry and related sectors of the Nigerian economy,” he said.

Igali also warned that the proposed funding mechanism could establish a dangerous precedent in public finance, whereby newly established government institutions would depend on deductions from funds already allocated to existing statutory agencies.

He said such an arrangement was inconsistent with sound corporate governance and fiscal policy, stressing that new institutions should have independent, predictable and sustainable funding structures.

“The principle of sound public finance requires that the establishment of new institutions should be accompanied by deliberate, independent and sustainable funding arrangements.

“It is inappropriate to weaken one institution in order to finance another, particularly when the existing institution is performing effectively and fulfilling its statutory mandate,” he said.

The PANDEF chairman further stressed that the Niger Delta had a legitimate interest in protecting the financial strength of the NCDMB, given its contributions to human capital development and economic empowerment across the region.

He said the board’s interventions had supported education, technical and vocational training, skills acquisition, enterprise development and the growth of indigenous businesses in Niger Delta communities.

According to him, reducing the fund’s resources would limit the board’s capacity to expand these programmes in a region that had historically borne the environmental and socio-economic consequences of oil and gas exploration.

Igali called on the National Assembly to critically review the funding provisions in Section 19 of the proposed Bill and identify alternative sources of financing for the proposed council.

“We call on the National Assembly to critically review the funding provisions contained in Section 19 of the proposed Bill and reject the proposed 20 per cent deduction from the Nigerian Content Development Fund.

“We believe that the proposed council deserves a dedicated, predictable and sustainable funding framework that will enable it to discharge its responsibilities without undermining the mandates and financial capacities of existing statutory institutions,” he said.

He added that the funding provision could be referred to the Executive for further review, if necessary, to develop a more appropriate and sustainable arrangement.

Igali disclosed that PANDEF had already communicated its position to the President of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, urging them to give the matter serious consideration.

The forum, however, reaffirmed its support for the Federal Government’s efforts to advance research, science and technology, insisting that the pursuit of new national initiatives should not come at the expense of existing institutions.

“We must not sacrifice the gains of local content development in the pursuit of a new national initiative.

“We urge the Federal Government and the National Assembly to protect and strengthen the NCDMB and its Fund, recognising their strategic contributions to indigenous capacity development, industrialisation, employment generation and economic diversification,” he said.

Also speaking, a member of PANDEF and former Permanent Secretary, Federal Ministry of Labour and Productivity, Dr Timiebi Koripamo-Agary, questioned the need to establish another institution to oversee research, science, technology and innovation, arguing that existing agencies should instead be strengthened.

She cited the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI) and the Projects Development Institute (PRODA) as institutions with existing capacities that could be enhanced to deliver on the proposed council’s objectives.

Recalling the contributions of indigenous technology institutions during the Nigerian Civil War, Koripamo-Agary noted that some of the agencies established to develop local technological capacity still existed but faced funding challenges.

“Why not think out of the box about how to strengthen the capacity of NASENI? There are other agencies that can do what is being proposed,” she said.

She also questioned the proposed funding source, suggesting that the government explore alternative revenue options, including taxation of telecommunications companies, rather than drawing resources from the Nigerian Content Development Fund.

“If it’s about communication, how about taxing them and deploying part of the money that they are making? And they are making so much money,” she said.

Koripamo-Agary further expressed concern over poor budget implementation and the rollover of allocations across financial years.

She urged the government to improve coordination among institutions, strengthen existing agencies and deploy available resources more effectively, arguing that Nigeria could pursue new initiatives without weakening institutions already performing related functions.

World.title: Photos: Adeleke sworn in for 2nd term; says ‘Let’s heal our past wounds’
World.content:
Governor Adeleke of Osun taking his oath of office for a second term tenure.

By Shina Abubakar, Osogbo

As Governor Ademola Adeleke took oath of office for his second term tenure, he has charged the Osun State political class to allow the wounds of the past to heal and collaborate to develop the state.

Governor Adeleke spoke while addressing hundreds of dignitaries and residents who thronged the Osogbo township stadium to be part of his inauguration.

He disclosed that citizens, irrespective of political affiliations, must unite for the collective good.

His words: “Fellow citizens, we must heal the wounds of the past and unite for our collective good. I charge the Osun political class to embrace elite consensus, transparency, good governance and local content”.

The governor commended the resilience of the citizens and residents of the state to safeguard democracy, saying their commitment has become a national model.

“Today is a triumph of the people’s will. I give all glory to God and deeply thank the people of Osun. Their commitment to democracy is today a national model,” he said.

2nd term focus

On his administration’s focus for the second term, he said the target of the government will focus on citizens’ welfare, infrastructure expansion, industrialisation, agricultural transformation, digital economy, tourism industry, wealth creation, and youth and women’s development among others.

“As growth depends on steady power supply, we will immediately set up the Osun State Electricity Regulatory Commission. This is in line with the power sector law I signed earlier this year.

“Job and Wealth creation will be at the heart of our second term. We will establish a digital hub in each of our three senatorial districts. This is to drive job creation in the digital economy.

“In education, we will recruit more teachers and speed up school rehabilitation. We will expand bursaries and scholarships, keep tuition affordable, tackle cultism, and revive our technical colleges.”

Osun local government crisis

On the issue of local government crisis, Adeleke said: “I am glad to announce that Mr President has intervened in the local government matter. In the next one week, the crisis will be fully resolved. Once this is done, our administration will ensure the rehabilitation of the remaining 102 primary health care centres.”

Earlier, the deputy governor, Kola Adewusi took oath of office at 11:24a.m. followed by that of the governor whose oath of office was administered by the Chief Judge, Justice Oyebola Adepele-Ojo at exactly 11:34am.

Vice President Shettima, Ooni, others

Meanwhile, the Vice President, Senator Kashim Shettima led dignitaries from all spheres of life to the inauguration.

The National leader of the APC, Chief Bisi Akande; Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa; former National Secretary of the party, Senator Iyiola Omisore, PDP’s National Treasurer, Prince Diran Odeyemi and former Presidential candidate of the Labour Party, Datti-Baba Ahmed, were also in attendance.

Also, the Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Ogunwusi joined other traditional rulers including the Alaafin of Oyo, Oba Akeem Owoade, Oluban of Ibadan, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, Soun of Ogbomoso Oba Ghandi Olaoye, Ataoja of Osogbo, Oba Jimoh Olanipekun, who arrived the venue earlier for the inauguration.

The governor’s elder brother, Dr. Deji Adeleke, led captains of Industries and the Adeleke family including the Afro beat star, David Adeleke, Mrs Modupe Adeleke-Sanni, Mr. Tunji Adeleke, Shina Adeleke (Shina Rambo), Adebayo Adeleke (B-RED) among others.
