World.title: Child Stunting Still Unacceptably High In Nigeria, Says FG
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

The Federal Government has said that child stunting remains unacceptably high in Nigeria, despite several achievements recorded in the area of child and maternal health indicators.

World Health Organization (WHO) described stunting as impaired growth and development that children experience from poor nutrition, repeated infection, and inadequate psychosocial stimulation.

The country currently has the second highest burden of stunted children in the world, with a national prevalence rate of 32 per cent. Various study statistics indicate prevalence among children under five ranges between 31.5 per cent and 39.5 per cent.

While declaring open the 10th Annual Conference of the Association of Nigeria Health Journalists (ANHEJ) in Abuja, Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, Daju Kachallom, said about four in ten children under five are affected by stunting in the country.

Speaking on the theme, “NHSRII: From Policy to Tangible Impact,” Kachallom said three years after President Bola Tinubu launched the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (NHSRII) in December 2023, all 41 presidential health-sector commitments have been achieved, and 12 of the 13 health indicators tracked have improved.

She said 3,526 primary health centres have been revitalised, with 900 more under way. The share of participating facilities supported by the Basic Health Care Provision Fund in 172 MAMII local government areas with at least two midwives or community health extension workers has risen from 12 to 91 per cent.

Skilled deliveries in those facilities rose from 4.8 million in 2023 to 7.9 million by mid-2026. In the 172 LGAs that carry more than half of maternal deaths, maternal deaths fell by 17 per cent and newborn deaths by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2025.

Measles and rubella vaccination has reached 100 million children, and more than 17 million girls have received the HPV vaccine. Health insurance enrolment has grown from about 16 million to nearly 24 million Nigerians.

But Kachallom said: “Stunting remains unacceptably high, affecting about four in ten children under five. Nigerians still tell us that care costs too much and that its quality is uneven.”

She added that even with nearly 24 million enrolled in health insurance, coverage remains at only about one in ten, and the country does not yet have enough health workers where they are needed most.

She also lamented poor implementation of resolutions, noting that before this year’s Council of Health meeting, only 412 of 740 expected reports were received, with ten states recording implementation scores below 40 per cent.

“A resolution that is never implemented is just another announcement,” she said.

Presenting its scorecard, the Nigeria Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) said enrollees rose from 16.2 million in 2024 to over 24.09 million as at third quarter of 2026.

NHIA said over 100,000 women and newborns were reached through the CEmONC and Fistula-Free programme as at August 2026, while 6,059 women received treatment for obstetric fistula. Facility-based maternal mortality case-fatality rates declined by 22 per cent, from 1,042 in 2024 to 810 in 2026.

The Institute of Human Virology Nigeria (IHVN) urged health journalists to uphold accuracy and ethical responsibility and to move beyond reporting challenges to documenting solutions.

President of ANHEJ Joseph Kadiri said the conference theme, “Nigeria’s Health Sector Renewal Investment: From Policy to Tangible Impact,” speaks directly to one of the most important questions confronting our healthcare system today which is how we can ensure that policies, reforms and financial investments translate into better health outcomes for ordinary Nigerians

World.title: Beyond Protocol Purism: Why Nigerians in South Africa Welcome an Envoy Who Refuses to Whisper
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Abiodun Abidoye

​When big men rise, little men tremble.

​When a patriot that truly cares about the welfare and safety of his people comes on the scene, the cowards and traitors murmur.



​When light comes, darkness cries and inevitably flees.

​It is in this context that we need to see and acknowledge the phenomenal rise and triumphs that Ambassador Femi Fani Kayode has recorded since his sojourn in South Africa as the Nigerian High Commissioner.



​He has shaken the table and made Nigerians hold up their heads with pride again in a nation in which they have been subjected to the sort of discrimination and indignities that can best be imagined.

​I view Professor Badejo as one of those small minded men who simply cannot bear the fact that Ambassdor Femi Fani Kayode is succeeding where archaic souls and career diplomats like him failed and who may be fronting for a number of individuals who feel threatened by the meteoric rise of Nigeria’s most popular and most loved Ambassador.



​In his recent essay, Jankara Diplomacy, Professor Babafemi A. Badejo invokes the bustling, informal commerce of the historic Jankara market in Lagos to caricature the newly accredited High Commissioner of Nigeria to South Africa. While the scholarly excursion of Professor Badejo from Kautilya to the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations makes for brisk reading, his selective invocation of protocol overlooks repeated violations of diplomatic norms and human dignity directed against Nigeria and its citizens, to which only the High Commissioner had the courage to respond.



​First, the factual record in Pretoria contradicts the alarmist portrait of a mission teetering on the edge of expulsion. On 13 November 2026, Chief Fani Kayode presented his Letter of Credence to President Cyril Ramaphosa at the Sefako Makgatho Presidential Guest House as the first substantive High Commissioner of Nigeria to South Africa in four years. Even Professor Badejo concedes that the formal address of the envoy, delivered in traditional Nigerian attire, was executed with panache and appropriately recalled the historic sacrifices of Nigeria during the struggle against apartheid.



Yet when the segment of Nigeria, delivered last among fifteen envoys, was cut off from the live broadcast while others aired, Professor Badejo treats the silence of Nigeria as a virtue rather than questioning whether denying an accredited envoy equal sovereign courtesy violated the spirit of the Vienna Convention.



​Even more glaring is the selective amnesia surrounding the official provocations that followed. When a South African presidential spokesperson publicly branded the Nigerian High Commissioner a liar over whether President Ramaphosa had intervened, only to fall mute when video evidence surfaced, and even went so far as to accuse President Bola Tinubu of lying regarding afrophobic attacks in South Africa, where were the purists preaching the Vienna Convention?



Similarly, when a Minister in the South African Presidency broadly labelled Nigerians as drug dealers, was that not an egregious breach of diplomatic comity and international norms?

Yet across the foreign policy establishment, only High Commissioner Fani Kayode stood up to defend the honour of Nigeria and its leadership.



​The same double standard applies to the safety and dignity of Nigerian nationals and diplomatic personnel on the ground. Under the Vienna Convention, a receiving state bears a solemn obligation to protect the dignity of a diplomatic mission and ensure peace and order around foreign nationals. When marching mobs descended on Sunnyside in Pretoria, a neighbourhood widely known as Little Lagos, taunting Nigerians to provoke a violent clash while declaring that Nigerians must not be permitted into South Africa or allowed to marry and have relations with South African women, the silence of commentators like Professor Badejo was deafening.



Even when the High Commissioner himself was subjected to humiliating treatment by airport officials on a Friday as he prepared to depart, an incident witnessed by over a hundred travellers that forced him to reschedule his flight until Sunday when he finally departed, and which he chose with remarkable restraint not to weaponise publicly, there was no outrage from those now lecturing him on protocol.

​Far from causing a diplomatic rupture, the subsequent 17 November engagement between High Commissioner Fani Kayode and the Director General of the Department of International Relations and Cooperation of South Africa, Zane Dangor, was constructive. Crucially, the High Commissioner used that very meeting to place the safety, treatment, and unresolved deaths of Nigerians in South Africa squarely on the bilateral agenda. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola has since affirmed that the matter is closed, and the subsequent consultative visit of Chief Fani-Kayode to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja, where he dismissed social media rumours of a recall, underscored institutional alignment rather than isolation.



​More importantly, the defence of subtle diplomacy by Professor Badejo rings hollow when measured against the lived experience of Nigerians in South Africa over the past four years. From wherever he is based, Professor Badejo cannot fully appreciate the extent of Nigeria phobia on the ground, making it imperative that High Commissioner protect the dignity of Nigerians in practical, visible ways.

During the prolonged absence of a substantive High Commissioner in Pretoria, hundreds of Nigerians were reported killed, including high profile attacks and disputed deaths in custody that yielded little justice, while thousands more were repatriated amid recurring waves of afrophobic hostility, scapegoating, and consular bottlenecks.



To ordinary Nigerians working, studying, and building businesses in Johannesburg, Pretoria, Cape Town, and Durban, years of timid, behind the scenes orthodoxy felt indistinguishable from official abandonment, doing nothing to deter prejudice against Nigerians or compel accountability from host authorities.



​That context explains why so many Nigerians across the diaspora, and commentators at home, have hailed the posting of Chief Fani Kayode as a long overdue turning point, with admirers even arguing that his vocal defence of national dignity exemplifies the energy that the broader foreign policy leadership of Nigeria ought to project. When a major African nation rebuilds its presence in Pretoria after a four year vacuum, it needs an envoy who commands attention and challenges discrimination openly, not one content to blend into the diplomatic wallpaper.



​It is equally telling how quickly sections of the foreign policy establishment and entrenched diplomatic circles rush to weaponise protocol purism against an envoy whose public resonance disrupts comfortable bureaucratic inertia. Too often, criticism disguised as concern for diplomatic etiquette reflects institutional discomfort, as some career diplomats appear envious of the rapid impact of Ambassdor Fani-Kayode and seem eager to undermine a visibly effective political appointee who refuses to treat quiet passivity as statecraft.



​Respect for the Vienna Convention and unapologetic defence of Nigerian citizens are not competing imperatives.



The early tenure of High Commissioner Fani Kayode in Pretoria has paired an insistence on bilateral parity and public accountability with direct engagement through the Department of International Relations and Cooperation and consultations with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Abuja.

Far from diminishing Pan Africanism, confronting discrimination against Nigerians honestly while strengthening bilateral channels offers a far more durable foundation for genuine brotherhood between Nigeria and South Africa.

World.title: OK Movement Pulls Nationwide Structures Out of Obi’s NDC
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

.Group withdraws ward, council, state mobilisation machinery

.Begins talks with other parties ahead of 2027 elections

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The OK Movement has withdrawn its nationwide political structures and campaign support from the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), following what it described as the decision by the party’s presidential candidate, Peter Obi, and the party leadership to discontinue their political relationship with the movement.

The movement announced the immediate termination of all its campaign, mobilisation and operational engagements with the NDC, directing its structures at the ward, local government and state levels to disengage from the party’s activities.

It also disclosed that it had commenced consultations with other political parties and prospective presidential candidates ahead of the 2027 general election, promising to announce its preferred political platform and candidate in due course.

The announcement, signed by its National Director General, Hon. John Ozyl Ughulu, on Friday, on behalf of the national leadership, signals a potentially significant realignment within the opposition political landscape as parties and political groups intensify preparations for the 2027 elections.

The movement said it had been formally informed that Obi and the NDC had decided to discontinue their political relationship with it, describing the development as regrettable but insisting that it respected their decision.

“Following this development, the National Leadership of the OK Movement has resolved to officially discontinue all campaign, mobilisation and operational support for the NDC Party, effective immediately,” the statement said.

It added that all its political structures and operational engagements across the country had consequently been withdrawn from the NDC’s campaign and mobilisation activities.

Although the movement did not disclose the circumstances surrounding the breakdown of the relationship, its statement contained pointed observations about leadership, political management and the handling of disagreements.

It argued that effective leadership required capacity, competence, integrity and the ability to resolve disputes, build bridges and unite people rather than exploit internal divisions.

According to the movement, leadership should not be driven by personal interests, self-centred ambitions or the pursuit of supremacy but by selflessness, accountability and the willingness to place collective interests above individual considerations.

The group also appeared to question the NDC’s ability to translate its considerable social media following into electoral strength, arguing that online popularity must be backed by organised grassroots participation to produce meaningful electoral outcomes.

The statement read: “We recognise that the NDC has a considerable social media following which, if properly organised and translated into meaningful grassroots political participation, could deliver significant electoral benefits.

“The responsibility for converting that support into electoral strength now rests with the party and its leadership,” it stated.

On its next political direction, the OK Movement said it was already engaging other political parties and potential presidential candidates whose political visions, leadership capacities and ideological commitments aligned with its established principles.

It maintained that its nationwide organisational structures, grassroots presence and mobilisation capacity positioned it as an independent political force capable of influencing the outcome of the 2027 elections.

The movement further declared that its political identity and organisational structures were not owned by any individual or political party, stressing that its decisions would be determined independently.

“The OK Movement remains independent in its identity, organisational structure and political decisions. No individual, political party or political interest owns this movement,” it said.

It listed integrity, fairness, equity, justice, competence, accountability and national unity as its non-negotiable principles, insisting that it would not compromise them for political convenience or allow intimidation, manipulation and personal ambitions to determine its political direction.

The national leadership also acknowledged that the withdrawal could disappoint members who had developed political and emotional attachments to the NDC, but urged them to distinguish between their individual political preferences and the collective institutional decisions of the movement.

It assured members that anyone wishing to maintain their relationship with the NDC or pursue a different political direction was free to do so without intimidation or hostility.

However, it urged coordinators, volunteers and supporters across the country to remain calm, disciplined and committed while awaiting further directives from the national leadership.

The movement expressed appreciation to members for their sacrifices, resources and commitment to building its structures across the country, assuring them that their contributions had not been wasted.

Reaffirming its determination to remain politically relevant ahead of the next general election, the group declared that its withdrawal from the NDC should not be interpreted as a retreat from the political arena.

“The OK Movement is not retreating. We are repositioning, reorganising and preparing for the next phase of our political journey,” it declared.

World.title: In Defence of Jankara Diplomacy: When Quiet Diplomacy Has Not Worked
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Olabisi Dare

Professor Babafemi Badejo’s Jankara Diplomacy is elegantly written, learned, and with respect mistimed.

It is right about the Vienna Convention. It is right that diplomacy is a conservative trade. It is right that an envoy must act “within the limits permitted by international law” under Article 3(1)(b).



Where it misses the point is on timing and context. For years, Nigeria has practised the quiet, correct, conservative diplomacy that Badejo prescribes in Pretoria. And for years, Nigerians in South Africa have been killed, their shops looted, their properties destroyed, and their dignity questioned, often with what many Nigerians reasonably perceive as complacency, if not insensitivity, from the South African authorities.



Quiet cables did not stop the killings. Quiet démarches did not stop the xenophobic protests. Quiet dialogue did not produce accountability.



That is why there is a need, at this point, for what my Egbon, derides as ‘Jankara/Areaboy’ diplomacy. Jankara is not anarchy, as he himself admits. Jankara has rules which are flexible rules, loudly negotiated, in full view of the market. And sometimes, when the other side has stopped listening in the quiet room, you must take the matter to the market square so that everyone hears.



Chief Femi Fani-Kayode did not invent Nigeria’s grievance. He gave voice to it. His presentation on November 13, 2026 — in Babanriga, with panache, recalling Nigeria’s frontline sacrifices against apartheid — was exactly what a proud nation should expect. His subsequent insistence that Nigeria would not be erased, even from a livestream, was not vanity. It was symbolism. To many Nigerians, that cut-out felt like a metaphor for a larger erasure.



Was the language robust? Yes. Was it undiplomatic by the textbook? Perhaps. But diplomacy is not only about pleasing the host government. It is also about protecting nationals and signalling resolve — the very duty imposed by Article 3(1)(a) and (b).



On the MFA’s Reset, this is why the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ reaction deserves applause, not derision. In its Press Statement No. MFA/PR/2026/304 of November 17, 2026, the MFA did precisely what a mature foreign ministry should do: it reaffirmed that the relationship is “founded on African solidarity, friendship and mutual respect,” it insisted on “diplomatic engagement in resolving outstanding matters,” and it announced that it is reviewing the comprehensive report, including the discussions at DIRCO.

That is not a rebuke. That is a reset.



It tells Pretoria: we will not escalate, but we have heard our envoy and we have heard our people. It tells Abuja’s envoy: your message has landed, now let the Ministry manage the process. And it tells both capitals: the message must be clear to both sides — Nigeria will not accept insensitivity to the treatment of its nationals, and South Africa must understand that African solidarity cannot be one-way. That balanced reset is statesmanship.



That is precisely why there is no recourse or need, on either side, to initiate a recall.

South Africa has not declared the High Commissioner persona non grata under Article 9(1) of the Vienna Convention, and it should not. Nigeria has not recalled its High Commissioner, and it should not.

A recall now would be a victory for escalation. It would reward those who want a rupture between Africa’s two largest economies. It would leave Nigerians in South Africa without a champion in Pretoria, and it would leave South African investments in Nigeria exposed to retaliatory populism.

The High Commissioner’s presence in Abuja on November 23, 2026 for routine consultations — to submit reports, receive guidance, and prepare his family’s relocation — should be taken at face value. Consultation is not recall. Review is not reprimand.



What Pretoria needs is not a silent envoy who will look away while Nigerians suffer. What Abuja needs is not an envoy who will humiliate a host for sport. What both need is what the MFA has now imposed: a firm message delivered, followed by calm, structured dialogue.



Let the jankara moment pass. Let the market hear that Nigeria is serious. Now let the diplomats return to the quiet room but this time, with South Africa fully aware that Nigeria’s patience is not infinite, and with Nigeria fully aware that its strength lies in disciplined follow-through, not in perpetual shouting.

That is not Jankara versus diplomacy. That is Jankara in service of diplomacy.

*Ambassador Olabisi Dare is a Nigerian career diplomat and international civil servant with over 27 years of field and desk experience across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. He is widely known for his work with the African Union Commission (AUC), where he served as Head of the Humanitarian Affairs, Refugees and Displaced Persons Division

World.title: FG Pledges More Investment in Energy Sector
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

The Federal Government has pledged to deepen investment, strengthen local industrial capacity and promote infrastructure development in the energy sector as part of efforts to achieve energy security and accelerate Nigeria’s economic transformation.

The Secretary to the Government of the Federation (SGF), Senator George Akume, made the commitment in Port Harcourt at the 10th Africa Energy Summit, organised by the Solewant Energy Training Institute (SETI), a subsidiary of Solewant Group.

The summit, with the theme, ‘Scaling Innovative Industrial Capacity for Africa’s Energy Security,’ brought together policymakers, investors, energy professionals and other stakeholders to discuss strategies for strengthening Africa’s energy sector.

Akume, who was represented by his Special Assistant on Technical Matters, Prof. Babatunde Bolaji Benerd, said energy security went beyond having abundant natural resources, stressing that the country must develop the capacity to produce, process, transport and distribute energy reliably and affordably.

He said the Federal Government, under President Bola Tinubu, was implementing reforms aimed at improving the investment environment, increasing domestic production and supporting industrial growth.

“The current administration is pursuing reforms aimed at improving the investment climate, strengthening domestic production and creating conditions for productive activities,” he said.

The SGF said the implementation of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) had provided a framework for improved governance, clearer institutional responsibilities and increased investment across the oil and gas value chain.

He added that the government was promoting domestic gas utilisation, compressed natural gas (CNG) development, energy infrastructure and reforms in the electricity sector.

Akume also called for a broader approach to local content, saying Nigerian participation in the petroleum industry should translate into the development of competitive businesses capable of manufacturing equipment, providing specialised services, creating jobs and competing internationally.

Also speaking, the Special Adviser to the President on Energy, Olu Verheijen, represented by Dr Oluseun Amoda, said ongoing reforms had helped improve investor confidence and unlock fresh investments in the sector.

She said executive orders and policy directives introduced by the administration were designed to provide fiscal incentives, reduce contracting timelines and costs, and strengthen local content.

According to her, the reforms had contributed to investment decisions valued at more than $8 billion in oil and gas projects.

Verheijen said the growing participation of indigenous companies in the industry presented opportunities for Nigerian businesses to expand their operations and develop technical capacity.

She said oil and gas projects required fabrication, engineering, drilling services, equipment, logistics and maintenance, creating opportunities for local enterprises.

She, however, stressed that local content should not become protection from competition but should help Nigerian companies compete globally on cost, quality and reliability.

Verheijen further urged investment in technical manpower, including welders, inspectors, process safety engineers and project managers.

Earlier, the Group Chief Executive Officer of Solewant Group, Solomon Ewanehi, said Africa must move beyond discussions about its natural resources and focus on investments capable of translating them into industrial growth and prosperity.

He said the summit should increasingly serve as a platform for decisions, partnerships and practical solutions to the continent’s energy challenges.

Ewanehi stressed that Africa’s energy future required collaboration, investment, innovation, skills development and deliberate efforts to build strong local industries.

World.title: Pharmacists Debunk Ban on Camosunate, Demand Retraction of Edo Committee’s Claim
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Kemi Olaitan in Ibadan

The Association of Industrial Pharmacists of Nigeria (NAIP) has called on the Edo State Consumer Protection Committee to retract its reported declaration that an antimalarial drug marketed by Geneith Pharmaceuticals Limited, Camosunate, is not approved for use in Nigeria.

In a statement jointly signed by its National Chairman, Aminu Bankole Ezebuilo, and National Secretary, Rosemary Lawson, the association insisted that the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) remained the statutory body responsible for determining the registration and regulatory status of medicines in the country.

NAIP, the technical and professional arm of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria (PSN), described the reported declaration as misleading, warning that such pronouncements could undermine public confidence in Nigeria’s pharmaceutical regulatory system.

The association maintained that NAFDAC had not withdrawn its approval for Camosunate, which contains the artesunate-amodiaquine combination, stressing that decisions concerning the approval, suspension or withdrawal of medicines must be based on scientific evidence and established regulatory procedures.

According to NAIP, NAFDAC has the statutory responsibility to register, regulate, suspend, withdraw or cancel the registration of medicinal products whenever necessary, following appropriate investigations and scientific assessments.

While acknowledging the responsibility of government institutions to protect Nigerians against counterfeit, substandard, falsified and unsafe medicines, NAIP cautioned against confusing suspected adverse drug reactions, consumer complaints or ongoing investigations with formal regulatory decisions.

NAIP warned that unverified public statements concerning registered medicines could create unnecessary panic, weaken patients’ confidence, disrupt pharmaceutical supply chains and expose legitimate manufacturers to reputational damage.

The association also expressed concern that such developments could discourage investment in Nigeria’s pharmaceutical manufacturing industry, particularly at a time when the country is seeking to expand local production, improve access to quality-assured medicines and reduce dependence on imported pharmaceutical products.

The association urged the Edo State Consumer Protection Committee to review its position and publicly retract its assertion regarding Camosunate, in line with NAFDAC’s official clarification on the medicine’s regulatory status.

It also called on government institutions, public officials and consumer protection agencies to ensure that public statements concerning the safety and regulatory status of medicines are supported by credible scientific evidence and authoritative regulatory information.

While reaffirming its commitment to patient safety, the association clarified that its intervention was not intended to shield any pharmaceutical company from legitimate regulatory scrutiny but to promote scientific objectivity, institutional accountability and fairness.

It maintained that the fight against substandard and falsified medicines should not become a platform for spreading misinformation about quality-assured products, insisting that genuine consumer protection must be anchored on scientific evidence and established regulatory principles.

“Public health requires facts, not fear. Regulation demands evidence, not assumption. And national pharmaceutical development requires partnership, not avoidable confrontation,” the association declared.

World.title: AVA Capital Convenes Stakeholders’ Brunch To Chart Financing Path for $1trn Economy
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

AVA Capital Plc has convened stakeholders from agribusiness, commercial banking, development finance and the capital market for a private wealth brunch focused on rethinking corporate finance strategy in Nigeria’s agribusiness sector.

The session, hosted in Lagos recently with the theme ‘The $1 trillion Economy: Rethinking Corporate Finance Strategy in Nigeria’s Agribusiness,’ formed part of AVA Capital’s $1 trillion Economy Private Brunch Series.

Speaking at the event, Managing Director, Investment Banking, AVA Capital, Mr. Abiola Hammed, highlighted the sector’s economic significance, noting that agriculture contributed 26.15 per cent of Nigeria’s GDP in Q2 2026.

However, he observed that the sector accounted for only 6.63 per cent of total bank lending as of June 2026, underscoring the need for alternative financing solutions, including commercial paper, credit guarantees and other capital market instruments.

Emphasizing the objective of the engagement, he said: “At the end of these conversations, what we want to achieve is to link capital to opportunities.”

Sharing industry perspectives, Chief Operating Officer, Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited, Mr. Nzubechukwu Anisiobi, discussed the company’s growth from trading 200 metric tonnes to over 50,000 metric tonnes of agricultural commodities annually, attributing its expansion to vertical integration across sourcing, logistics, storage, processing and exports.

A major highlight of the brunch was the unveiling of AVA Capital PLC’s November 2026 Agriculture Sector Report, Farm to Balance Sheet: Rethinking Corporate Finance Strategy in Nigeria’s Agribusiness.

The report examines the sector’s economic contribution, financing gaps, investment opportunities and corporate finance strategies for sustainable growth.

Among its key findings, it highlights the disparity between agriculture’s contribution of 2 6.15 per cent of Nigeria’s GDP in Q2 2026 and its 6.63 per cent share of total bank lending as of June 2026.

It also identifies export processing and integrated oil palm as priority investment opportunities, while highlighting the importance of supply chain integration, operational scale and appropriate financing structures in improving business profitability and attracting investment.

The report further provides practical guidance on leveraging commercial paper, development finance, corporate bonds, equity and structured commodity finance to support agribusiness expansion.

The event featured two moderated panel sessions exploring risk-sharing mechanisms, credit guarantees, capital market access, credit ratings, corporate governance and structured financing for agricultural businesses.

Panelists included Simisola Ojumu, Executive Director, Technical, NIRSAL Plc; Arese Ugwu,

Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, NASD Plc; Oladele Adeoye, Chief Rating Officer and Executive Director, Operations, DataPro Limited; Nzubechukwu Anisirobi, Chief Operating Officer, Sunbeth Global Concepts Limited; Chinedu Okere, Managing Director, ARN Foods Limited; and Adesuwa Asemota, Group Head, FMCG, Access Bank Plc.

The discussions reinforced the importance of stronger collaboration between financial institutions and agribusinesses in unlocking capital, strengthening the agricultural value chain and supporting Nigeria’s broader economic ambitions.

World.title: REAN Elects First Female President, New Executive Committee
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The Renewable Energy Association of Nigeria (REAN) has elected a new executive committee to steer the association’s affairs for the next two years, with Damilola Asaleye emerging as its first female president.

The election followed the association’s Annual General Meeting (AGM) in Lagos.

The association also held its conference on Tuesday, with the theme ‘Strengthen Collective Action in Driving Nigeria’s Renewable Energy Growth.’

The newly elected executive committee comprises Asaleye as president; Joseph Inyang, vice-president; Onyinye Okere, treasurer; and Happy Amos, head of programmes and partnership. Ridwan Adelaja was elected head of communications, while Motunrayo Akinfala remains chief executive officer.

Speaking shortly before the election Wednesday, Ayo Ademilua, the outgoing REAN president, commended the executive officers for their support during his tenure, describing them as outstanding partners in progress.

He thanked God for sustaining him and his executive committee through their two terms in office.

Ademilua also urged members to sustain the association’s culture of peaceful engagement and democratic leadership as it prepared to elect a new executive. He stressed that members’ votes rather than internal conflicts, should determine leadership positions.

“The voices of our members count by vote. We do not need to fight to maintain our leadership,” he said.

He appealed to the incoming leadership to regard their positions as a responsibility of service rather than personal privilege.

Regarding members’ welfare, Ademilua said his administration had prioritised creating business opportunities and improving access to financing for renewable energy companies.

According to him, REAN worked with about five commercial banks to develop financing products for renewable energy projects, including solar home systems, equipment importation, productive-use energy equipment and commercial and industrial solar installations.

In her remarks after being declared winner of the election, Asaleye, REAN’s first female president, sought the support and cooperation of all members.

She pledged to build on the association’s existing work, sustain its progress and take it to greater heights.

Asaleye also commended the electoral committee for conducting a free and fair election and thanked members for entrusting her with the leadership position.

Meanwhile, the association presented awards of recognition to some members of its Board of Trustees, former executive officers and partners for their contributions to its growth.

World.title: An entire farming region in South Africa is quietly under attack
World.content:
A region in the Cape Winelands where drugs have taken over. Image: Pexels

The Cape Winelands is home to some of the world’s best wines.

But an entire region, the Breede River Valley, is under attack, at least according to the most recent data from the South African Police Service (SAPS).

Crime rises across 9 wine farm towns in 3 municipalities

Every single town in the Breede River Valley, the Western Cape’s largest wine and fruit producing region, is struggling with drug-related crime.



The largest rise in drug-related crime was in De Doorns. Between July and September, drug-related crime more than doubled.

Despite this drastic rise, De Doorns isn’t the town recording the most drug-related crimes; that title goes to Worcester.

The town recorded an 18.4% rise and set a record for the number of drug-related crimes recorded in the area.



Worcester accounted for 66% of the Breede Valley’s drug-related crime cases.

Robbery with aggravated circumstances rose 48.9%, and theft out of a motor vehicle rose 29.6% in Worcester.

Residential burglaries also rose 14.5% during the three months between July and September.



Then in Rawsonville, drug-related crime rose 40.5%, and other serious crime, a category that includes theft, rose 69.7%.

In Robertson, drug-related crime is up 46.1%.

Petty thefts and contact-related crimes rose 27.6% and 16.7%, respectively.



Touws River has also reached its peak, with drug-related crime rising 53.3% in the second quarter.

Drug-related crime in Ceres has also peaked, with it rising 21.7% compared to the same period last year.

But the crimes aren’t limited to drugs.

In each town, one or more other crime categories are rising significantly.



Thefts, robberies, and burglaries are the main crime culprits.

But even serious offences like murder and kidnapping have increased.

Police Precinct % Rise in Drug-Related Crime De Doorns 107% Touws River 53.3% Robertson 46.1% Rawsonville 40.5% Bonnievale 26.1% Montagu 23.1% Ceres 21.7% Worcester 18.4% Ashton 18.4%

The reality of drug-related crime in the Cape Winelands

SAPS views a rise in drug-related crime reporting as positive, since it requires police intervention to be recorded.



However, the rise in other serious and contact crimes suggests otherwise.

In the Cape Winelands, drug-related crime is up 14.5%.

Contact crime is up 11.7%, and other serious crimes, including theft, are up 7.4%.



Crime in only 8 of the 32 categories SAPS reports on has declined.

World.title: The storm safety checklist South Africans should know this weekend
World.content:
Dark storm clouds gather as SAWS issues severe weather warnings for the weekend. Image: Unsplash

With severe thunderstorms and heavy rain forecast in parts of South Africa this weekend, motorists and residents should take precautions before conditions turn dangerous.

Floodwater can rise quickly, cover roads and hide damaged surfaces.

A road that looks passable may become dangerous within minutes.



Here is how to stay safe during the weekend storms

Never drive through floodwater

If you reach a flooded road, turn around and find another route. Do not assume your vehicle can make it through, even if the water looks shallow.

Floodwater can sweep vehicles away, while strong currents may hide potholes, debris or damage to the road.

If your vehicle stalls in rising water, leave it if you can do so safely and move to higher ground.

Do not stay behind to save your car.

Get indoors when thunder approaches



If you hear thunder, move indoors or into a fully enclosed vehicle with the windows closed.

Avoid sheltering under trees, near poles or in open areas. Stay away from rivers, dams and swimming pools during storms.

Protect your home from rising water

People living in low-lying areas should watch for rising water and be ready to move to higher ground.

Keep important documents, medication and a charged mobile phone close at hand.

If authorities advise you to evacuate, leave early rather than waiting for water to reach your home.

Stay away from fallen power lines

Heavy rain and strong winds can bring down trees and power lines.

Do not touch fallen cables or approach them, even if they appear to be inactive.

Keep children away and report the danger to the relevant authorities.

Check warnings before travelling

Check the latest South African Weather Service (SAWS) warnings and road updates before leaving home.

If conditions become dangerous, delay your journey. Keep your phone charged and make sure you know how to contact emergency services.

The safest decision during severe weather is often to stay put and wait for conditions to improve.

World.title: Good news for South Africa’s takeaway and fast food industry
World.content:
One part of South Africa's food industry is doing better than expected. Image: canva

South Africa’s takeaway and fast food businesses are performing better than traditional restaurants, according to new figures from Statistics South Africa.

The latest Food and Beverages report shows that income at takeaway and fast-food outlets increased by 2.2% in real terms in September 2026 compared with the same month last year.

This is in contrast to restaurants and coffee shops, which recorded a 10.2% drop over the same period.



The figures suggest that takeaway businesses are holding up better, while sit-down restaurants are facing a tougher time.

Fast food sales are still growing

Food sales at takeaway and fast food outlets increased by 2.2% in September compared with September 2025.

Income from bar sales also increased by 6.9%, although this makes up a very small part of the takeaway sector.



Overall, takeaway and fast-food outlets recorded a 2.2% increase in real income.

This is a notable difference from restaurants and coffee shops, where food sales fell by 10.4% and bar sales dropped by 10.9%.

Takeaways also performed better over the last three months

The difference between the two sectors can also be seen in the figures for the third quarter of 2026.



From July to September, takeaway and fast-food outlets recorded a 0.3% increase in real income compared with the same period in 2025.

Restaurants and coffee shops, meanwhile, recorded a 1.5% decline.

Catering services performed even better, with real income increasing by 2.7% over the same three months.



When comparing the third quarter with the second quarter of 2026, takeaway income increased by 1.5%. Catering income grew by 1.6%, while restaurant income slipped by 0.2%.

How much money are takeaways and restaurants making?

In rand terms, restaurants and coffee shops still brought in more money than takeaway businesses during the third quarter.

Restaurants recorded income of R13.7 billion between July and September 2026.



Takeaway and fast food outlets brought in R12.6 billion, while catering services recorded R4 billion.

However, takeaway businesses saw stronger growth compared with the same period last year.

Income at takeaway and fast food outlets increased by 8.8% in rand terms, compared with 5.2% for restaurants and coffee shops. These figures are measured before inflation is taken into account.



It’s important to note that while the latest figures show that takeaway businesses are performing better than sit-down restaurants, they do not prove that South Africans are switching from one to the other.

The Stats SA report measures how much money businesses bring in. It does not track individual customers or explain why people choose one type of business over another.

World.title: Level 4 warning: Flooding, hail threaten parts of KZN and Free State
World.content:
A car drives through floodwater as heavy rain threatens parts of KwaZulu-Natal. Image: Unsplash

Severe thunderstorms could bring flooding, hail and damaging winds to parts of KwaZulu-Natal and the Free State on Saturday, 28 November.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has issued a Yellow Level 4 warning for eastern KwaZulu-Natal.

A separate Yellow Level 2 warning covers the Free State and parts of North West.



Yellow Level 4 warning for eastern KwaZulu-Natal

The Yellow Level 4 warning covers parts across parts of eastern KwaZulu-Natal, including areas around Pietermaritzburg, Durban and Richards Bay.

SAWS expects severe thunderstorms that could flood roads, settlements and bridges.

The storms could also produce large amounts of small hail and damaging winds that may damage infrastructure.

Residents should avoid crossing flooded roads and streams and take care when travelling during heavy rain.

Another warning for parts of North West and Free State

The Yellow Level 2 warning covers areas across parts of North West and Free State, including areas around Klerksdorp and Welkom.

SAWS expects severe thunderstorms that could cause localised flooding on susceptible roads, low-lying areas and bridges.



The storms could also bring large amounts of small hail and damaging winds, which may cause localised damage to infrastructure.

People in the affected areas should remain alert, avoid flooded routes and follow weather updates.

World.title: New figures reveal a worrying trend for South African restaurants
World.content:
South Africa’s restaurant industry is facing a difficult period, with new figures showing that restaurants and coffee shops brought in significantly less money in September than they did a year ago.

Statistics South Africa’s latest Food and Beverages report shows that income at restaurants and coffee shops fell by 10.2% in real terms in September 2026 compared with September 2025.

This means that after taking inflation into account, the sector earned less money than it did during the same month last year.



The figures also show that the decline was not limited to food sales.

Restaurant food and drink sales take a knock

Food sales at restaurants and coffee shops fell by 10.4% in September compared with the same month last year.

Bar sales also dropped, falling by 10.9%. Other income, however, increased slightly by 1%.



The figures follow a difficult August, when restaurant income fell by 4.4% compared with August 2025. This is a sharp change from July, when restaurant income increased by 11.2% year-on-year.

The wider food industry is also under pressure

The figures show that restaurants are not the only part of the food industry facing challenges.

Overall, income across the food and beverages industry fell by 3.4% in real terms in September compared with the same month in 2025.



The industry also recorded a 2.3% drop between August and September, after falling by 3.4% between July and August.

Looking at the full third quarter of the year, from July to September, total industry income was down by 0.2% compared with the same period in 2025.

Restaurants and coffee shops recorded a 1.5% decline over the same period.



How much money are restaurants bringing in?

Although restaurant income has fallen after inflation is taken into account, the amount of money businesses brought in was still higher in rand terms.

Across the third quarter of 2026, restaurants and coffee shops recorded income of R13.7 billion. This was 5.2% higher than the R13.1 billion recorded during the same period last year.

Across the entire food and beverages industry, income reached R30.3 billion during the quarter, up 7.2% year-on-year.



However, these figures are measured at current prices and do not take inflation into account.

This means that while businesses may bring in more money in rand terms, they are still earning less once rising prices are considered.

Stats SA’s figures measure business income, not profit. They also do not show how many customers visited restaurants during the month.



The report covers restaurants and coffee shops, takeaway and fast-food outlets, and catering services.

World.title: All Blacks make shock captaincy call for England clash
World.content:
Jordie Barrett (R) will emulate brothers in Beauden (L) and Scott (C) in captaining New Zealand. Image: Adrian DENNIS / AFP

Jordie Barrett will become the third member of his family to captain New Zealand when he leads an under pressure and much-changed All Blacks in their Nations Championship third-place playoff against England on Saturday, 28 November.

Kick-off is at 18:40 (SA time).

READ | FIVE people Rassie Erasmus may have been calling during Springboks ‘watch party’



Heaviest loss

New Zealand coach Dave Rennie’s side return to Twickenham just a week on from their record 37-12 defeat by England – their heaviest loss to any northern hemisphere side – at the same ground.

Inside centre Jordie Barrett, a 29-year-old veteran of 88 Tests, becomes the third Barrett brother to lead the All Blacks, after Scott and Beauden, who are also named in the match-day 23.

Jordie Barrett replaces regular captain Codie Taylor as skipper, the hooker one of several players ruled out through injury.

Rennie has made six changes to his starting side as they look to finish 2026 on a high, with the 2027 Rugby World Cup in Australia less than a year away.

Beauden was captain when New Zealand suffered a shock 35-28 defeat by Wales a fortnight ago – the All Blacks’ first loss to the Welsh in 73 years.

“I think anyone who would have worked with Jordie would know that he’s very impressive, got great game understanding,” coach Rennie told reporters on Thursday.



“He’s been great in our leadership group, and he’s taken over the captaincy role when Codie’s left the field last week and a couple of weeks ago, so it was a pretty straightforward decision for us.”

‘Hurt’

Another defeat would be New Zealand’s third on the trot and take Rennie’s record in his first year as coach to seven wins and six losses – the All Blacks’ worst set of results since 1949.

It would also be the first time that England have won three Tests in a row against New Zealand.

Dave Rennie has now lost five of his 12 Tests as New Zealand coach following a 37-12 Nations Championship defeat by England at Twickenham. Image: Adrian Dennis / AFP

“Last weekend hurt,” said Rennie.

“We own that performance. We’ve been really honest with ourselves about where we fell short.”

He added: “Most of our issues last week were our own undoing …

“Our lineout’s got to be better, the quality of our kicking game’s got to be contestable if we’re doing that, so we can apply pressure. Our skill-set just weren’t clinical enough.

“We made double the amount of errors that England did with half the amount of ball.

“It hasn’t been a lot of time on the grass (training), but we’ve put a lot of time into those key things, and if we get that part of the game right, then we’ll be in the hunt.”

Hooker Asafo Aumua, loose forward Anton Segner, scrumhalf Cortez Ratima, flyhalf Richie Mo’unga, midfielder Leicester Fainga’anuku and wing Rieko Ioane, replacing the injured Will Jordan, come into the starting XV.

Damian McKenzie moves from flyhalf to fullback, with scrumhalf Cam Roigard and fullback Beauden Barrett dropping to the bench.

England coach Steve Borthwick named his side on Wednesday, giving a first Test start to back-row Greg Fisilau and recalling fullback Freddie Steward in two of five changes to his starting side.

Prediction

England to win by 10 points

Teams

England

15 Freddie Steward, 14 Tommy Freeman, 13 Henry Slade, 12 Seb Atkinson, 11 Will Joseph, 10 Fin Smith, 9 Jack van Poortvliet, 8 Ben Earl, 7 Greg Fisilau, 6 Ollie Chessum, 5 Alex Coles, 4 Maro Itoje (captain), 3 Joe Heyes, 2 Luke Cowan-Dickie, 1 Ellis Genge

Replacements: 16 George Bell, 17 Xavier Numia, 18 Pasilio Tosi, 19 Josh Lord, 20 Ethan Blackadder, 21 Cam Roigard, 22 Timoci Tavatavanawai, 23 Beauden Barrett

Assistant referees: Andrea Piardi (Italy), Eoghan Cross (Ireland)
