World.title: Bill 7 Petition: Constitutional Court Rules on Whether Parliament Followed the Constitution
World.content:
The Constitutional Court is set to deliver judgment on Friday in a petition by the LCK Freedom Foundation which contends that the Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025, the law that began in Parliament as Bill 7, was passed in breach of the procedure the Constitution lays down for its own amendment.

The judgment in LCK Freedom Foundation v The Attorney-General, Cause No. 2026/CCZ/006, was set for 09:00 hours in room number two of the Supreme Court of Zambia in Lusaka. The foundation confirmed the date in a public notice it issued in Lusaka on Thursday.

The petition grew out of the way Bill 7 became law. After the Bill was enacted as Act No. 13 of 2025, the LCK Freedom Foundation moved to the Constitutional Court to challenge the validity of the Act, on the grounds that the law was passed contrary to the procedure the Constitution requires for amendments.

The organisation’s challenge does not stop at procedure. It also contends that the Act undermined the basic structure of the Constitution, which places the content of the amendment, and not only the manner of its passage, before the court.

The foundation said its first concern was about ownership of the supreme law. In its notice, it said the case went to the heart of how the Constitution might be changed and who might change it.

That concern was set out in one line.

“The Constitution belongs to the people of Zambia, and any amendment must follow the procedure it prescribes,” the foundation said.

Its second concern is whether Bill 7 met that standard. The LCK Freedom Foundation said the judgment would determine whether the amendment process followed for the Bill complied with the procedure set by the Constitution, the very point on which the petition was filed.

The third concern is the reach of Parliament. The foundation said the ruling would set an important precedent on the limits of the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution, giving lawmakers a clear boundary for any future amendment.

Its fourth concern is the protection of the Constitution’s core principles. By asking the court to find that Act No. 13 of 2025 undermined the basic structure of the Constitution, the petitioner is seeking a ruling on whether some parts of the supreme law can be altered by ordinary amendment at all.

The fifth concern is the place of the public in constitutional change. The foundation said the decision would also settle the right of the people to take part in changes to the Constitution, a point that follows from its position that the document belongs to the people of Zambia.

The Attorney-General is the respondent and defends the State’s position on the process through which Bill 7 became law.

The ruling will therefore answer the question that led to the petition, whether the amendment was lawfully made, while also drawing the line for every future attempt to change the Constitution.

The LCK Freedom Foundation has invited members of the public to attend the delivery of the judgment at the Supreme Court in Lusaka.

World.title: Solwezi DAO encourages Kalumbila residents to form companies
World.content:
Kalumbila District Administrative Officer (DAO) Frank Siatwinda has called on residents of Kakaindu Village to form companies and strategically position themselves to compete for business opportunities and contracts offered by mining companies operating in the area.

Mr Siatwinda says community members should move away from merely complaining about unemployment and instead take advantage of opportunities created by the government through the Local Content Act which prioritises local contractors.

Speaking during a community engagement meeting organised by Transparency International Zambia (TIZ) in Kalumbila District, Mr Siatwinda said residents have the potential to secure contracts by forming companies and becoming innovative.

He said losing employment in the mines should not mark the end of one’s livelihood, as former mine employees can establish businesses and continue working with mining companies as contractors.

Mr Siatwinda also encouraged residents to explore business opportunities beyond the mining sector particularly through local authorities, the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) and Ward Development Funds.

He said community members should be proactive and willing to compete for available opportunities rather than expect things to come easily.

World.title: Lightning kills two pupils
World.content:
Two pupils have died, while 49 others sustained injuries after the roof of a one-by-three classroom block at Mweru Primary School in Nchelenge District was blown off by strong winds during a heavy downpour.

Luapula Province Commanding Officer Lucky Mukondya confirmed the incident to ZANIS, saying it happened at around 13:00 hours yesterday, Thursday 26, 2026.

Ms Mukondya identified the deceased as 11-year-old Grace Chishimba and Catherine Chongo, both of Dyson Village.

She said part of the brick wall supporting the roof also collapsed into the classroom while Grade three pupils were writing their end-of-term examinations.

Ms Mukondya said the 49 injured pupils have since been admitted to St. Paul’s Mission Hospital, where they are receiving medical treatment and are reported to be in stable condition.

She added that the bodies of the two deceased pupils have been deposited at St. Paul’s Mission Hospital Mortuary, awaiting postmortem examinations and subsequent burial arrangements.

World.title: Uganda: 15,000 Young People Acquired HIV in 2023, 80 Percent of Them Girls, Parliament Warns
World.content:
Uganda's ambition to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 could be undermined by inadequate HIV prevention awareness and limited access to services among young people, Parliament's Committee on HIV/AIDS and Related Matters has warned.

The warning follows the committee's assessment of learning institutions in northern Uganda, where it found that many young people aged 15 to 24 still lack adequate knowledge about HIV prevention.

The committee, led by its chairperson, Stephen Kisa, the MP for Luuka South County, said the information gap, coupled with stigma and inadequate prevention services, threatens progress in the fight against HIV.

"Many young people lack adequate knowledge about HIV prevention. If we do not close this information gap now, we risk losing the gains we have made," Kisa warned.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At UNITE Unyama Campus, Dean Pario Lot Ewaku told the committee that HIV prevalence among the institution's approximately 600 students is below five per cent.

The institution works with nearby health facilities, maintains confidentiality and uses trained peer educators to promote HIV awareness.

However, Ewaku identified inadequate funding, deep-rooted stigma and a lack of clear intervention guidelines as persistent challenges.

Stigma also discourages some students from testing and seeking information or services, raising concerns about whether existing interventions are reaching those who need them.

At Gulu University, students and health workers cited staff shortages, inadequate condom supplies and the location of the HIV service unit as barriers to accessing prevention and care.

The concerns point to gaps not only in awareness but also in the availability and accessibility of services within learning institutions.

At Gulu Senior Secondary School, head teacher Irene Mwaka said the school works with partner organisations and student clubs to promote HIV awareness among its more than 3,000 learners.

However, she called for increased funding, noting that the school's day-school arrangement limits its ability to monitor learners beyond school hours.

Student leader Moses Okello said peer-to-peer engagement was essential in encouraging open discussions about HIV/AIDS and breaking the silence surrounding the epidemic.

He also called for continuous teacher training to equip educators to support learners seeking guidance without judgment.

The concerns raised in northern Uganda come against the backdrop of national figures showing that young people continue to account for a significant number of new HIV infections.

Uganda AIDS Commission estimates indicate that approximately 15,000 people aged 15 to 24 acquired HIV in 2023, with adolescent girls and young women accounting for about 80 per cent of infections in this age group.

Close 

Preliminary results from the 2025 Uganda Population-Based HIV Impact Assessment (UPHIA) put HIV prevalence among young people aged 15 to 24 at 1.5 per cent, compared with 2.0 per cent among young women and 1.0 per cent among young men.

The figures highlight the disproportionate burden of HIV among young women and the need to strengthen prevention interventions targeting this population.

Despite the challenges, Kisa said Uganda could still achieve its 2030 target if investment in awareness campaigns and accessible, youth-friendly HIV services is prioritised.

The committee's findings point to the need for learning institutions to strengthen prevention education, improve access to HIV testing and other services, address stigma and equip teachers and peer educators to guide young people.

For Uganda, the challenge is to ensure that the national ambition to end AIDS as a public health threat is matched by practical interventions in the schools and universities where young people spend much of their time.

World.title: Mali: Mali Remains Strategic for Russia Despite Heavy Losses, Investigator Says
World.content:
Russia is unlikely to pull out of Mali despite losing more than 10 percent of its forces there, an investigator who tracks Russian military deployments told RFI. Lou Osbourn co-founded All Eyes On Wagner, a collective of journalists and cybersecurity analysts. She said the losses prove that Russian fighters are taking part in operations alongside Malian troops and that "Africa remains an area of interest for Moscow".

The United Kingdom's The Guardian newspaper - which had access to the leaked records through a media consortium that includes RFI - reported on Tuesday that 349 Russian fighters were killed in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026.

It based its tally on death certificates held by Russia's national statistics agency, Rosstat, but said that the real figure was probably higher because deaths can take time to be registered.

Two hacking groups obtained the records: Cyber Partisans, which is linked to the Belarusian opposition, and Ukraine's Silent Crow. Moscow does not publish its military losses in Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Russian mercenaries from the Wagner group arrived in Mali in late 2021 to support the country's military rulers. In June 2025, Wagner handed over its operations there to the Africa Corps, a unit under Russia's defence ministry.

The Guardian linked most of the 349 deaths to fighting with armed groups. The records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July, 2024, when Tuareg separatists and fighters from JNIM, a group linked to al-Qaeda, ambushed Malian troops and Wagner fighters near Tinzaouaten, close to the border with Algeria.

Another 43 Russians died on 25 April, 2026, when JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front launched coordinated attacks across Mali. General Sadio Camara, Mali's defence minister, was killed in the offensive.

Russian forces withdrew from the northern city of Kidal by the following morning, and Malian troops and the Africa Corps retook it on 6 October.

Osbourn tells RFI why she trusts the leaked figures and what they reveal about Russia's role in Mali.

France rejects 'absurd' Russian claims of direct involvement in Ukraine war

RFI: The leaked records list 349 Russian fighters from Wagner and then the Africa Corps killed in Mali over three years. Is that a significant toll?

Lou Osbourn: Yes, it's quite high. It's more than 10 percent of their force. The deaths also line up with specific events - the battle of Tinzaouaten and the more recent fighting.

RFI: You're talking about the coordinated attacks of 25 April, when several places were hit at once and Mali's defence minister, General Sadio Camara, was killed?

LO: Yes, that's right. It shows they suffered heavy losses. The figures are particularly interesting because the Russian authorities revealed so little about the deaths of Wagner fighters and later Africa Corps fighters. We looked into this ourselves, especially around the time of Tinzaouaten.

RFI: That was in July 2024, when Tuareg separatists and jihadists from JNIM laid an ambush...

LO: Exactly. Even the fighters' families weren't told at the time. There was a blackout on the information. What's interesting about these figures is that they show Russia did record the deaths.

RFI: The leaked figures put the toll at 70. That's also how many the armed groups claimed to have killed at the time.

LO: Yes, absolutely. It was a traumatic experience for Wagner.

RFI: The group's biggest defeat in Africa?

LO: Absolutely, the group's biggest defeat. What's very interesting is that the official records amount to a kind of acknowledgement of the defeat. But that acknowledgement was never made public.

Why Russia remains dependent on medicines made by the West

RFI: These figures come from Rosstat, Russia's national statistics agency, which was hacked by two groups, Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow. Do you have any doubts about how reliable the figures are?

LO: We have few doubts, for two reasons. We know one of the hacking groups and it generally doesn't tamper with the documents it obtains. That gives us some confidence in the source.

The numbers also fit what's happening in the countries concerned. There's been a lot of talk about Mali, but the records list deaths in many African countries. In Niger, for example, there were very few - two, if I remember rightly. Russia's involvement there is very limited. Our estimate was around 200 people.

RFI: Two hundred fighters?

LO: Two hundred Africa Corps fighters. When you compare the number of deaths with what we know about how many fighters are deployed, the figures look realistic and consistent.

RFI: You've said 349 Russian deaths in Mali is a high figure. Does it also show how involved Russia is alongside Malian forces?

LO: Yes. It shows they take part in military operations and that their role goes beyond training.

RFI: Which is something we knew...

LO: We did, but this gives us another concrete piece of evidence. It shows they're operating alongside the Malian army.

RFI: The leak gives no figures for Malian soldiers killed in recent years. If nearly 350 Russian fighters were killed, how many Malian soldiers might have died? Thousands?

LO: I think the toll is probably two or even three times as high. We know there are usually only a handful of Russian fighters embedded in small Malian army units. Sometimes there's one Russian fighter for every five Malian soldiers. So the Malian army's losses are probably much higher than Russia's.

'Working in Russia is like being a deep-sea diver', BBC's man in Moscow tells RFI

Close 

RFI: The hack of Russia's statistics agency revealed that at least 500,000 Russian soldiers were killed on the front in Ukraine between February 2022 and August 2026, or 700,000 if those reported missing are included. Could those losses put Russia's presence in Africa in doubt?

LO: I don't think so. Russia sends far fewer people to Africa and its troop numbers there are fairly stable. In countries where it's establishing a presence, it has only around 100 people. The Africa Corps runs operations in both Africa and Ukraine and rotates its troops.

Africa also matters politically to Russia. It helps Moscow win allies and gives it a way to try to stretch Western military resources in Ukraine and elsewhere. So Africa remains an area of interest for Moscow, and I doubt the release of these figures will lead to a withdrawal.

RFI: After the 25 April attacks in Mali, which killed 43 Russian Africa Corps fighters, Russia seems to be getting even more involved. Despite the cost in lives, the deployment still seems strategically important to Moscow, especially in Mali.

LO: Mali remains strategic because Russia uses it as a base for some of its activities. It was from Mali that Russian forces went into Burkina Faso and Niger. Resources are also at stake, and Mali matters to Russia politically.

For a year now, we've heard every three months that Russia is going to pull out. It's still there, and I find it hard to see why it would leave now. I don't think it will.

This interview was adapted from the original audio in French by David Baché.

World.title: Southern Africa: Crowded Waters - Can Southern Africa Steer Mozambique Channel Security?
World.content:
analysis

Rising international interest and insurgent activity at sea should push regional states to reassess their maritime commitments and capabilities.

Visits to Mozambique and Madagascar in November by Lieutenant General John Brennan, Deputy Commander of United States (US) Africa Command (AFRICOM), underscore the Mozambique Channel's growing strategic weight.

Alongside the channel's significance as a global commercial shipping route, AFRICOM highlighted Islamic State Mozambique's (ISM) developing maritime capabilities and the security of Cabo Delgado's multibillion-dollar onshore and offshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) investments.

The US and Madagascar then signed an Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement facilitating logistical cooperation in maritime patrols, military exercises and humanitarian operations. The agreement comes amid US concerns about Madagascar's deepening military ties with Russia.



These developments coincide with disruptions to Middle Eastern energy exports caused by the US-Iran war, which reinforce the strategic significance of Southern Africa's offshore energy projects. Continued disruptions to global shipping also underline the importance of alternative routes around Southern Africa, including the Cape of Good Hope and the Mozambique Channel.

They also follow October's inaugural South Africa-European Union (EU) Peace, Security and Defence Dialogue, after which Cosmin Dobran, Director for Peace, Partnerships and Crisis Management at the European External Action Service, advocated greater Southern African Development Community (SADC) involvement in securing the channel.

US encouragement for Mozambique to join regional maritime information-sharing arrangements, together with proposals for expanded military exercises and bilateral training, signals a greater emphasis on operational cooperation. The US is not alone. This month, an Indian Coast Guard vessel visited Maputo to conduct joint training and deliver naval spare parts. In March, India's Navy conducted joint surveillance of Mozambique's exclusive economic zone.

The channel's maritime security was also a focus of the recent 13th France-South Africa Strategic Defence Dialogue. France's longstanding military and commercial interests in the channel are entangled with unresolved sovereignty disputes with Madagascar over the Îles Éparses and with Comoros over Mayotte, which complicate regional maritime surveillance and operational cooperation.

The maritime dimension of the Cabo Delgado insurgency has intensified this year. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data analysis identifies 34 potentially maritime-related events involving ISM by mid-November, compared with 29 in 2025, 30 in 2024 and 20 in 2023. These include vessel seizures, abductions of fishers and sailors, extortion of coastal communities and clashes with naval forces.

Several incidents demonstrate the insurgents' ability to operate in coastal waters and occasionally target larger vessels, such as the May 2025 attack on the Russian research vessel Atlantida off Cabo Delgado.

In April, ISM intercepted a Tanzanian fishing vessel off Cabo Delgado, seizing its cargo and demanding a ransom before allowing it to continue to Tanzania. In May, insurgents reportedly seized at least 12 boats off Mocímboa da Praia and Macomia.

This expanding maritime activity poses rising security risks to commercial vessels operating in or transiting northern Mozambican waters.

The growing concentration of offshore energy infrastructure warrants careful consideration. In November, Italian energy company Eni began drilling for its second floating LNG project, Coral North, and expects to reach a final investment decision on a third floating LNG facility by 2027.

TotalEnergies resumed onshore and offshore construction of its US$20 billion Mozambique LNG project in January, and Mozambique's government has approved the revised development plan for the US$26 billion ExxonMobil-led Rovuma LNG project.

Locating floating production facilities roughly 50 km offshore may afford some protection from the insurgency, but distance alone no longer guarantees the security it once seemed to offer. Persistent maritime criminality, including drug trafficking networks operating between Mozambique and the Makran coast of Iran and Pakistan, and the wider proliferation of cheap drones and uncrewed vessels add to the risks.

Threats to commercial operations, and even unsuccessful attacks, would have disproportionate consequences for investor confidence and continued operations. The March 2021 Palma attack prompted the TotalEnergies-led Mozambique LNG consortium to declare force majeure, which was lifted only in 2025.

Nor should maritime insecurity and criminality in the northern Mozambique Channel be viewed solely through the prism of the insurgency. Cabo Delgado was a hotspot for transnational illicit trade long before the conflict began in 2017. Maritime trafficking networks that benefit from poorly monitored coastlines and weak oversight would continue to pose serious challenges even if the insurgency were resolved.

Protecting commercial investments must also not come at the expense of coastal communities. Fishers in northern Mozambique have experienced violence by both insurgents and security forces. Securing offshore energy developments and international shipping does not necessarily address the wider maritime insecurity these communities face.

The US and other international partners are tackling maritime security challenges in the same area where South Africa established counter-piracy patrols under Operation Copper in 2011. In 2012, the operation was formalised as a framework for trilateral maritime security cooperation between South Africa, Mozambique and Tanzania.

Successive South African presidential authorisations for Operation Copper have linked the deployment to implementing SADC's Integrated Maritime Security Strategy (IMSS).

The increasingly complex threat environment, expanding commercial interests and the growing involvement of international security actors should prompt a public review of Operation Copper, and of whether it genuinely contributes to implementing the IMSS. No long-range maritime patrols have been conducted under Operation Copper for four consecutive financial years, owing to the unavailability of South African naval vessels.

Southern Africa increasingly faces the problem of coordinating several overlapping mechanisms, which makes such a review essential. These include SADC's IMSS and its Standing Maritime Committee, as well as the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment. This month, the Code's signatory states adopted a regional maritime security strategy and agreed to move towards establishing a combined maritime task force.

Close 

Two SADC member states, Tanzania and South Africa, will be chair and deputy chair respectively. This gives both countries an opportunity to shape wider regional maritime security cooperation and promote greater alignment with SADC's maritime security priorities.

Regional states have also leveraged EU financial and technical support to establish the Regional Maritime Security Architecture. Madagascar hosts the Regional Maritime Information Fusion Centre, which works with Seychelles' Regional Coordination Operations Centre to facilitate information sharing and coordinated responses to maritime threats.

International interest in the Mozambique Channel has long presented opportunities for geopolitically minded countries. However, the current proliferation of security initiatives makes coordination essential.

At next year's SADC Standing Maritime Committee meeting, member states should assess how their maritime security commitments and activities can better complement existing Western Indian Ocean arrangements, and ensure that international assistance supports collectively identified regional priorities.

States that cannot implement their maritime security commitments risk having their priorities determined by those that can. As international recognition of the Mozambique Channel's strategic significance grows, Southern African countries must actively shape and deliver maritime security cooperation in their own backyard.

Timothy Walker, Consultant, ISS Pretoria

World.title: Eritrea: Eritrea Accuses Ethiopia of Using Maritime Diplomacy to 'Camouflage Its Irredentist Ambitions'
World.content:
Addis Abeba — Eritrea has accused Ethiopia of using maritime diplomacy and regional security forums to mask what it described as territorial ambitions in the Horn of Africa, escalating tensions amid renewed disagreements over Ethiopia's pursuit of Red Sea access.

In a statement issued Thursday, Eritrea's Ministry of Foreign Affairs accused the Prosperity Party government of seeking to "manufacture a veneer of international legitimacy" around its demand for "sovereign sea access," which Asmara characterized as territorial revisionism.

The statement follows Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's address to the House of Peoples' Representatives on Thursday, November 26, in which he rejected claims that Ethiopia intends to invade Eritrea, but reiterated that access to the Red Sea remains a strategic imperative to be pursued through dialogue.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Now they say, 'Ethiopia is going to invade Eritrea, Ethiopia will wage an invasion for the Red Sea'--we will not wage an invasion. Invasion is not needed; we want it peacefully and through dialogue," Abiy told lawmakers, likening Ethiopia's maritime ambitions to the natural course of the Abay River.

Abiy claimed Ethiopia had made repeated efforts to pursue economic cooperation with Eritrea, including proposals to extend electricity infrastructure, build roads and jointly develop a port, but said the Eritrean government had rejected them.

"We have made high efforts with the Eritrean government to develop together," he said, citing a proposal to supply electricity at Ethiopian domestic prices and jointly undertake infrastructure projects.

He also said Ethiopia had undergone a "strategic awakening" after its political elite failed to properly recognize the country's Red Sea interests, arguing that neighboring countries should recognize the long-term strategic implications of the issue.

Abiy further warned that Ethiopia's size and population meant instability within the country would have far-reaching regional consequences, cautioning against scenarios involving millions of Ethiopians moving into neighboring states.

"Because we are a large population; our disturbance disturbs many," he said, arguing that Ethiopia's stability was central to wider regional peace.

He also pointed to shifting geopolitical dynamics, including the potential opening of Arctic shipping routes, arguing that these could alter the Red Sea's strategic importance in the coming years.

Eritrea, however, said Ethiopia's maritime diplomacy was increasingly being used to normalize the involvement of a landlocked country in Red Sea security arrangements. It cited a late-October maritime security and search-and-rescue workshop in Addis Abeba, supported by the European Union.

The workshop brought together naval representatives from Puntland and Somaliland alongside representatives from Djibouti. Asmara argued that including Somali regional administrations while bypassing the Federal Government of Somalia undermined the sovereignty of a recognized coastal state.

Eritrea also cited the Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa, held in Bahir Dar from October 23-25, where National Intelligence and Security Service Director General Redwan Hussein argued that Ethiopia should have a role in Red Sea security arrangements given the waterway's strategic importance and growing involvement of global powers.

Redwan maintained that Red Sea security was not a responsibility reserved exclusively for coastal states, a position Eritrea said reflected Addis Abeba's efforts to expand its role in regional maritime affairs.

The Eritrean statement further cited Field Marshal Birhanu Jula's November 13 remarks in Mekele, in which he reportedly asserted that Dogali, Gundet and Adulis belonged to Tigray and made claims concerning Somalia's port of Zeila. Asmara described the remarks as part of a broader territorial narrative advanced by Ethiopian political and military officials.

It warned that repeated territorial assertions by senior officials, alongside threats to secure maritime access through force, challenged regional sovereignty and internationally recognized borders. The statement invoked Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of states.

Close 

Asmara also rejected Ethiopia's maritime rationale, arguing that landlocked countries are entitled to access the sea through negotiated commercial arrangements but have no unilateral right to ports, naval deployments or arrangements that compromise the sovereignty of coastal states.

Eritrea claimed it had previously offered Ethiopia access to the ports of Assab and Massawa, including proposals in 2000 and 2002 to facilitate humanitarian assistance, which it said Addis Abeba rejected. It also accused Ethiopia of squandering opportunities for cooperation following the 2018 peace declaration between the two countries.

The statement reiterated a position shared by Egypt, Somalia and Sudan that Red Sea security and governance should remain the responsibility of littoral states, citing the October 4 El Alamein Joint Declaration, which reaffirmed freedom of navigation while emphasizing coastal states' role in Red Sea governance.

World.title: Ghana: Why Ghana Is Moving to Protect Its Traditional Palm Spirit and What It Could Mean for Producers, Consumers and the Country's Global Reputation
World.content:
opinion

GHANA is on the verge of doing for Apio what Scotland did for Scotch Whisky and what France did for Cognac. Across the world, some of the most successful products are not simply commodities. They are products whose value is inseparable from the places, traditions and communities that produce them.

The country's traditional palm-based spirit, distilled exclusively from fermented palm sap, is deeply rooted in local knowledge, rural livelihoods and cultural identity. Through the development of a Geographical Indication (GI), Ghana now has an opportunity not only to preserve this heritage but also to transform it into a source of long-term economic value.

A geographical indication identifies products whose qualities, reputation or characteristics are linked to a specific place of origin. Around the world, GI protection has helped transform local products into globally recognised brands while protecting producers from imitation and misuse.

Why the examples of Cognac and Scotch Whisky matter

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Related Articles

According to BNIC industry figures, Cognac generated approximately €2.22 billion in export sales from 143.6 million bottles sold in nearly 139 countries during 2025, supporting around 14,500 direct jobs and 72,500 livelihoods. Likewise, Scotch Whisky exports were worth approximately £5.3 billion in 2025, with 1.34 billion bottles exported to more than 160 global markets. These figures illustrate that the value of protected spirits comes from authenticity, origin, quality standards and reputation built over generations.

Ghana's palm heritage

For generations, palm trees have supported livelihoods through palm wine tapping, palm oil production, food processing, medicines, construction materials and trade. Palm wine tapping remains one of Ghana's oldest traditional occupations.

What producers stand to gain

A stronger identity for authentic palm-derived Apio could create more stable demand for palm sap, improve market opportunities for traditional distillers and encourage younger generations to remain engaged in a centuries-old occupation.

A strategic opportunity for Ghana

In 2025, Champagne generated approximately €5.7 billion in sales, Cognac generated €2.22 billion in exports, and Scotch Whisky exports exceeded £5.3 billion globally. While Apio will not achieve similar values overnight, these examples demonstrate the long-term economic potential that can emerge when authenticity, reputation and origin are protected.

Close 

A defining opportunity for Ghana

There are only a handful of products that become ambassadors for their countries. Cognac is inseparable from France. Scotch Whisky is inseparable from Scotland. Tequila is inseparable from Mexico. Ghana now has an opportunity to place Apio among that distinguished group of origin-linked products.

That is why Ghana is moving to protect Apio. Not simply to safeguard a traditional spirit, but to unlock the economic potential of one of the country's most distinctive cultural assets and lay the foundation for a future in which Apio stands proudly alongside the world's most respected protected spirits.

Conclusion

Protecting Apio as a Geographical Indication is not merely a legal exercise. It is an investment in Ghana's culture, economy and future competitiveness. The success of Champagne, Bordeaux, Scotch Whisky and Tequila demonstrates the power of geographical indications to transform local products into internationally respected brands. Ghana now has an opportunity to build a similar success story around Apio.

By protecting authentic palm-derived Apio and ensuring that the benefits reach palm wine tappers, distillers and rural communities, Ghana can create a model of inclusive development rooted in its own traditions and resources. Ultimately, this is not only about protecting a spirit, but also about protecting a heritage, a livelihood and a uniquely Ghanaian story.

The writer is an International Consultant and Head of Geographical Indications, Ghana Industrial Property Office, Accra.

World.title: Kenya: Nairobi Airspace to Close Temporarily
World.content:
Nairobi — Nairobi's airspace will be temporarily closed on three dates between November and December to facilitate scheduled national military activities.

The temporary restrictions will affect flights on November 27, December 4 and December 12, with authorities advising travellers to anticipate possible changes to flight schedules.

According to a notice issued by Kenya Airways, the first closure will take effect on Friday, November 27, between 12:00hrs and 13:20hrs.

The subsequent closures are scheduled for December 4 and December 12, running from 10:30hrs to 12:30hrs on both dates.

The national carrier cautioned that some flights may experience schedule adjustments during the affected periods.

Passengers travelling on the three dates have been advised to check their flight status through the Kenya Airways website or mobile application before heading to the airport.

Kenya Airways said it was coordinating with the relevant authorities to minimise disruptions and would communicate directly with passengers whose flights are affected.

The temporary airspace restrictions are linked to scheduled national military activities, although further details of the exercises were not provided in the notice.

Travellers have been urged to monitor airline updates and confirm their departure times to avoid inconveniences.

World.title: Kenya: No, Photo of Kenyan Senator Tabitha Karanja and Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua With Bundles of Cash Is Doctored
World.content:
No, photo of Kenyan senator Tabitha Karanja and former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua with bundles of cash is doctored

IN SHORT: A photo circulating on Facebook appears to show the two politicians with an open bag full of cash between them. But the original photo, posted by DCP TV, shows no bag or money.

An image posted on Facebook supposedly shows Kenyan senator Tabitha Karanja in conversation with former deputy president Rigathi Gachagua, with an open bag containing bundles of cash on a table in front of them.



The accompanying caption reads: "Gachagua is a business man with his briefcase party DCP according to him Tabitha Karanja is now a gitungati, but Hon. Gathoni Wamuchomba HSC, MP who defended him during his impeachment is a mole. Mkora sana."

"Gitungati" is a Gikuyu language term for a dedicated servant or patriot. The Agikuyu are an ethnic community native to central Kenya.

The Kiswahili phrase "Mkora sana" translates to "what a crook".

Gachagua was Kenya's deputy president from 2022 until his impeachment and removal from office in October 2024. He later founded the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), which he leads.

Karanja, who was elected senator in 2022 on a United Democratic Alliance (UDA) ticket, had voted in favour of some of the charges against Gachagua during his impeachment.

But on 9 October 2026, she announced that she had left UDA for Gachagua's DCP and would contest the Nakuru governorship in the 2027 general election.

In contrast, Githunguri MP Gathoni Wamuchomba, who defended Gachagua during his impeachment, later fell out with him amid accusations that she was a state "mole". In November 2026, she appealed for reconciliation.

This image has also been posted here, here and here. But is the photo genuine? We checked.

Doctored photo

A Google reverse image search revealed that the circulating image had been doctored.

We found the original photograph on DCP TV's official X account. The caption reads: "Incoming Nakuru Governor Tabitha Karanja Meets DCP Party Leader Rigathi Gachagua. Welcome to DCP Mama Keroche."

Unlike the circulating version, the original image does not show an open bag of cash in front of the two politicians.

The bag and cash have been digitally added to the version circulating on Facebook.

World.title: Nigeria: 2027 Politics Watch - From Delta Aide's Resignation Over Killings to INEC's Nine-States Hit By Political Attacks
World.content:
An aide to the Delta governor resigned over campaign killings as INEC named nine states affected by political attacks. Seyi Makinde's campaign denied plans to withdraw for Atiku Abubakar, who challenged the APC's claims on housing delivery and job creation.

The political fallout from Monday's deadly political violence in Delta State widened with the resignation of Tonia Gbemre, an aide to Governor Sheriff Oborevwori, as the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) identified nine states where political attacks have occurred since open campaigns began in August.

While National Security Adviser Nuhu Ribadu pledged impartial protection for political actors and voters, efforts to build a common opposition front faced a fresh test as Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde's campaign denied plans to withdraw in favour of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar. The former vice president also challenged the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) over its claims on housing delivery and job creation.

Delta governor's aide resigns as INEC names nine states hit by political attack

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Ms Gbemre, a senior special assistant to Mr Oborevwori, resigned over the killings in Uduere community, Ughelli North Local Government Area, and what she described as persistent intimidation of opposition supporters.

In a resignation statement shared on Facebook and reported by PREMIUM TIMES on Thursday, she accused the administration of failing to adequately protect citizens.

"I am a mother. I cannot continue to watch our children being killed just because of politics," she said.

She urged the governor to caution local government chairpersons, political leaders and community stakeholders against actions capable of restricting opposition campaigns.

Mr Oborevwori had visited the affected community and directed security agencies to apprehend those responsible. No response from his administration to Ms Gbemre's specific allegations was available for this roundup.

The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) also called for an investigation and prosecution of the perpetrators, following the House of Representatives' intervention detailed in Wednesday's Politics Watch.

In neighbouring Edo State, Governor Monday Okpebholo on Thursday denied allegations linking him, the APC or its supporters to Wednesday's attack on members of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Benin City.

Speaking at an APC campaign rally, the governor suggested that the violence resulted from a confrontation among opposition supporters, an account the police have not established.

Against the backdrop of these attacks, INEC Chairman Joash Amupitan told the Strategic Election Security Conference in Abuja on Thursday that political attacks had occurred in Lagos, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Ebonyi, Delta, Cross River, Oyo and Benue.

He warned that insecurity could discourage voter participation, endanger electoral personnel and undermine acceptance of election results.

Mr Amupitan also questioned a provision in the electoral guidelines requiring security personnel to act on the instructions of presiding officers or other INEC officials when arresting electoral offenders.

Mr Ribadu, speaking at the same conference, pledged that security agencies would remain neutral and protect voters, candidates and electoral personnel before, during and after the elections.

"Security agencies will discharge their responsibilities impartially and in accordance with the law," he said, according to Vanguard.

The reported remarks of the INEC chairman did not

present a comprehensive incident count or a breakdown of arrests and prosecutions across the states he identified.

Makinde's campaign denies withdrawal plan as opposition consultations continue

The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation on Thursday night dismissed reports that its presidential candidate was negotiating to withdraw from the 2027 race in favour of Atiku, according to Nigerian Tribune and The Nation.

The organisation insisted that Mr Makinde remained committed to pursuing the presidency on the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) under his RESET Nigeria agenda.

The denial followed remarks by the governor in an interview with media personality Chude Jideonwo, in which he expressed confidence that he, Atiku and the NDC's Peter Obi would reach an arrangement to challenge President Bola Tinubu.

Mr Makinde distinguished the proposed arrangement from the merger of opposition parties that produced the APC ahead of the 2015 presidential election. He did not disclose how the arrangement would work or identify which contender, if any, would relinquish their presidential ambition.

Thursday's statement rejected the specific claim of a withdrawal in Atiku's favour without necessarily ruling out other forms of opposition cooperation.

Atiku continues to campaign under the African Democratic Congress (ADC), although the 5 November Federal High Court judgement nullifying his presidential candidacy is under appeal, with the party also applying for a stay of execution. No order granting the stay had been confirmed as of Wednesday evening.

Meanwhile, the Coalition for Democracy reaffirmed plans to hold its second summit in Abuja on Monday, 30 November.

In a statement issued on behalf of the coalition by Salihu Lukman, the parties said consultations would continue despite their decision to suspend campaign activities on the day of the summit.

The coalition intends to adopt three documents: the National Covenant for Democratic Renewal, the Framework for Opposition Unity and the National Reform Programme. An agreed mechanism for selecting a common presidential candidate has yet to be publicly announced.

As PREMIUM TIMES examined in its latest State of the Race, the expiry of the ordinary statutory deadline for voluntary withdrawal and substitution of presidential candidates complicates the opposition's options. An agreement to support one contender would not automatically remove the others from the ballot.

The ruling party is also confronting disagreements over its campaign arrangements.

The Imo State chapter of the APC on Thursday rejected an offer by Federal Capital Territory Minister Nyesom Wike to help coordinate Mr Tinubu's re-election campaign in the state.

Mr Wike had on Wednesday requested additional campaign responsibilities in Imo and Kwara states. The Imo APC maintained that its existing leadership was capable of conducting the campaign.

In Kaduna, Governor Uba Sani urged northern political leaders to support Mr Tinubu's re-election and develop a governance blueprint ahead of a northern bid for the presidency in 2031.

The president's Chief of Staff, Femi Gbajabiamila, also led a delegation to former military rulers Ibrahim Babangida and Abdulsalami Abubakar in Minna, Niger State.

Mr Gbajabiamila told journalists that Mr Babangida reaffirmed his support for Mr Tinubu, while Mr Abubakar, chairman of the National Peace Committee, appealed for peaceful elections.

Atiku challenges APC's housing and employment claims

The APC Presidential Campaign Council on Thursday said the Tinubu administration had facilitated the financing and delivery of more than 26,000 housing units and generated 525,100 jobs in the real estate and construction sectors over the past three years.

The council's spokesperson, Dele Alake, said the Ministry of Finance Incorporated's real estate investment fund had provided more than â¦158 billion in mortgage financing to 2,269 homebuyers as of 31 October.

He said beneficiaries could access mortgages at an annual interest rate of 9.75 per cent, with repayment periods of up to 20 years.

Atiku challenged the APC's claims, arguing that rising energy and manufacturing costs were making housing increasingly unaffordable.

In a statement issued on Thursday by his Director of Strategic Communication, Phrank Shaibu, the former vice president cited reports that 11 listed manufacturers spent approximately â¦842 billion on energy between January and September 2026.

A PUNCH analysis of the companies' unaudited financial statements put their combined expenditure at â¦841.99 billion, a 7.4 per cent increase from â¦784.08 billion recorded in the corresponding period of 2025.

According to the same PUNCH analysis, Dangote Cement and BUA Cement accounted for â¦797.44 billion, or 94.7 per cent, of that expenditure, which includes the cost of electricity, diesel, petrol and gas.

The concentration in two cement producers limits the conclusions that can be drawn about manufacturing businesses generally.

Atiku questioned the inclusion of unfinished and inherited projects in the government's housing figures and demanded evidence supporting the number of jobs attributed to its interventions.

"A building site is not a completed home. An inherited project is not proof of fresh delivery. A mortgage approval is not a house key," he said.

The APC's statement says 10,328 housing units under the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development are at various stages of completion. It also distinguishes between units financed and those delivered through the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria, while describing some employment opportunities as estimates.

PREMIUM TIMES' review of Federal Housing Authority records shows that the 337-unit Bwari housing project listed by the APC commenced in March 2022, during the administration of former President Muhammadu Buhari.

The records also show that the FHA's Apo/Guzape estate, where the APC lists 1,200 housing units, was already under development when the then Minister of State for Works and Housing, Umar Ibrahim El-Yakubu, inspected the site on 16 November 2022.

Although both developments predate the Tinubu administration, the extent of construction undertaken under each administration remains unverified.

Atiku proposed improving electricity supply to industries and introducing a transparent, targeted subsidy for domestically refined fuel to reduce production costs.

His statement did not quantify the proposed subsidy's fiscal cost or specify an implementation timetable.

A subsequent APC response addressing his specific objections was unavailable for this roundup.

The competing claims leave unresolved questions about how many housing units have been completed and occupied, their affordability to intended beneficiaries, and how many of the reported jobs represent actual employment rather than projections.

Kano judicial controversy and fresh nomination disputes

The Kano State APC Presidential and Gubernatorial Campaign Council has opposed a petition requesting a National Judicial Council (NJC) investigation into the circumstances surrounding the January 2024 Supreme Court judgement affirming Governor Abba Yusuf's election.

The petition, dated 24 November, was submitted by Suleiman Malali on behalf of a group called Concerned Nigerian Citizens.

The council argued that the petition misrepresented the governor's account of his discussions with Mr Tinubu before the judgement, a controversy that had earlier prompted the ADC to demand the president's resignation or impeachment.

Close 

No finding of judicial misconduct or decision by the NJC on the petition was available.

In Jigawa State, the Federal High Court in Dutse ordered the reinstatement of ADC primary election winners in seven legislative constituencies, according to reports by Daily Post and Nigerian Tribune on Thursday.

The outlets reported that Justice Muhammad Ibrahim Buba held that the substitution of the affected candidates was unlawful and directed the party and INEC to recognise the original primary winners.

PREMIUM TIMES has not independently examined the judgement.

The ruling concerns specific legislative nominations and does not resolve the separate litigation over the ADC's national leadership and presidential nomination, detailed in Wednesday's Politics Watch.

In Bauchi State, the Young Progressives Party (YPP) challenged the eligibility of APC deputy governorship candidate Farouk Mustapha at the Federal High Court in Abuja.

The YPP alleged that Mr Mustapha did not satisfy applicable party membership requirements before the APC's governorship primary.

The allegations remain to be determined by the court. No judgement disqualifying Mr Mustapha or response from the defendants was available for this roundup.

INEC's Monday audit deadline puts Saturday's mock accreditation under scrutiny

By Monday, 30 November, resident electoral commissioners are expected to submit comprehensive technical audit reports on Saturday's nationwide mock accreditation and result-upload exercise.

Mr Amupitan issued the directive during Wednesday's meeting with resident electoral commissioners, with further details reported by PUNCH on Thursday.

The exercise will test the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and automated safeguards intended to detect inconsistencies in polling-unit results before they are uploaded to the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV). The sample ballot papers will not carry the names of registered political parties.

INEC previously announced that 17,676 polling units would participate in the exercise, scheduled for 8:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. on Saturday. The commission has published the list of participating polling units.

Saturday's simulation is not an election and cannot, by itself, establish the reliability of the entire electoral process.

The Monday deadline provides a specific accountability benchmark ahead of the 16 January presidential election: whether INEC will publish the audit findings, disclose the operational failures encountered and explain how it intends to correct them before voters go to the polls.

A LOOK AT HOW THE TRUMPS SPEND THEIR THANKSGIVING HOLIDAY THROUGH THE YEARS

TRUMP SAYS AIR FORCE PILOTS DESCRIBED A ROUND UFO FLYING THREE TIMES FASTER THAN AN F-22 FIGHTER JET

CENTCOM'S THANKSGIVING MESSAGE TO TROOPS 'IS ONE OF DEEP GRATITUDE' FOR THEIR 'EXCEPTIONAL WORK' PROTECTING US

TRUMP PAUSES TURKEY PARDON TO SALUTE US TROOPS GUARDING STRAIT OF HORMUZ: 'WATCH OVER AND PROTECT'

"And you're seeing some big victories, aren't you? Knocking them out left and right, knocking out the launchers, knocking out the missiles, knocking out left and right. Amazing job you're doing, Brant," Trump said.

US RACES TO BUILD BUNKERS ACROSS MIDDLE EAST AS IRANIAN STRIKES THREATEN AMERICAN TROOPS

"In my opinion, they're not very smart. They're making big mistakes. They've made a lot of mistakes. Their economy is down the tubes," the president said of Iran.

"Every day the stellar F-16 squadron is conducting missions across the Middle East to defend our interests and our assets. Like few people could ever even think about. World.content:
Thursday delivered us quite possibly the greatest slate of Thanksgiving football games of all time, and it ended with a bang.

Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills stunned the Kansas City Chiefs at the buzzer, 13-10, thanks in large part to a blocked punt in the waning seconds. The Bills deflected the kick, it was returned by Greg Dortch to Kansas City's 39, and Tyler Bass drilled the long field goal to walk it off.

It was the perfect day of football — including two stunning comebacks in Detroit and Dallas. Again, I'd argue it was the greatest Thanksgiving slate ever.

BUFFALO BILLS OUTLAST KANSAS CITY CHIEFS IN DEFENSIVE STRUGGLE TO MAINTAIN TOP SEED STATUS IN AFC

Of course — because we can't have nice things — it didn't come without some controversy at the end. In another stunning turn of events, this one actually worked against the Chiefs!

Incredible. Again, seeing a call go against the Chiefs was shocking. You just don't see it. You haven't seen it during the Mahomes era. Not saying I agree with the call, by the way, because I'm not sure I do.

World.title: Treasure hunters searching a field uncover 5,500-coin hoard hiding 'national treasure'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Archaeologists in Norway have uncovered an extraordinarily rare 1,000-year-old coin minted during the reign of Viking King Olaf Haraldsson, better known as Saint Olaf, inside the largest Viking Age coin hoard ever found in the country.

The discovery, announced by the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo, marks the first time a coin of this type has been found in Norway since 1924.

The Olaf coin went on display Nov. 20 at the Historical Museum in Oslo — part of the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History — as part of a new exhibition showcasing the Mørstad Hoard.

PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE

The hoard was originally discovered on April 10 by metal detectorists Vegard Sørlie and Rune Sætre in Rena, Innlandet County, and the site has since been secured and investigated for further research.

Officials said the latest count puts the cache at 5,500 coins, though researchers believe the total could soon exceed 6,000.

The star of the hoard, officials said, is a coin depicting Haraldsson, who ruled from 1015 to 1028.

Haraldsson, who became a saint after his death, occupies "a unique place in Norwegian history," officials said.

RARE COIN BEARING FACE OF KING WITH INFAMOUS NICKNAME UNEARTHED AFTER 1,000 YEARS

"Fewer than 20 of his coins have survived to the present day, and most have been found outside Norway," the release said.

"Only four examples of the type found in the Mørstad Hoard have previously been discovered, including just one in Norway."

The new coin was spotted by archaeologist Anne Skogsfjord, who immediately ran to tell a colleague about the find.

Officials said the coin was initially thought to be Anglo-Saxon and had been roughly sorted into the group of coins issued by Æthelred II.

MYSTERIOUS FIND BENEATH FIELD LEADS MAN TO MASSIVE TREASURE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES

"I could see that it read ONLAF R+ NORMANORV … Could this really be a coin of Olaf Haraldsson that I was holding?" Skogsfjord said. "And it was! It was a very special moment."

She added, "I realized that we had found a national treasure."

"When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge."

The coin dates between 1024 and 1028, and officials said it may have been in circulation for up to 25 years before it was deposited in the hoard.

Featuring a cross on both sides, the coin shows how Olaf used currency to legitimize the Christian faith and establish himself as a Christian king of European standing, according to numismatics expert Svein H. Gullbekk.

CLICK HERE TO 

The museum added, "Few archaeological and historical sources can be directly linked to Olaf Haraldsson himself. Numismatic sources — the coins — were closely connected to the king."

Gullbekk said in the release, "Olaf Haraldsson himself decided what these coins should look like, and perhaps he was present when they were struck. It is entirely possible that this very coin from Mørstad was once held in the king's own hand."

Hanna Geiran, Norway's director general of cultural heritage, said the coin "is not only a rare object, but also tangible testimony from a time when the foundations of the Norwegian kingdom and the Christianization of the country were laid."

"When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge," said Geiran, the museum noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"This St. Olaf coin is yet another reminder of how extraordinary this find is."

Looking ahead, the museum said that research on the coin hoard will continue "for a long time to come."

"Every single coin must undergo the same thorough process before entering the museum collection," added officials. "Numismatists, archaeologists, conservators, collection managers and photographers are all involved."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The Mørstad Hoard joins several other significant European coin discoveries unearthed in recent months.

Earlier this year, archaeologists in Germany uncovered 11 ancient Celtic coins at a construction site — the largest hoard of its kind ever found in the region, dating back more than 2,000 years.

World.title: Josh Holloway reveals Kevin Costner's high standards on the Yellowstone set before his exit
World.content:
Josh Holloway is pulling back the curtain on what life was like on the set of "Yellowstone."

The neo-Western series created by Taylor Sheridan dominated TV for all five of its seasons. The success of Sheridan's crowning achievement also led to multiple prequels and spinoffs.

The "Yellowstone" universe is a powerhouse, and Holloway played a major role. He starred as villain Roarke Morris in season three of the series, and very briefly appeared in season four.

LUKE GRIMES SAYS HE HASN'T SPOKEN TO KEVIN COSTNER SINCE 'YELLOWSTONE'

Josh Holloway reveals what Kevin Costner was like on the "Yellowstone" set.

Now, he's shining a light on what Kevin Costner was like on set, and the high standards and work ethic the legendary actor brought to the series.

Holloway recently appeared on the "Inside of You" podcast hosted by Michael Rosenbaum, and explained that Costner wasn't afraid to call himself out on set when he didn't perform at a high level.

ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN GIVES STARS TWO CHOICES: 'MAKE SURE THAT YOU DON'T F--K UP... OR YOU QUIT'

"What I was impressed with with him, he did a close-up with me where he’s telling me about the rules or something, and he did it, and he just went inside and he was like, ‘Ah, that sh*t was lazy.’ And then he came up and I was like, ‘He cares. He’s still working.’ And he brought it. He's in this. So, I was impressed with that. You know, that he’s still keeping his standard high. I respected that. I was like, ‘Hell yeah,'" Holloway explained.

You can watch Holloway's comments in the video below starting around 1:05:00, and let me know your thoughts at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

'YELLOWSTONE' STAR NEAL MCDONOUGH REFUSES TO WATCH HIT SERIES FOR ‘PAINFUL’ REASON

It's worth noting that while Costner might have held himself to extremely high standards on set, his time on "Yellowstone" didn't end in great fashion.



Costner infamously split from the show during the mid-season split in season five, and never returned to ever play John Dutton again.

His exit, which led to plenty of reports of feuds behind the scenes, resulted in the final "Yellowstone" episodes feeling a bit rushed and an ending that never truly felt complete.

Don't get me wrong. The conclusion of "Yellowstone" was always clear to anyone paying attention, but without John Dutton, something just felt a little unsatisfied.

World.title: Google Gemini may expose private emails to reviewers
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Think about everything sitting in your Gmail inbox right now. Maybe there's a conversation with your doctor, a recent bank statement or a personal message you never intended anyone else to read. Your Google Drive may hold years of private documents. You probably don't spend much time thinking about who might see that information beyond the people you share it with. But what happens when you connect those services to Google's Gemini AI assistant?

An independent researcher has raised concerns about how Gemini handles information retrieved from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The findings prompted questions about whether some private content could end up in conversations reviewed by humans.

We contacted Google, and the company confirmed that some information retrieved from connected Gmail and Drive accounts may be seen by human reviewers under certain circumstances. Google stressed that these connections are off by default. Here's what you should know before giving Gemini access to your personal information.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

AI CHATBOT PRIVACY: WHAT YOUR AI MAY KNOW ABOUT YOU

Researcher raises concerns about Google Gemini privacy

An independent researcher using the name thisisme6598 published findings on GitHub, raising questions about the way Gemini retrieves information from connected Gmail and Google Drive accounts. The researcher tested Gemini using a personal Google Account with connected apps enabled. According to the published findings, Gemini sometimes retrieved information from emails or files during conversations without someone explicitly asking it to search Gmail or Drive. For example, the researcher described asking Gemini whether an internet service bill seemed too expensive. During some tests, Gemini reportedly retrieved billing information from Gmail, including payment amounts, account details and confirmation numbers.

In certain instances, the researcher reported that Gemini returned several sentences directly from an email and, in some tests, the entire email, including its headers. The researcher argues that this behavior creates a privacy concern because information retrieved into a Gemini conversation may become eligible for human review. However, the published findings do not establish that a human reviewer actually accessed the researcher's emails. Google told CyberGuy that the reported retrieval was standard behavior for someone who had voluntarily connected their apps. The company also emphasized that retrieved files remain visible only to the authenticated account holder and are not exposed publicly through this process.

Can human reviewers see your Gmail and Drive information through Gemini?

Yes, under certain circumstances. Google's own Connected Apps privacy documentation confirms that trained human reviewers, including service providers, may review a subset of information processed through Gemini's connected apps. That information can include summaries or excerpts from relevant Gmail messages and Google Drive documents.

In some cases, Google acknowledges that reviewers may see a complete email or file if it is short or especially relevant to the request. Google also says human reviewers may access some Gmail inbox content when investigating abuse or harm or responding to submitted feedback.

The company uses these reviews to evaluate Gemini's responses and improve its services.

Simply using Gmail or Google Drive does not subject your private content to this review process. The concern involves information retrieved after someone voluntarily connects those services to consumer Gemini. Google says it does not train generative AI models directly on someone's entire Gmail inbox or Drive. However, relevant information processed during Gemini conversations may be used for model improvement, depending on account settings. Google specifically warns against connecting apps containing confidential information someone would be uncomfortable having a reviewer see.

What Google told CyberGuy about Gemini privacy

We contacted Google directly to ask whether human reviewers could access Gmail messages or Drive files processed through the consumer Gemini app. We also asked whether the company had changed its privacy disclosures, notified existing customers and provided ways to prevent human review. A Google spokesperson told CyberGuy:

"Gmail and Google Drive’s core privacy protections remain unchanged, and your private emails and files are not reviewed by humans simply by using Gmail, Drive, or built-in Workspace features. Connecting those apps to the consumer Gemini app is off by default — it’s an optional way to get more personalized, time-saving answers across your Google apps when you want them. Users can disconnect their apps in Gemini settings at any time without losing access to Gemini’s core features."

Google also confirmed that when someone connects their apps to consumer Gemini with activity saving enabled, a small subset of conversations may undergo human review. Those conversations can contain relevant information retrieved from connected services. Before trained service providers review the material, Google says it separates the conversations from the associated Google Account and takes steps to reduce identifying information. The company also disputes the suggestion that the researcher's findings demonstrate public exposure of private files.

Did Google change its Gemini privacy promises?

Another part of the controversy involves changes to Google's public privacy disclosures. In Oct. 2023, Google published a blog post about its approach to generative AI privacy. The company said that content from Gmail, Docs and Drive accessed through Bard's Workspace extensions would not be seen by human reviewers or used to train the Bard model.

On Oct. 16, 2026, Google added an update to that same blog post. The new language explains that Google has introduced additional optional features allowing people to connect Workspace information to other Google services. Google says that when someone enables these newer features, a subset of the information may be used to train generative AI models, depending on their settings. It may also undergo human review in limited circumstances. The researcher argues that the change represents a reversal of Google's earlier privacy commitment.

However, Google's original statement concerned Bard's Workspace extensions, while the updated disclosure addresses newer connected features. The available evidence does not establish that Google quietly changed the underlying handling of information in existing connections. We asked Google whether people who previously connected their accounts were notified about the updated disclosures or asked to provide additional consent. Google's response did not directly address those questions. Instead, the company emphasized that the newer connections are optional and can be disabled. That leaves an important question about how clearly Google communicates changes to its AI privacy practices, particularly as new features gain access to more personal information.

APPLE TIGHTENS MAC SECURITY AS AI AGENTS SEEK YOUR FILES

What happens to your information after human review?

Google says it disconnects conversations from the associated Google Account before sending them to trained service providers for routine review. The company also takes steps to reduce personal information. However, removing account identifiers does not necessarily eliminate every sensitive detail contained in an email excerpt or document summary.

Google's Gemini Apps Privacy Hub explains that conversations reviewed by service providers may be retained for up to three years, even after someone deletes the corresponding activity from their Google Account.

Turning off Gemini's History setting, previously called Keep Activity, prevents future conversations from being used to train generative AI models unless someone submits feedback. However, Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes, including with help from human reviewers.

On Nov. 16, 2026, Google announced changes to its Gemini privacy controls. Under the previous policy, Google retained conversations for up to 72 hours when Keep Activity was turned off. Under the new policy, Google will retain conversations for approximately two months when History is turned off. The company is rolling out these changes globally over several weeks.

How to protect your Gmail and Google Drive privacy

If you use Gemini, it's worth checking which accounts and services you've connected. You may find that you don't need every feature enabled. Here are some settings worth reviewing.

Disconnect Gmail and Drive from Gemini

Google groups Gmail and Drive under Google Workspace in its connected-app settings. Here's how to check the connection on a computer.

Go to gemini.google.com and sign in to your personal Google Account.

and to your personal Google Account. At the bottom of the sidebar, click Settings (which may appear as Settings & help).

Select Personal Intelligence .

. Click Connected Apps .

. Find Google Workspace , which includes Gmail and Drive.

, which includes Gmail and Drive. Click More options (the three-dot menu) next to Google Workspace and select Disconnect.

Follow any on-screen instructions to complete the change.

If you see a different menu, look for Connected Apps in Gemini's settings. Google offers different connection controls depending on account eligibility and available features. You can reconnect supported services later if you decide to use them.

Turn off Gemini History (formerly Keep Activity)

If you want to prevent future conversations from being used to train Google's generative AI models, review this setting.

Visit Gemini Apps Activity .

Sign in with the Google Account you use for Gemini.

with the Google Account you use for Gemini. Find the History or Keep Activity control near the top of the page.

Click On to open the available options.

to open the available options. Select Turn off or Turn off and delete history (which may appear as Turn off and delete activity).

Follow the confirmation prompts.

Turning off History stops future chats from being used to train generative AI models unless you choose to submit feedback. Some connected apps, including Google Workspace, become unavailable. Google may still process conversations for security and safety purposes. Depending on whether the latest privacy update has reached your account, conversations may be retained for up to 72 hours under the previous policy or approximately two months under the new policy.

WHAT YOUR INTERNET PROVIDER, WEBSITES AND ADVERTISERS SEE

Turn off AI training without deleting your Gemini history

Google is introducing a separate privacy control that lets you keep your Gemini conversation history while opting out of generative AI model training. If the new setting is available on your account, here's how to find it on a computer.

Go to gemini.google.com .

Click Settings.

Select History.

Uncheck the box next to Chat content including text & uploads.

including Also make sure Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares is unchecked if you see that option.

Click Turn off to confirm.

Google says future chats will no longer be used to train generative AI models unless you submit feedback. However, human review may still occur for other service improvements and safety purposes. If you want to prevent Gemini from retrieving information from Gmail and Drive, disconnect Google Workspace separately.

Delete previous Gemini conversations

Disconnecting an app does not automatically delete information from earlier Gemini conversations. Google says Gemini may still use information from previously saved chats even after you disconnect the original app. That's why it's important to both disconnect the app and delete conversations containing sensitive information.

Open Gemini Apps Activity at myactivity.google.com/product/gemini .

. Sign in to your Google Account.

to your Google Account. Click Delete above your activity.

above your activity. Select All time if you want to remove your saved history.

if you want to remove your saved history. Confirm the deletion.

Remember that previously reviewed information may remain subject to Google's separate retention policies, even after you delete your activity.

Avoid sharing sensitive information with AI assistants

Think carefully before giving an AI assistant access to confidential documents or personal communications. If you don't need Gemini to retrieve information from Gmail or Drive, leave those connections disabled. Also, remember that uploading a document directly into Gemini creates a separate privacy consideration.

Google says uploaded content may be used to improve its services when History, previously called Keep Activity, is enabled, potentially with help from human reviewers. Whether that content is used to train generative AI models also depends on your training settings and whether you submit feedback.

Does this Gemini privacy concern affect business accounts?

Google says the connected-app disclosures involved in this controversy apply to personal Google Accounts using consumer Gemini. Business, Enterprise and Education accounts covered by Google Workspace commercial terms have different privacy protections. According to Google's response to CyberGuy, customer data governed by those commercial terms is not reviewed by humans or used to train foundational AI models.

If you use Gemini through an employer or school, your organization's settings and agreements determine which features are available and how information is handled. The important point is that the consumer Gemini privacy rules discussed here should not automatically be applied to commercial Workspace accounts.

Kurt's key takeaways

I can understand why someone would want Gemini to search their Gmail or find a document buried in Google Drive. We've all wasted time digging through old emails looking for something we need. Having an AI assistant do that work sounds pretty appealing. But I think Google has a responsibility to make the privacy implications much clearer before someone connects an account. Most people probably don't expect information pulled from their private emails to become part of a conversation that could eventually be reviewed by another human being. I appreciate that Google responded to our questions and explained the safeguards it uses. Still, I would have liked a more direct answer about whether existing customers were notified when the privacy disclosures changed. If you're giving an AI assistant access to years of personal information, you deserve to know exactly how that information might be handled. Personally, I'd leave Gmail and Drive disconnected unless I had a specific reason to use those features.

Would you trust an AI assistant with access to years of your private emails if you knew some of that information could be seen by human reviewers? Or has Google crossed a privacy line, even with your permission? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.
