World.title: Ontario family business says $500K weekly in Trump tariffs is forcing production to U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A family-owned packaging business in Niagara, Ont., says it’s paying half a million dollars in Trump tariffs weekly and will be f orced to move production to the U.S. next month.

Stanpac manufactures packaging for ice cream brands including Chapman’s, Baskin-Robbins and Van Leeuwen. Founded in 1949, the company has six locations in North America.

Since 1973, the company has been a major employer in West Lincoln's community of Smithville, where brothers and co-presidents Andrew and Matt Witt were raised. But tariffs are forcing a difficult reckoning within the company.

“Right now, we’re paying $500,000 per week in U.S. tariffs, which is much more money than we take in,” Andrew Witt told CBC.

Brothers and co-presidents of the food packaging business Stanpac, Andrew Will, left, and Matt Witt say the 50 per cent tariffs will force it to move production from Canada to the United States. (Diona Macalinga/CBC)

The company has requested relief from the federal Ministry of Industry but "there doesn't seem to be a clear path forward," said Murray Bain, vice-president of marketing at Stanpac.

As a result, Stanpac is set to move specialized equipment for producing ice cream containers and plastic milk bottle lids to their facilities in Texas and New Jersey, the owners say.

With about 500 employees at their Smithville headquarters, Stanpac estimates it may need to cut 70 per cent of their staff in the coming months. The company is looking to move affected production staff to different departments within the Smithville location before they commit to layoffs, Bain said.

Company charged 50% tariffs

Stanpac exports paperboard ice cream packages, glass milk bottles and other food service packaging, with about 80 per cent of its production going to the U.S., the company says.

The United States is currently subjecting such products to 50 per cent tariffs, according a White House list of goods subject to tariffs under Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act of 1930.

Since the 50 per cent tariffs came into effect on Aug. 22, Stanpac's tariff payments have exceeded the company's entire revenues, it said in a Nov. 16 press release warning that it will run out of money in the near future without government support.

“It’s not a viable business in Niagara,” Matt Witt said. “I don’t know that [the federal and provincial governments] understand how urgent it is and that every week, our cash reserves are depleting.”

350 jobs at risk: MP

Niagara West MP Dean Allison raised Stanpac's plight during the House of Commons’ question period on Nov. 17.

“This is an unsustainable amount for a business and operation for over seven decades,” he said. “Three hundred and fifty jobs are at risk just before Christmas.”

Niagara West MP Dean Allison raised Stanpac's plight during question period in the House of Commons on Nov. 17. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the government is still talking with the U.S. about relieving tariff pressures. (CBC News)

In response, Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said “Canadian workers and businesses that are facing pressures from these unjustified and illegal tariffs will be supported by the government of Canada,” adding that situations like Stanpac's are of “great concern” to the federal government.

“We're obviously engaged in discussions with the United States to be in a position to relieve this tariff pressure,” LeBlanc said. “But we’re not going to wait … for an agreement that is possible with the United States to stand up and defend workers and do the right thing and support those jobs.”

$44B in federal support for those facing U.S. tariffs

The 2026 federal budget sets aside nearly nearly $44 billion to support workers, businesses and industries affected by U.S. tariffs.

This includes “$20.6 billion to help tariff-affected firms adapt, grow, diversity markets and maintain industrial capacity, ” the Department of Finance Canada said in a statement.

Affected firms may qualify for loans, the department said.

Stanpac applied for support in September through the Federal Economic Development Agency for southern Ontario's Regional Tariff Response Initiative, Bain said. The company has not yet received any funding, he added.

Andrew Witt believes money from reciprocal tariffs the Canadian government introduced on Sept. 6 should be used to offest U.S. tariffs paid by Canadian businesses.

But the Department of Finance told CBC Niagara that counter-tariffs are “not a revenue-raising policy.”

Instead, they are intended “to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses, defend industries harmed by unjustified U.S. tariffs, and help Canadian producers compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market.”

The Witt brothers are still hoping that 11th hour assistance from the federal government could keep Stanpac's manufacturing — and jobs — in Ontario.

“A lot of the people that work here, we went to high school with,” Matt Witt said. “There’s generations that have worked here.”

“We really take pride in being from Smithville,” he added. “We don’t want to leave.”

World.title: Small businesses worry potential consumer pullback could cut into critical holiday sales
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's the most wonderful — and most important — time of the year for retailers like Kristi Wozniak: the holiday shopping season.

"It's very big," said Wozniak, owner and founder of Keylime Activewear in Sherwood Park, Alta. "We are in our busiest season right now for sure."

Wozniak says a quarter of her sales come from holiday shopping, with December being their busiest month.

But sales have been down recently compared to previous years, and she's worried that shoppers slowing their spending could cut into those critical holiday sales.

"Customers are definitely more cautious where they're spending their dollars," Wozniak said.

She's not alone. As small businesses struggle with tariffs and rising costs, some are worried that less spending by consumers this holiday season could deal another blow.

Kristi Wozniak, owner of Keylime Athletics, stands beside a sign advertising discounts at her storefront in Sherwood Park, Alta. (Submitted by Kristi Wozniak)

In a survey of 1,675 of its members from across the country, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business found that the holiday season is an important part of the financial outlook for four in 10 respondents. And 73 per cent of that group said a pullback in spending posed the biggest threat to holiday sales.

"In times of worsening affordability in the middle of a trade war, lack of consumer demand has actually been a key threat for many small businesses," said Ryan Mitton, the CFIB's director of legislative affairs for B.C.

And retail sales data from Statistics Canada shows consumers might, in fact, be trying to cut down on their spending.

Retail sales ticked up in September by 0.8 per cent — but that was driven mostly by a jump in how much consumers were spending at gas stations. And an early estimate for October forecasted a 1.5 per cent drop in retail sales.

Those figures give a "very weak kickoff point" for retail sales in the last quarter of the year, according to Michael Davenport, a senior economist with Oxford Economics.

He says high gas prices due to the war in Iran have been squeezing household budgets, while the weak job market and volatility in financial markets are weighing on consumer's confidence. And while consumer spending has been pretty resilient throughout the year despite some of those factors, he expects they'll cause Canadians to spend less in coming months.

"All of these factors are kind of coming together, we think, to lead to a bit of a slowdown in consumer spending growth towards the end of 2026 and early 2027."

WATCH | What chatbots can miss hunting for Black Friday deals: Black Friday deal hunting with AI? What chatbots can miss | Duration closed caption 3:34 Canadians are increasingly turning to AI to help hunt down Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals, but as CBC’s Philippe de Montigny explains, the chatbots might be missing some of the best bargains.

If holiday sales do take a hit, Wozniak says it could leave her with less cash to order new stock in the new year and force her to cut back some hours for staff.

"[If] we didn't make enough money for the previous season, now we're looking for cashflow options," Wozniak said.

She's stopped purchasing from some of her U.S. suppliers due to tariffs and to keep down costs related to shipping and the unfavorable exchange rate between the Canadian and U.S. dollar.

But rising manufacturing costs have still shrunken her profit margins in recent years, meaning she can't offer massive Black Friday discounts on clothing at Keylime like big box stores can.

Despite that, she's offering deals on gift cards and discounts that scale with the number of items shoppers buy, which she hopes will be enough to get buyers through the door — and spending some of their cash.

"We do want to attract the customer into the store," Wozniak said. "We try our hardest."

World.title: With World Cup and Olympic berths at stake, revamped Canadian women's team could begin new chapter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The 2026 FIFA Men’s World Cup proved to the world that Canada is a soccer nation.

This Saturday, at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium, the Canadian women’s national team can amplify that reputation.

With a win over Panama at the CONCACAF W championships, the women’s side has a chance to clinch a berth to the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

That entails decisively conquering an opponent they beat 1-0 in 2022 — which came with an allegation of “spying” levied against them . The complaint never reached the disciplinary committee because there was no evidence.

Canada has won the continental tournament twice before but is looking to secure qualification to next year's World Cup hosted by Brazil. The Canadians are placed ninth by FIFA rankings, and Panama is 54th.

While there is always a pause to think about the worst-case scenario, the Canadian women's team goes into this tournament very well prepared. Their recent series against Denmark left with one win (in penalty shots) and one loss but a lot of lessons learned. After a loss 4-3 against Denmark on Thanksgiving Monday at BMO Field in Toronto, head coach Casey Stoney told the media that it was necessary to “keep context and not panic.”

Context is essential for this tournament and Stoney understands what is at stake.

It is not impossible for Canada to qualify for the World Cup nor the Olympics if they don’t win against Panama, but the path is far more difficult. A journey that Stoney and the team would likely want to avoid.

Stoney, a legend on England’s national women’s team with 130 caps, learned some hard lessons, on losing in transition and the need to kill the game quickly. Something they will need to do with Panama.

Canada’s storied backline will not have Vanessa Gilles, one of its strongest players, who is unavailable due to injury.

But this team will boast a fresh and clinical group of attackers — something missing from previous iterations of this team after the retirement of the world's top international goal scorer and Canada’s skipper, Christine Sinclair, in 2023.

Kaylee Hunter, the 18-year old phenom from Calgary, will be back with a team of seasoned players including Jessie Fleming, 2026 NWSL Defender of the Year Janine Sonis, and Kadeisha Buchanan.

Hunter just renewed her contract with AFC Toronto in the Northern Super League (NSL). She made a name for herself on the international stage when she scored a hat trick against France at the U20 Women’s World Cup in Poland during the September window.

Hunter is the top youth player in the country and has chosen to stay in Canada and compete at the highest level. This is a particularly poignant move after Hunter was part of the AFC Toronto club that won the Diana B. Matheson Cup after beating the Montreal Roses in the NSL Final.

The Canadian women's national side features five players from Canada’s domestic league, including fellow attacker Delaney Baie Pridham — who scored her first international goal in the Toronto match against Denmark.

The attacking line is punctuated by Olivia Smith of Arsenal FC, and also midfielder Simi Awujo of Manchester United FC, both of whom are enjoying success in goal scoring and in wins in the Women’s Super League (WSL).

Marie-Yasmine (Mimi) Alidou plays midfield for the Montreal Roses and will support attackers as club rivalries are put aside for the country. All need to be finding the back of the net.

Instead of turning a new leaf of attacking prowess, Canada should be thinking about planting deep roots, says Amy Walsh, soccer commentator and former captain of the national team.

Walsh, a Canada Soccer Hall of Fame inductee, says that a new approach doesn't have to be drastic, but this team has to find its form.

“It has to reaffirm its identity as one of the toughest teams to play against, that lock down defensively,” Walsh said. “So you put [clinical finishers and defensive strength] together, and I think it allows this foundational style of play, this philosophy, to take shape and put down roots.”

The women's national team has not beaten a top 15-ranked team in Stoney’s tenure that began in January 2025.

A shift away from former mainstays

With a change in roster announcements and the exclusion of players who were once considered mainstays, the shift is important considering what is at stake. Nichelle Prince (119 caps with the senior team) was named as a practice player.

“Those conversations are not easy to have,” Stoney admitted on a media call following the squad announcement. Stoney said that when she spoke with Prince, she said it was Prince’s choice.

Another player to not make the roster was Adriana Leon (132 caps).

Stoney said it was simply because Leon had not featured regularly at her club San Diego FC. She says that getting “consistent minutes” is a priority in selection. Game experience offers an opportunity to stay sharp for an intense campaign with the national team, preparedness in fitness, and practiced in game IQ.

WATCH | Is Canada ready? Women's roster revealed: Is Canada ready? CANWNT roster revealed & CANMNT 2026 report card | Duration closed caption 17:39 The CANWNT roster is out ahead of crucial World Cup and Olympic qualifiers. On Soccer North, Mackenzie Barwell and Amy Walsh break down the squad, give the CANMNT a grade for its 2026 season and preview the CPL Final between Atlético Ottawa and Cavalry FC.

This is the first match with consequences that the Canadian women's national program has played since 2024. They have had international friendlies but nothing this consequential.

Stoney says that they have spent a lot of time preparing and want to qualify for both Brazil and Los Angeles, but also challenge the United States for the CONCACAF title. A win against the reigning CONCACAF W champions would boost their confidence moving towards a World Cup year.

Walsh agreed that the team is up for the challenge.

“I think they come into this understanding what's on the line, and I think they're very well prepared, and they understand the task in front of them, but they also understand how to get success playing ‘Stoney Ball.’”

Stoney Ball considers that structural pieces can be tweaked but also how a “team-first mentality” is essential.

The team has faced ups and downs but its culture and identity are one that has always carried a firm belief in the collective.

With this next chapter for Canada, the game plan must be to demonstrate how lethal, decisive and unflappable it can be.

Stoney leads the charge with seasoned vets and young blood to write a new chapter for Canada women’s soccer.

World.title: Focker-In-Law isn't terrible. It's just a sitcom
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There is a fairly simple way to avoid seeing how far the mighty have fallen. Just avoid finding out where they fell from.

When it comes to the probably-too-cutely-titled Fockers franchise, that seems to be the recipe for success. Because following 2010's Little Fockers, 2004’s Meet the Fockers and finally, the normally titled comedy that started it all, 2000's Meet the Parents, there’s really only one way to avoid disappointment: Only watch the entries earning their buck off the punny name of our titular Gaylord (though he'd much prefer you call him Greg) Focker. Or skip them all and just stick to the seminal indie smash success whose title didn’t lean on him at all.

Clearly, some critics didn't take this advice when heading into Focker-In-Law, the newest iteration of the Ben Stiller-led comedy premise. So far holding the second-lowest Rotten Tomatoes score of the critically panned sequels, the film's dour reception appears to broadly circle the same complaints. Too broad. Too cliche. And — aside from the bubbly Focker-in-law herself, Ariana Grande — too dour . That means you, Ben Stiller.

That, though, is true only if you don't judge it on face value. Because really, what else did you expect? If it was for a return to the heights of Jay Roach's "original" — itself a sort-of remake of the 1992 comedy of the same name — you're out of luck. But if comparing it to the intentionally broad, necessarily formulaic, situation-comedy field that the bloated Fockers franchise has found itself in, it's ... fine? Mostly? Watchable, let's say. And that's all these things are going for.

WATCH | Focker-In-Law trailer:

Because more than 25 years after his famously awkward, increasingly idiotic protagonist turned a meeting with exacting father-in-law Jack (Robert De Niro) into a cavalcade of I Love Lucy-esque disasters of his own moronic making, Greg is left with few to no grounded choices. What else to do but what director/co-writer (and Zoolander co-writer) John Hamburg opted for here: a feud between overbearing Greg and his son (Skyler Gisondo) Henry's impossibly perfect, ex-hostage-negotiator girlfriend, Olivia (Grande)?

If you're waiting for some type of subversion, keep waiting. The central conflict — and its resolution — is about as hard to guess as what, exactly, Samuel L. Jackson is going to find in the cockpit in Snakes on a Plane.

Take it from Greg's long-suffering wife, Pam (Teri Polo), to whom director Hamburg even needs to give an expositional line about how Greg only acts this insane on family trips. (If not, why wouldn't she have divorced him yet?) Greg is now older than Jack was during the events of the first film. Wouldn't it be crazy if it were his turn to play the Jack to his own son's new flame?

Cue the most basic, least innovative evolution to allow this repeated framing to occur, once again. Greg is now the one to suggest strapping Olivia into the lie detector chair, to battle Olivia in a bizarrely high-stakes race by unsuspecting pedestrians (though this time on ludicrously slow bikes instead of sedans).

But there's one new complication thrown into the mix, in that all the while, he's still desperately and pathetically trying to earn the affections of his family — and of Jack, which he attempts with unsettling, pseudo-romantic passion.

This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows Ben Stiller, left, and Robert De Niro in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)

The solution

For high-concept features doomed by both their initial originality and unexpected success, there are few options to keep them rolling as a series. And, as Fockers' consistent box office success in the face of equally consistent negative reviews shows, there's one method that can keep at least the money rolling in: Become a sitcom.

That is, figure out a way to put your characters in the exact same situation with the near-exact same logline as before. For The Hangover, simply lose a different friend — or have him kidnapped this time. In Home Alone, perform a narrative reset by losing Kevin all over again. But have him lose his parents instead. And always: have every character constantly remark on how ridiculous it is this is all happening again, so the audience doesn't have to.

The sitcom format works for television, as the pilot is expected to showcase a formula to revisit later. But it's different for film, where the original is expected to be its own self-contained story. How do you have your character face the same problem again when previous entries had them surmount whatever central flaw brought the problem about in the first place?

If you're Home Alone, it's simple: Just get a new kid for the (somehow) four sequels beyond Macaulay Culkin. For Focker-In-Law, the solution is even simpler: Have Greg revert to the same psychotically self-conscious behaviour he's exhibited in every film so far, despite the character development with which the previous films ostensibly all ended.

While Jack has long ago accepted him into his coveted "circle of trust," Focker-In-Law continues to set up hypothermia-inducing ice-plunges and pants-ripping dog attacks largely around Greg's obsessive need to continue impressing him.

And the rest of the cast is left as shallow supporting acts to gawk at the unbelievably short-sighted choices made by this grown man, who presumably has a 401(k) and a consistently paid mortgage, yet also just burned his eyebrows off after pouring nearly a full bottle of whisky onto a flaming pan.

There is the parallel plotline: Greg's competition with Olivia's funny — if, once again, one-dimensional — and powerful perfectionism. In fact, the only person who seems to have changed much is Jack. Previously a meat-eating traditionalist, this Jack is now, inexplicably, a vegan on a health kick who immediately takes to Olivia and Henry's relationship, arguing that sexually active couples should be allowed to share a room and even complimenting the gorgeous vegan meal she cooks as Greg's burnt steak smoulders untouched on the plate.

This image released by Universal Pictures and Paramount Pictures shows, from left, Eduardo Franco, Beanie Feldstein, Teri Polo, Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller in a scene from Focker In-Law. (Atsushi Nishijima/Universal Pictures)

This does work against Focker-In-Law's success in a vacuum. Where Greg's neuroses could be excused when he was up against an unbelievable monster, he becomes much harder to empathize with when up against normal humans. A doubly strange double-down: Stiller's protagonist genuinely becomes the least likeable player in his own movie.

Still, the undeniable unoriginality is not enough to make Focker-In-Law unwatchable. Greg's daughter's live-in boyfriend, Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), endears with the hilariously earnest patter he showed off in his criminally short turn in Stranger Things.

Then there is Grande's typical, unflappable comedic timing, which picks up the pace whenever things really start to drag. And there is the no longer novel yet ever-present formula, reheated and presented once more.

Again, it's nothing even close to the serviceable, interesting first entry, in a franchise that should probably now be sorted by pre- and post-Focker. But otherwise, it is … fine?

World.title: 2,000 wild species live in our homes with us, study finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

You probably have way more housemates than you think, and most of them have at least six legs, a new study suggests. And if you find them, scientists say there are reasons why you shouldn't put them outside.

Homes in Canada and the U.S. are inhabited not just by humans and their pets but by at least 2,000 other species, from Asian lady beetles to a huge diversity of spiders to the occasional alligator, reports the study published this week in Ecology .

Bradley Allf, the Colorado State University ecologist who led the study, said the findings showcase "the ways in which we're not so separate from nature despite the many ways we try to wall it out."

Allf said his goal was to treat the indoors like the savannah or rainforest and get a sense of what the ecosystem looks like in the relatively new but growing habitat created by humans.

There's already evidence that it's full of ecological mysteries "right under our nose that we don't know very much about."

This green anole was submitted to the Never Home Alone project from a home in Raleigh, N.C. That was among the species that lead research Bradley Allf contributed to the project. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)

How science got inside so many people's homes

Allf and his team didn't explore people's homes, as scientists had in a previous study . Instead, they launched a citizen science (also known as community science) project called Never Home Alone on the iNaturalist app. It invited ordinary people to send photos of wild species they found indoors. Those species were then identified by a team of experts.

WATCH | The Great Wild Indoors -- Insects hiding in your home: The Great Wild Indoors – Insects Hiding in Your Home | Duration 1:01 We think our homes are ours alone, but they are actually shared by many insects.

The project received more than 23,000 photos from 3,000 people in every U.S. state and every Canadian province (though not all territories) between 1996 and 2024. Most were from homes, but some were also from offices, schools, airports and other buildings.

And while experts were able to identify more than 2,000 species, the researchers believe there were more, since nearly half the observations could only be identified as belonging to a more general grouping (such as combfoot spiders), rather than as individual species. About 52 per cent of species were observed only once.

The most common species in our homes (besides us)

The most commonly recorded species in the study did include some pests, as expected. The varied carpet beetle, which can damage carpets, furniture and clothing, was No. 4, for example.

But No. 1 was the Asian lady beetle, which came as a surprise to Allf.

"We know almost nothing about what they're doing inside," he said. "And yet, they're found in hundreds of homes across the U.S. and Canada."

(CBC)

Catherine Scott is an arachnologist from Memorial University in St. John's who co-authored the study and identified many of the spiders.

"I was surprised by the diversity of spiders found indoors," she said.

While there were lots of expected species such as cellar spiders (the long-bodied cellar spider was the fifth most common in the study) and false black widows, which spin cobwebs, the bold jumping spider was also frequently reported.

"They're big and flashy and not particularly known as a house spider," she said.

But Scott noted that the most commonly reported species aren't necessarily the most common, as people tend to notice larger, more brightly coloured things that move around more.

Allf said the fact that spiders, which are predators, are so common is evidence that indoor spaces are "a real ecosystem … where species are eating one another or where there's food webs."

This is one of the most recent observations from the Never Home Alone project. Submitted from Fort George, B.C., it's been tentatively identified as a hobo spider. Spiders were among the most common types of animals found, and there was a huge diversity. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)

But he said there are lots of questions about how creatures live and interact within that ecosystem, including cellar spiders: "How often do they eat? How do they meet other cellar spiders and reproduce?"

He hopes studies like this will begin to help answer such questions.

Why you shouldn't put them outside

Allf acknowledged that many people's gut reaction when encountering other species in their homes is to squish them or take them outside.

But in fact, for many species, the indoors is their natural habitat. They're adapted to the controlled climate and food resources and are more protected from predators there.

"If they go outside, it might be a more dangerous place for them," Allf said.

This Asian lady beetle was submitted to the project from Longeuil, Que. This was the species most commonly submitted to the project in North America. (Never Home Alone/iNaturalist)

He gave the example of German cockroaches, a species he said has never been found outdoors.

"I think there's probably many more species like that that we just don't know about yet."

Allf suggested that when people find an organism from another species in their home, they should consider whether it's dangerous or bothering them.

"If the answers to those questions are no, then maybe just leave it there."

Scott noted that spiders are in people's homes for a reason.

"They're doing their job eating insects," she said. "They're natural pest control and they don't want to bother you, so try to coexist."

What citizen science can do

Jeremy Kerr is a University of Ottawa ecologist who has developed and used citizen science apps extensively in his research on butterflies and bees, but wasn't involved in the Never Home Alone project.

He said he loves the name and the concept and suggested it might make people feel more connected to nature and appreciate its value.

"I think there's something to be gained by simply recognizing that nature is everywhere, and maybe by extension, it's worth being curious about it," he said.

So far, he said, this is a very small citizen science database compared with larger ones containing hundreds of thousands to billions of observations that allow researchers to answer detailed questions about species such as birds. More observations about indoor ecosystems would be valuable, he said, providing a better idea of the dominant species in different regions, for example.

In fact, the Never Home Alone project is ongoing and accepting observations from around the world.

Scott hopes the publication of this study will encourage more people to contribute.

World.title: This suspected North Korean operative said he had an IT company in Toronto. It wasn't real
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Aku Alatao seemed like the perfect job applicant to create a cryptocurrency and design a website for the Canadian startup Bananacoin.

His resumé boasted lots of previous front- and back-end coding experience. He had his own IT company based in Toronto and he was eager to get started right away.

"Aku, let me ask you a question. What do you think of Bananacoin? I'm not sure if I like the name Bananacoin," company executive Clark Shelley said to Alatao during an online job interview this past summer.

"Yeah, maybe it is very good," Alatao replied.

He got the job. The company offered to start him at $8,000 per month. He said he would work remotely.

But there was a catch — Bananacoin wasn't real and neither was Aku Alatao.

For the last year, the fifth estate has investigated multiple suspected North Korean operatives posing online as Canadian residents. They have been able to secure remote jobs in Canadian companies and government, their paycheques propping up the heavily sanctioned regime.

@neilunosoftware This is my company going to the Moon. —AkuAlatao891113

Alatao has been presenting himself around the world as the founder and CEO of Toronto-based Neiluno Software.

But according to our research and experts, Alatao is a suspected North Korean operative working under a false Canadian identity.

Watch the full documentary, "For Hire: North Korea's IT Army," from the fifth estate on YouTube , CBC Gem or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

To find out more about him and the scheme he is involved in, we created a fictitious crypto company, Bananacoin, and posed as potential employers looking to hire him.

Alatao proved to be a phantom. As we tracked his operation online and around the globe, he was everywhere and nowhere and certainly not where he claimed to be based in Canada.

Sanctions and cybercrime

North Korea is a closed-off country.

Ruled by leader Kim Jong Un, the state has been wracked by mismanagement and economic sanctions aimed at curbing its nuclear ambitions and human rights violations.

So to make money, experts say, the regime has turned to crime — including counterfeiting currency, trafficking heroin and massive multibillion-dollar crypto hacks.

According to cryptocurrency intelligence firm TRM Labs, North Korea-backed hackers stole $7.4 billion in crypto in 2026.

The regime has also trained an army of information technology workers to get remote IT jobs around the world — including in Canada.

One U.S. Department of the Treasury estimate put the total take from North Korean IT work at nearly $800 million from the U.S. for 2024 alone.

WATCH | Posing as a potential employer: 'Hiring’ a North Korean operative posing as a Toronto resident | Duration 3:30 For more than a year, the fifth estate has been tracking North Korean operatives suspected of using fake and stolen identities to work online jobs in Canada and funnel funds back to Pyongyang. To learn more about the scheme, the team set up a fake company to recruit a suspected operative masquerading as a Toronto resident. Here’s what they uncovered in the process.

Cybersecurity expert Evan Gordenker, who has led more than 150 investigations into threat actors and testified before a United Nations hearing on North Korean IT workers, estimates there are thousands involved in this scheme.

"Fraud has been their job for, in most cases, at least six years, but in some cases even much longer than that and they're a well-oiled machine," Gordenker told the fifth estate in an interview.

In early 2026, the fifth estate received a tip regarding a cache of documents on the computer programming website GitHub. It contained passports, resumés and other documents North Korean IT workers use to ply their trade. It was left available for anyone with an internet connection to access.

Using open source intelligence tools and an artificial intelligence agent tasked with looking for specific quirks associated with North Korean IT workers, we scanned thousands of Github accounts to see what else might be available on public websites.

What we found surprised us. Alongside fake IDs and fake resumés were working documents, including digital notebooks, shopping lists and photos that appear to have been taken inside North Korea.

Metadata for this photo, linked to a suspected North Korean IT worker’s GitHub account, indicates the photo was taken inside North Korea. (Devops920719/GitHub)

In the middle of it all emerged one particular account that caught our attention, alleycat1 , owned by Toronto-based Aku Alatao.

According to Ontario corporate filings, Alatao registered his company, Neiluno Software, in April 2025.

But when we visited the registered address in Toronto, a converted house on a busy commercial strip in the west-end district of Etobicoke, we found a fast-food restaurant on the main floor and another unrelated small business in the basement. The building owner told us he'd never heard of Alatao or Neiluno.

Internet phantoms

When we looked into Neiluno's employees listed on its website, they were largely internet phantoms — strange accounts with changing names, connected to gambling websites and cryptocurrency ventures.

The company website also listed former clients. One of them, Aqualoan, was connected by cryptocurrency experts to North Korea and the theft of $50 million from crypto firm Radiant Capital.

When we invited Alatao to an online interview to discuss Bananacoin, using false identities ourselves, we weren't sure what to expect.

He logged onto the meeting a few minutes early, eager to discuss the details of our proposed project.

"I imagine you're taking on multiple projects. You must be busy," the fifth estate host Mark Kelley, posing as Bananacoin CEO Clark Shelley, asked in the interview

"It is no problem to work for this project all day," Alatao responded.

Among Neiluno's advertised portfolio project was a fake Forbes website, which the real Forbes confirmed was inauthentic. (Neiluno.io)

"Your company, Neiluno, I see its head office is based here in Toronto?" Shelley asked.

"Yes," he said.

When asked where he was personally located, Alatao stumbled, pronouncing the Toronto suburb of Etobicoke incorrectly multiple times before providing the fake Etobicoke address where the fifth estate had confirmed neither he nor his business was.

When the topic of money came up, Alatao asked to be paid in cryptocurrency.

"They would love to move money across cryptocurrency where once a transfer is done, it is done," Gordenker said, adding "from there, making it invisible and having it disappear into the bytes and bits of the blockchain space, and really the many blockchains that they use, is totally trivial for them to do."

We asked Alatao for a regular bank account, and he sent us the details for a CitiBank account in his name. CitiBank declined to comment on the record.

Providing his ID for our fictitious payroll, Alatao sent a picture of an Ontario driver's licence we determined to be fake. The licence number was invalid, the photo appeared to be a cutout from a picture he had used in an online profile and the address was that same Etobicoke address that Neiluno and Alatao had no connection to.

A photo of a fake Ontario driver’s licence provided by Aku Alatao. (Aku Alatao)

North Korean IT workers often enlist the help of domestic facilitators in the countries where they pretend to be. Facilitators help them keep the scheme going by completing tasks the worker cannot do remotely, like opening a bank account or receiving mail.

Local facilitators also get paid to host laptop computers that the North Koreans remotely work from, fooling their employers into believing they are based in a friendly location like Canada or the U.S.

We told Alatao during our interview that he would need to do all his work from a company-provided laptop in the hopes that we could locate him or a Canadian facilitator working with him.

The day after our interview, Alatao emailed to tell us there was an urgent matter that required him to be out of the country.

"I am currently navigating some significant personal matters involving my girlfriend in Indonesia, which requires my immediate departure for that country tomorrow," he wrote. "This absence is anticipated to last several months. I believe I have no issues working for this project there."

He gave us an address in Cirebon, Indonesia, for delivery of the laptop and a contact name: Aisyah Isaa, who appeared on the Neiluno website as an employee

Indonesia-based Aisyah Zahira Isaa was one of multiple employees listed on the Neiluno website. (Neiluno.io)

Cirebon is more than 220 kilometres east of Jakarta. We hired a freelance journalist there to investigate and keep up the appearance that we were trying to legitimately get a Bananacoin company laptop to Alatao.

The address turned out to be the home of Isaa's parents and neither she nor Alatao was there.

The parents called their daughter, who gave us two addresses in Jakarta — one was a co-working office space in a building in the centre of the city, the other was a home in the suburbs.

Our freelancer went to the office building. Seeing no sign of Neiluno, he arranged to meet Isaa at her home.

Throughout a nearly hour-long discussion — during which our freelancer identified himself as working with the CBC — Isaa said that she had met Alatao in Singapore at a tech conference and that she had been working with him for about a year. Neiluno's CEO wasn't in Indonesia, she said. He was in Hong Kong or possibly back home in Canada, where she believed he grew up.

Isaa later sent emails to CBC explaining that she knew nothing about Alatao or any scheme that he may have been running and had connected with him online just a month prior, contradicting her statements from her conversation with our freelancer in Jakarta.

It seems we were not the only people trying to find Alatao. About a week prior, in Neiluno's Telegram channel, someone posted wondering if the channel's owner had "disappeared."

The reply came two days later, stating that the Neiluno's owner had just returned from a sailing trip that was extended due to stormy conditions.

A member of the Neiluno Software Inc. chat on Telegram wondered about the apparent disappearance of the company’s leader. (Telegram)

Wherever he was, it seemed that Neiluno's founder and CEO was a difficult man to pin down.

"It's so easy for the North Koreans because for most ordinary citizens, I don't think the implications of doing some of these things is really registering," said Gordenker, "Certainly they're not registering, ‘Oh, this could be assisting a sanctioned country and I could be helping with illicit finance.'

"Even people who are saying this is a little bit suspicious typically don't figure out the whole scope of the scheme. And that's partly a function of people just not understanding how serious this could be. But moreso, I think this is a function of people don't understand that they are being used. They're pawns in this grand scheme."

On one online profile, Aku claimed to be based in Rehoboth Beach, Del. According to other accounts, he graduated from a university in Hong Kong and another in Ankara, Turkey, in the same year. (Peopleperhour.com)

Alatao had heard from Isaa that something wasn't right about the conversation she had with our freelancer.

"She stated that two individuals approached her and proceeded to record video and audio using concealed equipment," Alatao wrote. "They have accused our organization of fraudulent activity, which has understandably caused Aisyah considerable distress."

We agreed to meet online and clear up the whole matter. Again, Alatao showed up to our video call as scheduled.

When we informed Alatao that we had been by his office address in Toronto and no one had heard of him or Neiluno Software, he told us he had moved the office, but did not say to where.

We also wanted to ask Alatao about a photo we had found online. In June 2025, X account @browsercookies posted two photos. The first was a picture Alatao had used on a personal website. The second was a photo of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un at a state event in 2020. In the crowd behind Kim, there is a smiling, clapping person sharing a striking resemblance to Alatao.

Oh hell ya, DPRK. Holler at your boy sitting behind the man himself, Kim Jong Un. Look top left.. He also has profiles on LaborX, Lancers[.]JP, etc. @aptwhatnow @Narcass3 @meow_mfer @blackbigswan #DPRK https://t.co/yt5HoZAVRD —browsercookies

The fifth estate could not independently verify that the man in the crowd was Alatao, but North Korea experts we interviewed said it could be him.

"This event was the first event when Kim Jong Un's aunt was reintroduced to the public after Kim Jong Un had her husband executed ," Gordenker said.

"That someone with a vaulted position, that could be so close to Kim Jong Un, is also out here scamming Canadian companies means that scam is so profitable and he is so successful at this sort of thing that he has really earned his way there.

"I think you've probably stumbled into one of the more elite attackers that the North Koreans have for their cyber force," Gordenker said.

This photo was made available by the Korean Central News Agency in January 2020. (Reuters)

When we asked Alatao during our interview if he was in North Korea and if he was North Korean, he responded "no."

When we pressed him on whether was in fact a North Korean operative, he said: "I don't know what you mean" and that the allegation was "very weird."

He told us we had him mixed up with someone else and left the meeting.

World.title: Danielle Smith’s hold over UCP takes centre stage as 7,000 members registered for annual meeting
World.content:

Alberta's United Conservatives kick off their fifth annual general meeting under Premier Danielle Smith Friday, a gathering expected to reveal much about the party’s future a little more than a month after a divisive referendum.

In the days after the vote, Smith said the UCP would not be turned into a vehicle for independence.

But party unity remains elusive.

Several constituency association presidents have refused to sign pledges backing the results, meaning the independence issue remains a live one heading into the weekend.

Smith herself has advocated for conservatives to band together, suggesting she expects a “really robust [and] fun” debate at the annual meeting.

“We sadly always seem to try to find the things that blow us apart. I keep on wanting to try to find the things that will draw us together,” Smith told longtime separatist Cory Morgan in a recent interview .

Some attendees, though, expect these fissures to come into public view on the convention floor over the course of the weekend.

“I think she’s going to get absolutely surprised at the AGM,” said Martin Belanger, a social media influencer who has been a vocal proponent for Alberta independence on his channel, Martyupnorth.

“If people think that Jeff Rath getting up in front of the mic last year and saying, ‘Who here is pro-independence?’ [was notable] … You’re going to get a moment like that, after moment, after moment.”

Jeffrey Rath, co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project, speaks at a referendum watch party in October. At last year’s AGM, Rath received a standing ovation at a microphone after challenging Alberta Premier Danielle Smith. (John Ulan/The Canadian Press)

For Belanger and others in his camp, frustration lies with Smith’s approach to Ottawa.

“Some people are fed up with negotiations,” Belanger said.

“In this big tent, we have different paths, and she’s trying to shove us down one path. I don’t think she’s genuine when she says she wants that discussion, because some of her actions of late don’t reflect that.”

Remarks expected from 3 conservative premiers

More than 7,000 members have registered for the event at Calgary’s BMO Centre. On Friday, candidates for the UCP board will deliver speeches.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson are expected to deliver remarks later in the day.

British Columbia Premier Lorne Doerkson looks on during the swearing-in ceremony at Government House in Victoria on Nov. 20. Doerkson and Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe are expected to deliver remarks on Friday at the 2026 United Conservative Party annual general meeting. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)

During the event, members will vote for eight people to join the party’s board while also voting on proposed policy matters. Smith will deliver a keynote address Saturday morning.

It will be a balancing act for Smith as she is tasked with appearing as though she has a reasonably united party behind her, without conceding too much ground to the separatists in the party, said Lisa Young, a professor of political science at the University of Calgary.

“I would imagine that there’s a substantial number of party members who are sympathetic to the idea that they have to set aside their differences, because this is the last convention going into an election,” Young said.

“What proportion of the members those are … it’s anyone’s guess, really.”

Resolutions on land acknowledgements, washrooms

Members will also vote on a series of grassroots policy resolutions during the meeting. While non-binding, they signal the desires of party faithful and have influenced party legislation in the past.

For instance, at last year’s annual general meeting, Smith pointed to recent legislation that she said was inspired by the “attack” on psychologist and media personality Jordan Peterson.

“That came from you. That was your policy last AGM. We're calling it the 'Peterson law,’” Smith said during her speech to delegates.

As she has at AGMs past, Smith will hold an “accountability session” in front of members on Saturday.

Delegates cast their votes at the United Conservative Party annual general meeting in Calgary on Nov. 4, 2023. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

This year, delegates will debate policy resolutions that will be voted on by members during the convention, including:

Ending the use of land acknowledgements by the government, as well as all publicly-funded institutions and entities.

Adopting policy that would “protect the safety and privacy of women and girls in schools and public facilities,” including washrooms and change areas.

Mandate that Alberta use "all available legal avenues” to challenge federal land claims, including Indigenous claims that "may infringe on private property owners and their rights."

Pass legislation that would require an MLA who departs their party to sit as an independent member and seek a renewed mandate from voters before joining another party.

Notably, there are no policy resolutions tied to the notion of separating from Canada to be debated.

Near the site of the convention, some people opposed to the UCP government's priorities have promised to hold a sort of “accountability” session of their own, saying there will be “costumes, signs, music” and other forms of protest.

“There are so many awful issues!” the Calgary Raging Grannies wrote in a post on Facebook.

Who will sit on the party's board?

To many, the biggest thing to watch over the weekend will be the results of the board elections. Half of the provincial board is elected each year, with winners going on to serve two years.

Going into the next election, this group will set the rules and the processes for nomination and platform development, making this key to the party’s future, said Colin Aitchison, managing director of western Canada with Enterprise Canada.

“I think a lot of the party membership … they want the party to be best positioned to beat the NDP and Naheed Nenshi in the next election,” said Aitchison, who was a former spokesperson for the UCP under ministers Adriana LaGrange and Nicholas Milliken.

“In order to do that, you need to have a unified leadership at the top, and one that supports the current leader and their agenda.”

Some running for the party board have dismissed the idea that the disagreements that have emerged over past months can be resolved simply by supporting a unity principle.

“A strong leader should welcome a board willing to speak candidly on behalf of its members,” wrote Vince Byfield, a board candidate, on his Substack .

“Sometimes that means offering support, sometimes it means proposing alternatives, and sometimes it means saying that members have serious concerns about a particular decision. None of those actions is inherently disloyal.”

Board election results are expected to be delivered on Saturday evening, just before the adjournment of the annual general meeting.

World.title: The bizarre twists and turns of Colombia’s supermarket hostage siege
World.content:
Blackout drunk kidnappers, false statements by De La Espriella, and bogus accusations against hostages leave a trail of chaos and doubt.

Shortly after 76 hostages were liberated from the Exito Supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, corporate media broadcast a video of two of the men they claimed were involved in the attack.

​The two men, Carlos Tapia and Daniel Díaz, appeared in handcuffs, being escorted by police from the scene of a tense 18-hour standoff between criminals and police.

The media, with information from President Abelardo de la Espriella, suggested that Tapia and Diaz were two of four surviving members of the gang that attacked the supermarket.

​De la Espriella praised the operation he said “came off perfectly,” and released a video of himself mocking two different men, who police say were the actual kidnappers, together with one more person who was killed in the operation.

The president also released a video of himself making demands into a walkie-talkie, falsely claiming that he was in charge of negotiations with the hostage-takers.

According to the indictment from the Prosecutor’s Office, all negotiations and communications with the three hostage takers were handled by Colombia’s anti-kidnapping police unit, the GAULA.

​Tapia and Díaz were released by police just a few hours later, and cleared of any wrongdoing after police confirmed the men were hostages rather than hostage-takers. De la Espriella confirmed shortly afterwards that the men were innocent of any crimes.

​The two men have since both spoken with Colombian media, in interviews in which both men claimed they were mocked by De la Espriella and treated badly by police before being cleared.

​A third man, Edgar Díaz, was also falsely accused by police. He released a video to social media as well, claiming that not only was he mocked and verbally abused by the President, but also robbed of a gold chain by police. Diaz says he was leaving a gym where he works as a personal trainer, in the same mall as the Exito, when he was grabbed by men who appeared to be armed.

The stories of the falsely accused hostages aren’t the only odd parts of the official story surrounding the stand-off between 3 nominally armed men and hundreds of marines, police, snipers, helicopters, and riot police in the city of Cali.

​One of the hostage-takers was killed by police when they entered the supermarket around 1 a.m., after the hostage-takers missed a deadline of 12:30 to release all hostages.

​According to police, the three men attempted to rob an armored car transporting money around 8 a.m., but the car had already left by the time the men arrived. For unclear reasons, the three decided to take nearly 100 people hostage in the Exito supermarket instead, which is part of the same “mega-mall” where the men allegedly intended to carry out the hijacking.

​Two of the men carried long guns that, again according to police, were “traumatic weapons” (similar to Airsoft rifles, the weapons fire foam bullets meant to be non-lethal), and one was armed with another that resembled a shotgun.

Early in the morning, before the men blocked windows in the supermarket, Colombian media captured one of the men from a distance clad in black tactical clothing, body armor, and what appeared to be a heavy steel helmet with a facemask.

​Many of those who were held hostage, speaking with media, said the men were drinking heavily throughout the day, with one witness going as far as to say they were “blind drunk” by the end of the day.

​Workers at the Éxito, who were also taken hostage, said the men set up large speakers, blasted music, and demanded to be given bottles of whisky.

​The two men who survived the police assault that liberated the hostages were asleep when police entered the Éxito, likely why they survived, according to multiple witnesses.

​Confusing matters even further, the wife of the man who was reportedly killed by police, Javier Humberto Muñetón Zapata, had spent the previous 14 hours speaking with local media in Cartagena, looking for her husband, who she believed to be among the hostages.

​She says they lived nearby and went to the mall every day, and that her husband had a membership at the same gym where Diaz works. She claims she began searching for her husband, who had promised to drive her to work and bring pastries from the supermarket, after he suddenly stopped replying to texts.

​She showed Blue Radio a text message at 8:12 a.m. from her husband that said, “Okay, I’m going to pop into Éxito, and I’ll pick you up right away.”

​She claims that her husband ran a small business, regularly drove her to work, and has no criminal record — a fact that has since been confirmed by Cartgena’s mayor. She has made multiple statements to the media asking for clarification and more information, claiming he could not have been involved in any crimes.

Early statements by police, shortly after the hostage situation began to unfold, put the number of hostages at 50. After two releases of hostages by the nominal gunmen, police stated they believed 20 hostages remained as evening approached.

​Shortly after the operation to enter the Éxito, police released details about their raid, claiming that they had “drilled holes in the walls and inserted cameras,” allowing them to identify the kidnappers and estimate the number of hostages.

​They also stated they had men on the roof, in the warehouse of the supermarket, and stationed at the interior entrance to the Éxito, which connects to the mega-mall.

​But more than 70 hostages remained when the raid was successfully carried out.

The attackers claimed in a letter to authorities that if the store was entered by police they would detonate explosives placed near the entrances, killing the hostages.

Police later revealed there were no explosives, and the men were bluffing.

​The two men who were captured alive (and reportedly asleep), Juan Camilo Torres Manco, 33, and Jhon Albeiro Mejía Blandón, 44, are both from Antioquia and have previous convictions for “violent” crimes, according to police.

​Both men appeared intoxicated in videos shortly after they were captured. De la Espriella released a video in which he berates the two men, telling them, “You thought you could just kidnap people and get away with it? Welcome to the miracle country.”

​The bizarre details of the event, as well as misreporting by the media, inaccurate and even contradictory statements by police throughout the day, and general confusion, led some critics of De le Espriella to claim the entire event was staged.

De la Espriella’s efforts to insert himself into the situation, and false claims made by the president, worsened that dynamic.

​There is no evidence currently to support those claims, but with a story that is just straight-up strange, we can see how some people came to that conclusion.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: De la Espriella calls on US to prosecute Petro in response to call to “resign now”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the US Justice Department to “investigate, prosecute and hopefully jail former President Gustavo Petro after the latter called on the people to “rise up” and “restore real democracy.”

De la Espriella addressed the nation at the end of a day of anti-government marches that mobilized tens of thousands of people throughout Colombia.

Petro led the march in Cali and called on his supporters to “rise up,” call a general strike and force the president to “leave now,” less than four months after De la Espriella took office.

Reiterating fraud accusations and the president’s business ties to paramilitary warlords and drug traffickers, the former president told the crowd that “it is not about waiting until 2030; an illegitimate government must leave now.”

A government whose policy goes against the people must leave now. A government whose policy builds hunger and death for the people of Colombia must leave now. Life must be restored, democracy must be restored, and the slogan “Abelardo, resign now!” must become the slogan of the majority of the Colombian people. An agreement will eventually be made to transition back so that the Constitution of Colombia and the laws in favor of the Colombian people prevail. But from here on out—and that is why we must move to a national strike, that is why we must move to a general strike—within the people’s right of expression and decision, an illegitimate government that goes against the interests of the Colombian population must leave now. Gustavo Petro

De la Espriella told Petro that he would never accept they “attack democracy, promote a coup d’état or attempt to destroy Colombia, just as he did when he was a guerrilla fighter.”

The president claimed that the former President and congressional opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “have no moral authority whatsoever. However, as I tell you, I will not accept them attacking democracy, attacking institutionality, or promoting a coup d’état in an attempt to destroy Colombia.”

De la Espriella repeated his threat to extradite his predecessor if requested to do so by the administration of his ally, US President Donald Trump.

I make a direct call to the judicial authorities of the United States so that investigations related to acts of corruption, drug trafficking, or any other criminal conduct move forward with full rigor and the independence of the judicial system in the United States. Petro’s government was a criminal enterprise, and international laws and provisions were violated. The United States has jurisdiction to investigate him, prosecute him, and hopefully imprison him. Let the North American justice system act, let the whole truth be known, let the evidence be examined, and let those found responsible answer before the law without regard for anything other than the application of the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president has tried to criminalize the opposition and the former government ever since taking office in August without much success.
