World.title: Mexico Swings to US$298M Trade Surplus
World.content:
MEXICO · ECONOMY · TRADE

Mexico swung back to a trade surplus in October 2026, selling US$86.01 billion of goods abroad and buying US$85.71 billion, INEGI, the national statistics institute, said on Friday 27 November. The gap of about US$298 million compares with a deficit of US$606 million in September.

For US readers, the numbers show how closely Mexican factories and American buyers are tied. Export growth of more than 30% in a year is led by electronics, and imports grew slightly faster.

Exports outside the oil sector reached US$84.27 billion, up 31.2%. Oil exports were US$1.74 billion, down 3.4%.

The balance counts merchandise only. Services such as tourism and the money migrants send home are not in it.

Non-oil exports to the United States rose 36.8%, and manufacturing exports outside the auto industry rose 41.3%. Oil imports cost US$6.03 billion, up 52.7% in the month.

The month also reverses a short run in the other direction. August had closed with a surplus of about US$605 million before September’s deficit, so the balance has swung twice in three months.

Over the first nine months, exports totalled US$627.19 billion, up 30.4%. Among goods, electrical and electronic equipment surged 73.6%.

Car and truck exports rose 5.6%, with sales to the United States up 7.2% and sales to other markets down 3.3%. Over the first ten months of 2026, exports totalled US$713.20 billion, up 30.3%, and imports totalled US$703.65 billion, up 27.9%.

That leaves a cumulative surplus of about US$9.55 billion by our subtraction, close to the US$9.25 billion INEGI reported for January to September.

What Prediction Markets Say On Polymarket, about US$13,000 had been traded by 27 November, 9:01 a.m. ET, on whether the USMCA trade pact between the United States, Mexico and Canada is extended in 2026. Traders gave that outcome 4.8%. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Mexico is a major supplier of cars, electronics and farm goods to US shoppers, so these flows reach American prices and jobs directly. A surplus this thin leaves little cushion if tariffs or weaker US demand cut exports.

It is not yet clear whether October’s swing marks a lasting change, since September showed a deficit of US$606 million. INEGI also publishes a seasonally adjusted balance, which removes regular calendar swings, but that figure is not confirmed here.

World.title: Chile Jobless Rate Hits 10.0% as Jobs Fall
World.content:
CHILE · ECONOMY · JOBS

Chile’s unemployment rate reached 10.0% in the three months from August to October 2026, the national statistics institute INE reported on Friday 27 November. It stood at 9.8% in July to September and 8.4% a year earlier.

The figure arrived one day after Chile’s conservative president, José Antonio Kast, told more than 500 business leaders to hire and invest. For US investors who hold Chilean assets, it shows a labour market weakening just as the government asks companies to expand.

Key Facts What Unemployment hit 10.0% in August to October 2026, up 1.6 points from 8.4% a year earlier.

Who INE, Chile’s national statistics institute, published the data on Friday 27 November 2026.

Why Employment fell 0.4% in a year while the number of people seeking work grew 1.3%.

Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction market, gives 58.5% to no change at Chile’s December meeting (27 Nov, 9:01 a.m. ET).

Chile’s unemployment rate has climbed to a round 10%, and fewer people hold jobs than a year ago, even as more people look for work.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Chile unemployment Email address Follow

More people are looking for work, but fewer are finding it. The labour force grew 1.3% from a year earlier, while the number of employed people fell 0.4%, INE said.

The number of unemployed people jumped 19.7% in the year, INE’s figures show. Women were hit harder, with their jobless rate at 10.7%, up 1.9 points, against 9.4% for men, up 1.2 points.

In the Santiago Metropolitan Region the rate reached 10.5%, up 1.9 points from a year earlier, INE said. Jobs in information and communications there fell 23.5% and manufacturing jobs fell 9.4%.

The rate has crept up through the autumn: 9.5% in May to July, 9.6% in June to August and 9.8% in July to September, INE’s earlier releases show. Participation, the share of working-age people who work or look for work, rose 0.3 points to 62.2%, while the employment rate fell 0.7 points to 56.0%.

Job quality slipped as well. Wage jobs with a formal contract fell 2.6% in a year, while the informal share of employment rose to 27.0%, up 0.8 points, according to INE.

Total hours worked fell 1.0% in the year, and the average working week slipped to 36.3 hours. Nationally, employment fell 18.9% in information and communications, 11.5% in other services and 4.7% in manufacturing.

On a seasonally adjusted basis, which strips out regular holiday and harvest swings, the rate was 9.9%, up 0.3 points on the previous quarter. That suggests the rise is more than a seasonal blip.

Kast told the business leaders on Thursday 26 November: “Inviertan, contraten, a jugársela por Chile” (our translation: invest, hire, go all in for Chile). He asked them to restart postponed projects and avoid layoffs where possible and noted that his government turns one year old on 11 March.

Rosario Navarro, president of Sofofa, Chile’s manufacturers’ federation, answered: “Recibimos ese llamado con claridad” (we received that call clearly). She proposed a pact between companies, workers and the government on training, retraining and the flexibility to promote formal employment.

Gonzalo Arenas, the government’s spokesperson, said on Tuesday 24 November that a cabinet reshuffle would not change the picture. In his words: “el desempleo va a estar igual y la falta de crecimiento va a estar igual” (the unemployment will stay the same, and so will the lack of growth), adding that the measures aim to overcome unemployment and the cost of living over the medium and long term.

A weaker job market usually eases wage pressure, which the Central Bank of Chile weighs when it sets interest rates. The bank’s next rate decision comes in December.

What Prediction Markets Say On Polymarket, about US$46,000 had been traded by 27 November on the Central Bank of Chile’s December decision. Traders gave 58.5% to no change, 36.5% to a quarter-point rise and 3.5% to a rise of half a point or more. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

For US readers, the data matters because Chile is a US free-trade partner and the world’s top copper producer. A jobless rate at this level adds to doubts about consumer spending there.

INE has not said how much of the rise comes from people returning to the labour market. The next reading, for September to November, will show whether the climb continues.

How High Is Chile’s Unemployment Rate Now?

INE put it at 10.0% for August to October 2026. That is higher than both the previous quarter and a year earlier.

Why Is Chile’s Unemployment Rising?

Employment is shrinking while more people search for work. Losses are led by information and communications, other services and manufacturing.

What Does It Mean for Chile’s Central Bank?

Weak hiring can ease wage pressure, one input the bank weighs. Its next rate decision is due in December.

Sources: INE Chile, national unemployment release for August to October 2026, 27 November 2026; INE Chile, release for July to September 2026, 29 October 2026; remarks by President José Antonio Kast and Sofofa president Rosario Navarro at the Sofofa annual industry meeting, 26 November 2026; remarks by government spokesperson Gonzalo Arenas, 24 November 2026; Polymarket, 27 November 2026, 9:01 a.m. ET.

World.title: Somali Clan Leader Rallies Armed Fighters
World.content:
A clan leader's call to be ready comes weeks after a disputed state election, with the state government silent and key details unconfirmed.

Soldiers of the Somali National Army stand guard on a street in Burhakaba, the town in Bay region near this week's fighting. File photo, 28 February 2013. (Photo: AMISOM Public Information, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

SOMALIA · BRIEF

Hundreds of armed local fighters gathered in Beledweyne, a city in central Somalia, on Thursday 26 November, according to an account we could not independently confirm. A clan leader told them to prepare for “a significant task” in the coming days.

Ugaas Yusuf Ugaas Hassan, paramount traditional leader of the Hawadle clan in Hiiraan region, visited the fighters at the Lamagalay camp and in the Hiiraan Bile area on the city’s northern outskirts. His title, ugaas, means traditional clan leader, and he did not say what the task is, where it lies or when it begins.

What Hundreds of fighters were reported assembled; we could not confirm the number.

Where Beledweyne, capital of Hiiraan region in Hirshabelle, a state in central Somalia.

Open The task he announced, its targets and its timing are unknown.

As of. 27 November 2026, 13:30 GMT

A clan leader’s call to be ready comes weeks after a disputed state election, with the state government silent and key details unconfirmed.

Beledweyne is the capital of Hiiraan region in Hirshabelle, one of Somalia’s federal member states. The fighters were said to be equipped with military gear and paid salaries, but that account comes from a single Somali source and we could not verify it.

With Ugaas Yusuf were federal lawmaker Abdirahman Ahmed Osman Gurey, Mayor Duale Adan Garase, elders and military officers. Gurey told the fighters: “The struggle is underway, and we hope it will not be prolonged.”

File photo, 27 February 2013: a Somali soldier on guard in Burhakaba, with army and African Union vehicles behind him. (Photo: AMISOM Public Information, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ugaas Yusuf told them: “We have reached a point where it is being said that you are nothing and have no say.” He added: “Prepare yourselves; in the coming days, we will undertake a significant task.”

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Guinea-Bissau's junta pushes its vote to 2028” Get the brief

The mobilisation follows a disputed state election. On Saturday 24 October, Hirshabelle lawmakers re-elected President Ali Abdullahi Hussein Gudlawe, who has led the state since 2020, in Jowhar, the state capital, by 81 votes to 13, the state House speaker Abdihakim Luqman announced.

In a communiqué issued on 12 November, after consultations, Hawadle elders said the vote lacked sufficient consultation, especially of Hiiraan residents, and called for a conference of clans, politicians and elders. On Sunday 15 November, at a demonstration in Beledweyne, Ugaas Yusuf said his community would not reverse its opposition despite pressure.

At the end of October, armed Macawisley fighters, community militias that have fought the al-Qaeda-linked insurgent group al-Shabaab, seized parts of the Hiiraan administration compound in Beledweyne. One account says this followed Hirshabelle’s dismissal of regional governor Mohamed Hussein Mohamed, who refused to leave.

One account says clashes on 19 November between local militia fighters and Djiboutian troops of the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), the African Union force in the country, left at least one fighter dead and six wounded at Ugaas Khaliif Airport, Beledweyne’s airport. We could not confirm this or a reported flight suspension at the airport.

The stakes reach beyond one city, because militias that fought al-Shabaab now face a state government whose legitimacy their elders reject. The federal electoral rules are also in flux, as our report on Somalia’s party-list voting law explains.

The Hirshabelle administration had published no response to the mobilisation or the warning on Friday, and we could not reach it. Still unknown are who pays and equips the fighters, and whether Mogadishu or the African Union will mediate.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Ugaas Yusuf Ugaas Hassan?

He is a prominent traditional leader of the Hawadle clan in Hiiraan region. He has said publicly that his community will not drop its opposition to the state election.

What are the Macawisley fighters?

They are community militias that have fought al-Shabaab in central Somalia. We have not confirmed whether the fighters seen this week belong to them.

Has the Hirshabelle government responded?

No public response had appeared as of 27 November 2026, and we could not reach the administration. We will report its position when it is stated.

World.title: Freetown Floods Beat City Drainage Defences
World.content:
Freetown had no flood this size since 2022, the Red Cross says, until one night of rain exceeded the capacity of its flood defences.

Photo: David Hond / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

SIERRA LEONE · FLOODS

Rain that fell for about six hours in the early hours of Monday 3 August 2026 overwhelmed flood defences in Freetown, the capital of Sierra Leone. It was the city’s worst flood emergency since 2022.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), a global humanitarian network, set out the damage on 18 August 2026. The European Union followed on 24 August with humanitarian funding for the Sierra Leone Red Cross Society.

Key Facts Who Sierra Leone Red Cross Society, a national relief charity, backed by the Red Cross federation.

What Flash floods hit Freetown on 3 August 2026, killing four people and affecting 8,915.

Money Red Cross emergency fund release of about US$444,000; EU aid of about US$192,000 via the Red Cross.

When The relief operation started on 13 August 2026 and runs for four months.

As of. 27 November 2026, 13:30 GMT

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Guinea-Bissau's junta pushes its vote to 2028” Get the brief

Freetown had no flood this size since 2022, the Red Cross says, until one night of rain exceeded the capacity of its flood defences.

The IFRC’s operation document says Freetown had not faced a flood emergency of this magnitude since 2022, “largely due to sustained investments in drainage improvements” and other flood measures by the government and its partners. That record ended with one night of rain.

The document says the rain on 3 August 2026 “exceeded the capacity of existing mitigation measures and generated humanitarian impacts far beyond normal seasonal flooding patterns.” Dense housing, slope failures and soil erosion made the damage worse, it adds.

File photo: a street in Lumley, Freetown, one of the districts named among the worst hit on 3 August 2026. (Photo: Victor turay / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

The National Disaster Management Agency (NDMA), Sierra Leone’s state disaster body, said on 4 August that the rain lasted six to seven hours in the early hours of Monday. It reported three deaths in Metchem Community, where a wall collapsed on a five-year-old girl, her mother and her grandmother.

The agency also said two children were missing, and that more than 300 houses in Portor Community, in the Juba Hills, were completely flooded. At 44 Femi Turner Drive (the IFRC places it in Goderich), a perimeter wall fell and three vehicles were washed away.

By 18 August the IFRC counted four deaths, 1,763 families (8,915 people) affected and more than 700 houses flooded or damaged. It also found 18 community boreholes contaminated and one community school damaged, with thousands of people displaced.

The two accounts differ, as early counts often do: the agency listed three dead and two children missing, the IFRC four dead. The IFRC places the fourth death in Portor Community and does not say whether any children were found.

Besides Portor and Metchem, the IFRC names 44 Femi Turner Drive in Goderich, Regent Road in Lumley, Bonga Town and settlements along the Cain Water Stream among the worst-hit places. Many residents had little time to leave because the rain fell overnight, it says.

The IFRC released 370,924 Swiss francs (CHF), about US$444,000, from its Disaster Response Emergency Fund (DREF) for an operation that runs from 13 August to 31 December 2026. Part of the money, CHF 23,413 (about US$28,000), is budgeted for livelihoods and basic needs such as cash support for traders and small businesses.

The European Union delegation to Sierra Leone announced EUR 175,000 (about US$192,000) in humanitarian aid in Freetown on 24 August 2026. The EU says the money goes through the Sierra Leone Red Cross Society as part of its contribution to the IFRC emergency fund.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

The EU says its money helps the Sierra Leone Red Cross assist 5,100 people in 27 flood-affected communities, the same number the IFRC operation targets. It pays for cash transfers, emergency shelter, water and sanitation, livelihood recovery and health support.

Dollar figures use RT, a financial data provider: one Swiss franc closed at US$1.1965 on 27 November 2026, and one euro at US$1.097 on 26 November. The IFRC reports in Swiss francs, and the EU in euros.

For readers in the United States, the stakes are relief money and health, and background on the country is in our Sierra Leone Explained 2026 guide and our geopolitics explainer. The IFRC said that contaminated boreholes raise the risk of diarrhoea and cholera, and that health authorities were monitoring cholera, acute diarrhoea and malaria.

The danger had not passed when the IFRC wrote. Persistent rain keeps the soil saturated, it said, and more communities in Freetown and other districts faced a higher chance of flash floods, erosion and local landslides as the rainy season continued.

The IFRC says there is a “critical need to enhance risk awareness, strengthen community-based early warning and preparedness systems”, which points the response toward warnings rather than new drains. The operation ends on 31 December 2026, and we found no government cost estimate or announcement of new drainage works after 3 August.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why were the 2026 floods so damaging in Freetown?

The Red Cross federation says the rain was heavier than existing flood measures were built to handle. Dense neighbourhoods on slopes and eroding soil made the damage worse.

Is there a health risk after the floods?

Yes. Contaminated boreholes raise the risk of diarrhoea and cholera, and health authorities were watching for outbreaks when the Red Cross wrote.

Who is paying for the relief?

The Red Cross emergency fund and the European Union are backing aid through the Sierra Leone Red Cross Society. The government has not published its own cost estimate.

World.title: Tanzania Cabinet Backs a Real Estate Law
World.content:
Tanzania's Cabinet has cleared the way for a bill to regulate developers, brokers and managers, but the draft, the regulator's powers and the timetable are still unknown.

File photo, 2019. Downtown Dar es Salaam, Tanzania’s largest city, seen from the harbour with a passenger ferry in front. (Photo: Dicksonpicha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Tanzania: Politics

Tanzania’s Cabinet, the government’s top decision-making body, has approved the drafting of a law to regulate the real estate industry, the Ministry of Lands, Housing and Human Settlements Development said in comments published on Friday 27 November 2026. The ministry did not state the date of the Cabinet decision.

Upendo Matotola, the ministry’s director of Real Estate, said officials are already writing the bill. Once an initial draft exists, it will go to industry stakeholders for review before it reaches Parliament.

What. Cabinet, Tanzania’s top government body, approved drafting a real estate law; the decision date is unstated.

Next. The draft goes to industry stakeholders, then Parliament; no dates have been announced.

Tanzania’s Cabinet has cleared the way for a bill to regulate developers, brokers and managers, but the draft, the regulator’s powers and the timetable are still unknown.

The approval comes about 17 months after a 1 July 2025 interview in which Matotola said that the ministry had gathered industry input and that the draft review was with government authorities for scrutiny before Parliament. The plan still needed Cabinet and parliamentary approval at that point.

She said then that the planned law should create a regulatory body, and that the ministry was finalising the land policy before seeking Cabinet and parliamentary approval. Developers at the time asked for an authority focused on development rather than a purely regulatory one.

The Dar es Salaam skyline with the Indian Ocean on the horizon. File photo. (Photo: Ali Damji, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

One developer, who was not named, said the industry needs guidelines and clear terms that encourage growth. It is not known whether the planned authority will have a development role.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Guinea-Bissau's junta pushes its vote to 2028” Get the brief

The ministry set up a Real Estate Unit in July 2022 to coordinate and promote the industry. The law is meant to complement that work with specific legal provisions for the industry.

The law now being drafted would add a regulatory body to that work, the ministry says. It would oversee property developers, brokers, managers and other participants.

Matotola said in July 2025 that the lack of oversight had let substandard properties flood the market. She has argued that investors need reliable market data.

“Investors need accurate data to make informed decisions and avoid risky investments,” she has said. She added that reliable market information would ensure fair pricing.

On 7 July 2026, at the 50th annual Dar es Salaam International Trade Fair, then Lands Minister Leonard Akwilapo said the proposal for a Real Estate Regulatory Authority had passed key government processes and was at an advanced stage. “We have reached a good stage,” he said, adding that the ministry was completing the remaining procedures before the plan goes to the Cabinet.

He said the regulator would ensure that only registered practitioners offer real estate services. Akwilapo has since been replaced, and State House, the president’s office, named David Silinde, formerly deputy minister for agriculture, as the new Minister for Lands, Housing and Human Settlements Development on 25 November 2026.

We covered the wider changes in our report of the reshuffle of 26 November. Silinde now holds the portfolio that is drafting the bill.

Industry voices welcomed the idea in July 2026. Stephano Kamote, market manager at the property firm Eager Sky Co Ltd, said: “A regulator will make the market more attractive because investors will have greater confidence that they are dealing with recognised professionals.”

Batuli Sogora, marketing manager at Venny Construction and Real Estate Co Ltd, a construction firm, welcomed the regulator after years of calls from the industry. “We have been pushing for this regulator for many years,” Sogora said.

Independent analyst Oscar Mkude said on 27 November that a law would formalise the property market, and protect buyers and investors. He warned that “the main risk is that this is another layer of bureaucracy in an already bureaucracy-heavy country.”

Mkude said excessive administrative powers could discourage investment and favour financially stronger or well-connected players, leaving smaller developers struggling. He said the law should anticipate future change without adding excessive bureaucracy.

For foreign investors and diaspora buyers, the ministry’s list of gaps describes the risks they face today, from unregistered brokers to opaque pricing. A licensing regime and market-data rules could change how a buyer or fund checks a Tanzanian property deal.

The ministry has not said what the bill will contain, how the regulator will be funded or what powers it will hold. No date has been announced for the stakeholder consultation or for Parliament.

Matotola said the timeframe depends on stakeholder feedback and further reviews. The next visible step is that review of the initial draft.

Readers can follow property and policy stories on our Tanzania page. Any date for the review will matter to developers, brokers and buyers alike.

Related coverage: Tanzania Splits Foreign Ministry in Two

Frequently Asked Questions

What has Tanzania’s Cabinet approved?

It has approved the drafting of a law for the real estate industry. The ministry did not state when the Cabinet decided.

Who would the new regulator oversee?

According to the ministry, it would oversee property developers, brokers, managers and other participants. Its powers and funding have not been set out.

Why does it matter to foreign buyers?

Rules on licensing and market data could change how overseas buyers check a deal. Until the bill is public, the detail is unknown.

Sources: Ministry of Lands, Housing and Human Settlements Development, statements of its Director of Real Estate, 1 July 2025 and 27 November 2026; Minister Leonard Akwilapo, remarks at the 50th Dar es Salaam International Trade Fair, 7 July 2026; State House statement, 25 November 2026.

World.title: Tanzania Splits Foreign Ministry in Two
World.content:
Tanzania now has a ministry devoted to its work in the East African Community, the regional bloc, separate from diplomacy. Until now that work sat inside the foreign ministry.

File photo, 2013. The statue of Julius Nyerere in Nyerere Square in Dodoma, Tanzania's capital. (Photo: Mchiriku, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Tanzania: Politics

President Samia Suluhu Hassan has split Tanzania’s foreign-affairs ministry in two, creating a separate Ministry of East African Cooperation, according to a State House statement announced on Wednesday 25 November 2026. State House, the president’s office, also divided the Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries into two, so that two ministries became four.

On Friday 27 November, at a swearing-in ceremony for the new appointees at State House in Dar es Salaam, Samia explained why she had separated East African work from diplomacy. The reasoning is below.

Key Facts Who. President Samia Suluhu Hassan announced the split in a State House statement on 25 November.

What. Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation became two ministries; Livestock and Fisheries also became two.

Who leads. Mahmoud Thabit Kombo keeps foreign affairs; Angellah Kairuki, formerly the technology minister, heads East African Cooperation.

Why. Samia says East African matters had been overshadowed inside the combined ministry.

As of 27 November 2026, 14:00 GMT

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Guinea-Bissau's junta pushes its vote to 2028” Get the brief

Tanzania now has a ministry devoted to its work in the East African Community, the regional bloc, separate from diplomacy. Until now that work sat inside the foreign ministry.

The statement turned the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and East African Cooperation into the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation plus a new Ministry of East African Cooperation. It also split the Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries into a Ministry of Livestock and a Ministry of Fisheries, and said the changes were meant to strengthen the performance of government.

The president gave her own reasons on Friday 27 November at State House in Dar es Salaam. She said East African cooperation matters had been overshadowed by the wide range of work handled by the combined ministry.

Aerial view of Dodoma, Tanzania’s capital, seen from the International Space Station. File photo, 2009. (Photo: NASA, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Samia said her recent visit to Uganda showed her that many of the issues discussed centred on East African cooperation, so a dedicated ministry was needed. She said the change is meant to give the East African cooperation agenda greater focus and momentum.

The new ministry takes its name from the East African Community, the regional bloc that Tanzania belongs to. Mahmoud Thabit Kombo stays foreign minister, while Angellah Kairuki, formerly minister for communications and technology, now leads East African Cooperation.

Who Got Which Job

Dr Bashiru Ally, who headed the combined Livestock and Fisheries ministry, leads the new Ministry of Livestock. Hamis Mwinjuma, known as MwanaFA, becomes minister for Fisheries.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

David Silinde, formerly deputy minister for agriculture, moves to head Lands, Housing and Human Settlements Development, and Beng’i Issa takes the technology ministry. Dr Ayub Rioba, a former head of the Tanzania Broadcasting Corporation, the state broadcaster, replaces Gerson Msigwa as government spokesperson, and our report of the reshuffle of 26 November carries the earlier details.

In a smaller reshuffle on Wednesday 5 July 2023, Samia had already turned the Ministry of Finance and Planning into the Ministry of Finance. The same change created a Ministry of Planning and Investment.

For a US diplomat, investor or aid group, the split changes whom to call. Regional matters now have their own minister in Kairuki, while fisheries and livestock have separate ministers in Mwinjuma and Ally.

Related coverage: Tanzania Cabinet Backs a Real Estate Law

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Tanzania create a separate East African Cooperation ministry?

President Samia Suluhu Hassan said the topic had been overshadowed inside the combined ministry. She wants the agenda to have its own focus and momentum.

Who runs the new ministries?

Angellah Kairuki leads East African Cooperation, Dr Bashiru Ally leads Livestock and Hamis Mwinjuma leads Fisheries. Mahmoud Thabit Kombo keeps Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation.

World.title: Accra Eviction Leaves One Dead, Five Hurt
World.content:
A railway clearance in central Accra ended with one person dead and five soldiers hurt, and the mayor’s claim about Nigerian nationals is unconfirmed by police.

The Kwame Nkrumah Interchange at Circle in Accra, where the planned Sky Train network was to have its central terminal, pictured in June 2023. (Photo: Goldenwabbit, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Society: Ghana

One person died and five soldiers were hurt on Wednesday 25 November 2026, as police and troops cleared an Accra railway settlement. Linda Ocloo, the Greater Accra Regional Minister, confirmed the toll at the scene near Kwame Nkrumah Circle, a major junction and bus hub in central Accra.

Rio Times membership One dollar for your first month. All premium analysis. Enter your email and the link comes by mail. Privacy Send me the offer

Accra’s mayor, Michael Kpakpo Allotey, said on 26 November that some Nigerian nationals led the resistance, a claim police have not confirmed. He named nobody, and he spoke of one injured soldier where the minister counted five.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Key Facts Who. Regional Minister Linda Ocloo and Accra Mayor Michael Kpakpo Allotey, with police and soldiers.

What. One person died and five soldiers were hurt as a railway settlement was cleared.

Where. ECOMOG Railway Lane, a squatter settlement behind the STC intercity coach station, near Circle, Accra.

Open. We found no police statement, no named suspect and no confirmation of the mayor’s claim.

As of. 27 November 2026, 13:00 GMT

A railway clearance in central Accra ended with one person dead and five soldiers hurt, and the mayor’s claim about Nigerian nationals is unconfirmed by police.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

A fire on Monday 16 November 2026 destroyed more than 100 wooden structures, many used as homes and businesses, near a bus yard, Ghana’s Fire Service said. One man died returning for his motorbike, a separate case, and the cause of the fire has not been officially established.

On Tuesday 17 November, Ocloo said the whole settlement would be cleared. At the scene on Wednesday she said it was the third fire there.

Kwame Nkrumah Circle, known as Circle, is a major road junction and bus hub in central Accra. The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA), the city government, joined police, troops and the regional administration on Wednesday.

ECOMOG Railway Lane is the local name of the settlement, not the West African peacekeeping force of that name. Ocloo, as Greater Accra Regional Minister, is appointed by the President, with Parliament’s approval, to represent him in the region and direct its administration (Article 256 of the 1992 Constitution).

Allotey ordered a 40-day “decongestion” drive from Monday 9 November 2026, with police and the Korle Klottey Municipal Assembly, a local council. It cleared hawkers and roadside stalls at bus stops including Circle, and reached Lapaz, another Accra district, on Tuesday 10 November.

The AMA’s communications head, Gilbert Nii Ankrah, said the drive runs 40 days to reclaim bus stops and ease traffic before Christmas. Okaikwei South MP Ernest Adomako criticised the destruction of traders’ goods in a sweep at Circle on 9 November.

Between 9 and 25 November 2026, the city assembly cleared stalls at bus stops, and the regional administration and the assembly then cleared a railway settlement after a fire, citing traffic relief before Christmas for the bus-stop drive (the AMA) and safety after the fires for the railway clearance (Ocloo). Ocloo has warned that anyone who returns to rebuild will be prosecuted, and no relocation date has been announced.

The Clash on the Railway Line

Police and troops moved into the settlement, behind the STC intercity bus station, to clear wooden structures along the line towards Agbogbloshie. Agbogbloshie is a market district of Accra.

Allotey said stones were thrown at the team as it arrived on Wednesday, that warning shots followed and that a stone hit his leg. Ocloo said some residents resisted and that reinforcements were called.

Ocloo said at the scene on Wednesday that she could not establish how the person died. “Unfortunately, we lost one life,” she said, and the five injured soldiers are being treated at the armed forces’ 37 Military Hospital in Accra.

Ocloo said at the scene on Wednesday that residents had quickly begun raising new wooden structures. She said officials therefore had to return with enforcement to save lives.

Ocloo warned that anyone found coming back to redevelop the site will be prosecuted. She said officials had met the community and set up an eight-member committee that promised no redevelopment.

Ocloo said officials were making plans to relocate residents, but she gave no date, no place and no number of residents affected. Residents with problems, she said, should turn to the AMA and the Greater Accra Regional Coordinating Council, the regional administration.

Independence Arch in Accra, in a file photo. It does not show the demolition or the Circle settlement. Photo: Ijon / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Accra (Ghana) Email address Follow

The Mayor’s Unconfirmed Claim

In a radio interview on 26 November, Allotey said some Nigerian nationals led the resistance on the line from Circle towards Agbogbloshie. He said: “It is the Nigerians [who] decided to attack us.”

He gave no names, and we have not seen a recording of the interview or any police finding that supports the claim. As of 27 November 2026 we found no police statement on the clash and no comment from the Nigerian High Commission, Nigeria’s diplomatic mission in Accra.

It is not known how the person died, who the person was, how many lost homes, or where they will be moved. No date for relocation has been given, and the nationality of anyone involved in the clash is not established.

Circle is where intercity coaches and city buses meet, and the clearance took place beside the STC coach station. The mayor’s claim concerns nationality, and no police finding on it has been published.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened at the railway line near Circle in Accra?

Police and troops cleared a railway settlement, some residents resisted, and a person died while soldiers were hurt. Regional Minister Linda Ocloo confirmed the toll at the scene.

Have police confirmed the mayor’s claim about Nigerian nationals?

No. Mayor Michael Kpakpo Allotey made the claim in a radio interview, and we found no police statement or public comment from the Nigerian High Commission.

What happens to the people who lived in the settlement?

Ocloo said officials were making plans to relocate residents but gave no date or place. She warned that anyone who rebuilds on the site will be prosecuted.

World.title: Costa Rica Holds 58% of the World’s Quetzals as Northern Forests Vanish
World.content:
Costa Rica is home to nearly six of every ten resplendent quetzals left on Earth, according to a new study that puts the species’ total population at about 334,000 birds, less than half of the most recent published figure. The research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Bird Conservation International, estimates that about 193,900 quetzals live in Costa Rica’s highland forests and another 83,700 across the border in Panama. Together the two countries hold roughly 83% of the global population.

The remaining birds, about 56,500, are spread across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua, where the study found that the bird’s breeding forests have been cut roughly in half in three decades.

Lead author Edward H. Backus, an independent scholar based in Oregon, worked with four co-authors, among them Sofia Solórzano of the National Autonomous University of Mexico and Knut Eisermann of Bird Studies Guatemala. The team combined satellite forest records for 1990, 2011 and 2021 with elevation data to map cloud forest between 1,500 and 3,000 meters (4,900 and 9,800 feet), the band where quetzals nest.

They found about 864,000 hectares (2.1 million acres) of core breeding habitat still standing across Mesoamerica in 2021. Some 361,000 hectares (892,000 acres), close to 30% of the forest that existed in 1990, had disappeared. The losses were far from even. El Salvador lost 73% of its quetzal breeding habitat over the period, Mexico 65%, Guatemala 53%, Nicaragua 52% and Honduras 37%. Costa Rica lost 8%, or about 32,800 hectares (81,100 acres), and Panama 5%.

The difference comes down largely to one mountain range. The Cordillera de Talamanca, which runs from Costa Rica into Panama and includes La Amistad International Park, holds a single block of breeding forest of about 442,000 hectares (1.09 million acres). The next largest, in Guatemala’s Sierra de las Minas, covers about 50,700 hectares (125,000 acres), less than one-eighth the size.

Protection also sets the south apart. Of the roughly 388,000 hectares (958,000 acres) of core habitat the study mapped in Costa Rica, about 371,000 hectares (917,000 acres) of quetzal habitat lay inside protected areas in 2021. The bird continues to turn up in new corners of that network, including a first record at a Cartago refuge last month.

The quetzal is divided into two subspecies, and the study shows them on very different paths. The northern form, found from Mexico to Nicaragua, lost 51% of its breeding habitat between 1990 and 2021. The southern form, found only in Costa Rica and Panama, lost 7%.

On that basis the authors recommend that the International Union for Conservation of Nature move the species from Near Threatened to Vulnerable on its Red List, and they argue the northern subspecies warrants a higher category still. Habitat for the species as a whole shrank 26% between 2000 and 2021, just under the 30% threshold for a threatened listing but within the study’s margin of error.

The authors identify the conversion of forest to farmland and pasture as the main threat. They also point to climate pressures on cloud forest, including drought, fire and the loss of cloud cover, a concern already documented in the drying of Monteverde.

The population figure carries real uncertainty, the authors caution. It rests on assumptions about how many birds a given area of forest supports, and field counts are sparse and were made with different methods at different times. For Costa Rica and Panama the team assumed 50 birds per 100 hectares (247 acres) after halving the upper field estimates to avoid overcounting.

Even so, the new total is a sharp downward revision. A rough estimate published in 2023 by Alan F. Poole, a co-author of the new paper, had put the population at about 770,000.

The authors single out the Talamanca highlands as a priority for long-term monitoring. The quetzal is also among the main draws of a birdwatching sector that has become a growth area for Costa Rican tourism, which leaves the country holding both the largest share of the species and the largest stake in what happens to it.

World.title: President Puts Illegal Gold Mining Losses at Crucitas Near $2 Billion
World.content:
President Laura Fernández said Wednesday that illegal miners have taken about $2 billion in gold from Crucitas, in northern Costa Rica near the Nicaraguan border. She called the figure preliminary and did not explain how it was calculated. Speaking at her weekly press conference at Casa Presidencial, Fernández described the mining as a blatant violation of national sovereignty and said the problem was getting out of the government’s hands.

She blamed the Legislative Assembly, saying a negotiated solution has been available for nearly three years without becoming law. Fernández said the gold belongs to Costa Rica and that its value could have paid for roads, schools, health services and pensions. She said an ounce was trading at $3,674 this week, which in her view raises the cost of every month without a solution.

The $2 billion estimate is not new. Former ruling-party legislator Pilar Cisneros cited the same figure in June, and no methodology was released with Wednesday’s statement. The president also pointed to a 61.3% rise in Nicaragua’s gold exports, without saying how much of that gold she believes came out of Crucitas.

On enforcement, Fernández said authorities have made 537 apprehensions in Crucitas, 243 of them tied to immigration status and illegal gold extraction. Police seized 2,000 sacks of mining sediment in the most recent operation. Security Minister Gerald Campos said recent operations in Crucitas and nearby Conchudita cost the state more than 30 million colones (about $67,000). Those operations have included US helicopter support for the crackdown on illegal gold mining. Fernández also linked the mining zone to the smuggling of cocaine, crack and marijuana and to human trafficking.

She said the excavations and settling ponds used by the miners threaten aquifers and forest and estimated that restoring the area would cost more than $20 million. She questioned whether restoration would hold while illegal mining continues. Crucitas was the site of a proposed open-pit gold mine that never opened. Costa Rica banned open-pit metal mining in 2010, and the deposit has since drawn illegal miners, whom the government says cross mainly from Nicaragua.

The government’s proposal would allow the gold to be auctioned, with proceeds going to education, health and security. Opposition blocs including the National Liberation Party and the Broad Front have held it up with motions in the Assembly. Fernández also asked lawmakers to advance a separate bill that would toughen penalties for illegal mining, even if the broader Crucitas plan remains stalled.

Presidency and Finance Minister Rodrigo Chaves has said he would recommend that she call a referendum on the proposal. Fernández has said she is considering putting Crucitas gold mining to a national vote but has not decided. The president is scheduled to meet Friday, Nov. 27, with residents of San Carlos, Cutris, Crucitas and nearby communities to discuss new measures.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens 4 Days of Walk-In Driving Tests in San José
World.content:
If you have had trouble landing an appointment for your practical driving test, you get four days next week to skip that step. From Monday, Nov. 30, through Thursday, Dec. 3, you can show up at Ciudad Vial in San José and take the test with no appointment and no login to the online booking system.

The days are split by vehicle, so go on the one that matches yours. Car tests for the B1 license run Monday, Nov. 30, and Tuesday, Dec. 1. Motorcycle tests for the A1, A2 and A3 licenses run Wednesday, Dec. 2, and Thursday, Dec. 3.

Testing runs from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. on all four days, longer than the usual schedule. That includes Tuesday, Dec. 1, a national holiday. Sindy Coto, director of Educación Vial, the road education office of the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT), said staff will work that day because many people are expected to use the day off to take the test.

Expect company. When the office ran the same walk-in format for motorcycles only in the last week of October, 1,279 people turned up over five days. Arriving early gives you the best chance of getting through. Ciudad Vial is the MOPT testing track beside Parque de la Paz, in southern San José.

You still have to meet the normal requirements. You must have already passed the theory test, and you need a valid ID in good condition. Bring the vehicle you will test in, along with its circulation permit (derecho de circulación) and its technical card (tarjeta técnica vehicular). The examiner needs to confirm the vehicle is legally on the road before you drive it on the track.

Pay the 5,000-colón test fee (about $11) before you go. You can pay at any authorized bank or financial institution, and you need to bring the receipt with you. You also need a medical certificate (dictamen médico) issued within the last 180 days. If yours is older than that, get a new one before you go.

Two groups will be turned away. If you already have a practical test appointment booked, you cannot use the walk-in days. And if you failed the practical test recently, you have to wait out the 20 business days that must pass before a retake. The system blocks both cases automatically, so there is no way around it at the gate.

It is worth practicing before you go, in a year when nearly half of all driving tests have been failed. In the October session, 940 riders passed and 339 failed, a pass rate of 73 percent.

The mistakes that failed people were basic ones. Riders put a foot down or crossed the lines in the parallel-line and zigzag exercises, ignored road signs and pavement markings, knocked over or brushed cones, and forgot to use their turn signals. Educación Vial is asking everyone to arrive well prepared.

Coto said the October session produced very good results, which is why the office is repeating it and adding car tests this time. Educación Vial said the walk-in days are meant for people whose work or study schedules have kept them from finishing the process of getting a license.

World.title: Costa Rica Will End 2026 Short of Its 2019 Visitor Record, Forecast Shows
World.content:
Costa Rica is on course to receive about 3.05 million international visitors in 2026, a gain of 3.6% over last year that would still leave us short of the record 3.14 million who arrived in 2019, according to a projection by the Center for Tourism Studies (CET). The center’s scenarios range from 3.03 million to 3.08 million.

Reaching the central figure would require November and December to roughly match the 594,530 arrivals recorded in the same two months of 2025, according to a Tico Times calculation based on the published figures. The year began at a record pace. The first quarter brought 1,033,777 visitors, 11.3% more than a year earlier and the first time that period had surpassed its 2019 level, the CET reported.

The growth stopped there. From January through October, arrivals by all points of entry totaled 2,454,330, an increase of 4.5%, and all of that gain came in the first three months. April through October brought 1,420,553 visitors, nearly unchanged from the same stretch of 2025.

Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), said the cumulative growth largely reflects the strong first quarter. The most recent months were weaker. October brought 144,010 visitors, 1.1% fewer than a year earlier and the third consecutive monthly decline, after drops of 5.1% in August and 2.4% in September. Across the three months, the country received 14,767 fewer visitors than in the same period of 2025, Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) figures show.

Flight schedules have thinned along with arrivals. The CET counted 523 weekly flights to Costa Rica in the third week of November, compared with 609 a year earlier, and 82 routes against 90. All 14 routes that were discontinued served Juan Santamaría International Airport near San José, which now has 94 fewer weekly flights, while Liberia gained eight. The capital’s airport has lost arrivals for seven straight months as Guanacaste has grown.

CET director Víctor Umaña said airlines reassign aircraft according to cost and demand, and that routes to San José, which are the most sensitive to price, are the first to be cut. Former Tourism Minister Gustavo Segura attributed the capital’s decline to the exit of the low-cost carrier Spirit, ticket prices, oil prices and the country’s international image.

Analysts also point to the high cost of visiting and operating in Costa Rica, an appreciated exchange rate, weak transport infrastructure, insecurity and growing competition from Mexico, the Dominican Republic, Colombia and the rest of Central America. The high season runs through early April. Arrival figures for November, expected next month, will give the first reading on whether the forecast holds.

World.title: King Tides Peak on Costa Rica’s Pacific Coast and Run Through Saturday
World.content:
If you are on Costa Rica’s Pacific coast this week, expect the sea to come higher up the beach than usual through Saturday. Unusually high tides, often called king tides, peaked before dawn Thursday and will return each early morning and afternoon until Nov. 28. The University of Costa Rica’s oceanographic information unit, MIO-CIMAR, forecast the highest water between 2 a.m. and 4 a.m. Thursday. Golfito, on the southern Pacific, was expected to see the highest tide at 3.48 meters (11.4 feet).

Puntarenas, Bahía Herradura, Uvita and Bahía Culebra were each forecast at 3.08 meters (10.1 feet). The Gulf of Santa Elena, in northern Guanacaste, was forecast at 3.05 meters (10 feet) and Quepos at 2.87 meters (9.4 feet). Two things are stacking up. Tuesday’s full moon lined up the sun, Earth and moon, which produces the strongest tides of the lunar cycle. On top of that, El Niño has warmed the Pacific, and warmer water expands and raises the average sea level.

That extra height is what pushes seawater into streets and homes that normally stay dry, even when there is no rain or storm. MIO-CIMAR oceanographer Rodney Mora said the conditions can cause flooding and coastal erosion. The places to watch are low-lying coastal neighborhoods. During the last episode, from Oct. 26 to 31, high tides flooded homes in Puntarenas, where residents of Barrio El Carmen reported water up to their knees. The National Emergency Commission confirmed damage at Playa Zancudo, in Golfito, and Playa Preciosa, near Puerto Jiménez.

If you live or are staying close to the shoreline in those areas, move vehicles and anything that can be damaged by salt water off low ground before the early-morning and afternoon high tides. The water arrives on a schedule, so you have time to prepare. On the beach, you will have much less sand at high tide. Set up well above the wet line, and do not leave a car parked on the sand or beside an estuary mouth, because those are the first places the water reaches.

Swimming and boating are not ruled out. MIO-CIMAR said the tides by themselves do not create generally adverse conditions for bathers or for navigation. If you have booked a night tour during turtle nesting season in Guanacaste, ask your guide whether the tide changes the timing.

The Caribbean coast is not affected. The difference between low and high tide there is about 60 centimeters (2 feet), which is normal. Pacific tides are expected to return to their usual range on Sunday, Nov. 29. MIO-CIMAR updates its forecast every six hours at miocimar.ucr.ac.cr.

World.title: Costa Rica Doctors Call a February Strike as Surgery Waits Average 449 Days
World.content:
Costa Rica’s largest doctors’ union is calling on general practitioners, specialists and medical residents across the public health system to prepare for a general strike starting in February 2027, a move that could hit hospitals, clinics and the waiting lists millions of patients already depend on.

The National Medical Union (UMN) announced the call on Wednesday at a press conference alongside the nurses’ union ANPE and Siprocimeca, which represents medical professionals at the Costa Rican Social Security Fund (CCSS). The unions said the strike would cover both regular and overtime shifts. No specific start date has been set.

UMN president Randall Cabrera Garita said the union’s central demand is that the CCSS cancel a new set of rules on overtime pay. According to the union, the changes cut pay for work outside regular hours, including the extra shifts and on-call duty that keep many hospital services running, and could push more doctors out of the public system.

Cabrera also warned of what the union described as a creeping privatization of public health care. The unions argue that money meant for hospitals, clinics, local EBAIS health posts and new staff positions could instead flow to private providers, and they object to cuts in payments tied to programs meant to shorten surgery waiting lists.

A report published hours after the announcement brought that concern into focus. Massimo Manzi, executive director of the Costa Rican Health Chamber, which groups private providers, said the CCSS completed a market study last week on contracting private services for outpatient consultations, diagnostic tests and surgeries. Manzi said 24 providers took part. The CCSS had not responded to press questions about the study by this morning.

Manzi said the chamber wants providers outside the Greater Metropolitan Area included, and proposes contracts that would activate only when patients wait longer than the limits set by a Health Ministry decree. Any deal would have to follow Costa Rica’s public procurement law. The idea of paying private doctors to ease the backlog has been under discussion since earlier this year.

The scale of the backlog explains why both sides are pushing. The CCSS reported in late October that the average wait for surgery stood at 449 days, down from 535 days in April 2023. It also reported 816 people who had been waiting since 2021 or earlier, and an average wait of 769 days for a first orthopedic consultation.

The unions listed other grievances, including staff shortages, the departure of specialists, saturated emergency services and lagging infrastructure. They also cited the effects of the Public Finance Strengthening Law and the Public Employment Framework Law on pay. The UMN said the state owes the CCSS more than 4 trillion colones (about $9 billion), and complained that the government has blocked the appointment of a union representative to the CCSS board of directors.

Cabrera said the union has asked for a meeting with CCSS Executive President Mónica Taylor to discuss the demands before any walkout. The union said escalation can still be avoided if authorities open a dialogue, but that the strike call stands until the contested decisions are reviewed. Taylor had previously said the CCSS is reviewing its overtime payment tables. The institution had not issued a public response to the strike call by this morning.

The threat comes after a difficult year of labor conflict in the public health system, from a nurses’ strike at Hospital México in August to a nationwide health workers’ strike threat in September over unpaid salaries. Hospitals have also struggled with capacity, with some patients in Liberia waiting days in a chair for a bed.

The CCSS is the backbone of health care in Costa Rica. Workers, employers and legal residents, including foreign retirees and others with residency, are required to pay into the system, and most of Costa Rica relies on its hospitals and clinics. How the institution answers the unions over the coming weeks will help decide whether patients face a disruption in February, and whether more of their care ends up being delivered by private providers paid with public money.

World.title: Costa Rica Sloth Rope Bridges Reach 410 With 22,000 Crossings
World.content:
Costa Rica’s sloth rope bridges are drawing international attention, with The Associated Press publishing a feature yesterday on the conservationists and caretakers working to keep the sloths in the trees. The story begins behind a beachfront hotel in Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, where a small crew strings rope from one trunk to the next. To a passing tourist it looks like little more than a clothesline. To a sloth it can be the difference between staying safely in the canopy and coming down to the ground, where dogs, cars and power lines are waiting.

The work is led by The Sloth Conservation Foundation, founded by British zoologist Rebecca Cliffe, who has spent close to 20 years studying the animals on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. Her team has now installed roughly 410 rope bridges, most of them in places where roads, houses and hotels have opened gaps in the forest.

The design is deliberately simple, usually a single line. Cliffe says that for animals built to live in the trees that is enough, giving them a way over a gap they could not otherwise cross. Unlike monkeys, sloths cannot jump. Cliffe has a name for the problem, microfragmentation. A break of just 2 or 3 meters (about 7 to 10 feet) between neighboring treetops can force a sloth to look for another route, and the other route is often the ground or an electrical cable.

Making matters harder, sloths tend to stick to the paths they learned when young, even after the landscape around them has changed. Cliffe began experimenting with bridges nearly two decades ago after working at the Sloth Sanctuary of Costa Rica in Penshurst, where she kept seeing animals brought in after dog attacks, collisions with vehicles and electrocutions. With almost no funding, she started hanging single ropes.

Cameras mounted on some of the bridges have since recorded more than 22,000 wildlife crossings, and sloths are not the only users. Today the team responds to sightings at hotels and private properties, plants trees and works with neighbors to reconnect their lots. The ropes are not permanent. Tropical sun and rain wear them out in four or five years, and they have to be replaced.

The paradox is that Costa Rica is a celebrated reforestation success. A 2023 OECD report put forest cover at 59 percent of the national territory, up from about 21 percent in 1987. But geographer Carlos Morera Beita of the National University points out that much of that regrowth took place on old pastureland, in a countryside still divided up by farming. Sloths have proven more adaptable than scientists once believed, getting around through pastures with scattered trees, living fences and vegetation along rivers.

Those links matter, he says, because an isolated sloth has a hard time finding food, shelter and a mate. In his view bridges fix specific choke points, but lasting protection depends on keeping existing forest standing, restoring biological corridors and stopping further fragmentation. Back at the Sloth Sanctuary, founder Judy Avey-Arroyo cares for the animals that cannot go home.

Her work began when she and her husband took in an orphan named Buttercup, and today the sanctuary houses sloths with severe injuries or disabilities along with babies whose mothers were killed by cars, dogs or power lines. The smallest are raised in incubators and fed milk, while older juveniles move on to leaves, time outdoors and climbing practice. Avey-Arroyo says a mother cannot really be replaced.

A young sloth spends about a year learning which leaves are safe, which plants to avoid, how to move through the forest and even how to deal with parasites, and orphans that miss those lessons can struggle in the wild even when they look healthy. Accepting that some of her animals will never return to the forest, she says, is the hardest part of the job.

Climate change adds another layer. Small patches of forest heat up and dry out faster than continuous forest, and sloths control their body temperature by moving between sun and shade. Cliffe says extreme heat can drain their limited energy reserves while cold can interfere with digestion, so her group is planting shade trees alongside the bridges.

Scientists still lack reliable estimates of how many sloths Costa Rica has or whether their numbers are rising or falling. Cliffe’s team is testing thermal imaging drones, trained detection dogs and field surveys to find out. Two rescue centers in the region take in around three sloths a day, but without historical data no one can say whether that figure is climbing. Costa Rican conservation groups have separately backed a U.S. bill to ban sloth imports.

The idea is spreading beyond the Caribbean. On the southern Pacific coast, Alturas Wildlife Rescue Center and the state utility ICE are installing eight rope crossings along the coastal highway between Dominical and Uvita to cut down on wildlife being hit by traffic or electrocuted. Four were in place by late September.

The best outcome, Cliffe told the AP, would be for the bridges to become unnecessary once the trees grow close enough for sloths to move freely on their own. Until then she believes their future rests on many small acts, a tree planted here and a rope hung there. She calls it “the cumulative power of many individual actions” and says that is what keeps her hopeful.

World.title: Expect Two Weeks of Night Lane Closures on Costa Rica’s Route 1 Near Naranjo
World.content:
If you drive Costa Rica’s Route 1 at night, expect lane closures and a short detour near Naranjo for the next two weeks. Crews are demolishing the former Naranjo toll station on the Bernardo Soto Highway. Work runs from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m. and started today. The Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) and the National Road Council (CONAVI) expect it to take about two weeks, with partial lane closures while crews are on site.

If you are heading from San Ramón toward Alajuela, you will be moved onto a temporary lane that runs alongside the old toll station. That is the direction drivers take toward San José and Juan Santamaría International Airport, so it affects night trips in from Guanacaste, San Carlos and the western Central Valley.

The overnight schedule keeps the work out of rush hour, but you should still leave extra time, especially if you have a late-evening or early-morning flight. Slow down as you approach the work zone, follow the temporary signs and do what the crews on site tell you. They will be working next to moving traffic in the dark.

The Naranjo station has not charged a toll since September 1, 2025. Authorities suspended collection that day at Naranjo and at Río Segundo de Alajuela, citing constant backups at Río Segundo and changes tied to the highway project at Naranjo. The booths stayed in place after the toll ended.

In April 2026, then-President Rodrigo Chaves ordered both toll stations removed, calling the unused structures an unnecessary obstacle for drivers. Crews began demolishing the Río Segundo booths in late April. The Naranjo structures stood until this week. Transportation authorities say taking down the Naranjo station is part of the San José to San Ramón highway expansion. Removing the abandoned booths clears an obstacle from the road, improves safety and ends vandalism at the unused site.

World.title: CCJ rules government cannot grant the same land twice, voids 2019 title
World.content:
CCJ rules government cannot grant the same land twice, voids 2019 title

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) has ruled that once national land has been granted, it is no longer national land and cannot legally be granted a second time.

In its decision, the court declared a 2019 Minister’s Fiat Grant issued to Rudolph Ramirez null and void, and dismissed an appeal that sought more than $2 million in compensation over a 14 acre parcel at Cats Caye.

Senior Counsel Eamon Courtenay, who appeared for the Government of Belize, said the court ordered that the appellants be refunded $2,878.20 and that they pay the government’s costs.

Courtenay said the ruling overturns the principle established in the Andre Vega decision, under which holders of a second title could seek compensation at market value.

“The first title is good and the second title is not good. It is null and void, and if you get that second one you have nothing. So you can’t claim market price,” he said.

He said the decision helps to restore integrity to government land titles and confirms, at the level of the country’s highest court, that two valid titles cannot exist for the same property.

According to Courtenay, the government has had to pay out millions of dollars in past cases involving duplicate titles. He said the CCJ described the practice of issuing a second title as an abuse of power.

The court was also critical of the state of land records at the Ministry of Natural Resources and stressed the need for accurate record keeping.

Courtenay agreed, saying people buy, sell, invest and borrow on the strength of the land register.

“Public officers must keep the records, they must be accurate, and you cannot have political interference in records keeping in any part of the public service,” he said.

He argued, however, that this case was not one of error. According to Courtenay, when Ramirez learned in 2008 that title to the land had already been granted and raised it with the minister at the time, he was told a title would be issued anyway.

World.title: Mexican Ambassador says CFE curtailment due to high power demand
World.content:
Mexican Ambassador says CFE curtailment due to high power demand

By Zoila Palma: Mexican Ambassador to Belize Ana Luisa Vallejo Barba says that CFE’s power curtailment is due to high power demand in Mexico.

The Mexican Ambassador says that the Embassy has been involved in discussions surrounding BEL and CFE.

“We have been involved, and I think it has been very fruitful, because sometimes there are some misunderstandings because of the cuts-and it is not because of the lack of payment that is usual in our case, in our house. But in Mexico, we are committed to waiting for Belize to be ready, but we are not cutting. Some of the cuts has been because of the natural demand in Mexico and the production that has some problems or lack of energy, but it is not because Mexico is cutting because of lack of payment,” Vallejo said.

In addition, the Mexican Ambassador confirmed that in parts of Mexico during peak times and high demand, there are frequent blackouts.

“Yeah, exactly. Sometimes during the year, when the demand grows, it is very difficult on the peninsula to get the flow of energy, and that is why us, Belize, is affected-but not because Mexico is closing or directed to Belize; it is because of the natural process,” she added.

World.title: Belize Coast Guard celebrates 21 years of service to Belize
World.content:
Belize Coast Guard celebrates 21 years of service to Belize

By Zoila Palma: On November 26, 2026, the Belize Coast Guard celebrated its 21st anniversary, marking more than two decades of dedicated service to Belize since its establishment in 2005.

“This year’s anniversary was a celebration of our institutional heritage, progress and the men and women whose courage, commitment and sacrifices have shaped the Belize Coast Guard into the institution it is today,” the Belize Coast Guard said.

The occasion marked several significant institutional milestones, including the unveiling of a monument honoring founding members, known as Intake Alpha, the establishment of the Belize Coast Guard Hall of Fame, and the recognition of our retired officers and sailors for their years of dedicated service.

The celebration also provided an opportunity to recognize the Mexican Naval Attaché for his contributions to strengthening the enduring partnership between the Mexican Navy and the Belize Coast Guard.

“We extend our sincere gratitude to Her Excellency Dame Froyla Tzalam, Governor-General of Belize; the Honourable Michel Chebat, Minister of National Security; and Chief Executive Officer Francis Usher for gracing this memorable occasion with their presence. We deeply appreciate their continued support and confidence in our institution,” the Belize Coast Guard added.

As the Belize Coast Guard celebrates 21 years of service, it honors those who laid the keel, recognize those who continue to stand the watch, and reaffirm the commitment to safeguarding Belize’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and maritime interests.

World.title: Usher: no confrontation with Guatemalan forces at Sarstoon since November 11
World.content:
Usher: no confrontation with Guatemalan forces at Sarstoon since November 11

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): There has been no confrontation between Belizean and Guatemalan forces at the Sarstoon since November 11, according to the Chief Executive Officer in the Ministry of National Security, Francis Usher.

“November 11th was the last time we had a confrontation between the Guatemalan Armed Forces and the Belizean forces, whether it be the Belize Defence Force Special Boat Unit or the Belize Coast Guard,” Usher said.

That incident involved a standoff in Belizean waters in which Guatemalan civilian vessels were reportedly enlisted by that country’s military.

Usher said Belizean patrols have continued without incident. He reported that as recently as this week, a patrol travelled up to Cadenas through the tributaries and creeks branching off the Sarstoon and around Sarstoon Island.

He confirmed that the larger Coast Guard presence deployed during the standoff has since been removed from the Sarstoon.

“But the reinforcements remain nearby,” he said.

Asked whether United States diplomatic efforts played a role in Guatemala standing down, Usher said one could speculate, but pointed instead to Belize’s own posture.

“We have maintained a consistent presence; we have ensured that we assert ourselves in our territorial waters, that we enforce our boundaries,” he said.

Usher restated Belize’s position on the boundary as “the centre of the river and around the southern portion of the Sarstoon Island,” and said there is “a coherent strategic plan in place.”

World.title: Ministry of National Security planning new intake for all three security forces
World.content:
Ministry of National Security planning new intake for all three security forces

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Ministry of National Security is planning a new recruit intake for the Belize Defence Force, the Belize Coast Guard and the Belize Police Department.

Chief Executive Officer Francis Usher confirmed the plan as the Coast Guard marked its 21st anniversary.

“We are in the planning phase of an intake for all three security forces: the BDF, the Coast Guard, and the Police Department,” Usher said.

Asked whether the Coast Guard needs to grow in light of recent developments at the Sarstoon, Usher said the forces need both more personnel and more technology.

“I think that we need to both increase in numbers, and we need to embrace the age of technology,” he said. “As we have technological advancements, there are more efficient ways to do many of the jobs that we had to do on foot or in person before.”

Usher said the aim is to ensure Belize can continue to defend its maritime and territorial integrity.

In the case of the Police Department, he said the goal is not only to fight crime but to deter it and “stop it before it ever occurs.”

No dates or recruit numbers for the intake were given.

The comments come weeks after an incident near Sarstoon Island in which Guatemalan military vessels confronted a Belizean patrol, and as a State of Emergency remains in effect in parts of the country.

World.title: Mostly sunny and mild Friday with little to no rain
World.content:
Mostly sunny and mild Friday with little to no rain

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize can expect a mostly sunny and mild Friday with little to no rain.

The National Meteorological Service says a mild and mostly dry airflow continues to dominate over the country.

Tonight, skies will be mostly clear and cool. Showers, if any, will be light and isolated.

Coastal areas will reach a high of 82°F (27°C) with a low of 68°F (20°C). Inland areas will hit 83°F (28°C), cooling to 63°F (17°C). The hills will see a high of 72°F (22°C) and a low of 58°F (14°C).

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region in the next 48 hours.

Today’s forecast was issued by forecaster Catherine Cumberbatch.

World.title: Halo BPO continues recruitment of work from home sales agents in Belize
World.content:
Halo BPO continues recruitment of work from home sales agents in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Halo BPO is still accepting applications for sales agents in Belize.

The positions are full time, work from home roles in outbound sales.

Agents earn BZ$9.00 per hour during training and BZ$10.00 per hour after training is completed. Commission and bonuses are paid on top of the hourly rate, and agents are paid weekly.

The company requires at least two years of sales experience. Experience in credit repair is a plus.

Applicants must also have a home internet connection with speeds of 85 Mbps download and 45 Mbps upload.

To apply, send a resume to [email protected] with your full name in the subject line.

World.title: Orange Walk student charged with driving without a licence
World.content:
Orange Walk student charged with driving without a licence

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police have charged Martin Jimenez, 19, a student of Orange Walk Town, with driving a motor vehicle while not being the holder of a Belize driver’s licence.

The stop was made around 11:48pm on Sunday, November 22.

According to police, officers on mobile patrol on San Francisco Street in Orange Walk Town pulled over a black F150 pickup truck.

An officer asked the driver for the vehicle’s documents. Police say the vehicle licence was valid through the end of November 2026, and the insurance was valid until February 19, 2027.

When asked for his driver’s licence, the driver reportedly told the officer he did not have one.

He was informed of the offence, cautioned and arrested, then escorted to the Orange Walk Police Station, where he was advised of his rights.

On November 23, Jimenez was formally charged. Police say he chose to remain silent.

He was granted police bail to appear in the Orange Walk Magistrate’s Court on Tuesday, November 24.

World.title: Traffic takedown
World.content:
A father holds his daughter as he watches a representative of the Island Traffic Authority remove the licence plate from his vehicle on Old Harbour Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A push by the Island Traffic Authority (ITA) to make Jamaica’s roads safer ahead of the Christmas season was welcomed by some motorists but criticised by others as an early-morning enforcement drive on Old Harbour Road left 42 motorists without licence plates by midday on Thursday.

The operation, conducted jointly by the ITA and the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) at the St Catherine-Clarendon border, forms part of the traffic authority’s ‘Fatal Five Road Safety Intervention Strategy’ which targets the five leading causes of traffic crashes

— speeding, improper overtaking, improper lane use, pedestrians in the roadway, and unsafe right turns.

According to ITA figures, 373 of the 415 vehicles inspected up to midday Thursday were found to be roadworthy. The remaining 42 vehicles were found to be in breach of some road rules, resulting in the drivers being ticketed and given 24 hours to complete repairs before being barred from the road, after the vehicles were stripped of their licence plates.

ITA Manager of Corporate Communications and Public Relations Dontae Matthews told the Jamaica Observer that while the initiative targets the five leading causes of fatal crashes, it includes other areas designed to make travelling on Jamaica’s roads safer.

He said the ITA will be conducting an audit of roads and making recommendations on issues such as road markings and pedestrian crossings. The ITA will also be expanding its public education on the use of the roads and enforcement activities such as the one conducted on Thursday.

According to Matthews, although the initiative is being rolled out to meet the festive season, it will continue into 2027.

He said the ITA hopes the intervention will continue to drive down road fatalities in Jamaica, which recorded 281 fatal crashes, resulting in 324 lives lost up to November 26 this year. This represents a four per cent reduction compared with the corresponding period in 2025.

“It will go into the next financial year as well, and we will be assessing the data over time, and we’ll be making tweaks if the five causes of fatalities change… amendments will be made, and we will target those five reasons as well… So, the Christmas season is very important, but we will be taking it beyond it, into the new year, and we’re hoping for a reduction in road fatalities,” said Matthews.

But the ITA’s enforcement activity did not find favour with all road users, several of whom complained that the checks were unfair and disrupted their daily business.
