World.title: Bank of England boss warns AI must benefit humans
World.content:
“It’s a bit like rearing children. You have to give them the chance to do things, but you also have to set some sort of boundaries as it were,” he said in an interview from his office in the Bank of England.

With the G20 presidency fast approaching, Burnham has said he wants to use the U.K. to establish “a single set” of global standards for AI.

U.S. President Donald Trump shot down any global oversight of the giant American companies dominating the development of the technology, which he has rebranded as "super intelligence."

Against that backdrop, Bailey called for more international testing and access to AI giants’ frontier models, which he said are “critical questions” as the U.K. takes on the G20 presidency.

The U.K. central banking chief will make that push internationally in his role as chair of the Financial Stability Board, a global watchdog for the financial system.

With the number of cyber incidents already rising, Bailey said AI models are being built on “the good, the bad, and the ugly” of human behavior, and are now training themselves.

World.title: Ukraine cajoles allies to keep Putin’s athletes out
World.content:
Ukraine has near-unanimous EU backing for keeping Russian athletes out of European sport, and wants the bloc’s new visa ban on Moscow’s combatants also applied to soldiers who compete on national teams, Bidnyi added.

With the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics on the horizon, the dispute is becoming a test of who’ll shape Russia’s return to world sport: governments, or federations and courts. Kyiv is desperate for Europe to coordinate its response before more restrictions are lifted.

Bidnyi said he presented three demands to EU sports ministers on Nov. 20: a ban on Russian symbols; verified neutral status for athletes; and funding cuts for federations that let Russians compete. He added that the proposals found “wide support.”

“I have heard no voice against it,” Bidnyi said. Asked whether all 27 EU countries are on board, he said that “almost all of them” had expressed willingness to make it a common position.

No propaganda in sport

On Monday, the European Commission proposed barring Russian teams and athletes from competing in the EU, which would also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European sports and cultural associations. The sanctions package needs the approval of all 27 member countries.

In addition, seven EU countries had written to European Council President António Costa and Commission President Ursula von der Leyen before the sanctions package was presented asking for tougher visa rules on Russian nationals.

World.title: Georgia: Police clash with Besiktas fans at Israel club game
World.content:
Turkey's Besiktas accused Georgian police of using "disproportionate" force during the game with Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva, which saw Besiktas fans unfurl a banner supporting Palestine.

A football game between a Turkish and an Israeli team in Georgia's Batumi was disrupted by violence, with UEFA due to assess the events on Friday.

Georgian police said 16 people were detained and three officers "sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions" during the match.

The police also accused some supporters of hurling stadium seats at security forces.

Turkey's Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were originally set to meet in Istanbul, but with the tensions between the two countries running high due to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, UEFA decided to move the match to Georgia for safety reasons.

Georgia denies police were deployed over Palestine support

During the Thursday game, Besiktas fans unfurled a banner, "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine," waved Palestinian flags and chanted anti-Israel slogans.

Tensions between the two teams were also noticeable on the pitch Image: Oto Davitadze/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

However, Georgian authorities insisted they did not intervene due to the fans expressing their support for the Palestinians.

"We categorically deny these reports and emphasize that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," said the Georgian Interior Ministry.

The violence ended with several Besiktas fans receiving medical treatment Image: Mirian Meladze/Anadolu/picture alliance

In turn, Besiktas accused the authorities of using "disproportionate force" against the fans, and Turkey's football federation condemned "the unacceptable attitudes, behavior and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium."

A Besiktas club employee told the AFP news agency that five Turkish fans were taken to a hospital for medical treatment.

The match was suspended for over half an hour due to the violence in the stands. Eventually, Danish referee Morten Krogh continued the game, which ended with Besiktas winning 2 to 1.

Besiktas players also displayed Palestinian symbols while celebrating their victory over the Israeli team Image: Celal Gunes/Anadolu/picture alliance

The Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Turkish government ministers close ranks with Besiktas

The unrest has prompted a diplomatic incident between Turkey and Georgia.

Turkish sources indicated Turkey's Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan discussed the clashes with his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili.

Meanwhile, Turkish Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak and Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci echoed Besiktas' accusations of "disproportionate" force used by the Georgian police.

In an online post, Bak pledged to continue "resolutely defend the rights of Turkish sport and our fans."

Turkish news agency IHA reported that the 16 detained Besiktas fans have been released due to diplomatic and legal steps ordered by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

According to Besiktas, Erdogan also spoke to the club chairman, telling the sports official he was closely monitoring the situation.

World.title: Airline Norse Atlantic files for bankruptcy, succumbing to aviation fuel costs
World.content:
The low-cost airline was only founded a few years ago and had been struggling to turn a profit. The spike in aviation fuel prices caused by the war in Iran has now driven Norway's Norse Atlantic into bankruptcy.

Norwegian low-cost airline Norse Atlantic's operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the carrier said on Friday.

The airline had warned on Wednesday that its financial situation was "critical," and suspended all flights the following day, saying it was urgently seeking emergency funding to fend off bankruptcy.

Like many commercial airlines, Norse Atlantic is highly exposed to the vastly increased jet fuel prices of 2026, attributable in very large part to the war in Iran and resultant tension throughout the wider Middle East.

What did Norse Atlantic say about the bankruptcy filing?

Norse had said slightly earlier on Friday that its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier's fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back. Initially the company said it planned to contest this claim, which would have rendered it effectively unable to operate.

But the announcement of plans to file for bankruptcy followed fairly soon after.

"The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution," Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Other companies in the group like the stock market-listed Norse Atlantic ASA parent company and the Norse Atlantic UK subsidiary are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said.

"The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations," Roald said.

The company said on Thursday that it planned to file for bankruptcy unless financing could be arranged and had warned: "There can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Founded just five years ago and based in Arendal in Norway, Norse Atlantic had a fleet of 12 planes and serviced a total of 14 destinations. It had recorded a net loss of $61.9 million (€56.5 million) in 2025, even before the additional economic strains caused by the war in Iran.

Why has the war in Iran put such strain on the aviation industry?

Small and lower-cost airlines are struggling in particular, but the aviation industry in general is facing severe problems amid the strains on global fuel deliveries caused by the conflict in the Gulf.

In early 2026, as the US launched attacks on Iran — soon leading to reduced traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — aviation fuel rapidly spiked, more than doubling in price at its peak.

It rose higher even than in the immediate aftermath of Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Although it dipped in mid-summer amid hopes of a resolution to the conflict, it rose once again as these faded and a stalemate developed.

This has posed the worst crisis for the industry since the COVID pandemic drastically reduced the volume of air traffic in 2020 and beyond, a much larger issue that many carriers were still struggling to recover from.

World.title: German lawmakers approve debt-laden 2027 budget
World.content:
11/27/2026 November 27, 2026 BSW: Left-wing populists seek path forward at annual party conference

Germany's left-wing populist BSW party is holding its annual conference on Friday and Saturday as it looks to remain relevant following a series of electoral defeats and internal splits.

The BSW was founded in 2024 by former Left Party politician Sahra Wagenknecht who leant her initials to the party's original name, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance or Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW). The founder herself stepped down as party leader in 2025 and the party officially changed its name last month to "Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason" – also still abbreviated as BSW.

After initial successes in European and eastern German state elections in 2024, the BSW failed to reach the minimum 5% required to enter parliament in the 2025 federal election. In September, the BSW crept into the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt with 5.3% of the vote but fell short in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin.

BSW split over stance on AfD

Ahead of its party conference in Dresden this weekend, the BSW has been split over its approach to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which with it shares some economic and geopolitical policies, such as support for trading relations with Russia and opposition to military support for Ukraine.

Like most other German political parties, the BSW has ruled out entering into any coalition with the AfD but, in Saxony-Anhalt, has already voted with the far-right on certain policies and has held talks over support for certain issues which an AfD minority government would want to implement.

The BSW intends to abstain from the vote for the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund as state premier for Saxony-Anhalt on December 8 – but ultimately cannot force its five lawmakers to do so in what will be a secret ballot.

The softening of the BSW's position on the AfD has the backing of founder Wagenknecht and the party's lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Claudia Wittig, who has slammed the policy of refusing to work with the AfD as "firewall idiocy."

"We're not cozying up to the AfD," she insisted, but said: "Let's not get tied up in knots over lies in the mainstream media."

Wagenknecht added: "Vibrant parties should have vibrant discussions about their future course, but we shouldn't accuse ourselves of things which aren't true. The BSW is not team AfD. Rather, we take voters seriously and want to implement political change to improve the lives of the majority."

But other founder members are resisting, writing in the Zeit newspaper this week that a "clear political distancing from the AfD" was a "foundational consensus" for the BSW.

"Just as it was right to reject the firewall, which only served the AfD anyway, so it is also wrong to make common cause with the AfD," they wrote, warning that the approach could morph into "political cooperation with AfD" which would "compromise the BSW and make it irrelevant in the long term."

They demanded: "No tolerance of an AfD government, no cooperation agreements, no abstentions from the vote for the state premier."

World.title: The Gambia election: Can Barrow secure a third term?
World.content:
President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term as Gambians vote on December 5. The election will test the opposition's appeal and the country's progress on democratic reform.

The Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended Yahya Jammeh's 22-year rule.

President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.

Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and five other candidates.

The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only female in the presidential race.

What matters to voters

The Gambia is still governed under its 1997 Constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.

A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.

Many Gambians have voiced concerns about a lack of economic opportunities Image: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.

"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC). "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."

Opposition parties say their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.

Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, says the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.

"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," Manneh said.

Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.

"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.

"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.

Jobs and the cost of living

Many voters say that their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.

What happens when you speak up? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The World Bank projects economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but says extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.

The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.

The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.

Alhagie Sama says young people need opportunities at home rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.

"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.

Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.

"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that unemployment goes beyond conventional definitions.

"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."

Election under observation

The IEC says 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.

Gambia Election 2026: Can the opposition win? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The election commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It says the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.

International observers are also monitoring the process.

Following an invitation from Gamian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.

The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.

"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," the UN's Deputy Special Representative for West Africa and the Sahel, Barrie Freeman, told candidates.

Under the pact , presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."

The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.

World.title: On the arrest of Informer TV owner and editor-in-chief Dragan J. Vucicevic: Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
World.content:
The arrest of media owner Dragan J. Vucicevic raises questions about whether Serbia is holding the people behind the country's pro-Vucic media accountable or whether this is another political power struggle.

"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.

The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June last year.

On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by the police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching" and he labelled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.

The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures" and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."

Ready to break free: How Serbia's media are changing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted political opponents of the previous government, activists and independent journalists.

Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?

Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.

Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.

Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.

"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.

Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.

Protesters in April 2025 called for media freedom and adherence to ethical standards outside the offices of the tabloid newspaper Informer. The sign on the left reads 'Colorful (fake) revolution? Colorful lie.' The sign on the right: 'Bottom, bottom of the bottom, des-Informer' Image: SPASA DAKIC/SIPA/picture alliance

"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.

"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."

Court cases and compensation

The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.

Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.

According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.

"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."

Members of the Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) met on November 4 to discuss an initiative to revoke TV Informer's broadcasting license Image: Milan Ilic/SIPA/picture alliance

On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.

Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).

Where did the money come from?

According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.

Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.

Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.

SNS lawmakers protest

Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.

The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.

Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.

On the day after the October 25 parliamentary election, protestors confronted Dragan J. Vucicevic (center) in the offices of Informer Image: @veljars/TikTok/REUTERS

Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.

"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.

A reckoning or an internal power struggle?

Vucicevic has been remanded in custody for 30 days.

The offence of causing panic and disorder through the media carries a prison sentence of between six months and five years.

Stevanovic points out, however, that the outcome of the case is not certain because the executive branch, the police and the Ministry of the Interior formally remain under the control of the outgoing government until such time as the Student List forms a new cabinet.

"What is happening now could be an internal power struggle within their own ranks, or an attempt by some prosecutors to clean up their records and ingratiate themselves with the new authorities, assuming what their wishes and intentions regarding Informer might be," she said. "Or it could be a serious manipulation, a staged arrest designed to portray Serbia abroad as a country carrying out revolutionary terror, which, of course, is not true."

World.title: Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
World.content:
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte faces trial in The Hague over his deadly war on drugs. The proceedings could also determine the political fortunes of one of the Philippines' most powerful dynasties.

Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.

For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.

It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.

Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.

With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.

Why is Duterte on trial?

Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.

During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.

Filipino woman who lost family to drug war takes on Duterte To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.

His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.

"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.

After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.

A 'way of governing'

Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.

"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.

"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.

"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.

Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.

Former president remains popular

The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.

Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.

His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.

"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.

Why was Duterte arrested?

Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.

The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.

For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.

What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.

Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.

Philippine cafe keeps alive memory of 'drug war' victims To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.

Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.

In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.

The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.

What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?

The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Duterte-aligned senators implicated in the ICC investigation could face arrest and transfer to The Hague, while Sara Duterte is still a leading contender for the 2028 presidency, despite an ongoing impeachment trial over allegations of unexplained wealth that could see her barred from public office.

Her brother, Sebastian Duterte, the mayor of Davao City, has also become a possible alternative presidential candidate.

DW speaks with Nobel laureate Maria Ressa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

By portraying the ICC proceedings as foreign interference and political persecution, the Duterte family hopes to preserve the political capital accumulated during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, Jayson Lamchek, a legal scholar at Western Sydney University, told DW.

Before her father's arrest, Sara Duterte's performance and trust ratings had been declining amid allegations that she had misused confidential government funds.

However, her ratings rebounded following his detention and have largely held up despite the ongoing impeachment controversies, Ronald Holmes, a political science professor at De La Salle University and president of polling firm Pulse Asia Research, told DW.

"A conviction or prolonged trial near election season will likely turn the 2028 vote into a direct referendum on the Duterte legacy, either rallying sympathetic voters against perceived foreign and domestic persecution or galvanizing opposition forces around demands for accountability," Holmes said.

For many Filipinos, however, the trial's significance goes well beyond the political rivalry between the two dynasties.

"Rodrigo Duterte's trial in the ICC is a milestone not only for the victims and families of the war on drugs but for the entire country," Jean Encinas-Franco, a professor of political science at the University of the Philippines Diliman, told DW.

"Duterte and his cabal ruled by fear and misogyny and held Filipinos under his iron grip. The Filipino people deserve an answer. The Filipino people deserve justice," she added.

World.title: Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
World.content:
War, poverty and disrupted schooling could put more girls in Iran at risk of child marriage, rights advocates warn.

For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly last year.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the conflict's impact.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband.

Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRA), said she had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.

What the figures show

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 in year measured roughly from March 2025 to March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

When marriage becomes an economic calculation

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson told DW that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs, and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her towards marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

War and displacement

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Few legal safeguards against child marriage

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

The concerns also extend to the online space. An HRA investigation published in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted or whether the war increased them.

All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What can be done to protect girls?

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he told DW. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

World.title: Philippines: VP Duterte says father's ICC case 'not a fair trial'
World.content:
Sara Duterte has said the ICC will not give her father a fair trial and that the Hague-based court wants to "make a statement." Duterte alleges the case against her father is politically motivated.

The Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Duterte, criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Thursday, saying it would not provide a fair trial for her ex-president father's crimes against humanity case.

She said the court would try to "make a statement."

Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.

What is expected at Duterte's trial?

The trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in ⁠court.

"I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.

Duterte said "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.

BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Why is Rodrigo Duterte at the ICC?

Prosecutors at the ICC ​accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.

He has been charged with three counts of crimes against ​humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.

Duterte is the first Asian former ​leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.

Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.

Duterte: ICC trial is politically motivated

The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.

She said both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.

"I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

World.title: ¿Quién va a ganar las elecciones? La probabilidad de cada mayoría según las encuestas
World.content:
Nuestro modelo ve probable un gobierno de PP y Vox. Pero no está garantizado: el PSOE tiene la tendencia a favor y la derecha se queda corta una de cada seis veces

Las encuestas se apagaron este lunes dejando esta foto: el PP es primero con el 31,4% de los votos en promedio, seguido del PSOE (29,1%), Vox (17,9%) y los Frentes, la suma de Frente Amplio y coaliciones con Podemos y otras fuerzas (6,8%). La tendencia de la campaña es un PSOE que crece: la ventaja del PP sobre los socialistas se ha reducido de casi seis puntos a poco más de dos. La suma de izquierdas también ha avanzado, aunque PP y Vox siguen rondando el 49% de los votos. Su ventaja es real, pero no definitiva: nuestros cálculos dicen que necesitan alrededor del 47% para llegar a los 176 diputados que dan el Gobierno.

Con estos sondeos, y conociendo sus errores: ¿qué probabilidad tiene cada resultado? Es la pregunta que responde nuestro modelo electoral.

El PP sería el partido más votado y el que más escaños conseguiría: 129 en nuestra estimación central. El PSOE rondaría los 116, Vox 61 y los Frentes, 12. El resto de fuerzas tendría alrededor de 32 escaños en total.

Pero esas cifras solo son el centro de un abanico. El PP se mueve en una horquilla entre 112 y 146 escaños. El PSOE, entre 100 y 133. Y Vox, entre 44 y 75. Los rangos son amplios a propósito: recogen cuánto se han equivocado las encuestas en elecciones pasadas y lo difícil que es traducir votos en escaños provincia a provincia.

La clave: ¿quién alcanzará la mayoría?

La gran ventaja de un modelo de predicción es que permite atribuir probabilidades a diferentes resultados, algo que los sondeos no hacen. Así podemos enfrentar la pregunta fundamental: ¿qué partidos tienen opciones de sumar una mayoría absoluta? El gráfico muestra el resumen.

El escenario central es claro: PP y Vox sumarían unos 190 escaños en el centro de nuestras simulaciones, por encima de los 176 de la mayoría absoluta. De las 21 encuestadoras que han estimado escaños en la última semana, 20 les dan mayoría. Por ejemplo, 40dB les dio 187 en su último sondeo.

Pero ese consenso no asegura el resultado. Nuestro modelo ve una mayoría absoluta de PP y Vox en el 87% de las simulaciones (contando con los asientos de UPN-PP). En un 7%, la consigue la suma de PSOE y sus aliados de 2023, sin contar Junts. En el 6% restante, ningún bloque llega y la llave vuelve a tenerla Junts. Esto asume que Coalición Canaria continua en el bloque del PSOE, pero esto puede cambiar: hay un 1,5% de simulaciones donde los canarios pueden apuntalar la mayoría de PP y Vox.

Aun así, creemos que las opciones de la izquierda son algo mayores de lo que dice el modelo. En las últimas semanas, los sondeos se han movido hacia la izquierda y ese movimiento puede seguir. Lo hemos comprobado en 37 elecciones —las generales desde 1993 y las autonómicas desde 2015—: las urnas se desvían de las encuestas en la dirección que llevaban estas. Por eso es más plausible una sorpresa hacia la izquierda. El problema es que no lo veremos, porque ya no pueden publicarse encuestas.

En resumen, pensamos que la mayoría de PP y Vox es probable al 83%, es decir, que se queda corta una de cada seis veces. Algo tan fácil o difícil como sacar un seis con un dado.

¿Qué dicen otras señales? Casi todas apuntan a lo mismo que el modelo. Con nuestra propia estimación con microdatos de 40dB., PP y Vox suman mayoría con 81-85% de probabilidad. Los mercados de predicción les dan un 88%, casi lo mismo. Y esta derechización coincide con lo que se votó en las autonómicas del último año (Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón y Extremadura).

¿Quién queda primero?

La pelea por el primer puesto está todavía más abierta. El PP saca más escaños que el PSOE en el 73% de las simulaciones, y el PSOE queda por delante en el 25%: una de cada cuatro. Si además contamos con la tendencia, esas opciones suben al 33%.

El PP convierte mejor votos en escaños. Por eso hay un 4% de simulaciones en las que el PSOE gana en votos pero el PP saca más escaños (lo contrario, que el PP gane en votos y el PSOE en escaños, casi nunca pasa).

El siguiente gráfico muestra la estimación de escaños para cada partido. Ahí se responden otras preguntas más pequeñas. Por ejemplo, la lista de Podemos en solitario solo consigue escaños en el 43% de las simulaciones, menos de la mitad. Y el partido de Alvise Pérez, Se Acabó La Fiesta, aunque ronda el 2% de los votos, se queda fuera el 79% de las veces. Entre los partidos pequeños, ERC rondaría los 10 escaños, EH Bildu 7, Junts y Adelante Andalucía 4, el PNV 3 y el BNG 2.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido. Funciona en cuatro pasos.

1) Promedio de encuestas. El peso de cada sondeo depende de su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador: las mejores cuentan el doble que una casa normal, el peso de una encuesta se reduce a la mitad cada diez días y de cada casa solo cuenta su último sondeo, para que no mande quien publica más. Lo hemos probado con 41 elecciones desde 2018: cinco días antes de votar, el promedio falla 1,5 puntos por partido de media. Cuando falla mucho es porque fallan todas las encuestas a la vez, algo que ningún promedio puede corregir.

2) Voto en cada provincia. Proyectamos ese voto a cada provincia con un modelo propio y mejorado, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026—. También explota los microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad para detectar tendencias nuevas y desviaciones de la historia de la región.

3) Incertidumbre. Es el paso más importante. La calibramos con los errores de las encuestas en 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia.

4) Simulaciones. Simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y repartimos los escaños de cada simulación según D’Hondt, con la barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción. Las probabilidades de este artículo son la proporción de simulaciones en las que ocurre cada cosa, y los intervalos recogen ocho de cada diez. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades salen bien afinadas: de los escaños que el modelo veía en juego, con probabilidades de entre el 25% y el 75%, los partidos ganaron 202, frente a los 195 que esperaba. Los 498 escaños que dimos como 99% seguros en 2019 y 2023 se cumplieron todos.

En los gráficos, Frentes agrupa a Frente Amplio y sus coaliciones con Compromís, Ara Més y Unidad del Pueblo Canario; Podemos va en solitario. Las encuestas son hasta el 23 de noviembre.

World.title: Voto útil con todas las encuestas: Las opciones de izquierda y derecha en cada provincia
World.content:
El modelo de EL PAÍS dice que hay 40 escaños en el aire. Consulta a qué partido le sirve más tu voto

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima los escaños en cada provincia, les asigna probabilidades, e incluso señala el llamado voto útil. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos actualizados con las últimas encuestas, publicadas hasta el 23 de noviembre.

En el primer interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 186 seguros, 121 probables y 84 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Voto útil: ¿qué voto ayuda a tu bloque?

Muchas personas votan para maximizar las opciones de un gobierno de izquierdas o de derechas. Quizás tienen un partido favorito, pero se hacen otra pregunta: ¿a qué partido de su bloque le sirve más su voto? Es lo que se llama voto táctico o estratégico. La respuesta cambia en cada provincia: por el método D’Hondt, un voto al PP y otro a Vox no valen lo mismo en escaños, porque uno de los dos suele estar más cerca de ganar el último diputado. Y lo mismo pasa con PSOE, Frente Amplio o BNG.

¿Cuál es el voto táctico en tu provincia? Puedes verlo en el mapa. Primero elige un bloque. Entonces el mapa mostrará, para cada provincia, el partido de ese espectro que tiene más probabilidades de ganar (o salvar) un escaño para su bloque.

Para un votante de derecha, existe voto táctico en 39 provincias. Hay 21 donde le conviene votar al PP (probablemente) y 18 donde le conviene hacerlo por Vox. A veces la diferencia es grande: en Gipuzkoa, Lugo y Ourense, un voto a Vox casi nunca decide un escaño, mientras que el PP se disputa el último con Bildu o el BNG. En Álava o Melilla, un voto al PP vale más de cinco veces lo que uno a Vox. Pero hay territorios donde un votante indiferente entre PP y Vox maximiza sus opciones eligiendo al partido de extrema derecha. Es lo que pasa en La Rioja, por ejemplo.

En la izquierda, el voto táctico favorece al PSOE en 34 de las 52 provincias. En 22 provincias es el único del bloque que mueve escaños en nuestras simulaciones, porque los Frentes y Podemos tienen números débiles en los sondeos. Hay excepciones en territorios con fuerzas locales: por ejemplo, en Lugo parece que un voto al BNG es mejor para los intereses del bloque, y en Ourense BNG y PSOE están casi empatados. Y ocurre algo parecido con Adelante Andalucía en Córdoba, con la Unidad del Pueblo Canario en Santa Cruz de Tenerife y con EH Bildu en Gipuzkoa.

En las provincias grandes, en cambio, el voto táctico se reduce. En Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla hay más de una opción dentro de cada bloque que puede ser competitiva.

Nuestra simulación también muestra otra cosa: mover un escaño es mucho más barato en las provincias más pequeñas. La probabilidad de que justo tu papeleta sea la decisiva es siempre minúscula (un voto cualquiera tiene una posibilidad entre 113.000 de decidir un escaño). Pero no es siempre igual de minúscula. En Lleida un voto al PP pesa casi seis veces más que la media: una posibilidad entre 20.000. Y en La Rioja o Ceuta, uno al PSOE pesa unas cinco veces más. En el otro extremo, un voto al PP o a Vox en Madrid vale la mitad de lo normal, en parte porque allí cada escaño cuesta más votos: hay unos 94.000 votantes por diputado, frente a 25.000 en Soria.

Una advertencia: esto no es una recomendación de voto. Es la aritmética de los escaños según las encuestas de hoy, que todavía pueden moverse y que son siempre una aproximación. Además, el voto táctico solo mide la probabilidad de mover un escaño, pero un voto puede tener utilidad para apoyar unas ideas o una formación incluso cuando no se traduzca en asiento del Congreso.

¿Cómo funciona el modelo?

El modelo parte de nuestro promedio de sondeos, lo proyecta a cada provincia con su historia y microdatos del CIS, y le añade la incertidumbre de las encuestas en el pasado. Después simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y contamos cuántas veces gana cada partido cada escaño. Así podemos clasificarlos en tres grupos: seguros, probables y en juego.

El siguiente gráfico muestra qué significan estas probabilidades. Puedes simular las elecciones una, dos, tres o cien veces para hacerte una idea intuitiva de cuántas veces se gana un escaño de cada tipo.

El modelo es sólido. Cada pieza la hemos puesto a prueba con otras elecciones generales. Por ejemplo, hemos probado varias formas de repartir el voto entre provincias, siguiendo técnicas habituales, y nos quedamos con la más precisa en votos y escaños.

El modelo es cauteloso. Y lo es por diseño: predecir cada provincia es difícil porque las encuestas pierden precisión a escala provincial. Un sondeo de 2.000 o 5.000 entrevistas no basta para estimar directamente el voto de Soria, Pontevedra o Castellón. Por eso no lo intentamos: lo que hacemos es usar el voto histórico de cada partido en cada provincia y lo que dicen en cada comunidad los microdatos del CIS, que acumulan decenas de miles de entrevistas. Además, las fuerzas locales no siempre salen en las encuestas y pueden sorprender al final: Teruel Existe gana escaño en una de cada cinco simulaciones. Y pasa algo similar con partidos pequeños en las provincias grandes: Podemos consigue un diputado por Madrid en el 60% de las simulaciones, y SALF, en el 24%. Si detectas cualquier omisión, escríbenos.

Y el modelo es confiable. Estas predicciones las hemos hecho muchas veces. Por eso sabemos que el modelo funciona y está bien calibrado. En 2023 dimos 189 escaños como seguros y se cumplieron todos, igual que en las dos elecciones de 2019 (156 y 153). Los que dimos como probables se cumplieron el 94% de las veces (365 de 388), en la parte alta del 75%-99% que prometíamos. Los errores de cada provincia se compensan en parte al sumarlos, así que el total es más fiable que cada provincia por separado. El modelo también acierta en el total nacional: en las generales de 2016 a 2023, los escaños de cada partido grande cayeron dentro de nuestra horquilla del 80% en 19 de 20 casos, más de lo prometido: es la cautela de la que hablábamos.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate el nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido.

Funciona en cuatro pasos. 1) Un promedio de encuestas que pondera cada sondeo por su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador. 2) Una proyección del voto a cada provincia con un modelo logístico, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026— y se alimenta también con microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad. 3) La incertidumbre de las encuestas, calibrada con los errores de 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia. 4) 20.000 simulaciones de las elecciones, repartiendo los escaños según D’Hondt con barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción.

Un escaño es seguro si un partido lo gana en más del 99% de las simulaciones; probable, entre el 75% y el 99%, y en juego, entre el 25% y el 75%. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades están muy bien afinadas: los escaños en juego se cumplieron 202 veces, frente a las 195 que predecía el modelo.

Para calcular el voto táctico usamos las mismas 20.000 simulaciones. En cada una añadimos (o quitamos) un puñado de votos a cada partido en cada provincia, y miramos si su bloque gana (o pierde) un escaño. Solo contamos cuando el escaño cambia de bloque. El resultado es la probabilidad de que un voto decida un asiento para su bloque ideológico. Los bloques son derecha (PP, Vox y SALF), e izquierda (PSOE, Frente Amplio, Podemos, ERC, EH Bildu, BNG y Adelante Andalucía). PNV, Junts y CC quedan fuera.

En los gráficos nacionales agrupamos como Izquierdas a Frente Amplio, Podemos y las coaliciones Compromís-Front Valencià, Unidad del Pueblo Canario y Ara Més-Front Ampli; en cada provincia aparecen por separado.
