World.title: Kampa Park Revitalization to Begin in March 2027, Main Work to Last Three Months
World.content:
The long-awaited revitalization of Kampa Park in Prague will begin in March 2027, with the main construction phase scheduled to last until the end of May.

Smaller-scale work will continue afterward, Prague 1 announced on Friday.

The park will remain open to pedestrians throughout the project, and access to local businesses and institutions will be maintained. However, the lawns and green areas will be temporarily closed and are expected to reopen once the main work is complete.



The project includes repairs to existing paths, the creation of new walkways, landscaping and the installation of new railings along the Čertovka stream. The park’s layout and character will remain unchanged.

Work will begin along the Čertovka stream, where surveys will be carried out to protect tree roots. The first phase will also include repairs to connecting paths and the walkway between Werich Villa and Sovovy Mlýny.

The contractor estimates this phase will take around 45 days.

Work on the main path is scheduled to begin in mid-April. Further improvements will include new street furniture and repairs to the children’s playground, with the detailed schedule still being finalized.

The park’s lighting is also being replaced with fixtures inspired by Prague’s traditional lanterns. Most of the work is expected to be completed this year, with some lamps near Sovovy Mlýny and in Odkolkovská Garden scheduled for replacement in 2027.

According to Prague 1 Councilor Kateřina Klasnová, up to 75 percent of the material from the existing paths could be reused in the new surfaces, reducing construction costs and the number of trucks transporting materials through the park.

The main paths and lawns are expected to be accessible again by the end of May 2027, allowing visitors to use the park during the summer.

World.title: Advent in Prague: Where to Order Festive Sweets, and Savor Mulled Wine
World.content:
From sweets to warming svařák and Christmas markets, the Czech capital offers many ways to embrace the holiday spirit.

Here’s a guide to help you savor the best of Advent in Prague this year.

Where to Order Luxury Christmas Sweets in Prague

If you’re not planning to bake this year but still want something special for your holiday table, Prague’s bakeries and cafés have you covered.



Myšák

For classic holiday sweets, Myšák’s e-shop (mysakdomu.cz) has you covered. Order a 500g box of traditional Christmas sweets for 1,445 CZK. You can also pair it with a Christmas cake, their signature Věneček egg liqueur, or a homemade syrup for mulled wine.

Known for its craftsmanship, Skála offers a 1kg assortment of 12 different Christmas sweets for 1,699 CZK. Pre-orders are available for specific dates, with slots still open during the festive season.

Etapa in Karlín

Etapa’s 450g Christmas box (1,050 CZK) combines Linzer cookies, caramel shortbread, chocolate hazelnut balls, and their signature beehives. A few holiday dates are still open, or you can stop by the café for extras.

Gluten-Free Christmas Sweets

For those avoiding gluten, Mezi Srnky provides both classic and gluten-free options. Their 400g boxes include gingerbread, rum balls, and Išelské cookies.

Where to Find the Best Mulled Wine and Eggnog in Prague

After sorting your sweets, take a walk through Prague and visit these places for warm drinks.

Mulled Wine Stops

Bjukitchen (City Center): Classic mulled wine alongside kid-friendly vanilla cocoa.

(City Center): Classic mulled wine alongside kid-friendly vanilla cocoa. Eska (Karlín): Known for its creative twist on Christmas drinks, including apple mulled wine.

(Karlín): Known for its creative twist on Christmas drinks, including apple mulled wine. Hrnek (Letná): Enjoy their secret recipe mulled wine served in a stylish onion-shaped mug.

Eggnog

Iveta Fabešová’s (Masaryčka building): Famous for her rich eggnog, available by the glass or bottle, making it a great gift option.

(Masaryčka building): Famous for her rich eggnog, available by the glass or bottle, making it a great gift option. Coffee Room (Vinohrady): try their seasonal eggnog-infused coffee, a must for coffee lovers.

Advent Markets in Prague: Intimate and Unique

Skip the crowded main squares and explore Prague’s smaller, cozier Christmas markets for a more relaxed holiday shopping experience.

The list of Prague cafés and bistros that invite you to a unique culinary experience would not be complete without Villa 63, which can be found on Hradešínská Street.

You can now also take a look at the neighboring property, which is named Zahrada 65.

World.title: Filmasia to Bring 16 Asian Films to Prague, Brno and České Budějovice
World.content:
The 22nd edition of the Filmasia Asian Film Festival will take place in Prague from December 3 to 13, bringing 16 films from Hong Kong, South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Vietnam.

The festival will also welcome filmmakers from Hong Kong and South Korea before travelling to Brno and České Budějovice in January and February.

This year’s theme is “the thread of fate,” connecting established filmmakers with emerging artists.



The programme is divided into five sections, alongside a special retrospective dedicated to director Wong Kar Wai.

The festival will open on Friday, December 4, at 7 p.m. at Bio Oko with Good Trip, a Hong Kong comedy about a seriously ill father and his daughter embarking on a road trip. Directors Norris Wong and Wong Hoi will attend the screening.

The festival will also revisit four films by Wong Kar Wai in the In the Mood for Wong Kar Wai section. Audiences can see Chungking Express and Fallen Angels on Saturday, December 12, followed by Happy Together and In the Mood for Love on Sunday, December 13.

“We are delighted to welcome several prominent figures from Asian cinema to this year’s Filmasia. Meeting filmmakers in person is extremely important to us, as it allows our audiences to discover not only the films themselves but also the stories, experiences, and countries behind their creation,” said festival director Karla Stojáková.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Filmasia (@filmasiafestival)

The festival will take place at Bio Oko in Prague from December 3 to 13, 2026.

Selected films will then be screened at Kino Art in Brno from January 6 to 23, 2027, and at Biograf Kotva in České Budějovice from January 27 to February 1, 2027.

All films will be screened in their original languages with Czech and English subtitles.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets Reveal Prices for Mulled Wine, Sausages and More
World.content:
Prague’s main Christmas markets will open on Saturday, November 28, with mulled wine priced at 100 CZK and sausages costing 180 CZK.

Organizers say prices for several popular refreshments have remained unchanged, while the sausage is the main item to have become more expensive.



The markets on Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will run until January 6, 2027, with stalls open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

The company Taiko, which organizes the markets, says Prague remains among the most affordable Christmas market destinations in Europe for food and drinks.

The price of mulled wine has remained at 100 CZK since 2024. A hot apple drink will cost 70 CZK, the same as last year.

The price of sausages has increased, however. The item rose from 160 CZK to 180 CZK during the Easter markets and will remain at that level for the Christmas season.

The company also points to the ingredients used at its stalls. The sausages are made exclusively for the markets and contain up to 97 percent meat, while the mulled wine is produced from grapes supplied by the Moravian winery Chateau Valtice.

Prices at Prague’s main Christmas markets:

Mulled wine: 100 CZK

Hot apple drink: 70 CZK

Sausage: 180 CZK

Hot dog: 90 CZK

Sausage in a baguette: 180 CZK

Langoš with garlic, cheese and ketchup: 200 CZK

Draft Pilsner, 0.4 litre: 80 CZK

Hot chocolate: 130 CZK

Spiral potato: 100 CZK

French fries: 185 CZK

Record number of performers expected

The 2026 programme will feature a record 5,329 performers. Activities will include weekend workshops for children, a St. Nicholas Day event and the traditional Christmas Eve celebrations.

On December 24, festive soup will be served on Old Town Square from 11 a.m. A performance of the Czech Christmas Mass is scheduled for 9 p.m.

For safety reasons, the organizers have not announced the exact time of Saturday’s tree-lighting ceremony. They are also encouraging visitors to spread their first visits across the weekend and avoid bringing bulky luggage to the markets.

World.title: Expedia to Acquire Czech Flight Booking Company Kiwi.com
World.content:
American travel company Expedia Group has agreed to acquire Czech flight booking platform Kiwi.com, bringing a change of ownership to the Brno-based business.

The transaction is expected to be completed by the middle of 2027, although the companies have not disclosed its value.

The acquisition will see the departure of Kiwi.com’s current majority shareholder, US investment fund General Atlantic, which has controlled the company since 2019. Co-founder Oliver Dlouhý, who holds a minority stake, is also expected to exit.



Expedia said the deal would strengthen its technology and expand its position in the European air travel market. Kiwi.com generated approximately €227 million in revenue last year, equivalent to around CZK 5.6 billion.

Expedia said the acquisition would give travelers access to a wider selection of flights and provide new opportunities for growth across its brands, including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.

Kiwi.com was founded in Brno in 2012 by Dlouhý and his business partners. The company became known internationally for its search technology, which allowed it to combine flights from airlines that did not necessarily have direct partnerships with the platform.

The company has since developed into an international flight retailer, focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence to improve its operations.

The acquisition comes after several years of restructuring at Kiwi.com, which faced financial difficulties following the decline in air travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company reduced its workforce by more than 200 employees in 2024. Earlier this year, it announced plans to cut approximately 250 jobs from a workforce of around 700.

Expedia Group was founded in 1996 as a division of Microsoft. It operates an online travel platform offering bookings for flights, accommodation, car rentals and activities, as well as technology services for corporate partners.

World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Residents of Prague and Brno can choose a living Christmas tree this year and give it a chance to grow in the forest after the holidays.

Both cities are offering small potted firs that can be planted in spring with the help of foresters.

In Prague, the Forests of the Capital City of Prague are running their Christmas fir project for the tenth consecutive year. The initiative, known as A Christmas Fir with a Future, allows people to buy a young silver fir for 150 CZK.

The trees, approximately 50 centimeters tall, have been grown in a forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can continue growing after Christmas.



The organizers acknowledge that the firs may not look like traditional Christmas trees. Their branches are often irregular, and each tree has its own shape.

The project also aims to support the return of silver fir to Czech forests. The native species (Abies alba) became scarce during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Where to buy a living Christmas tree in Prague

The potted firs are available at several locations, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-center and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to care for a potted Christmas tree

A living Christmas tree needs more attention than a cut one. It should remain outdoors in a cool place, such as a balcony or garden, for as long as possible before being brought inside.

The tree should be gradually acclimatized to the warmer indoor temperature. The room should ideally stay below 20 degrees Celsius, and the soil needs regular watering. Spraying the needles with water can also help.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back to a cooler environment gradually.

Even with careful handling, survival is not guaranteed. According to the Masaryk Forest Křtiny School Forest Enterprise, around 60 percent of the Christmas firs planted in previous years have successfully taken root.

World.title: Higher Prices, Fuller Hotels: Prague Is Becoming a Luxury City Break
World.content:
Prague is strengthening its position as a high-end tourist destination, attracting visitors willing to spend more on accommodation and services.

The Czech capital has ranked ahead of Vienna and Berlin in an international tourism index, while demand for luxury hotels continues to rise.

More than 2.3 million tourists visited Prague between July and September 2026, representing a three percent increase compared with the same period last year.



The city received a score of 92.7 out of 100 in the Global Tourist Perception Index, compiled by Data Appeal and Mabrian Intelligence. Vienna scored 85.6, while Berlin received 78.4.

The ranking assessed several aspects of the visitor experience, including satisfaction with accommodation, safety and the variety of tourist attractions.

According to František Cipro, chairman of the board of Prague City Tourism, the results reflect a shift in the city’s tourism profile.

“Prague clearly demonstrates that it is no longer a budget tourist destination, nor does it wish to be one,” he said.

The trend is also reflected in visitor spending. During the first half of 2026, Prague welcomed more than 3.8 million tourists, a one percent increase year-on-year. However, Mastercard payment data showed that spending by visitors from selected foreign markets rose by 18 percent.

Tourists from China and South Korea recorded the most significant increases in spending.

Accommodation figures point in the same direction. Almost two-thirds of guests staying in Prague hotels choose four- or five-star properties.

In 2025, the average price of a hotel room in the capital stood at around CZK 3,000 per night. In central Prague, the average rose to approximately CZK 4,100, while luxury hotels charged around CZK 5,800.

Demand for higher-end accommodation has remained strong despite rising prices. In September 2026, luxury hotels recorded an occupancy rate of 83 percent, their highest September result in seven years.

Germany Remains the Largest Source Market

Tourism continued to grow during the first nine months of 2026, with Prague recording more than 6.1 million visitors, a two percent increase compared with the same period in 2025.

Germany remained the largest source market for international visitors during the third quarter.

Some other markets also recorded notable growth. Visitor numbers from Taiwan increased by 27 percent, followed by Israel at 26 percent and Ireland at 23 percent.

World.title: How to Choose a High School in the Czech Republic: Open Days and School Fairs
World.content:
Choosing a high school is an important decision for students and their families.

School websites and brochures can provide useful information, but visiting schools in person offers a much better idea of what studying there is actually like.

Open days and high school fairs are two ways to explore the available options, meet teachers and students, and find out which school might be the right fit.



This is the first article in our series on choosing a high school in the Czech Republic.

Visit Schools During Open Days

Open days give prospective students and their parents the opportunity to look around a school before applying.

High schools open their doors to visitors, allowing them to explore classrooms, workshops and laboratories, meet teachers and current students, and ask questions about studying there.

An open day can help families find out more about:

Study programmes: What courses and specialisations does the school offer?

Admission requirements: What are the conditions for applying, and how does the entrance examination work?

Future opportunities: What options are available after graduation, including further education and employment?

School environment: What is the atmosphere like, and would the school be a good fit for the student?

Open days take place throughout the school year, with many schools organising them ahead of the application period.

Dates vary from one institution to another, so check individual school websites or use the online overview of high school open days to find upcoming events.

Compare Schools at High School Fairs

High school fairs offer another opportunity to explore different institutions without having to visit each one separately.

In Prague, one of the main events is SCHOLA PRAGENSIS, where visitors can meet representatives of secondary schools from different regions.

You can visit META stand at Schola Pragensis, Prague’s high school fair, taking place from 26 to 28 November at the Prague Congress Centre

– stand number 245 on the 2nd floor.

The META team of professionals will help you explore the options and answer all your questions.

Students and parents can compare study programmes, ask questions about admission procedures and learn more about individual schools directly from their representatives.

These events are particularly useful for students who have not yet decided what they want to study or are still considering several different options. Meeting representatives from multiple schools in one place can help narrow down the choices.

If you live outside Prague, you can also find a high school fair in your region.

Use Worksheets to Help Make Your Decision

Comparing schools, admission requirements and study programmes can quickly become confusing, especially when several institutions are under consideration.

Free worksheets are available to help students organise information, compare their options and think about what they want from their future school.

You can download the worksheets here.

World.title: Hungary rejects EU budget plans that would cut its funding, Magyar says
World.content:
Hungary will not accept any proposal for the EU’s next seven-year budget that reduces its funding, increases its contributions or places additional conditions on how the money can be used, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in Brussels on Friday.

Speaking to journalists after an extraordinary meeting of EU leaders, Magyar said Hungary’s priorities for the bloc’s next long-term budget, covering the period after 2027, were to preserve funding for cohesion policy and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).

He added that any new sources of funding should not place an excessive burden on Hungary’s national budget.

“The overall size of the budget is irrelevant, whether it is lower or higher,” Magyar said. “The amounts allocated to other chapters can be reduced, but from Hungary’s point of view, the key is that funding for cohesion and the Common Agricultural Policy must not decrease.”

Photo: MTI

If you missed it: PM Magyar says EU summit talks are entering their final stretch, but agreement remains elusive

Hungary opposes linking the EU budget to Ukraine funding

Magyar said Hungary could receive around €32–34 billion from the seven-year budget, leaving it with a net gain of approximately €15 billion over the period.

By contrast, he said, the proposal would provide Ukraine with as much as €100 billion and could open the EU budget to “unlimited” borrowing and interest payments. He said this was unacceptable.

According to Magyar, some member states support Ukraine and show solidarity with the country in their own ways, but they cannot accept being required to provide substantially larger amounts under central directives while facing difficult budgetary circumstances.

He said Hungary was not alone in its position, adding that the Visegrád Four and the 19-member Friends of Cohesion group also opposed cuts to cohesion and agricultural funding, as well as significant increases in member states’ contributions.

Photo: MTI

Hungary wants to decide how its support is spent

Magyar said Hungary intended to decide independently which healthcare or energy projects to support in Ukraine, and where.

“Solidarity with a country at war is necessary, but the member state providing the money must decide what it is spent on, how it is spent and how the spending is monitored,” he said.

He added that Hungary would continue to prioritise support for the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, including its ability to remain in the region and access healthcare and heating.

“Since we have the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, we must primarily support the continued presence of Hungarians living there, their healthcare and, for example, their heating,” Magyar said. “We will continue to do so.”

Magyar sees little chance of a December agreement

The prime minister said he saw very little chance of a compromise being reached in December on the basis of the current proposals.

He described Friday’s meeting as “completely unnecessary”, saying member states were further apart on the long-term budget than they had been on Thursday morning.

As no compromise was reached, EU leaders agreed to meet again in Brussels on 16 December and continue discussions until Christmas in an effort to reach a unanimous decision, Magyar said.

World.title: Budapest’s festive light tram fleet brings Christmas to the streets
World.content:
Budapest’s popular Christmas light fleet is returning on Friday, 27 November, bringing illuminated trams, a festive bus, a decorated cogwheel railway and a light boat to the Hungarian capital.

Budapest Christmas light fleet is back

The annual tradition, organised by Budapest Transport Company (BKV), has grown beyond the famous UV Light Tram, which has been running since 2009 and has become a familiar sight during the city’s Advent season.

This year’s fleet will feature seven decorated tram types, including the classic UV, the modern CAF Urbos 3/5 – which will be illuminated for the first time – the Combino, the TW6000 Hannover tram, the Ganz articulated tram, the upgraded KCSV-7 and the Tatra T5C5K2.

The festive vehicles will gather for a special procession on Friday. From 5 PM, they are scheduled to set off from Hungária depot, at 1 Brüll Alfréd Street, and travel along the route of tram line 1 as an illuminated convoy. The procession is expected to pass along the route after 6 PM.

Not only trams will bring the light

The wider Fényflotta, or Light Fleet, will also include a Santa Claus bus based on an Ikarus 280, the illuminated cogwheel railway serving the Buda hills, and a decorated boat on the Danube. The boat is also due to make its first journey on Friday.

BKV and Budapest’s public transport operator BKK will publish detailed timetables for the individual services on the BKK website and through the BudapestGO app.

Residents and visitors are invited to watch the launch along tram line 1 and enjoy one of the capital’s seasonal attractions as the Christmas period gets under way.

Read also: Budapest is beating Vienna and Prague in race for Christmas season visitors

World.title: VIDEO: Water main bursts in Budapest, flooding streets near Déli railway station
World.content:
A burst water main flooded several streets in Budapest’s District XII early on Friday, with water flowing from the Alkotás and Márvány streets junction towards Déli railway station and as far as Krisztina Square.

Videos posted on TikTok showed water streaming along Márvány Street and reaching the area around Déli railway station and the Déryné restaurant. Residents used sandbags to protect building entrances from the flooding.

Budapest Waterworks confirmed that the incident was caused by damage to a 200-millimetre asbestos-cement pipe at the junction of Alkotás Street and Márvány Street.

The company said its staff isolated the damaged section from the network at 2:56 am and called a vehicle recovery service to the scene. A repair team then began excavating the site. Repair work continued on Friday morning, with the company’s daytime crew taking over.

If you missed it: Hungary braces for freezing rain, heavy snowfall and huge temperature drops

Water service expected to resume in the afternoon

Budapest Waterworks said water supply to affected properties was expected to be restored in the early afternoon. To help residents during the interruption, an emergency water point connected to a fire hydrant was installed at the corner of Márvány Street and Győri Road.

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) told Index that the burst pipe had not caused disruption to public transport.

Footage shared on TikTok showed water flowing along Alkotás Road, past Déli railway station and towards Krisztina Square. The uploader said several streets had been flooded, while sandbags were placed at residential entrances to keep water out.

World.title: WATCH: Documentary titled “Role Models” examines Orbán and Dodik’s political friendship and business ties
World.content:
Transparency International’s Bosnia and Herzegovina chapter has released a documentary investigating Hungarian loans and business projects in Republika Srpska during the close relationship between Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik.

The documentary, titled Zagledani / Példaképek (“Role Models”), examines the economic background of the political relationship between former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and Milorad Dodik, the former president of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Serb entity, Republika Srpska. Transparency International in Bosnia and Herzegovina announced its release on Thursday.

The film follows Hungarian Exim Bank loans to Republika Srpska and investments by Hungarian companies, asking who benefited from the two politicians’ close ties and what the cooperation brought to local residents.

According to experts from Hungary and Bosnia and Herzegovina interviewed in the film, business figures close to Orbán gained access to projects in Republika Srpska on favourable terms, sometimes without competitive tenders, alongside the loans provided by Exim Bank, Telex writes. The filmmakers also question whether the bank was legally entitled to lend to the entity. A similar loan to North Macedonia is reportedly under investigation following an initiative by Hungary’s current prime minister, Péter Magyar.

Hungarian companies and a planned solar power plant

The documentary focuses in particular on the planned Trebinje 1 solar power plant near the southern Bosnian town of Trebinje, a project valued at around €50 million.

The concession was initially awarded to Republika Srpska’s state-owned electricity company, Elektroprivreda RS, before being transferred to a newly established company. Hungarian firm Lugos Renewables acquired a 70 per cent stake in that company without a public tender, according to the film. After Lugos withdrew from the project, its shareholding passed to another Hungarian company, Mayer NRG Kft.

Transparency International said it obtained the project documentation following several years of legal proceedings. The filmmakers also visited the company’s registered address in Budapest, but said they could not find its name even on the building’s intercom.

Film draws parallels between the two political systems

Shot during Hungary’s political transition, the documentary compares the governing methods of Orbán and Dodik, focusing on corruption allegations, the situation of independent media and efforts to restrict criticism of those in power.

The film features Hungarian and Bosnian experts, including Andrea Schmidt, Gergely Brückner, Siniša Vukelić, Csaba Lukács, Srđan Blagovčanin and Miklós Ligeti.

The documentary is available free of charge in Hungarian and Serbian on Transparency International Bosnia and Herzegovina’s YouTube channel.

Orbán and Dodik have remained close since Orbán’s election defeat in April. In late October, Orbán visited Dodik, who wrote on social media that “true friendship lasts forever”. The two were shown drinking rakija by a fireplace and later listening to folk music together around a campfire.

World.title: One in three Hungarians faces basic cost-of-living hardship, survey finds
World.content:
Around 2.6 million adult Hungarians are struggling with at least one basic living expense, according to a nationwide survey by the Equilibrium Institute.

One in three Hungarian adults – approximately 2.62 million people, or 33 per cent of the adult population – faces at least one basic cost-of-living difficulty, a new survey by the Equilibrium Institute has found. These include being unsure whether they can afford to heat their home, being unable to eat meat or fish at least every other day, or lacking the means to cover an unexpected expense of HUF 120,000 (EUR 320).

The difficulties often overlap. Around 1.3 million adults, or 17 per cent, face at least two of the three problems, while approximately 633,000 people – 8 per cent – struggle with all three.

Heating and food remain unaffordable for many

As winter approaches, 13 per cent of respondents said there could be a period in the next three months when they would not have enough money to heat their homes. A further 4 per cent said they would be unable to pay for heating at all, while 82 per cent were confident they could cover the cost.

Food affordability is an even more widespread concern: one in five adults said they would not be able to afford meat or fish at least every other day over the next quarter.

The survey found particularly high levels of hardship among older people. Among those aged 65 and over, 41 per cent said they could not afford regular meat or fish consumption. Nearly one-third were uncertain whether they could cover heating costs or an unexpected expense.

Unexpected bills could push households into difficulty

The survey also asked whether respondents could pay an unexpected HUF 120,000 bill, such as an urgent repair or an unforeseen medical cost.

While 57 per cent said they could manage the expense without difficulty, 22 per cent would struggle to pay it and 21 per cent could not cover it themselves. In total, 43 per cent would face serious financial strain from a single unexpected expense of this size.

The gap between education levels was pronounced. More than half of those with no more than eight years of primary education said they could not independently raise HUF 120,000. Among university graduates, the figure was just 4 per cent.

Women reported hardship at almost twice the rate of men across all three measures. Among women, 23 per cent were uncertain about heating, 28 per cent could not afford regular meat or fish, and 27 per cent lacked the means to cover the unexpected expense. The corresponding figures for men were 11, 13 and 14 per cent.

Hardship is not limited to villages

The findings show that deprivation is not confined to small settlements. People living in towns that are not county seats were most likely to report uncertainty about heating (21 per cent) and difficulty affording regular meat or fish (26 per cent).

Meanwhile, residents of villages were least likely to be able to cover an unexpected HUF 120,000 expense: 28 per cent said they could not do so themselves.

Respondents said they would need a monthly net income of HUF 300,000 per person for a modest standard of living, HUF 500,000 for an average one, and HUF 800,000 to live comfortably.

Most households expect little change in income

Looking ahead to the next three months, 53 per cent of households expect their income to remain unchanged, while 17 per cent anticipate a decrease. Only 29 per cent expect their income to rise.

Young adults were more optimistic: more than one-third of those aged 18–29 expected their household income to increase. Among people aged 65 and over, slightly more expected a decline than an increase.

The Equilibrium Institute said that 27 per cent of the adult population belongs to financially vulnerable groups that do not expect their income to rise in the near future. It also warned that the reserves of households whose finances are currently stable but who do not expect improvement may be limited if heating costs remain a strain.

World.title: Small Hungarian ice cream parlour wins 2026’s best Christmas fondant with smoky whisky creation
World.content:
A small ice cream parlour in Orosháza has won the 2026 Christmas fondant competition with a smoky whisky and hazelnut creation, beating two pistachio favourites. The Hóvirág Ice Cream Parlour’s sweet was chosen from a record 147 entries submitted by 24 producers.

The recipe combines whisky, caramel and hazelnut, with the creators keeping the alcohol in the filling. According to the makers, its alcohol content is 0.98 per cent.

The competition’s founders, Ádám and Gergely Kovács, told Index that they entered the same sweet in last year’s contest, where it came second in the professional category. This year, they also entered it for the overall award—and won.

The runners-up were Stühmer’s Sicilian pistachio fondant, which contains a whole pistachio, and a pistachio cream sweet from L’art Chocolate Workshop in Békéscsaba, enclosed in a pistachio coating.

A record field and new categories

The seventh edition of the competition attracted 147 Christmas fondants, which were tasted by nearly 250 judges and tasters. More than 13,000 pieces were sampled across eight categories. For the professional award, each producer could submit only two products to a six-member jury.

The traditional jelly category was won by Damniczki Confectionery in Székesfehérvár with its raspberry-filled Málna Inspiration, coated in raspberry-flavoured Valrhona Inspiration. Hungary’s most popular Christmas fondant remains the jelly variety, the organisers said.

This year’s other winners included Kézműves Confectionery in Gyula, whose Bíborfehér fondant won the professional category after its namesake cake won the 2026 Hungary’s Cake competition. Stühmer’s Rákóczi cottage-cheese fondant came second, while Ricsi Confectionery in Pápa took third place with a sea-buckthorn version.

New categories included high-protein and gourmet fondants, as well as an influencers’ favourite award. The gourmet prize went to Szent Korona Confectionery in Soltvadkert for its white chocolate Beriolette made with Frittmann Néró Rosé. Promenád Café in Balatongyörök won the new-flavour award with a salted butter caramel and pecan fondant.

What winning means for a small producer

The competition was created to give smaller workshops a chance to reach consumers alongside well-known brands. The founders said a category win can lead to a noticeable increase in orders, although the Hóvirág parlour was still taking orders through Facebook while its online shop was being prepared.

The founders said they had not been contacted by major retailers about the winning sweet. However, they believe award-winning flavours can influence the wider market over time. They recalled that after the first competition was won by a salted caramel fondant, similar flavours began appearing in other workshops and larger manufacturers’ ranges.

World.title: Hungarian workforce among 3,000 people transferred by energy giant BP
World.content:
British energy giant BP has agreed to transfer around 3,000 employees working in its finance operations in India, Hungary and Malaysia to Indian technology services company Wipro, in a move reflecting the growing outsourcing of corporate support functions.

BP transfers 3,000 employees to Indian company

The employees are expected to move to Wipro in 2027, subject to applicable conditions. BP will nevertheless retain oversight of operational standards and data, according to the companies’ announcement reported by Reuters.

The exact number of Hungarian workers affected has not been disclosed. BP employs more than 3,300 people in Hungary, with offices in Budapest and Szeged, as well as approximately 7,500 in India and 1,400 in Malaysia. Its total global workforce stands at around 93,700.

Two employees at BP’s Budapest office told Hungarian news outlet Telex that staff were informed of the changes on Wednesday morning. According to their unofficial estimates, between 400 and 600 Hungarian employees could be affected.

They said workers were expected to retain their existing roles when transferred to Wipro, and understood that their employment could be guaranteed for one year from March 2027. Neither the figures nor the reported guarantee have been officially confirmed by the companies.

The employees also suggested that Wipro could eventually use artificial intelligence to automate parts of the finance processes, potentially leading to staff reductions. However, they said they had received no official information about such plans. The company has not confirmed these accounts.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

BP seeks to simplify operations and reduce costs

BP is focusing on reducing its debt and operating expenses. Chief Financial Officer Kate Thomson said the partnership with Wipro would help improve the company’s finance operations and simplify processes. BP declined to tell Reuters what proportion of its finance workforce the 3,000 employees represent. Wipro has also provided no further details about the agreement.

The deal reflects a wider trend among multinational companies to transfer in-house support operations to specialist technology providers. Businesses are increasingly seeking to reduce costs and improve productivity through automation and artificial intelligence, while outsourcing can also move operational expenses off their own books.

Technology service providers, meanwhile, gain established teams and longer-term contracts. Pareekh Jain, founder of technology advisory firm EIIR Trend, told Reuters that such transfers are increasingly being considered as an alternative to redundancies as companies rethink their internal service centres in response to AI.

He said providers typically take over these operations through outsourcing agreements lasting three to five years, while hoping to secure additional work from the same clients. Wipro employs more than 240,000 people across 65 countries and provides technology services and business consulting. The transfer is expected to take place in 2027, although the precise arrangements for Hungarian employees remain unclear.

World.title: FM Anita Orbán: dozens of Hungarian companies willing to help rebuild Ukraine
World.content:
More than 40 Hungarian companies have told the government they are willing to take part in Ukraine’s reconstruction once the war ends, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced, following high-level talks between the two countries.

Hungary to help rebuilding Ukraine after the war

Speaking on Kossuth Radio on Thursday, Anita Orbán said post-war rebuilding had been among the subjects discussed during Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s visit to Transcarpathia on Tuesday. The talks also covered railway and road infrastructure developments and the possible opening of a new border crossing.

She said many Ukrainian industrial facilities had relocated to Transcarpathia, making the region an increasingly prosperous part of the country’s economy. Hungarian businesses, particularly those based in eastern Hungary, could benefit from participating in reconstruction projects, she added.

The minister did not identify the companies involved or specify which sectors they represent. The figure therefore reflects expressions of interest communicated to the Hungarian government, rather than confirmed contracts or reconstruction commitments.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Bilateral talks to continue in 2027

Orbán described Tuesday’s meeting between Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an opportunity to establish the main directions for renewed cooperation. The next step is expected to be a meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental committee in the first quarter of 2027. The two countries’ agriculture and economy ministers are also due to hold talks.

Energy cooperation was another topic. Orbán said Hungary already imports crude oil from Ukraine, and companies believe the volume could be doubled. Hungary, meanwhile, supplies diesel to Ukraine, generating revenue for Hungarian oil and gas company MOL.

The minister also discussed the gradual improvement in bilateral relations over the past six months. She said Ukraine had begun addressing the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, after which Hungary took steps towards opening one of the clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations.

Budapest has asked Kyiv to accelerate the implementation of language legislation adopted by the Ukrainian parliament. According to Orbán, Ukraine has promised to do so. She stressed that enforcement of the law had been included as a condition in the EU accession process, and said Ukraine could not make further progress if it failed to protect the rights of its Hungarian minority.

In case you missed it: Magyar and Zelensky discuss energy, trade and EU membership as Hungary and Ukraine seek closer ties

Hungary wants to stay outside Ukraine loan

Orbán also reiterated that Hungary would prefer not to participate in a proposed €45 billion loan programme for Ukraine. However, she confirmed that Budapest would not block the process.

Asked about Russia’s response to the Hungarian-Ukrainian meeting, she said the Kremlin had made no official or unofficial comment. Diplomatic relations between Budapest and Moscow remain in place, she added, describing Russia’s reciprocal response to the expulsion of ten Russian diplomats as normal diplomatic practice.

Separately, Orbán announced that Hungary would join the International Coalition for the Return of Ukrainian Children, which aims to support the safe return of children taken during the war and reunite families.

World.title: Serbia’s Student List Names University Professor as Presidential Candidate
World.content:
Serbia’s Student List on Friday presented a chemistry professor, Radomir Saicic, as its candidate for the presidential election scheduled for December 27, at a press conference in Belgrade.

Saicic said he was proud that the student movement – which led mass protests then scored a landslide win in parliamentary polls last month – had placed its trust in him.

“I joined the movement believing that a change of government only makes sense if there is a change in the system of values, including the way those in power treat citizens. That is why I will advocate for a sovereign Serbia in which the constitution is respected and every citizen can live with dignity,” he said.

“Life has taught me to take responsibility when times are hardest, and I am ready to take on that responsibility now,” he added.

Saicic accused the outgoing government led by the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS – which is still acting in a caretaker capacity – of continuing to undermine the state, stressing the need to restore public trust in institutions such as parliament, the government, the courts and the presidency.

“For years, the presidential office has been used to deepen divisions, while its constitutional powers have been exceeded,” he said.

“As president, I will act within the limits of my powers, publicly explain my decisions and demand the same accountability from other public office holders,” he continued.

Asked about the future of EU candidate state Serbia’s integration process with the bloc, which had stalled under SNS rule due to democratic backsliding, Saicic said he had “a fundamentally positive attitude towards Europe and European values”.

He highlighted the importance of values such as the rule of law, high-quality education, knowledge-based economic and industrial development, environmental protection and addressing climate change.

“These are all things we should develop to the greatest extent possible, not for the sake of meeting certain formal criteria, but so that we can truly become what we should be,” he said.

Saicic added that EU membership should be considered, but that Serbia must first make genuine progress in these areas.

Asked when the new government would be formed, Saicic said he expected it to happen well before the legal deadline, adding that consultations were underway.

Saicic was elected to parliament on the Student List in elections held on October 25. The Student List won 140 seats, well over the 103 won by the long-ruling SNS.

After that landslide win, Saicic has a good chance of winning the upcoming presidential election.

The SNS has meanwhile signalled that it may boycott the vote. Serbia’s former President and current head of the SNS’s parliamentary group, Aleksandar Vucic said he favoured boycotting it – but added that his party will make its final decision at its assembly on December 13.

By law, presidential candidate proposals need to be filed 20 days before the election, which means all candidates need to be nominated before December 7. It is not clear how the SNS could decide on its participation several days later.

Saicic, a professor at the University of Belgrade and member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, SANU, supported the student-led protests and was among those SANU members who signed a petition calling for Vucic’s resignation in June 2025.

Serbia’s constitution grants the President limited powers, including representing the country at home and abroad, promulgating laws, nominating a candidate for prime minister and commanding the armed forces. Executive power rests with the government.

World.title: Serbian Agents Tailed Foreign Election Observers in 2023, Searched Rooms
World.content:
Burgers and MacMahon were part of a 30-strong long-term foreign observer mission, on the ground for roughly a month, moving between cities to monitor the conduct of the election campaign, the financing, media coverage, and any potential misuse of state resources, before voting day itself and the process of counting the votes and processing any complaints.

Such missions are a common occurrence during elections across the continent.

Neither Burgers nor MacMahon had any idea they were being watched and first learned of the surveillance when they were contacted by BIRN. Burgers, however, said it was clear that tensions were running high.

The ruling Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, had been in power since 2012, a period characterised by growing state capture, shrinking media freedoms and the increasingly repressive actions of security bodies. Previous elections had been marred by allegations of voter intimidation, skewed media coverage and the flagrant misuse of state resources.

“From some opposition people we talked to, we heard that they were facing problems and threats,” Burgers told BIRN.

“In fact, we met one man who was later beaten up. You hear these stories quite often, but when you actually talk to the person, and then later you get a picture and a message: ‘No, I can’t meet with you because I’m in the hospital…’ That was shocking.”

At the time, there was a change at the top of BIA; director Aleksandar Vulin, a former political ally of the wife of 1990s Serbian strongman Slobodan Milosevic, resigned in early November and his deputy, Tomislav Radovanovic, took over in an acting capacity in December.

Radovanovic was previously a police attaché in France, and was then appointed head of the Special Investigative Methods Service of the Criminal Police Directorate, UKP, which carries out covert surveillance and recording in the field, as well as monitoring of telephone, electronic, and other forms of communication.

Previously, Radovanovic had spoken publicly about what he claimed was a parallel structure within the Ministry of Interior that had allegedly wiretapped then President Aleksandar Vucic, founder of the SNS; he accused officers behind the discovery of a huge cannabis operation – known as Jovanjica and which enjoyed protection from members of the security services – of trying to incriminate Vucic’s family.

Radovanovic is currently deputy director of BIA.

Nothing secret

World.title: Democracy Digest: V4 Remain Critical of Budget as EU Summit Ends Without Deal
World.content:
Criticism also came from the EU Commission. Speaking in Strasbourg, ahead of the EU summit, Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin warned that Costa’s compromise proposal for the bloc’s 2028–2034 budget could shift costs from Brussels to national capitals. “Cutting the Union budget will not necessarily bring savings for our member states,” he told the European Parliament. Governments would still need to invest in security and competitiveness, he argued, but would lose some of the benefits of pooling resources at the EU level. He also noted that the proposed budget would be smaller than the current one as a share of the EU’s gross national income. Polish PM Donald Tusk warned that cutting the budget would mean less security on the eastern flank and is, therefore, unacceptable. Czech PM Andrej Babis was also doubtful about an agreement. “It will be complicated and we will see if there is an agreement. I don’t think so,” he said on Wednesday before departing for Brussels. He also described the inclusion of Ukraine aid in the next multiannual financial framework as “not acceptable at all”. “I have the same veto power as the German Chancellor. I will fight for Czech interests,” he added.

While the V4 are united in their fight for keeping the cohesion and the agriculture funding intact, they remain divided on the question of financing Ukraine. The EU proposal envisages an additional 45-billion-euro loan for Ukraine, on top of the 90 billion euros already agreed for 2026 and 2027, to help keep the government working and defence investments afloat as the country enters the sixth year of war. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia had previously secured opt-outs from contributing to the loan, but German Chancellor Merz insists that all countries should be on board and has threatened to veto the budget if there is no alignment on the issue. For Kyiv, establishing a predictable and sustainable financing mechanism is crucial. Integrating support for Ukraine into the next EU budget would therefore seem a logical step. However, the idea remains politically contentious in several member states, many of which are already struggling with tight public finances and face the difficult task of balancing higher defence spending against the need to maintain social expenditure.

World.title: ‘Sheer Outrage’: North Macedonia Activists Vow to Intensify Protests After Femicides
World.content:
Women’s rights activists in North Macedonia are planning to take to the streets every other week in a campaign against gender-based violence, following a series of killings of women and girls that has sparked public outrage.

The initiative Nitu edna povekje [Not One More] held a protest in Skopje on November 25 to coincide with the start of the international campaign 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence. Its members say they will continue protests and road blockades, seeking both to push the authorities towards more concrete action and to build a stronger community of women and their supporters.

“We are all united against femicide,” Marija Arsenkova, an activist and member of Not One More said in an interview with BIRN before the November 25 protest.

The campaign follows the killing on November 3 of 17-year-old Biljana Kirik in Bogdanci, a small town in southeastern North Macedonia, allegedly by her 21-year-old partner.

World.title: Timeline: Two Decades of Government Takeovers of Turkish TV Channels
World.content:
The recent state takeovers of the prominent critical television stations Halk TV and Sozcu TV have drawn renewed attention to the Turkish government’s use of trustees to take control of media outlets.

But while the latest interventions may appear to mark a new phase in the pressure on critical television, state takeovers of broadcasters are far from new in Turkey. In different forms and using different legal justifications, they have been a recurring feature over the two decades-plus that Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power.

The early interventions to take control of broadcasters largely involved the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund, TMSF, pursuing debts originating from failed banks. Later takeovers have increasingly followed criminal and terrorism investigations or emergency decrees.

World.title: European Parliament Backs Vukovar Anniversary Resolution Criticising Serbia
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

The European Parliament on Thursday adopted a resolution on the 35th anniversary of the fall of Vukovar in eastern Croatia, urging Serbia to grant access to documents in wartime archives and cooperate to help find the remaining missing persons from the Yugoslav wars.

The resolution called for “the cooperation of the competent authorities to establish the fate and whereabouts of those still missing”.

It urged the Serbian authorities to “grant access to relevant wartime archives, disclose all available information on the locations of individual and mass graves, fight against impunity for wartime crimes, and facilitate the recovery, identification and dignified return of victims’ remains to their families”.

The Croatian border town fell to the combined forces of the Yugoslav Army and Serbian paramilitaries on November 18, 1991, who went on to commit numerous atrocities. By then, the town was largely destroyed.

The resolution also strongly condemned “all forms of denial, minimisation or glorification of war crimes”, noting the public honours paid to the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade in July this year.

It further called for educational, cultural and commemorative programmes that promote a “fact-based understanding of the Croatian Homeland War and the 1990s”, while encouraging reconciliation and respect for all victims.

The legacy of the 1990s war has long been a key issue of disagreement between Croatia and Serbia, and the resolution has sparked renewed controversy.

Ahead of the European Parliament vote, the resolution was criticised by Serbia’s student movement, which under the name Student List won Serbia’s recent parliamentary elections.

The student movement argued that there should also be recognition of war crimes committed against Serb civilians during the Croatian conflict. It said the resolution did not contribute to an “objective understanding of historical events” or to reconciliation.

It further argued that the draft resolution overlooks killings, persecution and mass displacement of Serbs, particularly during the Croatian military operations Flash and Storm in 1995.

“Responsibility for war crimes must be individual and established on the basis of evidence and final court judgments, rather than attributed to entire nations,” the student movement said.

Austrian MEP Helmut Brandstatter, from the Renew Europe liberal political group, had proposed an alternative resolution, centred on regional scope of responsibility. His proposal was supported by the RECOM Reconciliation Network, the Humanitarian Law Centre, the Humanitarian Law Center Kosovo, Documenta – Centre for Dealing with the Past, the Centre for Civic Education, Human Rights Action and the Association for Social Research and Communications.

But the media outlet N1 reported that Renew Europe gave up on its proposal after a few minor changes were made.

Among the material added to resolution was a line saying that “families of missing persons of all nationalities also continue to wait for answers”. It was also added that in 2010, Serbia’s then President Boris Tadic “paid tribute to the victims, apologised for the crimes committed there and stressed the importance of reconciliation and of establishing the fate of those still missing”.

The resolution instructs the European Parliament’s President to forward the resolution to the governments and parliaments of EU member countries, and those of the Western Balkan countries. However, there is no obligation for them to adopt the resolution themselves.

World.title: Romanian Far-Right Leader Charged With Inciting Violence
World.content:
Romanian prosecutors on Thursday charged hard-line right-winger George Simion with public incitement over remarks calling for members of the Central Electoral Bureau, BEC, to be “skinned in a public square”.

The investigation concerns a video Simion posted on Facebook in March 2025, after the BEC rejected Calin Georgescu’s presidential candidacy on the grounds that it did not meet the legal requirements.

Prosecutors say Simion’s remarks encouraged people to commit crimes.

“Through the video, the defendant urged the public to commit acts constituting serious criminal offences, namely extreme physical assaults, torture or murder,” said a statement issued by the General Prosecutor’s Office.

“The message posted on social media was delivered against the backdrop of a protest taking place outside the BEC headquarters on the same day. The demonstration escalated into violence, with property being set on fire and vandalised and gendarmes injured,” it added.

Public incitement is punishable in Romania with prison terms of three months to three years, or a fine. But if committed by a public official, the penalty increases from one to five years.

Simion dismissed the case as a “farce” and a “politically motivated dossier”. He denied wrongdoing.

Hundreds of his supporters gathered outside the General Prosecutor’s Office, where they chanted his name and accused the justice system of being politically manipulated. No incidents were reported.

Simion’s indictment comes as Romania cracks down on far-right rhetoric and incitement to violence.

Last month, prosecutors sent AUR vice-president and lawmaker Dan Tanasa to trial on charges of inciting hatred and discrimination against foreign workers after he urged people to “refuse orders which are not delivered by a Romanian” and “not to encourage the import of unqualified labourers from Asia and Africa”.

Prosecutors said his statements encouraged discrimination and could damage relations between citizens by undermining mutual respect. Although Romanian lawmakers enjoy parliamentary immunity for statements made in the exercise of their mandate, prosecutors said the immunity did not apply in this case.

Far-right former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu is also facing charges in three cases related to the promotion of fascist and other extremist ideas, as well as alleged complicity in undermining the constitutional order. Georgescu is also under house arrest in a separate case in which he is accused of defrauding a businessman of more than one million euros.

Georgescu, who emerged as the frontrunner in the first round of the November 2024 presidential election before the result was annulled, has denied any wrongdoing.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Radev ruling majority hikes municipal real estate taxes
World.content:
In a vote in the National Assembly on November 26, Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev’s ruling majority Progressive Bulgaria pushed through amendments that will push up municipal real estate property taxes.

The move runs counter to Radev’s pre-election claim that in power, he would not raise taxes.

The National Assembly approved the phased update of real estate tax assessments, approving the second and final reading of amendments to the Local Taxes and Fees Act. They provide for an increase of 30 per cent in 2027 and 35 per cent in 2028 and 2029. They will cover buildings, improvements and agricultural land throughout Bulgaria.

During the debate on the bill, Deputy Minister of Finance Lyudmila Petkova rejected the opposition’s accusation that regional differences are not taken into account. According to her, the location coefficient is included in the formation of the tax assessment. Some opposition parties described the changes as untimely.

Atidje Veli of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms countered: “The doubling of tax assessments for the next three years in the face of rising prices, the introduction of a number of new taxes, will further increase the cost of living.”

Temenuzhka Petkova of opposition GERB_UDF and Stoyu Stoev of We Continue the Change also criticised the amendments:

“With this centralised increase in the basic tax assessment, we achieve an increase in three taxes – building tax, acquisition tax and inheritance tax on such properties. Which we believe greatly increases the tax burden on Bulgarian citizens,” Petkova said.

“In such a period of crisis that is coming, and if this property bubble bursts, it should not finally happen that after three years the tax assessments will be higher than the market assessments,” Stoev said.

Deputy Minister Petkova rejected the accusations that the financial sanctions imposed are being doubled, not converted into currency:

“The updating of fines and sanctions is not a measure tied to the Euro Adoption Act. In fact, the updating of fines and sanctions is dictated by the fact that they have not been updated for more than 20 years,” she said.

The proposal of the Bulgarian National Assembly to reduce the tax due by 23 per cent for the purchase of a single home by parents up to the age of 29 was unanimously supported. The relief will apply if the sale price of the home is up to 300 000 euro, and the buyers are married, have at least one child and have no outstanding public debts.

World.title: Bulgaria’s National Assembly amends Corporate Income Tax Act, introducing one-off ‘excess profit tax’
World.content:
Bulgaria’s National Assembly voted on November 26 to approve the second and final reading of amendments to the Corporate Income Tax Act, which introduce a one-off “excess profit tax” in 2027 on banks and several other sectors.

The “excess profit tax” of 33 per cent will affect banks, insurance companies, food retailers with net sales revenue for 2026 of no less than five million euro, telecommunications companies, exchange bureaus and payday loan companies.

The tax base for the taxation of excess profits of companies falling within the scope of the bill will be the difference between the taxable profit for 2027 and the average value of taxable profits for the period from 2020 to 2025.

The amendments provide that 30 per cent of the tax can be transferred for specific purposes such as investments or the formation of reserves.

They provide that a taxable person who fails to indicate or incorrectly indicates data or circumstances leading to the determination of the tax due on excess profit in a smaller amount shall be punished with a property penalty in the amount of 100 000 to 500 000 euro.

The amendments also increase the so-called “weekend tax” from three per cent to seven per cent. This tax is levied on personal use of company assets, such as company cars.

Just as with the amendments to the Personal Income Tax Act earlier on November 26, the increases in fines and property sanctions for tax violations sparked debate, with sharp and repeated criticism from the opposition.

The problem the opposition pointed out is the replacement of the previous fines in leva with the same amounts in euro. This effectively doubles the penalties.

Assen Vassilev, leader of the opposition We Continue the Change, repeatedly asked for re-votes on the clauses with the fines. He called for them to be converted at the rate of 1.95583, as provided for in the law on the adoption of the euro.

Vassilev said that the National Assembly is setting a bad example for business and Bulgarian citizens, and MPs were violating their oath to be guided by the interests of the people, instead blindly carrying out the instructions of the Ministry of Finance.

Both Vassilev and Temenuzhka Petkova of GERB-UDF said that the almost twofold increase in fines is a violation of the Euro Adoption Act, but the head of the parliamentary committee on the budget, Konstantin Prodanov of Roumen Radev’s Progressive Act, said that the act was no longer in force.

Martin Dimitrov of Democratic Bulgaria said that the ruling majority had no explanation why taxes for Bulgarian companies were doubled, while for multinational global companies there was a precise currency conversion.

On November 25, the European Central Bank (ECB), in a letter made public in the media, said that the one-off windfall tax on banks in Bulgaria would affect lending, their capital resilience and the country’s economic growth.

The ECB said that it was not specified whether the tax would be levied in addition to the standard corporate income tax rate of 10 per cent. It said that the combined tax rate on profits classified as windfall profits could reach 43 per cent.

The central bank said that the additional tax burden could be passed on to customers through higher interest rates and fees on loans, lower deposit returns or stricter lending conditions. Banks could also restrict lending and the accumulation of capital buffers, the ECB said.

(Archive photo: EC Audiovisual Service)

World.title: Bulgaria’s Parliament doubles fines for individuals and companies breaking tax laws
World.content:
With the backing solely of Prime Minister Roumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria party, Parliament approved on November 26 the second and final reading of amendments to the Personal Income Tax that double the fines for tax law violations by individuals and companies.

This sparked fierce criticism from the opposition.

In amendments, all currently existing fines that are still written in leva are directly replaced with euro, with their numerical value being preserved, without respecting the principle of currency conversion at the fixed exchange rate.

For example, failure to file an annual tax return within the legal deadline will now be punished with 500 euro, compared to the previous penalty of 500 leva. If the fixed exchange rate were applied, the fine would be 255.65 euro, not twice as high.

For filing a tax return with false content, the current fine of 1000 leva is proposed to become 1000 euro next year. Employers who do not withhold and remit the tax to the budget will also be punished with a double penalty – the current 1000 leva will become 1000 euro, and in the event of a repeated violation, it will jump from 2000 leva to 2000 euro.

Martin Dimitrov of opposition Democratic Bulgaria said that if firms in the private sector took the same approach, they would be severely fined.

“And what are your motives for making a 500 leva fine instead of 500 euro?” Dimitrov said.

Assen Vassilev of opposition We Continue the Change said: “This is a very bad parliamentary practice – you make raises without motivation. When you wonder why inflation is high, remember this example”.

Alexander Ivanov of GERB-UDF accused the government of violating the Euro Adoption Act, which says that the conversion of prices and fees can only be at the rate of 1 euro for 1.95583 leva.

Milen Trifonov of Progressive Bulgaria said that some fines have not been changed for two decades and have lost their disciplinary character.

“For example, how would a person with huge incomes be motivated to file an annual tax return if he knows that he will be sanctioned with only 500 leva. Such a sanction does not work preventively,” Trifonov said.

However, Trifonov refrained from explaining that failure to declare large incomes, leading to large-scale tax evasion, entails quite severe sanctions, forced collection by the National Revenue Agency, and criminal liability under the Criminal Code.

He said that in many cases, tax laws only specify maximum fines, and this is to the benefit of taxpayers. “Tax inspectors have a proven practice of assessing what fine to impose based on the severity of the violation. For minor violations, they will impose low fines, not the maximum ones,” Trifonov said.

The ruling party rejected all the opposition’s proposals for strict adherence to the fixed exchange rate when converting fines from leva to euro. The DB’s proposal to increase the tax discount for early filing of a tax return and payment of the full amount of tax from 500 leva to 500 euro was also rejected. Instead, the correct conversion is applied here – 255 euro.

The majority of the other amendments to the Personal Income Tax Act were voted on with full support from all parties. These include an almost 70 per cent increase in tax rebates for children up to 500 euro for one child, 1000 euro for children and 1500 euro for three or more children, and a 1200 euro tax credit for a child who has a disability.

(Photo: parliament.bg)

World.title: BNB: Loans to households in Bulgaria in October 2026 up 20.5% on annual basis
World.content:
Loans to households and NPISHs (non-profit institutions serving households) in Bulgaria added up to 33.635 billion euro at the end of October 2026, an increase of 20.5 per cent compared with October 2025, Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) said in a regular report on monetary statistics on November 26.

This followed 20.7 per cent annual growth in these loans in September 2026, BNB said.

At the end of October 2026, loans for house purchases added up to 20 billion euro, an annual increase of 24.1 per cent, following 24.8 per cent annual growth in September 2026.

Consumer loans amounted to 12.589 billion euro. Compared with October 2025, this was an increase of 16.3 per cent (16 per cent annual growth in September 2026).

Deposits of Households and NPISHs were 57.799 billion euro at the end of October 2026.

This was an increase of 15.4 per cent compared with October 2025 (16.2 per cent annual growth in September 2026), BNB said.
