World.title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Türkiye open Makkah defense pact talks in Islamabad
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye opened talks in Islamabad on Friday on how to implement their Makkah defense pact, a Pakistani Foreign Office official confirmed to Arab News.

The Saudi and Turkish foreign ministers are expected to attend the two-day meeting on Nov. 27–28, which will focus on how the countries would put their mutual defense pledge into practice.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye signed the agreement in Makkah on Aug. 7 amid heightened regional tensions over the US-Israeli war against Iran. The pact commits them to treating an armed attack on any one of the three countries as an attack on all.

Türkiye completed ratification on Friday after President Recep Tayyip Erdogan formally approved the agreement, according to the country’s Official Gazette.

“The committee meetings have started,” a Pakistani Foreign Office official told Arab News on Friday late afternoon, giving no details of participants or the agenda.

Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif told AFP on Wednesday the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis would be among the issues discussed.

At their first committee meeting in Istanbul on Aug. 31, the three countries agreed to establish a permanent secretariat in Riyadh and pursue joint development and production of defense technology. At emergency talks in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the committee condemned attacks targeting Saudi cities and civilian facilities and confirmed retired Pakistani Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood as the alliance’s first secretary-general for a three-year term.

Islamabad police imposed temporary traffic restrictions to accommodate the foreign delegations. Heavy vehicles are barred from entering Islamabad and neighboring Rawalpindi via the motorway and Grand Trunk Road until 12:30 a.m. Saturday. The Faizabad Bus Terminal and part of the capital’s bus network are also affected, and two hiking trails in the Margalla Hills are closed Friday.

Most roads in Islamabad remained open to regular traffic on Friday, while police sealed off the Red Zone, which houses Parliament, the Supreme Court, federal ministries and foreign diplomatic missions. The government directed ministries and other federal offices in the area to work remotely for the day.

World.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo amid diplomatic spat
World.content:
KINSHASA: Uganda’s army said on Friday it planned to withdraw from a key DR Congo town and accused militias apparently allied to the Congolese government of stepping up attacks in the strife-torn eastern region.

The Ugandan announcement comes days after the DRC said it had summoned the Ugandan embassy’s head of mission over remarks by the country’s army chief.

The mineral-rich eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has been wracked by violence for more than 30 years, often drawing in its neighbors Uganda and Rwanda directly or through support for local armed groups.

Ugandan armed forces (UPDF) have been deployed in Ituri and North Kivu provinces on the DRC’s border with Uganda since 2021.

They were sent to back up the Congolese army against militants linked to the Islamic State jihadist group.

The Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), historically a Ugandan rebel coalition, was established in the eastern DRC in 1995 and regularly carries out killings in the deeply troubled region plagued by myriad armed groups.

The Congolese army is also fighting the armed FRN anti-governmental group, formerly known as the M23, which is backed by Rwanda, in the region.

On Monday, Ugandan army chief, Muhoozi Kainerugaba and son of President Yoweri Museveni, threatened on X to take control of the strategic Congolese town of Walikale in North Kivu province.

The FRN launched an offensive toward the town at the beginning of the month.

Kainerugaba — known for inflammatory posts on social media — had in a separate post also called for the unconditional surrender of the airport in Isiro, the provincial capital in Haut-Uele.

In response, Kinshasa announced the following day the summons of the Ugandan diplomat following what it called the “particularly serious” remarks.

The DRC “remains determined to ensure respect for its dignity and its institutions in the face of any form of provocation or interference,” it said in a statement.

On Friday, the Ugandan army spokesman said on X that it would “soon” withdraw its forces from the town of Lubero in North Kivu which is close to a front line in fighting between Congolese and FRN forces.

In a separate post, the spokesman accused militia forces, including some apparently allied to the Congolese government, of stepping up attacks on civilians.

“These negative militia forces have increasingly mounted attacks against vulnerable communities, massacring women and children such as the Bahema and Tutsi communities in Ituri and the North Kivu region,” he said.

“Under International Humanitarian Law (IHL), the UPDF retains the responsibility to extend protection to such vulnerable communities and will continue to do so whenever possible,” he added.

World.title: Trump backs Iraqi leader’s efforts to curb oil-smuggling
World.content:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said on Friday he supported Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s move to put Kurdistan’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control in an effort to curb smuggling.

Zaidi, who has vowed to fight rampant corruption in Iraq, has been cracking down on the illicit oil trade, arresting officials and challenging an Iran-backed armed group after smuggling was uncovered in its stronghold near Baghdad.

“We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state,” Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Zaidi’s decision was widely denounced by Kurdish authorities, with the regional government saying it was a “constitutional violation.”

Following Zaidi’s announcement on Tuesday, the state news agency INA cited what it described as an intelligence document that showed crude oil was being smuggled in tanker trucks from fields in Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah provinces into Iran.

It was then being blended with Iranian crude and exported to Afghanistan for domestic consumption, according to the document.

The document, which AFP has seen but could not authenticate independently, says Iranian and Iraqi crude are mixed in an effort to help Iran “evade sanctions.”

A security source in Baghdad told AFP this week that the government’s position is that “any smuggling to Iran or elsewhere is prohibited, and the entire international border must be secured.”

The United States, with which Zaidi has enjoyed close ties since taking office this year, accuses Iran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions.

World.title: France seeks German man in Channel migrant boat probe
World.content:
LILLE, France: France has issued an arrest warrant for a German national it suspects of involuntary manslaughter as part of an investigation into a series of clandestine migrant crossings to Britain, a prosecutor has said.

According to a joint investigation by several media outlets including French daily Le Monde and the BBC, the managing director of a small firm in western Germany, Marvin Reuter of MaRe Boote, is suspected of being one of the main suppliers of inflatable boats to people smugglers organizing journeys across the Channel.

The prosecutor in the northern city of Lille, Samuel Finielz, confirmed late on Thursday that five people had been arrested and a German national was briefly detained in his country as part of a probe since May last year into illegal Channel crossings and sinkings.

The five individuals, now held in pre-trial detention, were suspected of offenses including assisting illegal entry and residence as part of an organized criminal group, involuntary manslaughter, involuntary injury and endangering the lives of others, Finielz said in a voice note to AFP and other media.

Lille authorities in May issued an arrest warrant against “the German national implicated in this case,” he said, notably on charges of manslaughter and endangering the lives of others.

German authorities arrested then released him, and he is now required to appear before a Lille court “before the beginning of January,” the prosecutor added.

Reuter, 35, is contesting extradition to France, the BBC said, adding formal charges cannot be brought against him until he is extradited to France.

The BBC and Le Monde reported that UK authorities have estimated that boats or engines linked to MaRe Boote were involved in 29 percent of detected crossings in the first four months of this year.

At least 25 people have died attempting the crossing since the start of the year, according to an AFP tally based on official sources, including two women and a child, believed to be Eritrean, in September.

World.title: One catheter, no backup: how Gaza doctors stopped a bleeding brain
World.content:
GAZA: The team at Gaza’s Al-Shifa Medical Complex had one micro-catheter to work with. It would have to travel from the patient’s groin all the way into the arteries of his brain.

If it kinked, blocked or broke halfway through, there was no second one in the building.

“If it had any fault, blockage or break, we had no replacement,” Dr. Mohammed Amin Matar, head of radiology at Al-Shifa, told Arab News. “It was a risk.”

The doctors went ahead anyway, and it worked. Earlier this week the hospital announced it had sealed a ruptured aneurysm in a young man’s brain through a catheter, without opening his skull. Dr. Matar describes it as the first procedure of its kind in the Gaza Strip.

Al-Shifa, Gaza’s largest hospital, was raided by Israeli forces in November 2023 and again in March 2024. Israel said Hamas used the hospital as a command center, a claim Hamas denied.

The patient arrived with a severe bleed in his brain. A CT scan traced it to an aneurysm, a balloon-like bulge in the wall of an artery, in the left middle cerebral artery.

“A brain bleed is highly life-threatening,” Dr. Matar said. “Most cases die before they even reach hospital.”

The young man survived the first bleed, but the aneurysm was large and could burst again at any moment. Doctors kept him in intensive care for two to three days until he was stable, then decided they could not wait any longer.

“The case could not bear waiting,” Dr. Matar said. “The chance of a second or third bleed was very high, and it threatened the patient’s life.”

Outside Gaza, such procedures are carried out only in highly specialized centers, Dr. Matar said, because of how delicate and sensitive work inside the brain is. In Gaza, getting ready for it meant searching storerooms. The team spent close to two days gathering the specialized wires, micro-catheters and coils the procedure needs, which are different from those used in ordinary catheterization.

“We searched through all the consumables from before the war and after the war to find these tools,” Dr. Matar said. He credited his colleague, Dr. Maher Al-Zaanin, with helping to secure them. “Without him, this would not have been achieved.”

In the operating room, the doctors entered through the femoral artery in the groin and guided a catheter up into the carotid artery in the neck, then into the vessels of the brain. They steered the micro-catheter into the aneurysm and pushed a tiny metal coil through it. The coil fills the bulge and causes the blood inside it to clot, which stops fresh blood from flowing in and building up the pressure that causes a rupture.

Neurosurgeons, anesthetists, radiology technicians and nurses all worked on the case. Not everyone was sure it would succeed.

“There were a lot of questions about whether we could succeed or not,” Dr. Matar said. “Thank God, it was a success.”

The patient spent one day in intensive care and five days on a ward. He is now out of danger and under follow-up.

The unit where he was treated, Al-Shifa's interventional radiology and cardiac catheterization unit, reopened only about two months ago after being rehabilitated.

“We were preparing for procedures like this before the war,” Dr. Matar said. “But the war destroyed everything, and we went back to zero.”

In September, the same department treated two patients with brain vascular conditions by catheter, working alongside a visiting Egyptian consultant, the Palestinian news site Palsawa reported.

For patients like this young man, sending them abroad is rarely realistic. More than 21,000 patients in Gaza were on waiting lists for treatment outside the Strip as of Nov. 17, including 6,430 urgent cases, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry says 2,027 patients have died while waiting since the Rafah crossing closed.

“Waiting for weeks or months is not possible in any way,” Dr. Matar said. “These cases need urgent intervention. The most practical option is to treat them here, inside Gaza.”

The success has not changed the shortages around it. Many simple procedures at Al-Shifa remain on hold, Dr. Matar said, because the supplies they depend on have run out. Gaza Health Ministry data from early November showed that 508 of the 1,006 medical consumables it lists were unavailable. Of 902 trucks that entered Gaza between Nov. 16 and 22, six carried medicines and medical supplies, according to figures from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce cited by the UN humanitarian office, OCHA.

“The staff qualified to do these cases are here,” Dr. Matar said. “But sadly, there are not enough medical supplies.”

The people doing the work are also stretched. “Most medical staff working now are doing so almost without salaries, and without any alternatives,” he said, calling on international organizations to support both the supplies and the doctors and nurses who use them.

For now, the young man who reached Al-Shifa with a bleeding brain is recovering. In a hospital rebuilding from almost nothing, his doctors saved him with one catheter and nothing to spare.

World.title: Belgian authorities force Google to halt data center construction
World.content:
BRUSSELS: Belgian authorities have ordered Google to suspend construction of a data center in the south of the country because of a lack of proper planning permission, a regional official said Friday.

“We have identified a major offense: the illegal construction of a building covering three hectares,” or 7.4 acres, Nicolas Yernaux, spokesman for the Wallonia regional authorities, told AFP.

The “stop-work” order at the former mining site covering some 50 hectares in total comes after NGO Greenpeace accused Google of carrying on construction despite lacking the correct permits.

The regional authority said that inspectors visited the site on Thursday to inform Google representatives to halt construction.

The mammoth project has been locked in legal litigation for months after Google applied to amend the terms of its planning permission.

The application sought to allow a cooling system for the facilities using water drawn from the nearby River Sambre, whereas the initial project had envisaged air cooling, Belgian media reported.

The move stirred local opposition as severe droughts since spring exacerbated fears about tapping the river — and regional officials refused the application over the summer.

Google has challenged that decision in court and a hearing is scheduled for January.

But a report this week by Greenpeace Belgium said that drone footage showed work was still progressing in the meantime.

“The tech giant is currently continuing its work, even though in August the latest version of its planning permission to build this data center was revoked,” the environmental group said.

“The climate crisis will only intensify in our region. Against this backdrop, the construction of energy-guzzling behemoths cannot be allowed to go unnoticed.”

Google did not immediately respond to a request from AFP to comment.

The legal row over the Belgian data center is the latest confronting Google in Europe as tech giants push to build data centers to support the Artificial Intelligence boom.

In October Finnish authorities ordered work on two Google data center sites in the country to be halted until mandatory environmental impact assessments could be completed.

World.title: EU wheat extends gains on Black Sea disruption
World.content:
PARIS: Euronext wheat prices climbed to one-month highs on Friday as ongoing war disruption to Black Sea trade maintained expectations of strong demand for European Union supplies.

Gains on broader financial markets as AI-related investor worries subsided also helped to underpin Euronext as participants awaited the reopening of Chicago grain markets after Thursday’s Thanksgiving holiday.

March wheat, the most active position on Euronext, was up 1.5 percent at €241.25 ($264.89) a metric ton at 1220 GMT. The contract earlier reached €242 for its highest since October 20 and above a previous one-month peak of €239 on Wednesday.

Front-month December wheat rose 1.4 percent to €247.25 a ton after ⁠touching another one-month ⁠high at €248.25.

A Russian attack on two cargo ships carrying more than 100,000 tons of grain near the Ukrainian Black Sea port of Odesa this week has kept the focus on disruption to grain trade.

The strike further dampened hopes of a shipping truce in Russia’s war with Ukraine and raised ⁠the prospect of more demand shifting toward European Union exporting countries.

Weather forecasts projecting a cold spell in the Black Sea zone from next week could also curb exports because icy conditions complicate logistics, traders said.

Winter conditions could also hamper Russian efforts to ship grain on alternative routes via the Baltic Sea and the Arctic.

Traders were also assessing competition from cheaply offered wheat from Argentina’s harvest.

Argentina’s 2026/27 wheat production forecast, currently expected at 23.4 million tons, could be raised due to ⁠higher than expected ⁠yields as the harvest progresses, the Buenos Aires grains exchange said on Thursday.

However, reports of modest protein content could make the Argentine crop less attractive to milling wheat importers, traders said.

A large tender being held by Pakistan, which is seeking to buy 800,000 tons with a bidding deadline on Monday, is being watched for a gauge of export competition.

Nearly all recently sown soft wheat in France remained in good or excellent condition as of Monday, data from farm office FranceAgriMer showed.

Frosts in northern France on Friday were not expected to pose any risks to crops, traders said.

World.title: Kremlin urges Armenia to choose between EU and Moscow-led bloc
World.content:
MOSCOW: The Kremlin on Friday called on Armenia to make a “choice” between its EU ambitions and a membership in a Russia-led alliance ahead of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s talks in Moscow next week.

Russia has warned the former Soviet republic against joining the EU while remaining in the Moscow-led Eurasian Economic Union (EEU) in the past.

But Pashinyan, speaking on Thursday ahead of his December 3 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, ruled out abandoning a pro-Western shift.

Armenia’s “orientation toward the European Union and, at the same time, the desire to continue the integration process within the framework of the EEU do not correlate with each other,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.

“The desire, in economic terms, to sit on two chairs at once must either be confirmed or refuted by making some kind of choice,” Peskov said.

Peskov said the issue would be “the key item on the agenda” of Putin’s meeting with Pashinyan.

Earlier this month, Pashinyan said Yerevan plans to formally apply for EU membership by 2028.

The Russian-led EEU is expected to discuss the possible suspension of Armenia’s membership in December.

Russia, which has a military base in Armenia, still wields substantial influence over the small Caucasus country.

Peskov said “the issue of our base will be raised” during the Putin-Pashinyan meeting.

“This base is a very important element in ensuring security and stability in the region. It will certainly be interesting here to hear the position of the Armenian side,” he said.

On Thursday, Pashinyan repeated plans to gradually end Armenia’s decades-long reliance on Russian border guards, who patrol its frontiers with Turkiye and Iran.

Armenia’s relations with Moscow deteriorated sharply after Yerevan accused Russia of failing to protect it against its longtime foe Azerbaijan.

World.title: Iraq seizes smuggled oil bound for Sulaymaniyah as Baghdad tightens control
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security forces intercepted a truck carrying smuggled oil at the Chimen checkpoint in Kirkuk on Friday as Baghdad steps up efforts to fight oil smuggling and reinforce federal authority across the nation.

According to Iraq’s Security Media Cell, which reports to the Prime Minister’s Office, forces from the Kirkuk Operations Command seized a vehicle traveling from Basra to Sulaymaniyah, which was carrying a container labeled as plumbing materials and protected with customs seals.

Security staff got suspicious of the package and ran a scan, which revealed hidden oil.

The driver was apprehended, and the truck was confiscated for further investigation and legal action.

The seizure comes as Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi pushes for more federal supervision of border crossings in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region and oilfields in disputed territory as part of larger measures to curb smuggling and defend Iraq’s national resources.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump voiced support for Al-Zaidi’s efforts to establish state authority across Iraq, curb oil smuggling, battle corruption, and place all weaponry under government control.

The operation comes as Baghdad steps up its attempts to improve government management of transportation routes, border crossings, and the country’s oil resources.

World.title: Trump backs Baghdad’s push to assert federal authority across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – US President Donald Trump pledged support for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s attempts to establish federal authority throughout the country on Friday, as Baghdad prepares to place border crossings in the Kurdistan Region and numerous oilfields in disputed territory under federal control.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump praised Al-Zaidi’s efforts to fight oil smuggling, battle corruption, and place all weaponry under state control.

“We support Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions,” Trump said.

Washington’s backing is a diplomatic setback for the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), which has sought international support against Baghdad’s aspirations to strengthen federal authority over border crossings and oil resources.

Iraqi Kurdish officials have aggressively criticized Al-Zaidi’s decree, claiming it breaches the region’s constitutional rights and weakens Iraq’s federal structure.

Iraqi Kurdish Prime Minister Masrour Barzani urged the international community to protect the region’s constitutional rights. In contrast, Trump’s speech expressly supported Baghdad’s attempts to impose state authority throughout the country.

The support also indicates the improved ties between Washington and Baghdad under Al-Zaidi’s leadership.

A national conversation is set for December 1 to resolve remaining conflicts between Baghdad and Erbil in line with the Iraqi constitution.

The advances occur as Baghdad works to consolidate state power, establish national sovereignty, and create a unified Iraq that serves all residents, regardless of race, religion, or sectarian affiliation.

World.title: Under-attack Palestinians find unlikely ally in Israeli retired general
World.content:
As Sawiyah – The four Israeli soldiers stepped out of their car in the occupied West Bank, their faces masked, their uniforms unmarked and automatic weapons strapped across their shoulders.

They had entered a Palestinian olive grove but, little did they expect, the person there planning to tell them to leave could have once been issuing them orders.

A retired Israeli general, Eyal Ben Reuven, had come that day to the Palestinian town of As Sawiyah, on a mission to prevent some of the rampant violence against Palestinians by extremist Israeli settlers.

For the 72-year-old, joined by fellow battle-hardened veterans of the Israeli military, the violence is a stain on the institution in which they once served.

“I’ve fought in a number of wars. And unfortunately, I have reached the point where I have seen an evolution,” said the former military man with piercing eyes, who spent much of his career driving tanks.

The army is failing to act, he said, even when the violence has reached a level “I never could have imagined”.

Unrest has soared in the West Bank since the unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel, which responded with a massive military campaign in the Gaza Strip.

More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by the army or settlers in the West Bank since then. More than 50 Israelis have died in the same time in the territory, which Israel captured in 1967.

The olive harvest has become a flashpoint, with settlers attacking or stealing from Palestinian farmers on a nearly daily basis.

With the other former soldiers, Ben Reuven has set up a protective presence, a tactic more common among leftist activists who put themselves in the way in a bid to stop attacks against Palestinians.

– Army intervenes in harvest –

Clad in comfortable hiking attire and carrying walking sticks, it is difficult to imagine that some of the greying volunteers fought in intense combat.

Like good soldiers, they review instructions upon going out — they are there to assist the olive harvest, not to confront the settlers, and they will obey the army’s instructions.

A Palestinian human rights activist, Arafat Abu Ras, led the military men to a small olive grove. An old Palestinian woman was waiting to guide them and the soldiers, more accustomed to the battlefield than to farming, used sticks and small rakes to start knocking the olives off the trees, volunteering to do the work on the Palestinians’ behalf.

Almost immediately a military vehicle arrived. Under the humming of a drone, one of the serving soldiers shoved aside an AFP team to prevent filming, while another checked Abu Ras’s identity papers and ordered everyone to leave.

Abu Ras said that the olive farmers had coordinated with the army, which insists that Palestinians receive approval for their harvests in the occupied West Bank, arguing that it is for safety reasons.

“They say, ‘yes, yes’, and then the next day they come and force us to leave,” Abu Ras said.

After the serving soldiers arrived, a second vehicle came, this time with Israeli settlers. An official from a neighbouring settlement also ordered the olive pickers out, with troops saying it was a “closed military zone”.

The Israeli veterans, in line with their guidance, complied. They instead moved elsewhere with the farmers, hoping to prevent attacks on them.

“Our army is a joke,” fumed Yoel Feldschuh, a 77-year-old former air force brigadier general.

“Is it its role to shut an olive grove? What does the military have to do with that?”

Feldschuh made headlines when he was handcuffed and taken away by police in a similar action a month earlier.

Changing the behaviour of the military, he said, “will take a generation”.

– Rampant violence –

COGAT, the Israeli body responsible for civil affairs in the Palestinian territories, maintains that “security forces are deployed to ensure a safe olive harvest”.

But since September, the harvest has been marked by nearly 500 attacks, some of them fatal, according to the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din.

Amram Mitzna, an 81-year-old retired general, attributes the army’s inaction to the young ages of the soldiers, who have grown up under now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader.

“They consider every Arab an enemy who must be treated as such,” said Mitzna, who has also served as mayor of Haifa, Israel’s third largest city.

Netanyahu has allied himself with the far-right and championed a rapid growth of West Bank settlements, which are considered illegal under international law.

Netanyahu is fighting for political survival after losing ground in elections. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general seeking to succeed him, supports many of Netanyahu’s security policies but accuses him of yielding to “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank and vowed to crack down on extremist settlers.

In As Sawiyah, the former soldiers eventually finished harvesting the olives in a nearby area alongside a school, putting them in bags to be taken by Palestinian villagers.

While no one was injured, Ben Reuven remained deeply disturbed by how the young soldier acted during the altercation.

“When I saw him arrive, masked, shouting, kicking sacks of olives, I was ashamed.”

World.title: BP eyes deeper energy ties with Iraq as CEO visits Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – British energy giant BP has reaffirmed its commitment to expanding operations in Iraq following CEO Meg O’Neill’s first visit to the country and meeting with Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi in Baghdad.

According to the Prime Minister’s office, talks centered on developing oilfields and boosting exploration efforts, notably at Rumaila in Basra, Eridu in Dhi Qar, and Kirkuk, as Iraq aims to produce 10 million barrels of oil per day by 2032.

To reach output objectives, Al-Zaidi advocated for faster development, intensified field activities, and longer working hours.

Iraq’s Prime Minister also emphasized the need for collecting related gas and decreasing waste to improve domestic energy supply.

O’Neill reaffirmed BP’s commitment to expanding its activities in Iraq, utilizing sophisticated technology and technical experience to boost production and develop the country’s oilfields.

Following the meeting, O’Neill lauded Iraq’s objectives, workforce, and energy potential on LinkedIn, stressing prospects to enhance the company’s collaboration with Baghdad.

Along with its partners and the Iraqi operator, BP plays a critical role in Rumaila, Iraq’s biggest producing oilfield, providing technical knowledge to boost production and maximize resource recovery.

In Kirkuk, BP is engaging in a large rebuilding program involving oil, gas, electricity, and water infrastructure, with the first phase covering resources amounting to more than three billion barrels of oil.

The company’s growing presence is especially important as Iraq pursues foreign investment, modernizes its energy infrastructure, reduces gas flaring, and expands its oil production capacity.

O’Neill emphasized that combining Iraq’s immense natural resources and indigenous knowledge with BP’s technology and worldwide experience may provide significant benefits for both parties.

The visit highlights Iraq’s strategic significance to BP, as well as the company’s long-term engagement in growing the country’s oil industry.

World.title: Iraq and Bahrain to strengthen economic and diplomatic ties
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi met with Bahraini Ambassador Khaled Ahmed al-Mansour on Thursday, as the two countries work to repair and enhance their bilateral ties.

The envoy delivered congratulations from Bahrain’s King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa and underlined his government’s commitment to developing economic cooperation with Iraq, promoting mutual growth, and resolving common difficulties.

Both parties addressed ways to further collaboration across sectors, as well as regional and international trends, emphasizing the necessity of coordinating views and ensuring regional stability.

The meeting comes after Bahrain’s decision on November 7 to reinstate its ambassador to Baghdad, after Al-Zaidi’s historic visit to Manama on November 4, the first by an Iraqi prime minister since 2003.

Al-Mansour departed Baghdad in April due to increased diplomatic tensions over drone strikes on Bahrain by Iran-backed Iraqi forces.

The reinstatement of full diplomatic representation represents a major step forward in Iraqi-Bahraini relations, creating new potential for commerce, investment, and economic cooperation while improving Iraq’s links with its Gulf neighbors.

World.title: Baghdad cracks down on Kurdistan oil smuggling to Iran
World.content:
Baghdad – The Iraqi government’s crackdown on oil smuggling through the Kurdistan region targets routes used to move crude into Iran to help it evade sanctions, according to document cited by state media and a security official.

On Tuesday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi moved to put Kurdistan’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control in an effort to curb oil smuggling.

Following Zaidi’s announcement, the state news agency INA cited what it described as an intelligence document revealing that crude oil was being smuggled in tanker trucks from fields in Kirkuk and Sulaymaniyah provinces into Iran.

There, according to the document, it was being blended with Iranian crude and then exported to Afghanistan for domestic consumption.

The document, which AFP has seen but could not independently authenticate, says Iranian and Iraqi crude are mixed in an effort to help Iran “evade sanctions.”

The United States, with which Zaidi has enjoyed close ties since taking office earlier this year, accuses Iran of using Iraq’s economy to evade sanctions, and has previously sanctioned Iraqi individuals and companies for blending Iraqi and Iranian oil.

A security source in Baghdad told AFP that the government’s position is that “any smuggling to Iran or elsewhere is prohibited, and the entire international border must be secured.”

The source added that Zaidi’s crackdown on oil smuggling, whether in the Kurdistan Region or elsewhere in Iraq, is backed by the United States, which has sought to choke Iran’s economy.

The intelligence document also indicated that another smuggling route runs through border crossings to Turkiye, but it was not clear if Turkiye was the final destination.

A former oil ministry official told AFP on condition of anonymity that the Kurdistan region has long exported oil to Turkiye not only via a pipeline, but also in huge quantities in tanker trucks.

He added that “illicit crossings in the Kurdistan region are used to smuggle crude oil, including from other parts of Iraq, to neighboring countries,” including to Iran and onwards to Afghanistan.

For months, Zaidi has been cracking down on the illicit oil trade, arresting officials and challenging an Iran-backed armed group after smuggling was uncovered in its stronghold near Baghdad.

But the move to bring Kurdistan’s border crossings and several oil fields under federal control could sour relations with Kurdish authorities, who have denounced Zaidi’s decision while keeping the door open for talks.

World.title: Iraq sentences eight French Daesh members to life in prison
World.content:
Baghdad – An Iraqi court sentenced eight French nationals to life in prison on Thursday for joining the Daesh group, according to an AFP correspondent, as the country presses ahead with prosecuting thousands of suspected militants.



Another two French defendants were sentenced to 15-year terms on similar charges, while 10 people who were supposed to receive verdicts had those postponed to another date.



The Daesh group swept across Syria and Iraq in 2014, committing massacres and forcing women and girls into sexual slavery, while many supporters traveled from Europe and elsewhere to join its ranks.



Iraq’s prisons, already packed with Daesh suspects, have recently received thousands more detainees transferred from neighboring Syria.



The 10 who received their sentences on Thursday are among 47 French citizens put on trial in Iraq since September, having been brought from Syria last year.



The court had already sentenced 15 of the group to life imprisonment, while one person had received a 15-year prison term.



Among those still awaiting verdicts was Adrien Guihal, known as the person who voiced the Daesh claim for the 2016 Nice attack when an attacker drove a truck through Bastille Day crowds, killing 86 people. His verdict was postponed on Thursday to another date.



Also waiting were Thomas Collange, whose wife who had traveled with him to Syria was sentenced to 10 years in prison in France last year, and Quentin Le Brun, who appeared in a propaganda video.



Romain Garnier, who worked for the group’s radio operation, was given a life sentence on Thursday.



During their hearings, most of the suspects pleaded guilty, and all expressed regret over joining the group, with some asking to be repatriated to France.



During his session last week, Guihal spoke in a loud, clear voice, in contrast with other defendants, who spoke quietly and at times stuttered.



He claimed he had renounced the group’s actions. “I have changed a lot, I am a new person,” he said.



Collange, who converted to Islam in the early 2000s, said he regretted bringing his wife and kids with him to Syria, and had renounced the group since trying to escape in 2017.

– Thousands on trial –

France has repatriated hundreds of family members of militants, but has refused to bring back most of the men accused of involvement, leaving them to face justice abroad.



During their hearings, many defendants argued that they had only been to Syria, questioning why they are being tried in Iraq.



Baghdad is prosecuting them under its anti-terrorism law for joining Daesh, regardless of whether they operated in Iraq or Syria.



Iraq, backed by US-led forces, proclaimed victory over Daesh in 2017, and Kurdish-led forces supported by Washington defeated the group in neighboring Syria two years later.



Iraq, however, is still reckoning with the group’s legacy, with mass graves being uncovered and testimonies of Daesh brutality still to be investigated.



For years, Iraqi courts have handed down hundreds of life and death sentences to people convicted of terrorism offenses, including foreign fighters.



But some rights groups have denounced the trials as rushed and lacking due process.



In February, Iraq also received more than 5,700 Daesh detainees from over 60 countries after the United States transferred them from Syria, following years of detention in Kurdish prisons.



Trials for that group started on Sunday, with the first hearings involving Syrian nationals.

World.title: Asian stocks mostly rise as markets calm after tech rout
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stocks mostly rose Friday, with technology firms building on the previous day’s gains and enjoying a much-needed period of calm following the ructions at the start of the week.

With Wall Street closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, traders had no new business-driving catalysts heading into the weekend, though they remain on edge over concerns about the AI boom.

They were also keeping an eye on possible retaliation to Donald Trump’s proposed tariffs of up to 20 percent on some of the United States’ biggest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.

Seoul and Tokyo were the standouts on a generally quiet day on trading floors, with chipmakers SK hynix, Samsung and Kioxia enjoying healthy buying — having been among the most brutally sold during a rout earlier in the week.

Taipei, which also saw huge swings, was marginally higher.

Still, analysts warned that there would likely be more volatility to come as investors assess the outlook for the AI trade with questions over the vast sums pumped into the sector and profitability.

Also in view is the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision next month, with speculation swirling that it could opt for a hefty 50-basis-point hike instead of the usual 25 points.

Stocks in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Jakarta, Singapore and Manila also rose.

Wellington edged down as New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority, plunging the country into political uncertainty with an insurgent centrist party set to play kingmaker.

“In the absence of any new information the backdrop does remain fragile but for now investors have returned to equities with technology shares leading,” wrote Skye Masters at National Australia Bank.

“The test will be whether this improved sentiment can be sustained through to the end of the week as the US returns from Thanksgiving holiday.”

Oil prices extended Thursday’s gains of more than one percent amid fresh concerns over an escalation of hostilities in the Middle East after Tehran-backed Houthis struck a Saudi refinery, temporarily halting some operations. That came after an attack on another hub in the Gulf earlier in the week.

In company news, Japan Tobacco rallied more than four percent following a report that it was considering joining up with US giant Altria for a takeover of Britain’s Imperial Brands. Imperial jumped 13 percent in London on Thursday.

Japan Tobacco is dealing with a $8.9 billion hit after the Russian government seized all seven of its local subsidiaries, as relations with Tokyo worsen following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

World.title: 'Pakistan funding' row: CJP's Ashutosh Ranka sends defamation notice to Jitendra Singh, seeks Rs 3 crore
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Ashutosh Ranka has sent a defamation notice to Union minister

over his allegation that Ranka received funds from Pakistani politicians and a purported handler, demanding an unconditional public apology, withdrawal of the allegations and Rs 3 crore in damages.

In a post on X on Friday, Ranka said he would not tolerate Singh questioning his integrity and patriotism, asserting that his professional engagements with McKinsey, GAVI and other organisations were well documented and complied with India's tax and accounting laws.

"I have sent a legal notice to @DrJitendraSingh for his obnoxious remarks on me saying that I had received 'funds from Pakistan'," he said.

Ranka said he had secured admission to the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, and the London School of Economics through hard work.



He added that he had given up a high-paying job at McKinsey and a comfortable life in London to return to India.

"I have toiled hard in public life for the last two years to raise issues that matter to the people of India," he said.

According to a statement issued by the CJP, its legal cell served the notice on Singh through advocate Abhik Chimni. Ranka has proposed that the Rs 3 crore in damages be donated to a charitable organisation working for primary education in India.





The notice has challenged Singh to provide details of the alleged payments, including the names of the Pakistani politicians involved, amounts, dates, transactions and supporting documents.

"You did not name a single Pakistani politician who is using their personal or party funds to remit money to my client. You did not state a single amount, date, transaction, account, document, or source," the notice said.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Singh had alleged at a press conference in Bengaluru on November 3 that CJP founder Abhijit Dipke received funds from the United States, while Ranka received money from Pakistan.

He had also accused anti-India organisations and foreign-funded groups, including Pakistani politicians, of financing a campaign against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Singh further alleged that "self-styled activists" were manufacturing a false narrative around the exercise.

World.title: Diaspora outreach will have ripple effect on investments to state, says WB finance minister
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

West Bengal finance minister Swapan Dasgupta believes that engaging the global Bengali diaspora will trigger a cascading wave of foreign investment into the state.âMany people of Bengali heritage hold key positions and possess deep technical expertise at companies worldwide,â Dasgupta said in an exclusive interview, roughly a month ahead of the Government of Indiaâs Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (PBD) Convention 2027, scheduled in Kolkata from January 7 to 9. âHarnessing their goodwill can create a ripple effect. We are already in talks with corporate leaders, venture capitalists, deep-tech experts, and entrepreneurs of Bengali origin across the globe.âIn a related outreach towards the diaspora with deep technology roots, Dasgupta is also scheduled to attend Confluence 2027, a global business, investment and innovation summit in Silicon Valley next year, as a guest of honour. To be held between April 9 and 11, 2027, at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center in California; the summit will feature the Opening Keynote on The Bengal Renaissance 2.0 and a Capital Forum titled Build Bengal.âI am looking forward to participating in Confluence 2027 in Silicon Valley because it is vital for West Bengal to connect with a diaspora operating at the cutting edge of technology and driving innovations that have transformed the Western world,â Dasgupta said.âIt is regrettable that the brainpower that has contributed so much to the West has not yet shaped our own country to the same extent. We need to build a bridgeâto understand what they are looking for and what we can offer. By getting this conversation started, we can secure a brighter future for West Bengal.âSilicon Valley-based serial entrepreneur Rahul K Roy, founder and chairman of Confluence 2027, welcomed the West Bengal finance ministerâs decision to participate in the conference, which will spotlight the stateâs push to emerge as a premier investment destination.Ahead of PBD 2027âthemed Return to Roots: Reigniting the Diaspora Connect with Bharatâthe state government is actively gathering feedback, suggestions, and concerns from the global Indian and Bengali communities.âOne common criticism from Global Indians is that West Bengal historically lacked a conducive environment for innovation, agility, and a productive work culture," Dasgupta noted. âWe must change that perception and prove what is possible here.While we recognize that large-scale investments take time to materialize, our immediate focus is on expanding the capacity and footprint of existing branch offices in the state. âTalking about the outreach to the global Indian investorsâ community, especially those with connections in Bengal, Dasgupta said that the first modest step is to show-case a friendly investment policy which includes some amount of incentives. âIt is most important that we create an environment that is attractive for investments. And while these are early days yet, I remain optimistic,â he said.The PBD2027 convention will kick off important steps for a more organised outreach to the Indian diaspora from Bengal in the New Year, Dasgupta added.

World.title: Sharad Pawar's NCP backs Centre's delimitation Bill ahead of Special Session
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

(SP) on Friday supported the Centre's proposed delimitation Bill, which is set to be tabled during the special session of Parliament.

NCP (SP) leader Jitendra Awhad said that a consensus was reached after discussions with

, adding that the delimitation process is a constitutional requirement.

"The discussion wasn't about our party's official stance. The general point being made was that the delimitation process is a constitutional requirement," Awhad said.

"A decision has been made to support the delimitation process, and we will indeed support it. We will support the delimitation," he added

Meanwhile Shirur MP Amol Kolhe, the party's whip in the Lok Sabha, said any decision would be taken only after studying the bill.



"Sule had made the party's stand clear. We have to first study the draft of the bill, only then any decision can be taken," he said.

This comes after the party's national working president

, on Thursday, struck a softer tone on the Centre's proposal, saying it would be premature to oppose the legislation before its details were known.

"Let the bill come. Perhaps there could be something good in the Delimitation Bill," she told news agency PTI.





"Whether a bill is in the country's interest or not, opposing it just because you are in the opposition, or blindly supporting it because you are in power, is wrong for a healthy democracy. It is not necessary to oppose everything. We can also suggest improvements and say what changes should be made. There could be something good in it," Sule said.

It issued contempt notices to senior Tamil Nadu officials over alleged non-compliance with its earlier order.

Cabinet clears 50% increase in Lok Sabha strength until 2051

The Union Cabinet, chaired by PM Narendra Modi, has approved a proposal to increase the strength of the Lok Sabha by 50% across states, sources told TOI.

A bench of Justice Krishna Rao directed the speaker to reconsider the appointment and pass a reasoned order within 10 days. The petition was filed by senior Trinamool Congress MLA Sovandeb Chattopadhyay.

World.title: 'Mr C Joseph hates Sanatan': BJP hits out at Vijay govt after SC's Deepam rebuke
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The BJP on Friday slammed the Tamil Nadu government after the

issued contempt notices to senior state officials over the

row, accusing chief minister C Joseph Vijay of deliberately violating constitutional principles and hurting the religious sentiments of Hindu devotees.

BJP national president Nitin Nabin also hailed the SC order saying, "A historic victory for every devotee of Lord Murugan! By ordering the ceremonial lamp to be lit at the Thiruparankundram Deepathoon tomorrow and pulling up Tamil Nadu authorities for acting at the dictates of their political bosses, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has thoroughly exposed the INDI Alliance government's anti-Sanatan mindset."

"No political conspiracy can stop the sacred traditions of Bharat.



May the divine blessings of Lord Murugan protect all devotees and guide them on the path of courage and righteousness," he added.

Meanwhile, addressing a press conference, BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia alleged that the controversy had arisen because of the state government's hostility towards Sanatan traditions and the Hindu community.

"This press conference is being held on a very important issue relating to the Karthigai Deepam row, which has been created only because the government in Tamil Nadu and the chief minister there, Mr C Joseph, hate Sanatan traditions and the Hindu community.





This hatred is so deep that a chief minister who has taken an oath to protect and preserve the ethos of the Constitution has, prima facie, wilfully decided to violate it," Bhatia said.

BJP leader CR Kesavan also criticised the state government, calling the Supreme Court's direction to light the ceremonial lamp at the Deepathoon on Saturday a victory for devotees of Lord Muruga.

"The sacred Karthigai Deepam, which will now be lit at the Deepathoon atop Thiruparankundram Hill tomorrow, is indeed an emphatic victory and a true triumph for the implicit faith and sentiments of crores of Lord Muruga devotees," Kesavan said.

He accused the state government of using the controversy for political gains and alleged that its actions had hurt the sentiments of Hindu devotees.

"The dubious and dangerous divisive drama enacted and orchestrated by the TVK Congress government to perpetrate their vote-bank politics of communal appeasement deeply hurt and humiliated the sentiments of countless Hindu devotees," he said.

Kesavan further demanded an unconditional apology from Vijay, saying, "This TVK Congress government, led by Joseph Vijay needs to tender an unconditional apology immediately to the people of Tamil Nadu and crores of Lord Muruga devotees for betraying their faith."

The row centres on the lighting of the traditional Karthigai Deepam lamp atop the Deepathoon, a stone pillar on Thiruparankundram hill in Tamil Nadu's Madurai district. The dispute escalated after the Madras High Court directed that the ceremonial lamp be lit at the pillar, amid objections and competing claims over the site.

On November 20, the Supreme Court permitted the lighting of the lamp at Deepathoon on November 24 as a one-time interim arrangement.

However, the ceremonial flame was lit only at the customary Uchaipillaiyar mandapam and not at the disputed pillar, prompting contempt proceedings.

Then earlier Friday, the Supreme Court directed that the traditional lamp be lit atop Deepathoon on Saturday using the flame lit at the Uchaipillaiyar mandapam. It also issued contempt notices to Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, Director General of Police, Madurai Collector and other officials over the alleged non-compliance with its earlier order.
