World.title: Coffee planter killed in wild elephant attack in Kodagu, fourth death in Malnad region in a fortnight
World.content:
A 48-year-old coffee planter was killed in a wild elephant attack at Badragola village in Ponnampet taluk of Kodagu district in Karnataka on November 26 morning.

The deceased planter, identified as Keshavayya, had gone to place the newly-harvested paddy crop (kadiru) near the tomb of his parents in his coffee plantation around 7.30 a.m., a ritual, which was being performed following the celebration of Nerekattu on November 25 night.

This is the fourth death in Malnad belt in man-elephant conflict in the last fortnight. Jayamma, 65, died in an elephant attack at Chowdanahalli in Belur taluk of Hassan district on November 14. On November 16, Hafees Ur Rahman, 60, was killed by an elephant at Nagenahalli in the same taluk. Krishnamurthy, 53, a resident of Hennangi village in N.R. Pura taluk of Chikkamagaluru district died after attacked by an elephant on November 18.

How death occured

Keshavayya’s plantation is located adjacent to a forest area in Anechowkoor range. According to sources, the elephant was returning to the forest in the morning after roaming in the area during the night when it attacked Keshavayya.

The elephant is suspected to have turned aggressive either after coming in contact with a solar fence in a nearby plantation or when people attempted to drive it back into the forest.

Wild elephants had reportedly ventured into the same area twice and damaged coffee plants.

The incident occurred in an area where elephant movement was not frequent, unlike in other parts of the forest range, sources said.

Barricade work

Railway barricade work is currently under way near Badragola village. Completion of the project is expected to help monitor and manage elephant movement in the area, sources added.

Keshavayya is survived by his wife and three children. Forest officials handed over compensation of ₹5 lakh to the family on November 26. The remaining compensation will be released after the post-mortem report is received, an official of the Forest Department said.

World.title: Central Sanskrit University urges citizens to accurately record Sanskrit proficiency in Census 2027
World.content:
Central Sanskrit University, New Delhi, has urged citizens across India to accurately record their proficiency in Sanskrit when providing linguistic details for the upcoming Census.

Vice-Chancellor Shrinivasa Varakhedi made the appeal as part of the university’s “Mama Bhasha Sanskritam” campaign, an outreach initiative that aims to reach nearly 10 crore people.

According to the 2011 Census, only 24,821 people reported Sanskrit as their mother tongue.

Vice Chancellor Srinivasa Varakhedi highlighted Question 14 of the Census questionnaire, which records respondents’ mother tongue and other known languages. He emphasised that the Census is not merely a headcount exercise, but a vital instrument for documenting the nation’s cultural, linguistic, and social identity.

He urged citizens to provide accurate language details when Census officials visit. “The university appeals to all citizens to participate responsibly in Census 2027 and provide truthful, accurate information about their linguistic background. Those who genuinely identify Sanskrit as their language are encouraged to ensure it is recorded,” he said.

He stated that Sanskrit represents India’s invaluable intellectual, cultural, and civilisational heritage. It is not merely an ancient language but a living repository of India’s knowledge traditions, philosophical thought, and scientific wisdom.

Sanskrit has historically served as a major vehicle of India’s intellectual heritage, encompassing the Vedas, Upanishads, philosophical literature, ayurveda, yoga, mathematics, and astronomy. Its influence is also evident in the vocabulary, literature, and cultural traditions of numerous Indian languages, he added.

‘Mama Bhasha Sanskritam’ seeks to create greater awareness about Sanskrit and its continuing relevance in Indian society. The university plans to involve its headquarters, all campuses, Sanskrit schools and colleges, students, and voluntary organisations to drive the campaign. Awareness activities are being planned at prominent city and tourist spots, alongside door-to-door visits.

World.title: Awareness programme against child marriage held in Tiruchi
World.content:
To mark the International Day Against Child Marriage and highlight efforts to make Tiruchi a child-marriage-free district, a special awareness programme was organised under the Bal Vivah Mukt Bharat Campaign at Chathiram Bus Stand in Tiruchi on Friday.

The programme was organised by the Association for Voluntary Action (AVA), a development partner of NITI Aayog under the Aspirational Districts Programme, in collaboration with Just Rights for Children and the District Social Welfare Department, District Child Protection Unit, Anti-Human Trafficking Unit of Tiruchi Police, and District Legal Services Authority.

Vijayalakshmi, District Social Welfare Officer, Tiruchi, explained the adverse effects of child marriage, particularly the physical health risks and other challenges faced by children forced into early marriage. She stressed the need to protect children’s health, education, safety and rights.

She emphasised the importance of reporting child marriages and informed the public about helpline numbers, including 1098, 181, 1091, and 100, for reporting such cases and seeking assistance.

Thirumurugan, Chief Panel Advocate, District Legal Services Authority (DLSA), Tiruchi, explained the legal assistance available to prevent child marriages. He outlined the procedure for approaching the competent court to obtain preventive injunction orders, wherever necessary, to stop child marriages in the district.

Participants took a pledge against child marriage and launched a signature campaign.

Seetharaman, Deputy Commissioner of Police, Tiruchi Fort Range, and Balachandran, District Planning Officer-cum-Secretary, District Panchayat Office, Tiruchi, took part.

World.title: West Bengal Police begin analysing data of voters deleted in SIR
World.content:
The West Bengal police have started the process to analyse the data on voters whose names have been deleted from the electoral rolls during the special intensive revision (SIR) process and submit a report by the end of November.

On Monday (November 23, 2026), the Director-General and Inspector-General of West Bengal police’s Law and Order unit held a video conference with all the senior police officials from the districts and directed them to examine the details of all the deleted voters across 294 Assembly constituencies.

“All CSP and SSP are hereby requested to visit the website https://appeal.civicresearch.in/ and examine the data pertaining to their respective jurisdictions in connection with SIR adjudication and tribunal appeals against exclusion and inclusion across all 294 Assembly Constituencies of West Bengal,” a copy of the order seen by The Hindu read.

Directing to consider the matter ‘most urgently’, it also said that all the data available on the website shall be downloaded, carefully analysed and a comprehensive report in respect of the respective jurisdiction shall be submitted to this office positively by November 30.

Since Monday, teams from the local police stations across the State have started a house-to-house visit of all the deleted voters to check their documents, a process that has alarmed citizens and civil rights groups. In Howrah, police teams were also seen holding camps at the government schools where all such voters queued up with their papers and submitted the details to the officers.

A senior officer from West Bengal police, however, said that it is a routine exercise, while the office of the Chief Electoral Officer denied any knowledge of the survey. On Thursday (November 26, 2026), Opposition parties in West Bengal raised an alarm over the police allegedly visiting the homes of deleted voters to collect information and documents. The Mamata All India Trinamool Congress called it an intimidation tactic, while State poll officials denied any involvement.

Earlier this week the Supreme Court asked the Election Commission of India (ECI) to fast-track the appeals of deleted voters at tribunals and prioritise cases of those affected in upcoming civic poll areas.

The SIR process in the State was held from October 2025 to February 2026, just before the Assembly election. Nearly 91 lakh electors were deleted from the electoral rolls; they accounted for about 12% of all voters in the State before the start of the SIR.

According to an affidavit filed by the ECI in September, of the 27 lakh electors who were excluded from the electoral rolls on the ground of ‘logical discrepancies’, 22 lakh have filed appeals before the tribunal challenging their exclusion. The ECI’s affidavit added that 16.10 lakh appeals have also been filed against inclusions during the SIR. This puts the total number of appeals before the SIR tribunals at 38 lakh.

World.title: CM to lay foundation stone for lift irrigation scheme in Bagalkot
World.content:
Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar will lay the foundation stone for the Kadarakoppa-Anawal Lift Irrigation Project in Hoolageri village near Badami in Bagalkot district on Tuesday.

The project falls within the Bilagi Assembly Constituency and will help farmers in several surrounding areas, district in-charge Minister Vijayanand Kashappanavar said in Bagalkot on Friday.

He reviewed preparations for the event to be held in Hoolageri. Over 25,000 people are expected to attend the programme.

Adequate seating, drinking water and meals should be provided for the attendees, the Minister told Deputy Commissioner Sangappa and other officers.

The Minister directed officials to take the necessary steps to ensure the participation of approximately 15,000 female beneficiaries of various schemes.

District-level officials and tahsildars, Zilla Panchayat Chief Executive Officer Gajanan Bale, Superintendent of Police Siddharth Goyal, Additional Deputy Commissioner Manjunath Dombar and Chief Engineer of Karnataka Neeravari Nigam Limited Lakshman Nayak and others were present.

World.title: Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan accuses Keralam CM of trivialising issues of illegal phone tapping
World.content:
Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan has accused Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan of trivialising issues of illegal phone tapping and constant surveillance, instead of launching an immediate and comprehensive investigation into the allegations.

In an official statement here on Friday, Mr. Vijayan said that it was astonishing that the Chief Minister had chosen the Constitution Day itself to make a comment as though unconstitutional activities such as citizen surveillance was a normal occurrence.

Privacy is a fundamental right guaranteed to every citizen by the Constitution. Even while making serious allegations that the phones of Opposition leaders and even members of his own Cabinet are being tapped, the Chief Minister is attempting to trivialise the issue instead of announcing a serious inquiry, Mr. Vijayan said.

The political row was triggered on Thursday during a function held in the capital to observe the Constitution Day, wherein Mr. Satheesan had stated that his phone was being tapped and that he was under constant surveillance.

Addressing the gathering, Mr. Satheesan had remarked that the situation no longer caused him anxiety, as everyone was under constant surveillance. He had also added that he deliberately fed false information and made incorrect statements during phone conversations to mislead whoever was listening in.

Political scrutiny

The Chief Minister had then gone on to connect his remarks to broader concerns over how technology and artificial intelligence was taking over the world and George Orwell’s novel 1984. But Mr. Satheesan never made any mention of whom he suspected of carrying out the surveillance, which seems to have prompted the political scrutiny as well as this sharp reaction from Mr. Vijayan.

The Opposition Leader pointed out that if even the phone of the head of the State administration was being tapped, it amounted to a grave lapse in security. He challenged the Chief Minister to reveal who is behind the alleged snooping. Mr. Vijayan also demanded to know if the unauthorised surveillance and phone tapping was taking place in the State with the knowledge of the Home Minister.

Surveillance politics that subverts democratic institutions and civil liberties cannot be accepted under any circumstances, he said

He demanded that the government order a thorough probe into the phone-tapping allegations and reveal the entire facts before the public.

World.title: Even drumsticks are a luxury in Andhra Pradesh now
World.content:
Drumstick (moringa) prices have surged in Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh with a single piece selling for as much as ₹30 amid El Niño conditions, adverse weather and supply disruptions, putting the commonly used vegetable beyond the reach of some households. A family of four may need four to five pieces to prepare a dish, taking the daily expense to roughly ₹120 to ₹150.

At these rates, drumsticks are competing with chicken in household food budgets. The increase is particularly burdensome during Karthika Masam, when many Hindus observe Ayyappa Deeksha and prefer vegetarian food. Drumsticks are widely used in dishes such as sambar and tomato-based curries, and are consumed for their perceived medicinal benefits. Dried leaves and moringa powder are also used.

Veerisetti Lakshmi Narayana, popularly known as Errabbayi, president of the Guntur Vegetable Market Retail Merchants Welfare Association, attributed the high prices to a shortage of locally grown produce. He told The Hindu that local drumsticks were unlikely to arrive in the market for another two months and prices could remain high until then.

He also said that the increasing number of weddings this month and the traditional use of vegetarian food at weddings and religious functions were contributing to the high demand and prices.

Supplies are currently being brought in from other States, including Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra, he said.

Navya Kesana, a customer at the market, said the prices had come as a surprise. She was accustomed to paying ₹5 to ₹10 for a piece, but retailers were now quoting between ₹15 and ₹30.

Retailer V. Srinu said drumsticks had been selling at ₹25 to ₹30 a piece for the past two months, depending on the quantity purchased. A customer buying one piece would be charged ₹30, while those buying two or more could negotiate about ₹50 for two pieces.

Vendor Gadde Venu said drumstick availability had fallen sharply following the impact of the last three cyclones in the State. Another retailer said prices were fixed according to each piece’s quality and size and the procurement cost.

Retailers said wholesale prices were above ₹150 per kg. They estimated that 10 to 20 drumsticks made up a kilogram, depending on size.

A retailer who also grows drumstick trees said scanty rainfall, which he attributed to El Niño conditions, had hit the yield of his trees

World.title: Anjanapura and Kukkarahalli dhobi ghats to get washing machines and dryers
World.content:
The State government has issued an order to modernise dhobi ghats by installing washing machines and dryers to help the Madiwala community (traditional washermen) at Anjanapura dhobi ghat in Bengaluru and Kukkarahalli Kere dhobi ghat in Mysuru.

The Backward Classes Welfare Department has given approval for the development of these two dhobi ghats. They will be modernised at a cost of ₹75 lakh each, and the expenditure will be borne by the Karnataka Madiwala Machideva Development Corporation under the grant of ₹12.38 crore allocated for the current financial year.

A senior official from the corporation said, “We will issue a tender notification for the installation of machines soon. They are expected to be modernised in the next one or two years.”

G.D. Gopal, former member of the Karnataka State Backward Classes Commission, said, “After running from pillar to post, the department has finally approved the budget, and the work will start soon at both locations. In 2026-27 State Budget, former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah announced the project that had remained on papers for a long time.”

He highlighted that in ₹75 lakh, three washing machines along with dryers can be installed in both the locations. “I know it is not sufficient as there are hundreds of washermen but it is a small step before doing it on large scale,” he said.

When asked about the installation of water recycling units, Mr. Gopal said it was a good initiative but a costly affair as it requires funds in crores and periodical maintainance. “In drought conditions, recycling water can be a good solution instead of depending on borewell water and even tankers. Modernising dhobi ghats by installing washing machines is a first step,” he said.

World.title: Makkah Defence Alliance meeting in Islamabad concludes
World.content:
A meeting of the tripartite Makkah Defence Alliance’s top decision-making body concluded in Islamabad on Friday.

The third session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) was held in the federal capital, where authorities announced a public holiday and imposed special movement restrictions in view of the high-level gathering. A local holiday was also announced in Rawalpindi.

The meeting lasted approximately two-and-a-half hours. No official statement has been released since the meeting ended.

The SPDC comprises the foreign and defence ministers and top military officials of the three countries.

The discussions were expected to feature the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthi fighters in Yemen.

The Islamabad meeting was also expected to focus on finalising standard operating procedures (SOPs), establishing an implementation mechanism and defining coordination between the three countries’ political, defence and military institutions, a Pakistani official said.

Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said on Thursday that the foreign and defence ministers of Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan would participate in the meeting and the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia will obviously be one agenda point in the meeting”.

“It is very important,” he remarked.

Saudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks by Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, commonly known as the Houthis, targeting cities, oil facilities and shipping since fighting in Yemen’s civil war intensified in July.

“Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Asif said.

The alliance

The three countries signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement on Aug 7. The pact provides that an armed attack on any one member will be considered an attack on all, obliging the other two to extend assistance through available means, including military support.

The SPDC, which brings together the foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of defence staff of the three countries, is the alliance’s principal decision-making forum.

A permanent secretariat has been established in Riyadh to coordinate its work, with Pakistan’s retired Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood appointed as its first secretary general for a three-year term. A working committee comprising officials from member countries is also functioning.

Turkiye’s ratification of the agreement has completed the accession process for all three member states, but the alliance’s institutional and operational framework remains at what Asif described as a “nascent stage”.

“Initially, we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” the defence minister said.

The alliance has yet to publicly define its doctrine, the composition of forces, command arrangements or procedures governing a collective military response.

An emergency SPDC meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 had called for moving towards practical implementation of collective defence commitments, including arrangements for the rapid deployment of agreed forces and capabilities, subject to national laws.

Wider regional tensions

The alliance’s formation also comes against the backdrop of wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel.

While the three members share an interest in strengthening regional deterrence, their differing strategic priorities make it important to define the alliance’s scope without allowing it to become an instrument for wider military confrontation.

Asif declined to comment on how the alliance would respond to a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia, but identified Israel as a possible threat to other countries in the region.

“The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said.

Managing relations with Iran will be particularly important for Pakistan, which has sought to preserve diplomatic engagement with Tehran while deepening defence cooperation with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

A meeting in Tehran involving representatives of the three countries and Iranian officials, held on Pakistan’s initiative, reflected efforts to keep channels of communication open between the two sides.

Pakistan brokered a June accord that led to a brief halt in fighting between the US and Iran and laid out a roadmap for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear programme.

However, the truce collapsed, with Washington and Tehran accusing each other of violating the agreement, prompting months of shuttle diplomacy led principally by Qatar and Pakistan.

Asif said Pakistan had played “a very, very constructive role” between Washington and Tehran, but the outcome of ongoing mediation was “still fragile” and peace was “not yet embedded in a way people were expecting”.

Recent Pakistani military deployments, including JF-17 aircraft, drones and air defence systems such as the HQ-9, were made under bilateral cooperation predating the alliance, a security source said, adding that these existing arrangements would now become part of the trilateral framework.

Meanwhile, Turkiye has stressed the defensive character of the agreement and remained cautious about involvement in combat operations in Yemen.

World.title: Death toll from Baloch Colony building collapse in Karachi rises to 8
World.content:
KARACHI: The death toll from the collapse of an under-construction six-storey building near Karachi’s Baloch Colony area rose to eight on Friday after rescue workers recovered four more bodies from the rubble.

On Wednesday, three people were killed and 14 others injured when an under-construction building — reportedly being constructed illegally on a residential plot — collapsed. Another body was recovered on Thursday, taking the death toll to four.

On Friday, a Rescue 1122 spokesperson said the total number of bodies recovered from the rubble had reached eight.

The spokesperson, Hassaanul Haseeb Khan, added that 11 people were still missing according to reports submitted by their relatives at the information desk set up at the site of the collapsed building. He said it may not be advisable for the workers to provide a timeline for finishing the rescue and debris removal operation at this stage.

In an earlier statement, Rescue 1122 said an operation to recover bodies was under way.

“Rescue 1122 has located the bodies of more people trapped beneath the rubble,” the statement added.

Khan said that heavy machinery was also being used to remove debris, but that whenever a human body is spotted in the debris, the team stopped the machine operations and initiated manual work with extra care to recover the body. He admitted that this pace of the rescue operation may be causing concern for the relatives of the missing persons, who were protesting the slowness of the operation.

Newly-appointed East Deputy Commissioner Kashif Nabi Khuhro, speaking to the media, denied that the pace of the rescue operation was slow. However, he pointed out that the collapsed building was situated in congested and narrow streets, where it was relatively difficult to move heavy machinery.

Sindh Local Government Secretary Waseem Shamshad, who also served as director general of the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA), was removed from both posts on Thursday on the directives of Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah following the incident.

The CM ordered sweeping action over the incident while chairing a high-level meeting, further issuing directives for the removal of East Deputy Commissioner Nasrullah Abbasi, as well as Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) East Zubair Sheikh over “negligence”, a statement issued by the CM Office said.

In addition to the removal of the three officials, CM Murad further issued directives for the suspension of 16 SBCA officials and the initiation of an inquiry against them.

He directed the police to “immediately” arrest the building’s owner, Salman Tahir, and the builder, Zeeshan.

Moreover, he instructed that the building’s architect and structural engineer be included in the incident’s investigation to determine whether the construction complied with approved plans, building regulations and safety standards.

14 ‘illegal’ buildings in KAEHS to be demolished

The KDA’s Additional Deputy DG Farhan Kaiser visited the site on Thursday and told the media that their first priority was to remove the debris. He said that under the directions of the Sindh CM and LG minister, “illegal buildings” were being sealed across the metropolis.

He said that so far, 14 buildings had been sealed in the KAEHS after the building collapse and would be demolished in a second phase of the operation.

Kaiser added that it was the responsibility of the residents to report illegal buildings in their respective areas, and vowed to take action against the builders and owners of these buildings.

Members of the Chief Minister Inspection Team (CMIT), Bilal Memon and Anwar Shar, visited the scene and collected samples of the material used in the construction of the building for investigation purposes.

Rehabilitation secretary Rafiq Mustafa Shaikh, SBCA DG Abid Saleem, Rescue 1122 DG Brig. (retd) Wajid Sibghatullah Mahar and Rescue 1122 COO Dr. Abid Jalaluddin Shaikh also visited the site and supervised the rescue operation.

FIR registered

A first information report (FIR) of the incident was registered at the Tipu Sultan police station on Wednesday, on the complaint of an official of the Sindh Local Government Department.

The FIR, seen by Dawn, invoked Sections 302 (intentional murder), 119 (public servant concealing design to commit offence), 427 (mischief causing damage), 337-H(1) (hurt caused by rash or negligent act), 109 (abetment) and 34 (acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention) of the Pakistan Penal Code.

The building’s four owners — including Salman Tahir whose arrest the Sindh CM has ordered — its builder, architect, structural engineer and its contractors have been nominated in the FIR.

According to the FIR, the complainant alleged that poor-quality material was being used in the construction of the building. He claimed that the suspects, in collusion with the officials of various government departments, had been involved in constructing additional structures and not complying with the building’s approved plan.

This was why the building collapsed around 1pm, the complainant alleged.

Police have arrested four of the suspects, including one of the owners, Saad Tahir, and three contractors, who were produced before the judicial magistrate (south) today.

The judge granted police a five-day physical remand of the suspects.

World.title: Airline Norse Atlantic's Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
World.content:
Airline Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating unit has declared bankruptcy, the long-haul budget carrier said on Friday, succumbing to soaring fuel costs wrought by the war on Iran.

Norse Atlantic ASA, which is listed on the Oslo Euronext Expand bourse, and other group companies are not part of the filing and are still attempting to stay in business, the company said in a statement.

Norse Atlantic, which launched in 2022, on Wednesday warned that its financial situation was “critical”, and the following day said it had suspended all flights and that the board could file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secured funding.

Earlier on Friday, Norse said its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier’s fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back, a claim contested by the company.

“The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the company and the group to find a solution,” Norse CEO Eivind Roald said in a statement.

“The board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations,” Roald said.

The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the US-Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs skyrocketing.

Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), a wet-lease partner of the airline, said earlier that it would shift its UK operations to its own Boeing 777 fleet from Nov 26 after Norse Atlantic abruptly suspended operations, forcing the cancellation of two flights from London and Manchester.

Norse in 2021 signed long-term leases for nine Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft from Ireland-based AerCap Holdings and six Dreamliners from Singapore-based BOC Aviation Ltd. It later returned three of the planes to AerCap.

In October, PIA signed an ACMI (aircraft, crew, maintenance, and insurance) lease agreement with Norse Atlantic Airways to acquire two state-of-the-art Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners, one of which arrived in Islamabad on Nov 1.

A PIA spokesperson at the time said the addition of the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner would mark the start of the expansion of the airline’s fleet as it aimed to meet rising demand.

World.title: FO says reports of boat carrying Pakistani migrants capsizing off Libya remain unverified
World.content:
The Foreign Office said on Friday that there had been no “independent verification” of the reports of a boat carrying Pakistani migrants capsizing off the coast of Libya and that Pakistan’s embassy in Libya was “actively pursuing the matter” to ascertain facts.

It was reported earlier this week that at least 25 people from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Bajaur district were feared dead or missing after a migrant boat capsized near Libya.

According to reports, the victims’ families said they had received information from the agents who arranged the travel that a migrant boat en route to Europe had reportedly capsized in the Mediterranean Sea near Libya on Nov 21.

While there has been no official confirmation of the incident, the funeral prayers in absentia of several individuals have been offered.

The FO said in its statement that Pakistan’s embassy in Tripoli was pursuing the matter to ascertain facts, including the presence of Pakistani nationals on the reportedly capsized boat.

“The embassy has contacted the relevant Libyan government authorities, the International Organisation for Migration, and other relevant stakeholders.

“Further information will be shared as soon as verified details become available,” the FO statement said.

Previous boat tragedies

In April this year, more than 80 migrants including 20 Pakistanis were reported missing after a boat carrying around 120 people capsized in the Central Mediterranean after departing from Libya.

Most of the missing Pakistanis had travelled to Libya posing as Umrah pilgrims, while others were on visit visas to Azerbaijan, Egypt and Uganda.

Following the boat tragedy, the FIA intensified its crackdown on human smuggling networks, targeting agents operating illegal overland routes through Iran and Turkiye. The agency also launched investigations to trace the suspects’ assets and sought Interpol’s assistance in pursuing agents based abroad.

In October last year, 18 migrants were killed when a wooden vessel capsized off the coast of Libya, while 64 people, including 12 Pakistanis, were reported missing. The boat capsized off Surman due to high waves, only a few hours after setting sail.

In April 2025, four Pakistanis were among the 11 migrants found dead in a shipwreck near Libya’s Harawa coast.

In June 2023, at least 209 Pakistanis were among the migrants aboard an overloaded fishing boat that capsized and sank in international waters off Greece on June 14.

Witnesses estimated that between 400 and 750 people were aboard the vessel. The official death toll stood at 82, while 104 people survived, including 12 Pakistanis.

World.title: Indian police say they rescued 164 foreigners trafficked for cyber fraud
World.content:
Indian police said they had rescued 164 foreign nationals allegedly trafficked into the country and forced to commit online fraud, in a rare case involving victims from overseas.

Fraud compounds, where international scammers lure internet users into fake romantic relationships, cryptocurrency investments and betting platforms, are common in Southeast Asia.

While similar crimes are also widespread in India, it is much less common for the ringleaders to traffic foreigners into the country to perpetrate them.

A police crackdown on an international cybercrime network in a suburb of the capital New Delhi resulted in the rescue of 92 Indonesian nationals and 72 Malaysians, the force said.

The individuals were trafficked into India “on various pretexts, including promises of employment and lucrative opportunities”, it said in a statement late on Thursday.

“After their arrival, the foreign nationals were allegedly confined and compelled to participate in cyber fraud activities.”

Investigators have arrested a Malaysian national, whose role is “being investigated”, and identified two Indian handlers, police said.

A United Nations report estimated this year that at least 300,000 people have been trafficked into scam compounds across Southeast Asia.

New Delhi repatriated more than 2,400 Indians from cyberscam centres in neighbouring Myanmar in the past year, according to the foreign ministry.

World.title: SBP issues Rs200 commemorative coin to mark Mata Sahib Hasi Devi’s 200th birth anniversary
World.content:
The State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) has issued a Rs200 commemorative coin to mark the 200th birth anniversary of Pujya Mata Sahib Hasi Devi, the bank said in a statement on Friday.

Mata Sahib Hasi Devi was the fifth head of the historic Shadani Darbar located in the Hayat Pitafi area of Sukkur division’s Ghotki district.

According to the statement, the coin has been issued through the exchange counters of all field offices of the SBP Banking Services Corporation from Friday.

The coin is made of cupro-nickel, comprising 75 per cent copper and 25pc nickel. It measures 30 millimetres in diameter and weighs 13.5 grammes, the statement said.

It added that the face of the coin features a waxing crescent moon and five-pointed star in the centre, facing northwest in a rising position. Along the periphery on top of the crescent and star is inscribed “Islami Jamhuria Pakistan” (Islamic Republic of Pakistan) in Urdu.

Below the crescent, at the top of the two wheat springs with their arms curved upwards, is the year of issuance 2026. The coin’s value and “rupia” in Urdu script are inscribed on the right and left sides of the crescent and star, respectively.

Meanwhile, the back features a picture of Puj Shandani Darbar in the centre. The inscription “Pujya Mata Sahib Hasi Devi” appears at the top along the periphery, while the wording “200th birth anniversary” is written along the lower periphery.

The years 1826 and 2026 are written on the left and right sides of the picture, respectively, marking the 200th birth anniversary, the statement said.

Last month, Pakistan Post also issued two special commemorative postage stamps and a souvenir sheet for the 200th birth anniversary of Mata Sahib Hasi Devi to promote interfaith harmony and Sufi traditions in the region.

World.title: Pakistan seeks deeper cooperation with IAEA on nuclear security
World.content:
Pakistan looks forward to further deepening cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and international partners in support of sustainable nuclear security, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Friday.

The statement came as the 15th annual meeting of the International Network for Nuclear Security Training and Support Centres (NSSC Network), hosted by Pakistan in collaboration with the IAEA, concluded in Islamabad.

The meeting, held from Nov 23 to 26, brought together international delegates to discuss nuclear security training, capacity building and cooperation, the statement added.

A special event was also held at the headquarters of the Pakistan Nuclear Regulatory Authority (PNRA) to mark 20 years of Pakistan-IAEA cooperation in nuclear security. The event featured an exhibition of indigenous nuclear security technologies developed by Pakistan’s national industry.

Delegates also visited the Pakistan Institute of Engineering and Applied Sciences (PIEAS), where they were briefed on the country’s capabilities in nuclear engineering, research, education and training.

The programme included technical sessions, expert discussions and thematic presentations on emerging nuclear security challenges, institutional sustainability, human resource development and the future of international cooperation in nuclear security training.

At the concluding session, the chairman of the Pakistan Atomic Energy Commission (PAEC) underscored the importance of sustained international cooperation in strengthening nuclear security.

The IAEA’s unit head of the Division of Nuclear Security commended Pakistan for hosting the meeting, describing it as an important milestone in international nuclear security cooperation.

The statement said the meeting had provided a platform for member states to exchange expertise, strengthen national capabilities and identify future priorities.

Pakistan first hosted the NSSC Network’s annual meeting in 2016. Its return to Pakistan after a decade reflected the country’s sustained engagement with the IAEA and continued contribution to international nuclear security cooperation, the statement added.

In a video address at the opening session on Monday, IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi thanked Pakistan for hosting the meeting and highlighted the network’s role in translating nuclear security principles into practice.

A day earlier, Pakistan had called for keeping decisions on the use of nuclear weapons under human control and cautioned against the use of artificial intelligence (AI) systems to target nuclear command, control and communications systems.

Speaking at an open debate of the UN Security Council, Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah, said emerging technologies posed new challenges to international security and called for appropriate safeguards, regulations and confidence-building measures to prevent miscalculation and escalation.

World.title: Roads blocked, traffic congested in Karachi for 2nd consecutive day
World.content:
Karachi saw blocked roads and congested traffic for a second consecutive day on Friday as road closure alerts caused traffic to be diverted due to a protest around the Karachi Press Club (KPC).

The city’s traffic police earlier announced diversions around KPC ahead of an expected protest, advising commuters to use alternative routes to avoid inconvenience.

According to a press release, the traffic heading from MR Kiyani Chowk towards Saddar and Zainab Market would be diverted left from Coast Guards Mess towards the Sindh High Court (SHC) and Passport Office.

It added that Sharea Faisal could be closed temporarily at Avari traffic signal.

Traffic travelling from Sharea Faisal towards the airport would be diverted right from Avari traffic signal onto Fatima Jinnah Road, towards Cantt, School Road, CSD and Kala Pul, the release said.

According to updates issued by the traffic police, the road from Coast Guard towards Zainab Market and Sarwar Shaheed Road was closed to traffic at around 3:20pm in view of security.

Traffic from Coast Guard was being sent towards the Chowrangi Passport Office, while traffic coming from there was being directed towards Paradise Chowk, the traffic police said.

The road was later re-opened to traffic as of an alert at 6:05pm.

Drigh Road towards Karsaz and Sharea Faisal was closed to traffic at around 4pm, with traffic being rerouted from Drigh Road via the Rashid Minhas Flyover towards Millennium.

The road was opened about half-an-hour later, but an alert was issued for heavy traffic pressure as the traffic was only running in one lane, slowing the movement of vehicles.

At 5:22pm, the traffic police issued an update that the flow of traffic had been restored, with all lanes opened for traffic. It noted that peak hours were still ongoing but that traffic was being kept moving.

Another road closure alert was issued for the road from Avari Towers towards Mehran Hotel and Sharea Faisal at 5:10pm. Traffic is being sent via Avari Towers towards Fatima Jinnah Road, police said.

Motorists were earlier advised to avoid roads around the KPC and follow the traffic police’s instructions. The public was also urged to cooperate with law enforcement agencies and traffic police.

Commuters requiring assistance could contact the Traffic Police Rahnuma helpline at 1915, where representatives would be available round the clock to provide guidance.

The latest traffic updates are also available through Karachi Traffic Police’s social media platforms, the statement added.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
