World.title: Chinese American Fields Medalist Calls for Math Collaboration in AI Age
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019334/Chinese American Fields Medalist Calls for Math Collaboration in AI Age
World.content:
Arguing that artificial intelligence could help mathematicians solve difficult problems, Chinese American Fields Medal winner Shing-Tung Yau said humans still have a place in pushing mathematics to new heights.

“Mathematics is not in crisis. It will only get better,” Yau told Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper on Nov. 23, saying that much of the anxiety surrounding AI stemmed from an excessive focus on problem-solving rather than the broader pursuit of mathematical discovery.

Yau, the founding president of the Asian Mathematical Union, the first pan-Asian academic organization dedicated to mathematics, called for greater collaboration among mathematicians at the union’s launch ceremony on Tuesday at the Chinese University of Hong Kong. He added that rapid advances in AI offer Asian mathematicians a chance not only to catch up with their international peers but also to overtake them.

Over the past year, AI has made a series of remarkable breakthroughs in mathematics. In May, a model from American AI company OpenAI disproved the Erdős unit distance conjecture, a problem that had remained open for 80 years.

On Nov. 20, mathematician Levent Alpöge, working for American AI company Anthropic, unveiled a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most famous unsolved problems, developed with the help of the company’s AI system Claude. Mathematicians are now working to understand the reasoning behind the proof.

“In mathematics, it’s often only after we’ve repeatedly used a theorem over a long period of time that we know the proof is sound,” Yau explained to The Paper. He expects mathematicians to fully digest the proof of the Riemann hypothesis within five years.

“Whether the Riemann hypothesis was proved by a machine or the human brain, it’s an exciting achievement. To me, humanity’s goal is to pursue truth. As long as the truth can be discovered, there’s nothing wrong with using whatever tools we have to find it. Who gets the credit, I think, is secondary.”

Yau likened mathematical research to climbing mountains, saying AI could help mathematicians reach the first summit and open up paths to even greater heights.

“Climbing a mountain isn’t something one scholar can do alone,” he said. “Machines can speed up our collaboration by helping us bring together ideas from scientists around the world.”

In line with Yau’s emphasis on collaboration, the Asian Mathematical Union plans to recruit around 100 postdoctoral researchers annually: 50 selected by an academic committee, five each nominated by China, India, Russia, Japan, South Korea, and Iran, and 20 from other countries and regions. It also plans to regularly invite 25 senior mathematicians and 30 early career researchers from around the world to Hong Kong for research, academic exchanges, and training.

The union will focus on four areas: pure mathematics, applied mathematics, statistics, and AI.

On Oct. 11, another initiative led by Yau, the Yau Laboratory Alliance for Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, was established at Beijing’s Tsinghua University. The alliance focuses on AI models designed specifically for mathematics, AI-assisted mathematical proofs, and interdisciplinary applications.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Shing-Tung Yau speaks at a new book launch event at the National Library of China in Beijing, March 28, 2025. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019324/Farmers’ Markets for the Masses: The Key to China’s Vibrant Local Food Culture
World.title: Farmers’ Markets for the Masses: The Key to China’s Vibrant Local Food Culture
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019324/Farmers’ Markets for the Masses: The Key to China’s Vibrant Local Food Culture
World.content:
Zhong Shuru has been working at a university in the southern Chinese city of Zhuhai for years. But she still regularly drives three hours north to the outskirts of Dongguan City just to stock up on chicken from her mother’s village.

This kind of commitment to fresh local produce is far from unusual in southern China’s Guangdong province, home to just over 125 million people and the birthplace of Cantonese cuisine.

“In Guangdong, we have a saying: Without chicken, there is no feast,” said Zhong, an associate professor of anthropology at Sun Yat-sen University.

The province consumes a whopping 800 million chickens a year, and locals pride themselves on their ability to taste the difference between “good chicken” — free-range birds raised for over 200 days — and the battery-farmed broilers used by most fast-food chains.

This passion for high-quality produce has shaped the region’s entire food supply chain, helping local networks survive even amid the rise of modern supermarket chains and online delivery services.

Even today, city dwellers across Guangdong can easily access fresh meat, seafood, fruits, and vegetables at relatively affordable prices via a dense web of neighborhood food markets.

For Zhong, these markets — often called “wet markets” in English — have long been a source of fascination: They are a relic of the pre-supermarket era, but also a potential antidote to industrial food production.

This point struck Zhong keenly when she began a Ph.D. at Texas A&M University. She quickly realized that such markets simply didn’t exist in much of the United States — unless you count expensive farmers’ markets.

During her time in Texas, Zhong found herself surviving mostly on pizza and pasta dishes to save time — a habit that added “about 10 kilograms” to her weight, she recalled.

That was when she decided to launch a research project into China’s food markets, aiming to understand the role they played in feeding the country.

In the summer of 2016, she began a work placement at a market stall selling Spanish mackerel in China’s southern province of Hainan, where she spent over a year tracing the fish’s journey from the South China Sea to dinner tables across the tropical island.

Over the following decade, she would visit more than 200 markets all over China, writing books including 2025’s “Sustainable Food Consumption in China.”

At the core of her research lies a burning question: Are local markets destined to decline in an era that prizes convenience, or could they help promote a resurgence in sustainable eating habits?

A misunderstood market

But first, it’s necessary to clear up a few common misconceptions. For years, the term “wet market” has fueled all sorts of prejudices in the English-speaking world, where negative stereotypes about Chinese eating habits have a long history.

Zhong specifically recalls a member of her Ph.D. committee in Texas frowning as she introduced her research subject. “What are wet markets?” the person asked. “Sounds disgusting.”

It didn’t help that some markets in China were involved in the wildlife trade until China outlawed the trade in 2020, with the practice allegedly playing a role in spreading pathogens such as the coronavirus that caused the 2002–2003 SARS epidemic.

But in reality, the term wet market encompasses a huge variety of venues selling different kinds of fresh produce. Most do not sell livestock, let alone exotic animals.

The Singapore government coined the term in the 1970s, wanting to distinguish between markets selling “dry” preserved goods and “wet” produce such as fresh meat and vegetables, according to Zhong.

The term likely began being applied to Chinese food markets in the 1980s and 1990s — a period when China leaned on Singapore for guidance as it rapidly reformed its economy and integrated into the global market.

And while wet markets are now associated with China, their origins in the country lie partly with Western businessmen living in Shanghai and Guangzhou during the 19th century.

Before then, food in China tended to be distributed through open-air markets known as ji, which towns and villages across the country often held weekly.

As cities such as Shanghai and Guangzhou grew rapidly in the 1800s, farmers and vendors flocked in to set up informal open-air markets to serve their swelling populations.

In 1864, a British businessman and a French priest teamed up to open Shanghai’s first indoor food market. Though that venture was short-lived, it pioneered a business model later adopted by other businesses and government bodies.

That eventually led to the establishment of large-scale facilities such as Shanghai’s Sanjiaodi Market — a three-story building with vendors selling vegetables, meat, and snacks on different floors every day.

But the nationwide boom of such markets did not begin until the 1980s, when China embarked on economic reforms that legitimized entrepreneurship and turbocharged urbanization. Street vendors would later gain legal status as “self-employed traders,” allowing them to open stalls in formal permanent markets.

The push to build more food markets even gained political significance as new residents flooded into the cities. In 1988, China launched the cailanzi (literally “food basket”) project, which tasked local officials with ensuring a stable supply of affordable and high-quality meat, vegetables, fruit, and dairy products.

Mayors across China were pushed to expand the food supply, improve logistics, and regulate trade, cementing markets as a vital part of a city’s infrastructure. In 2013, Shanghai set a goal of doubling the city’s number of “standardized food markets” to 1,500 by 2020, to ensure it could feed a population expected to reach “nearly 30 million” residents.

Modern temptations

But these neighborhood markets have since come under pressure amid the rapid expansion of supermarket chains and later online delivery services.

In 1995, the French retail giant Carrefour became the first global supermarket chain to enter the Chinese mainland, as a “supermarket revolution” swept across the Global South.

Supermarkets quickly won over millions of Chinese consumers with their promise of greater convenience, food safety standards, and — occasionally — lower prices.

By 2019, China had nearly 27,000 supermarkets, some built on the sites of former local markets.

Much was lost along the way. By operating large-scale, standardized supply chains, the businesses effectively severed the link between swathes of shoppers and locally produced food.

Yet, many pockets of Chinese society refused to buy the narrative that freshness could be acquired with a click.

In Hainan, Zhong found that some locals still didn’t have a refrigerator at home — not because they couldn’t afford one, but because of local beliefs that livestock must be consumed within hours of being slaughtered.

Locals who “know their food” would visit markets twice a day to ensure every meal was prepared with the freshest ingredients — a stark contrast to Zhong’s experience in Texas, where she drove to a supermarket to stock up once a week.

Seafood connoisseurs were another group who invested in the freshest local ingredients. In Hainan and other coastal regions, one of the most sought-after products is xiao haixian — or “small seafood” — an umbrella term for a variety of small catches that even locals often couldn’t identify.

They are fished in coastal waters on the day of sale, often by small boats without onboard freezers. The lack of cold storage was a badge of honor for many fishers — a guarantee that their catch had come directly from the sea that morning.

Zhong had never seen xiao haixian stocked at a food market near her Guangdong home, until one morning she saw fish vendors already packing up at 6 a.m. — just hours after the small fishing boats had returned to the dock nearby.

She found a similar appetite for freshness nearly 1,500 kilometers away in Suzhou, a historic city near Lake Tai in eastern China renowned for its refined cuisine.

There, she met a vendor specializing in seasonal food: freshwater mussels and snails in spring, soft-shelled turtles and eels in summer. The highlight of the year was autumn, when markets filled with traders selling jitoumi — seeds from a local water plant used in sweet soups.

It is a delicate ingredient that requires hours of labor to clean and hand-shell, and its sales window is brief: By late autumn, it has disappeared from local markets, just as hairy crabs come into season and dominate the stalls in this part of China for just a few weeks each year.

With their focus on stable output, mechanical processing and long-distance supply chains, products like xiao haixian and jitoumi simply do not fit the supermarket business model.

But thanks to local food markets, these local treasures are still widely available — and their popularity, in turn, has helped traditional markets survive even amid the digital shopping era.

“China is fortunate to have a robust local food culture,” Zhong said.

A web of relationships

Another key takeaway from Zhong’s tour across more than 50 Chinese cities is that food markets have not just shaped tastes, but also strengthened people’s bonds with their land.

In Guiyang, capital of southwestern China’s Guizhou province, she observed how vendors used more than 20 different methods to process tofu. In the northwestern city of Yining, she learned how nomadic communities had developed a unique relationship with their cattle and sheep.

Perhaps the most dramatic case was the “snowbird” community in Hainan.

Every winter, an estimated 1.5 million people from northern China — mostly retirees — move to the tropical island province to escape the freezing weather. There, they must adapt to a way of life starkly different from what they are used to in their hometowns near the Russian and North Korean borders.

As Zhong discovered, local markets often become a key venue where “snowbirds” learn to navigate the island’s dialects, fish names, and love of bargaining. She recalled spending time with a woman called Aunt Mei, a 60-something who moves to Hainan with her husband for six months each year.

Mei was not a fan of saltwater fish back in northern China, but she was captivated by the colorful varieties at the market and decided to give them a taste. She tried mincing Spanish mackerel and mixing it with ground pork to make dumplings — the staple food in her hometown.

The fish dumplings struck the couple as unforgettably “fresh,” sparking Mei’s passion for saltwater fish. After the local market closed, she teamed up with several other “snowbirds” to purchase fish directly at the docks.

Drawing on geographer David Seamon’s term, Zhong likens ordinary people’s experience of food markets to a “place-ballet”: By frequenting these markets, people develop a life rhythm in sync with their place, deepening their understanding of local food, culture, and communities. For “snowbirds” like Mei, learning this “place-ballet” helps them adapt to life on their new island.

For locals, relationships built around the market can also help them weather difficult times. In Shanghai, Zhong met a fish vendor who had kept a stall for three decades and maintained contact information for over 4,000 customers.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, he repeatedly received phone calls from customers — especially older clients — who couldn’t access markets. In response, the vendor delivered more than 300 orders per day to his customers’ homes, to ensure they could still get the groceries they needed.

Every bite matters

Yet despite all their advantages, food markets across China face daunting challenges.

Many are losing customers to supermarkets and, increasingly, online retailers. Meanwhile, mismanagement persists, as many markets have shifted from state control to neighborhoods, private companies, and individual investors since the 1990s.

In many cases, the privatizations boosted efficiency but also led to underinvestment in drainage, ventilation, and waste management, damaging customer experiences and sparking conflicts between vendors and venue managers.

It was no coincidence that the blockbuster Chinese crime drama “The Knockout,” released in 2023, centered on a clash between a fish stall owner and rent-seeking managers at a Cantonese market.

“To run a fresh food market, you shouldn’t follow the mindset of a landlord who just collects rent,” Zhong said. “Instead, you should treat vendors as your most important asset and support them.”

Zhong tries to maintain a “neutral perspective” toward the modern food industry. Supermarkets are not all bad; their sophisticated supply chains allow Shanghai residents to buy mushrooms grown more than 2,000 kilometers away in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, or tropical fruits from across Southeast Asia. She also understands why exhausted young workers order food online rather than spending hours buying groceries at their local market.

But she also worries about the hidden costs of such convenience. Supermarkets and e-commerce platforms often trumpet their “direct sourcing, no middlemen” business model in China, telling consumers they can provide unbeatable value.

What they don’t mention is their disproportionate bargaining power over farmers. During a recent research trip to Guangdong, Zhong found some growers were reluctant to work with platforms even when offered large orders, fearing they would have to accept massive discounts, customize production, and become trapped in a dependent relationship with the conglomerates.

Local flavors can disappear, too. Standardized retailing favors food suited for mass production and long-distance transportation. True local flavors, however, have to be found near the field. Cantonese people can only buy their favorite variety of chicken at a local market, and to truly taste maolaguo, a wild tomato, one must visit Guizhou in person.

According to Zhong, to preserve the flexibility and diversity of China’s food markets, both governments and consumers need to shift their mindsets.

In recent years, some markets have undergone refurbishment to look sleek and appeal to young customers, a move criticized for gentrifying neighborhoods. “Not every market needs cafés and flower shops,” Zhong cautioned.

Instead, market managers and local governments should focus on addressing vendors’ and consumers’ actual needs: better lighting, waste management, and parking. Ultimately, a market won’t be sustainable if it is not embedded in local connections, according to Zhong.

As for consumers, Zhong encourages them to try things out: accepting that farmers’ markets, like e-commerce apps, take time to navigate. She recalled that during her first days of fieldwork at the Hainanese market, she found bargaining in the local dialect unsettling. Now, she can confidently explore a new market and occasionally surprise her family with knowledge about local products.

“As consumers, we can vote with our mouths,” Zhong said. “Every bite matters.”

(Header image: A farmers’ market in Pu’er, Yunnan province, 2024. Courtesy of Graeme Kennedy)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.title: Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.content:
Amid nationwide classroom phone bans, “paper short dramas,” half-meter-long printouts of scenes from short dramas folded into the shape of a smartphone, have recently surged in popularity among Chinese primary school students.

“The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” “Reborn as the Heiress of a Tycoon,” and “The School Bully Forces Me to Date Him” are just a few examples of the stories now stocked by school-adjacent stores and e-commerce platforms, selling for as little as 1 yuan ($0.14), domestic media reported Monday.

In 2021, China’s Ministry of Education issued a notice stating that primary and secondary school students should not bring phones into the classroom, and any phone brought to school must be kept by the school. The ministry tightened this in 2025, banning phones and other electronic devices in school classrooms as part of a student mental health initiative.

Paper short dramas’ accordion-style design allow them to be easily concealed and taken into school. They typically contain scenes from multiple episodes, pairing screenshots with written dialogue.

Despite often containing adult, vulgar, and violent content — in “The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” for instance, a female character sleeps with a legendary CEO and becomes the envy of her peers — paper short dramas are marketed as toys, with some packaging citing toy-safety standards that are outdated or inapplicable to a paper booklet.

This marketing tactic allows sellers, who have not obtained permission from short drama producers to reproduce or distribute the content, to dodge copyright laws.

China’s short drama users reportedly reached nearly 664 million as of December last year. Industry estimates put the potential lost output value due to piracy at as high as 20 billion yuan.

In interviews with domestic media, some parents also reported concerns about the adult content in paper short dramas being available to children with no prior screening, saying that such stories might negatively impact their children’s values.

A hashtag related to paper short dramas on microblogging platform Weibo had garnered over 170 million views as of Thursday. Many commenters called the idea creative, terming it a “new kind of comic strip,” while others criticized it for exposing minors to harmful content.

“Products like this need tight control. Don’t let them poison kids,” one user wrote.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A box of different paper short dramas, each shaped like a smartphone. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.title: The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.content:
Zhong Weiting’s wife recently bought him a pair of trousers with four front pockets. They’re for the little metal objects he carries around — things that spin, slide, click, or flip open, some made from titanium and costing thousands of yuan.

Each day, he picks a few from a plastic organizer originally bought for socks. He plays with them in elevators, in his car, and at his desk, switching to quieter models when other people are around.

For Zhong, 32, they help relieve stress and keep his restless hands occupied. “I like the sounds they make, and knowing exactly how they’ll respond gives me a sense of certainty,” he tells Sixth Tone. “I feel a kind of electric tingling in my fingertips.”

For all their elaborate mechanisms, they’re just toys to fiddle with. And Zhong, an export salesman in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen who began collecting only in November 2025, already owns 25, including one he bought this month for 2,199 yuan ($330).

Across China, the toys have found a growing following under the name EDC, short for “everyday carry,” a term borrowed from an online subculture centered on practical gear such as pocketknives and flashlights. On social media, they’re also dubbed “cyber walnuts,” after the traditional Chinese pastime of rolling a pair of walnuts in the hand.

Among the most popular designs are sliders, known in China as “push cards,” whose metal plates produce a series of tactile clicks as they slide against each other. Some toys mimic the motion of revealing a playing card or recreate the sharp tap of a telegraph key, with adjustable resistance and sound on more elaborate models.

Basic models sell for less than 100 yuan, while stainless steel versions typically cost 300 to 500 yuan. Limited editions made from rarer metals or featuring elaborate designs can run into the thousands.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, online sales of EDC toys tracked by consulting firm Meritco Databank rose 55.5% to more than 45 million yuan, with nearly 500,000 toys sold, up 78% year on year.

The vast majority of the trade, however, still takes place within collector circles. While a few large brands sell openly on popular e-commerce platforms, smaller makers rely on private groups on Chinese super app WeChat to announce new releases, sometimes limited to just a few dozen pieces.

At an EDC exhibition in Beijing in October, organizer Fu Chunjun told domestic media that the community has a name for its growing obsession: the “men’s version of Pop Mart,” the Chinese collectible-toy company known for its blind boxes.

But when Zhong shows his latest purchases to friends, few understand the appeal. “They think, why should a plastic or stainless steel gadget sell for 500 yuan?” he says.

Idle hands

To buy a toy from one vendor at Shanghai’s EDC exhibition in April, Guo Songhao first had to draw one of two jokers from a deck of 21 playing cards.

He drew the big joker, securing a limited-edition knuckle roller, a small metal toy designed to be rolled and flipped between the fingers. “My luck was pretty good that day,” the 25-year-old Shanghai-based engineer tells Sixth Tone.

Organized by Laotiejiang, one of China’s oldest EDC brands, the exhibition brought together more than 100 brands and drew three times as many visitors as its 2025 debut. By the time Guo arrived that afternoon, many of the most sought-after toys had already sold out.

A friend who makes a living reselling EDC toys had traveled from northeastern China for the exhibition. After securing a 399-yuan VIP ticket through a lottery, he lined up for hours to get in half an hour ahead of regular visitors. When Guo caught up with him, his friend was carrying a bag containing more than a dozen toys worth tens of thousands of yuan. “He was there to stock up,” Guo says.

Guo first discovered EDC toys in high school but began collecting them in 2022. Still a student with little spare cash, he spent around 500 yuan on two spinners and a push card.

“I thought I’d stop after those three,” he says, even when the toys fell short of his expectations. “I couldn’t stop myself.”

Over the years, Guo estimates he’s bought and sold toys worth a combined 200,000 to 300,000 yuan, recovering what he spent on the hobby. One piece he bought for a little over 1,000 yuan later sold for 5,000 or 6,000 yuan.

Roughly 90% of those purchases took place in private WeChat groups, where Guo says some makers reserve new releases for repeat buyers, or give priority to collectors who already own all three of their earlier models.

While some brands increase production as demand grows, Guo says others deliberately restrict supply, leaving collectors who miss out on new releases facing higher prices on the secondhand market.

“Once everyone can buy it, people lose interest,” says Zhong.

Zhong recently tried to buy a slider he’d seen in numerous videos online. When he tried to add its maker on WeChat, the account had already been flagged for unusual activity following a flood of friend requests. Zhong eventually reached him and waited several more days to join the buying group, where nearly 1,500 people were vying for the first batch of just 200 toys.

He managed to get one, but no amount of adjustment produced a sound he liked. “The tactile feedback was atrocious,” he says. “It was really disappointing.”

He soon sold it on Xianyu, a popular Chinese secondhand marketplace, for 240 yuan, though he reckons it could have fetched more than 320. It was one of about 10 toys he recently sold, all priced below comparable listings.

Even secondhand, buyers expect these toys to look almost new, complete with their original boxes — a peculiar requirement for objects meant to be constantly handled. “I held on to the boxes, but my wife scolded me and told me to get rid of them, so I tossed them all out,” Zhong says. “That makes reselling things quite a hassle for me.”

After discovering EDC toys through online videos in 2025, Wang Yunfei, a master’s student at Shanghai’s Donghua University, began buying secondhand pieces to try different designs without losing too much money if he tired of them.

Over several months, he bought and resold toys worth a combined 2,000 to 3,000 yuan before growing weary of tracking new releases and prices. “I’ve archived those group chats,” he says, adding that he now rarely checks product announcements, spending more time on his studies.

Even Guo, after six years of collecting, has become harder to impress. He believes the market has expanded faster than the quality of its designs. “There are few people with real ideas, design ability, and taste,” he says.

During one spell of boredom, Guo switched to collecting actual walnuts, the traditional kind rolled in the palm. “I ended up buying a bunch of those, too,” he says.

New spin

Before founding 01EDC, now one of China’s leading EDC brands, Lin Tianfeng had simply set out to design a fidget spinner for himself.

In 2016, Lin, now 35, was repairing secondhand sweater-linking machines for his family’s business in southern China’s Guangdong province when he spotted a metal spinner on e-commerce platform Taobao and figured he could make one.

But factory after factory turned him down until a stainless-steel product manufacturer agreed to take his order. Lin commissioned a batch of about 20 three-bladed brass spinners, each weighing 120 grams — nearly three times the ideal weight.

Keeping a couple for himself, Lin tried selling the extras to fellow enthusiasts on Baidu Tieba, a Chinese discussion platform. “But nobody in China wanted these tie geda,” he says, using Chinese internet slang for EDC toys that translates to “little lumps of metal.”

A buyer in Singapore, however, spotted the spinners on Taobao and bought the remaining pieces. “He told me, ‘Your design is amazing. You’re a genius!’ I honestly thought he was trolling me,” Lin recalls. “But I figured, I’m not going to say no to money.”

Lin’s parents were less impressed. Unable to fathom why anyone would pay hundreds of yuan for a piece of metal, they stopped giving him money. At the time, he had just 75 yuan in his pocket.

Earning 10 yuan for every machine he repaired at the family shop, plus more for house calls, Lin managed to scrape together 3,000 yuan in less than two months. A business partner put up another 3,000 yuan, and with the Singaporean buyer’s help, Lin began reaching overseas collectors through Facebook groups.

“Our 6,000 yuan grew to over 10,000, then over 30,000, and then over 90,000,” he recalls. “It just snowballed.”

In his first year, Lin made more than 100,000 yuan in profit, mostly from spinners, all of which he gave to his family, plus an additional 10,000 yuan. “That’s when they believed I was building a business, not messing around,” he says.

Lin handled much of the work himself, sometimes spending 12 hours straight, from 2 p.m. to 2 a.m., meticulously cleaning brass spinners. And as collectors began favoring stainless steel and titanium alloys over brass, finding factories willing to work with the harder metals became increasingly difficult.

Of the seven factories Lin approached on one occasion, only one eventually agreed to take his order — after he spent hours drinking tea in its office. “They turned me down at first, as was to be expected,” he recalls. “I didn’t leave; I just kept sitting there until they finally agreed to handle one production run for me.”

For the first six years of his business, Lin had to keep finding manufacturers willing to take his orders. “It was a guerrilla-style operation, taking a shot here and a shot there, with no fixed base of operations,” he says.

In 2022, Lin finally bought his own machinery, set up a factory, and renamed his brand 01EDC. Most of Lin’s early customers were in the U.S. and Europe, though orders came from as far away as Brazil, where buyers were willing to pay $100 in shipping for a $60 toy.

“In China, the fidget-spinner craze of 2017 was followed by a second wave of interest during the pandemic,” Lin says. Videos demonstrating new designs on Bilibili and Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, drew more people into the hobby.

For men accustomed to collecting figurines or Gundam models, Lin says the pocket-sized toys had another attraction: They could play with them in public without attracting much attention. “Nobody thinks you’re childish,” he says.

Once reliant entirely on overseas customers, 01EDC — selling toys priced from 299 yuan to more than 3,000 yuan — now generates more than 70% of its sales in China, with Lin largely leaving exports to distributors. He estimates the number of Chinese EDC brands has grown from about a dozen in 2020 to more than 400 today.

“At home,” he says, “China alone is a whole world.”

Among his competitors are manufacturers selling near-identical designs under different names and at much lower prices. Many promote their toys on Douyin, and while Lin has struggled to take legal action, he acknowledges that some of the imitations are well made.

Wang, the Shanghai graduate student, once paid 189 yuan for a copy of a slider, less than half the price of the original. “In terms of feel, it’s practically indistinguishable from the original, although a few of the tracks aren’t as refined,” he says.

With hundreds of brands vying for collectors’ attention, Lin believes the bigger challenge now is coming up with original designs. “We’re not afraid of great products appearing,” he says. “We’re afraid of too many identical ones.”

Lin acknowledges that at 01EDC, too, the focus has long been on making reliable, well-crafted toys rather than experimenting with more imaginative designs.

“Next year,” he says, “we’re going to focus on something that really catches people’s eye.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A collector tries out a fidget spinner at an EDC toy exhibition in Beijing, Oct. 31, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.title: A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.content:
A Shanghai university is now giving each student and staff member up to 100 million AI tokens a week, saying that it hopes to make tokens a standard teaching resource equal to books, lab equipment, and databases.

University members may use the tokens to access a range of AI models and tools after signing in to the university website with their campus ID, as announced by Shanghai University of Finance and Economics’ (SUFE) official WeChat account on Nov. 21.

Tokens are the smallest pieces of information that AI models can process. Students can use them to debug code, clean data, conduct research, and even build their own AI agents.

China’s daily token consumption hit roughly 500 trillion in June, nearly four times that of December 2025. State-owned telecommunications carriers now sell token plans to consumers, with China Telecom’s cheapest plan costing 9.9 yuan ($1.50) a month for 10 million tokens — a 10th of SUFE’s weekly, per-person limit.

SUFE is the latest Chinese university to provide computing power and free token quotas to students and staff as a public resource, a trend that began earlier this fall.

Starting this September in Beijing, Tsinghua University began offering each student and staff member 1,000 yuan in “computing vouchers,” while Peking University offers a year of free access to Qoder, a cross-LLM AI coding assistant, and 3,000 credits a month. In the central Hunan province, Hunan University students receive 2 million tokens a day. Shanghai’s Tongji University also launched its own plan in October, giving students and faculty 100 million tokens a week.

“In the past, when you’d say a school had good infrastructure, you’d be referring to its gym and library,” Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, told domestic media. “Going forward, computing platforms, LLM data centers, and high-powered internet may be the important infrastructure of schools in the future.”

However, education researchers also report concerns that access to free tokens may fuel “idle teaching,” where teachers create assignments using AI and students submit AI-generated answers, creating a loop in which the work is completed but no real learning takes place.

“Measuring the value of token use is not about how many tokens are actually consumed but what kind of learning they advance in students,” Zhang Duanhong, director of the Center for Educational Policy Research at Tongji University, told domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.content:
“Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.

“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.

“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.content:
Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.

In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.

Service jobs — whether in finance, professional services, education, health care, or technology — cluster in big, wealthy cities, and so do the women who hold them. But while China’s educational and employment landscape has transformed dramatically, marriage norms haven’t. Census data show a strong and remarkably stable pattern of hypergamy, in which women marry men with higher socioeconomic status. This norm spans regions and educational backgrounds, meaning that urban women with higher degrees also tend to marry those who are more educationally and professionally advanced than they are.

This norm made sense in a world in which men were usually more educated than women. In a new reality where urban women are more likely to attend college and have a decent job, it becomes counterproductive for matchmaking.

Together, these three factors have contributed to a mechanical mismatch. But how can we quantify it? After all, no one can run a real-world experiment on national marriage rates.

To find the answer, we built a model of a counterfactual parallel world — one in which gender differences in education, occupation, and migration patterns in 2015 were the same as they were in the year 2000.

In that counterfactual world, the national singles rate, defined as the proportion of individuals who stay single from the earliest legal marriage age to the time they turn 45, falls by roughly 30% for women and 12% for men. In developed cities, the female singles rate drops by nearly 40%, and among highly educated women there, by more than half.

About one-third of this drop comes from the narrowing education gap; the other two-thirds comes from the reduction of service jobs in large cities available to women in this hypothetical world.

What does that mean for the future? While we do not have access to perfect projections, if the gender gap in educational attainment and service sector employment in developed cities merely widens at the same speed from 2015 to 2030 as it did between 2000 and 2015, our model suggests that by 2030, the singles rate among highly educated women in developed cities will rise to 15.2% — roughly one in seven. Meanwhile, among low-skilled men in less developed regions, it will rise from 8.7% to 12%, or about one in eight.

Of course, history is rarely linear. The Chinese government has made marriage rates and fertility rates a top priority, with local officials experimenting with all kinds of interventions and welfare policies to prevent marriage rates from entering a free fall. Some regions have even introduced cash rewards for newlyweds.

But our findings raise questions about the effectiveness of such policies, showing that financial incentives alone are not enough to reverse the trend. Using our model, we expect a subsidy as high as 10% of household income to lower the national female singles rate from 3.46% to 3.17% and the male singles rate from 8.17% to 7.89%.

This is because no amount of money can conjure up a partner who fits traditional expectations. Other interventions, such as encouraging more educated men to move to big cities or encouraging more educated women to move back to smaller cities, might work on paper, but they would raise serious gender fairness questions by effectively punishing educated women.

What is urgently needed is a rethink of hypergamic norms. Educated women should be celebrated as proof of the transformative power of education, migration, and hard work. They are no longer passive participants in a marriage market, but active planners of their own lives who can and should choose partners regardless of educational and financial status.

Men must also adjust their expectations to accommodate partners who may not meet hypergamic norms. And the gatekeepers of those norms — families and relationship gurus among them — must catch up with contemporary society, realizing that no single mode of relationship is the key to a fulfilling life.

It is likely that the red and blue on China’s marriage map will grow darker in the coming years. Yet nothing is set in stone. After all, even Carrie Bradshaw eventually found love.

Huang Zibin of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Wang Yushi of Hainan University, and Yang Yu of Peking University made equal contributions to this research.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.content:
Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.

The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.

Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

Excavation of the fourth site, Laohudun cemetery in Hubei, began this year. According to researchers, the area contains the highest concentration of Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) tombs in southern China.

At the site, archaeologists unearthed bamboo and wooden slips — writing materials used before the invention of paper — along with numerous inscribed lacquerware and wooden artifacts. The inscriptions cover a wide range of topics, including politics, military affairs, literature, medicine, folklore, and art, offering greater insight into society at the time.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Stone artifacts found at the Taohuahe site in Sichuan province. From the National Cultural Heritage Administration)

World.title: Boatwright debuts strong as Gilas routs Syria in FIBA World Cup qualifiers
World.content:
New naturalized Filipino Bennie Boatwright and star center Kai Sotto live up to the hype as Gilas Pilipinas pummels Syria to kick off its fifth-window campaign in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers

MANILA, Philippines – Syria had no answer to the towering might and pinpoint shooting of Gilas Pilipinas as the favored Filipino squad rolled to a dominant 97-58 win to begin its campaign in the 2027 FIBA World Cup Asian qualifiers fifth window in Seremban, Malaysia on Friday, November 27.

Long-awaited naturalized player Bennie Boatwright made sure to live up to the hype in his national team debut, tallying a big double-double of 16 points and 13 rebounds, while frontcourt partner Kai Sotto led the new twin-tower duo with 18 points and 10 boards in just 17 minutes.

“We only had a few practices with Bennie Boatwright, and yet, he’s fitting into us like a glove,” said Gilas head coach Tim Cone. “He didn’t go out and force anything, and stayed in what we do. From a coaching standpoint, you like it, because it wasn’t guys stepping out of what they do, it was really within what we’ve asked them to do, and that was really nice.”

“I just think that the more Bennie is with us, the more he’ll get comfortable, and know where his teammates are, and know where they like to get the ball. We’ll know more about him as we go along. We just see him elevating his game more and more when he’s with us.”

While Boatwright and Sotto set the tone in the first half on the way to a 43-32 lead, star forward Kevin Quiambao seized the spotlight in the latter two frames, as he led an offensive onslaught from deep to finish with a game-high-tying 18 points, all off a 6-of-8 shooting spree from three.

Thanks to a 29-13 third quarter pullaway that featured a 6-of-7 team clip from downtown, Gilas fully negated its slow start to lead by as many as 40, 95-55, and rise to a 5-4 record in Group E. Syria, meanwhile, stayed at the bottom of the six-nation group with a 2-7 card.

“These games this late in the qualifying, this late window five of six windows, they are so absolutely crucial at this point. We brought by far our best team, I think,” Cone said.

“Our size kind of took over the game at some point. We just controlled the boards. I think we won it like, 60-30, or something like that. When you could do that, you can run up the score, and we were able to run up the score.”



After losing to undefeated Australia (9-0), earlier in the day, 84-67, Iran fell to a 5-4 slate ahead of its crucial clash on Sunday, November 29, against Gilas, which now enjoys a three-game winning streak after losing four straight.

A sweep of the Malaysia leg can put the Philippines on top of its Iranian rivals to boost its chances of World Cup qualification after a stretch of heartbreaking windows. Gilas ends its qualifying run at home in Cebu City in late February 2027.

The Scores

Gilas Pilipinas 97 – Sotto 18, Quiambao 18, Boatwright 16, Gomez de Liaño 11, Perez 10, Phillips 10, Ramos 5, Edu 4, Millora-Brown 4, Newsome 1, Thompson 0, Rosario 0.

Syria 58 – Atli 12, Harrison 10, Albalbisi 9, Idelbi 6, Hermes 6, Maran 6, Abdullah, Y. 5, Michelsson 4, Nounou 0, Abdullah, K. 0, Majak 0.

Quarters: 18-18, 43-32, 72-45, 97-58.

– Rappler.com

World.title: DOH eyes faster upgrades for LGU-run hospitals in 2027
World.content:
The Senate finance committee recommends an additional P5.4 billion for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, pushing its proposed 2027 allocation to P15.58 billion

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Health plans to bring funds for the Health Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP) down to the provincial level in 2027, to speed up infrastructure projects and the decongestion of DOH-run hospitals.

The Senate finance committee recommended an additional P5.4 billion for HFEP, pushing the proposed allocation to P15.58 billion, Senator JV Ejercito said during plenary deliberations on the DOH’s proposed 2027 budget on Friday, November 27.

This comes after the House of Representatives approved only P10.09 billion for HFEP in its version of the general appropriations bill (HGAB), lower than the P14.54 billion allocated in the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“Admittedly, ‘yong pagiging centralized ay talaga naging problema…for the whole fund to be utilized. Kaya nga po siguro one reason ‘yan [na] P4 billion natanggal sa HGAB,” said Ejercito, the Senate finance committee chairman and the DOH’s budget sponsor.

“But dito sa ating committee, binalik natin dahil may bagong programa ang DOH under Secretary [Edwin] Mercado, that is to download ito sa provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will [be improved, capacitated], para po ma-decongest ‘yong DOH-run hospitals,” he added.

(Admittedly, HFEP being centralized became a problem for the whole fund to be utilized. Maybe that’s one reason why P4 billion was cut from the HGAB. But the Senate finance committee restored it because the DOH, under Secretary Edwin Mercado, has a new program, that is to download the funding to provincial hospitals and locally-run hospitals. So that they will be improved, capacitated, and to decongest the DOH-run hospitals).

With the limited funding, the DOH will also be prioritizing the completion of ongoing HFEP projects, particularly critical health facilities in remote and disadvantaged areas.

Ejercito said DOH-run hospitals, which are end-referral centers providing advanced or specialty care, currently have an average bed occupancy rate of 150%, especially with the implementation of zero balance billing (ZBB).

Since the ZBB rollout in July 2025, 4.2 million patients have benefited from the program in DOH-run hospitals, according to Ejercito. Recently, it was piloted in some hospitals run by local government units (LGUs).

In its version, the Senate realigned P19.8 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations or AICS, to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation or PhilHealth.

Ejercito previously said the funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the ZBB program. This includes P7.6 billion for DOH hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for LGU hospitals.

Aside from boosting the HFEP budget, the Senate also provided an additional P1.099 billion for health promotion, P1.599 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu Transition Program.

Phasing out MAP?

But if Senator Panfilo Lacson had his way, essential health programs would get even more funds while MAP would become a thing of the past.

MAP, previously called Medical Assistance to Indigent and Financially Incapacitated Patients or MAIFIP, has been tagged by watchdogs as “soft pork” and called a “politicized discretionary program.”

Acknowledging that the Senate might have to wrestle with the House regarding unfunding MAP, Lacson suggested introducing a special provision that would allow the remaining P16.2 billion for MAP in the proposed 2027 budget to be allocated to the chambers’ public assistance centers instead. He proposed having DOH personnel oversee the vetting process for claiming the medical aid.

Lacson said this was in a bid to eventually phase out the aid program.

“For next year, the DOH is planning to have a rules-based approach in granting medical assistance to qualified patients. They will, of course, study ‘yong inyong (your) proposal,” Ejercito replied. – Rappler.com

World.title: SKIT: What happened this time at COP31?
World.content:
Watch this skit to look back on how this year's heated climate negotiations went down

MANILA, Philippines – The world is warming, and world leaders’ discussions on how to address this problem were just as heated.

The 31st United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference (COP31) happened just as Filipinos started feeling the effects of a Super El Niño, which is expected to cause dry spells and drought all over the country over the next several months. With global temperature rise projected to cross 1.5°C within the next few years, this year’s COP was marked by calls for urgency.

Despite the intense negotiations running into overtime — making it the longest COP on record — no climate deal was reached.

What happened during climate negotiations over the past few weeks? Watch this video to look back on how it all went down. – Rappler.com

World.title: The coral reef watchers saving our ocean
World.content:
Filipino marine scientists and volunteer divers work together to keep an eye on coral reefs — a collective pursuit in protecting the country's marine environment

BATANGAS, Philippines – In front of a house along the mangrove coast in Calatagan, Batangas, rafts and boats sat moored.

Jessie delos Reyes, 50, a slight-framed man who has lived in this house all his life, calls these rafts his floating classrooms; for more than half his life, he has dived in and out of the waters of the marine reserve just a few minutes away from his house.

He is known as Kuya Jessie of the floating houses in Calatagan. His name is familiar to locals, tourists, students, and marine scientists who come here for fieldwork and retreat.

The weather was fair that Tuesday morning in November. I joined Jessie on one of his dives to check the corals in Buntong Gasang, a coral monitoring site. The spot is a few minutes off the coast and not that deep. Buntong Gasang is adjacent to the Verde Island Passage, the famous waterway at the heart of the world’s Coral Triangle.

We used the floating classroom to go to Buntong Gasang. A motorized boat pulled the raft from the coast.

Three more divers made up Jessie’s team that morning — men who make a living teaching water safety skills, divers for nongovernmental organizations. That Tuesday, they were all volunteer divers for Calatagan Reef Patrollers or Carepas, which Jessie founded in 2004.

On the floating classroom, they moved at ease with their scuba diving equipment. On the table was a green thermos filled to the brim with kapeng barako (barako coffee) and bread for a quick breakfast.

SITE. A motorized boat pulls the floating classroom to transport volunteer divers to the coral monitoring site. Photo by Franz Lopez/Rappler

They used a laminated coral health chart — composed of several shades of coral colors — from Australia’s University of Queensland. Divers hold this chart against the corals to compare colors and grade them properly.

When it turns 1 — or the palest shade of each color — it means the coral has bleached. Once they’ve identified the right shade of the coral with the chart, they write the grade on their slates. They submit these reports to authorities and experts.

During the dive, Jessie delegated tasks to the team. The safety diver entered the water first to check the current. Jessie laid the transect and collected data, with another diver tailing him to assist. Then another diver took photos and videos.

About 30 minutes later, after surfacing from the water, Jessie said there was good news and bad news. The good news: some of the corals that were bleaching a month ago showed signs of recovery.

“But the bad news is most of them were recently killed,” Jessie said after the dive. “There’s algae already. They were not able to recover.”

After many years of monitoring the corals in Calatagan, Jessie has become an advocate for “citizen science,” where community members work alongside scientists to monitor changes in the marine environment.

“The marine biologists, marine scientists, come and go,” Jessie said. “The community, even when their eyes are closed, even when they’re asleep, they know what’s happening in the community.”

TRANSECT. Jessie delos Reyes holding a transect tape aboard the floating classroom while on the way to the coral monitoring site. Photo by Franz Lopez/Rappler

The promise of citizen science

Coral scientist Wilfredo Licuanan has always dreamed of municipal fisherfolk checking the health of corals and reefs all on their own.

Licuanan, called Al by family and colleagues, is a De La Salle University professor who specializes in coral reefs. He established the SHORE Center, La Salle’s research center that pioneered a citizen science program on coral reef monitoring.

Al, 63, grew up in Diliman, Quezon City — the third generation in their family to study at University of the Philippines (UP). He took up marine science as an undergraduate, only learning to swim the summer before his first semester, before later shifting to zoology.

At the former Marine Science Center (now Marine Science Institute) at UP, he was a research assistant to the inimitable Edgardo Gomez, the center’s founding director. He eventually left the center and joined the La Salle faculty in 1997.

The next year, he started to manage the university’s Br. Alfred Shields FSC Marine Station in Lian, Batangas. The marine station lies in the western part of Lian, facing the Verde Island Passage and the West Philippine Sea. Its location is accessible to divers in the province, including volunteers from neighboring Calatagan.

Al said he has spent most of his time at the marine station as much as he could. Back then, it was still plain and bare, built like a bunkhouse along the coast in the remote part of town.

From 2014 to 2017, Al and his team at La Salle’s marine center surveyed reefs for a national assessment. The sheer scale of the work led them to develop further methods non-scientists could also use to assess coral communities and local reefs.

This eventually became the Alwan method. Alwan, a Tagalog word meaning “to ease,” evolved from the work of local and foreign researchers: an individual is trained to identify butterflyfish and target marine invertebrates and corals at a selected survey station.

By the end of the program, trainees are expected to know how to safely conduct a survey on their own, identify target species to determine reef health, and monitor bleaching triggered by climate change.

TRAINER. Wilfredo Licuanan stands on the bow as water safety training starts in waters off the coast of Lian, Batangas. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

Forty years ago, when Al started his coral studies, he did not deliberately set out to promote citizen science.

There are not enough scientists, and it would be impossible to regularly check on reef health without the help of people who are most frequently at sea: the fishermen, sea patrol, locals, lifeguards, and even recreational divers.

“Those methods were actually an early form of citizen science in the sense that they were developed in Australia so that people who can dive but do not necessarily have the science training [can] do surveys in the Great Barrier Reef,” Al said.

On the field

A few weeks after my Calatagan visit with Jessie’s team, I joined Al and his SHORE Center staff in La Salle’s marine station in Lian. They had started training people from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) on how to monitor reefs.

It was another Tuesday morning at sea. The water was cold, and I was swimming toward the reef crest in front of the marine station, following Al toward a jutting rock. He moved deftly in the familiar waters, while I tried to keep up.

As we swam, the seafloor visible beneath me started to fade, and all I could see was blue. A few moments later, a blanket of dead staghorn corals appeared. I knew they were dead because of the fuzzy texture. Algae had grown and taken over.

Above water, Al told me that amid the dead staghorn corals, there were new, living ones.

“I’ll point them to you,” he told me. We swam a bit more, and the live staghorn corals were hard to miss. Staghorn corals have branches, and these had white tips.

Al later told me that meant they were still growing. I asked him how there could be living ones among the dead. It’s the current, Al said. Corals may be spawning in another part of the reef, or in another reef altogether, and the coral eggs and sperm made it to the area due to the current.

SLATE. A diver takes note of target fish species on their slate. Photo from SHORE Center

A few minutes later, the BFAR staff who just finished water safety drills caught up with us at the reef. This was the first session of SHORE’s training for the BFAR. Among this session’s participants were the Carepas volunteer divers I visited in Calatagan weeks before.

Climate crisis and the decline of local reefs

Through the coral reef assessment from 2014 to 2017, Al and his team found a “marked decline” in the condition of local reefs in the past four decades (since the first assessment was conducted from 1976 to 1981).

Many of their assessment stations were in Luzon, specifically in the Verde Island Passage. The marked decline in conditions led the team to report then that “the establishment of marine protected areas, and other interventions in the past 40 years have not caused an appreciable impact on overall reef condition in general, except in particular localities.”

“Mostly, it’s climate change,” Al said in an interview before their fieldwork in Lian.

“I keep saying it’s the most visible manifestation of climate change,” he added. “Because when the water is hot, that is not a localized event. It happens in large sections of the sea.”

LEARNING. A research assistant from SHORE (right) helps a BFAR staff with her fins before the water safety training starts. Photo by Iya Gozum/Rappler

The world is already on track to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius limit that countries set to avoid the extreme impacts of climate change. At this point, drastic steps should already be taken to cut down greenhouse gas emissions.

Maintaining ocean health by protecting coral reefs, mangroves, and seagrasses can help cut down emissions. Australia and Turkey, co-presidents of this year’s largest climate summit, put the ocean at the heart of the conference, yet the talks broke down after a final draft deal failed to mention fossil fuels.

A way of life

Back in Calatagan, the coast opposite Jessie’s house was lined with mangroves.

“We planted those mangroves on September 2, 2002,” he told me after that morning’s coral monitoring session. “We have mangroves, we have seagrass, we have corals. The ecosystem here is complete.”

Jessie grew up in Calatagan. His parents fished for a living, and Jessie himself was a fisherman before he became part of the sea patrol, became a lifeguard, learned to dive, and eventually founded his volunteer divers’ group.

AFLOAT. The floating classrooms anchored in front of Jessie delos Reyes’ house in Calatagan, Batangas. Photo by Franz Lopez/Rappler

UNDERWATER. Jessie delos Reyes conducting coral assessment on November 3, 2026, in Calatagan, Batangas. Photo from Carepas

More than two decades ago, he attended a course that Al used to teach: marine biology for non-biologists. (“I taught it on the weekends,” Al told me in a separate interview. “Jessie was in the class.”)

Jessie has already seen it all: corals bleaching and recovering, the devastating impact of El Niño events in recent history, and typhoons that wreak havoc underwater.

His desire to protect the ocean is something he may have inherited from his parents, Jessie said

— from fisherfolk who were at sea every day and who saw what a healthy ocean looked like and what it could give them. – Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

This story was produced with the support of Informed Earth as part of the COP31 Ocean Virtual Reporting Fellowship.

World.title: SM Nuvali brings a new flagship mall – and traffic – to Laguna
World.content:
91st MALL. SM Nuvali in Santa Rosa City, Laguna on November 26, 2026, with its unfinished office tower in the background

SM's 91st mall distinguishes itself with an indoor garden inspired by Singapore's Gardens by the Bay

LAGUNA, Philippines – SM has built quite a mall in the south – its biggest in Laguna, to be exact.

SM Nuvali, which officially opened its doors to the public on Friday, November 27, is a spectacle. At 190,525 square meters, it’s SM Prime’s 91st mall and the fifth in the province alone.

But this flagship mall stands apart with its sprawling air-conditioned indoor garden and a glass-paned roof to let some sunlight stream in. On the floors above, restaurants and cafés overlook the patches of green, with playgrounds and a Paw Park.

“SM Nuvali is different because it brings together nature, sustainability, and thoughtfully curated retail experiences in one destination,” SM Supermalls president Steven Tan told Rappler. “At its heart is a garden within the mall, offering an outdoor-inspired environment that is air-conditioned and designed for comfort, while being LEED-certified.”

GARDEN. An indoor garden is the centerpiece of SM Nuvali. Photos by Leanne Jazul/Rappler

There’s a grand staircase, a community library called Book Nook with more than 10,000 books, and, on the top floor, a chapel.

Moviegoers can look forward to four regular cinemas, an IMAX auditorium with its own “IMAX Pods,” and two Director’s Club cinemas equipped with what SM calls the country’s first LED cinema screens.

MOVIE. SM Nuvali features the country’s first LED cinema screens. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

And though it’s new, it’s far from empty. If you’re going for food, you’ll find all the usual suspects, which Tan told Rappler was “carefully curated” – Din Tai Fung, Wildflour, Hoshino Coffee, among others – but some are showing up in Laguna for the first time, like Michelin Bib Gourmand awardee Some Thai, Golden Yolk, George & Onnie’s, and The Matcha Tokyo.

Tucked in the Food Hall is SM’s Game Park, where you can squeeze in a round of billiards or arcade games between meals.

MEALS. SM Nuvali brings Makati’s Scratch smashburgers down south. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

“Here, we can come together, enjoy a meal, and tell each other stories of our lives and our love,” Tan said at the mall’s opening gala on Thursday night, November 26. “We need community more than ever.”

Tan credited the Sy family “for their vision and passion to bring this development to the next level,” and then called SM Prime president Jeffrey Lim and Hans “Chico” Sy Jr. – son of Hans Sy and president of engineering, design, and development – to the stage.

CHEERS! (Left to right) Hans Sy Jr., Steven Tan, and Jeffrey Lim offer a toast during the opening of SM Nuvali. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

In the crowd too was Chico’s sister Hanna Carinna Sy, senior assistant vice president for marketing and leasing. The third-generation Sys are now helping to design the malls, giving the newer ones a touch of youth. And of course there was Hans Sy, who looked on like the proud father that he was. (READ: SM Harrison Plaza opening by end-2027 with entire floor for Gen Z)

“I cannot tell you enough how excited we are to welcome people to a brand new home in the South. But that will be for tomorrow,” Tan said. “So tonight, we hold this moment to ourselves and celebrate!”

TYCOON. SM Prime executive committee chairman Hans Sy poses during SM Nuvali’s opening night gala. Photo by Leanne Jazul/Rappler.

But about that traffic

Tomorrow, of course, means cars, and probably lots of them.

Even before the mall officially opened, motorists and residents had already been complaining online about worsening traffic along the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay Road, particularly around the traffic lights in front of the mall.

SM Nuvali sits right at the Santa Rosa-Tagaytay exit of the Cavite-Laguna Expressway (CALAX), mixing mallgoers with motorists entering and leaving the expressway. With the height of Christmas shopping season approaching, congestion could worsen even for motorists who simply use the expressway to get home or travel to Tagaytay.

Asked about the traffic situation, Tan told Rappler in a message: “We recognize the importance of managing traffic, especially with the area’s continued growth. SM Nuvali is coordinating closely with the relevant local government units and traffic authorities to support traffic management measures, including proper vehicle ingress and egress, traffic flow management, and coordination during peak hours to help minimize congestion and ensure a smoother experience for motorists and visitors.”

When Rappler visited the mall on Thursday, traffic had partly backed up to near the CALAX exit. That was before the general public could even enter the mall. – Rappler.com

World.title: X launches parental controls to help manage teen use
World.content:
The parental controls feature launch comes some 20 years after X, formerly Twitter, was built

MANILA, Philippines – Social media platform X on Thursday, November 26, announced it had introduced parental controls so that parents or guardians could better guide teens on their X usage and experiences on it.

The parental controls will not allow parents or guardians to read private messages, see searches or viewing history, post as their teen, or access a given teen account.

The social media platform, in its announcement, acknowledged that “while X is not designed for or promoted to children, and users must be at least 13 or older where required by law, we take extra care with the young people who are here.”



According to the X announcement, teen accounts “default to protected mode, sensitive media is restricted, and targeted advertising is blocked,” while parental controls give families further tools aside from these standard settings for teens.

The new parental control tools will let parents do the following:

see how much time their teen has spent on X over the past week

set limits on X usage

require approval for new followers (this also makes the account private)

limit For You recommendations and videos to accounts the teen already follows

control who can send direct messages to the account

filter specific words

turn off sensitive media content

see which accounts a teen has chatted with one-on-one (without seeing what they’ve written)

The X parental controls announcement is a long time coming. The feature addition is a first after about 20 years of operation, and comes after issues with X’s Grok AI chatbot being a vector for the generation of sexualized images or material featuring women and minors.

According to TechCrunch, while X is not generally aimed at teens, a 2024 study pointed to nearly a third of Gen Alpha kids as having an X account.

Michael O’Herlihy, head of safety at X, said in their press announcement that they aim to strike a balance between parental supervision and letting teens have some freedom to be themselves.

“Parents want practical tools, and teens deserve room to grow,” O’Herlihy said. “With Parental Controls on X, families can set the guardrails that fit their home, while teens keep ownership of their accounts and can see every change.”

A more thorough explanation of the parental control settings is available on this Help Center page. – Rappler.com
