World.title: Tulfo flags P71M in DOH-procured meds expiring in March 2027
World.content:
Sen. Raffy Tulfo. Senate PRIB / OS Raffy Tulfo

MANILA, Philippines – Sen. Raffy Tulfo flagged on Friday around P71-million worth of government-procured medicines set to expire by March 2027.

Tulfo expressed concern over expiring medicines during the deliberations on the Department of Health’s P274-billion budget for fiscal year 2027.

Article continues after this 

“P11-million worth of HIV/AIDS medicine, P43 million for family planning medicine, and 15 million for nutrition again is about to expire at mababaon sa lupa before January next year,” Tulfo reported, citing an unnamed informant.

(P11-million worth of HIV/AIDS medicine, P43 million for family planning medicine, and 15 million for nutrition again is about to expire and will be buried in the ground before January next year.)

According to Tulfo, 1.3 million cycles of Lynestrenol for family planning, 1 million tablets of Lopinavir or HIV/AIDS medication, 750 thousand sachets of ready-to-use supplementary food for nutrition will expire all by December 2026.

Meanwhile, 300,000 ampules of Diphenhydramine – a mental health medicine – worth P2 million is set to expire by March 2027.

Tulfo has long condemned DOH’s purchasing of expired or near-expired medicines after millions of pesos worth of such supplies were allegedly being buried. Previously, the Commission on Audit reported P39.8 billion worth of medicines and health supplies expired from 2015 to 2025.

Article continues after this 

For 2026, as of November, Tulfo’s informant reported around P216 million worth of expired medicines.

These include around P193 million worth of mental health medicines, such as Fluphenazine, Flupentixol and Valproic Acid; P23 million worth of remedies for HIV/AIDS.

Article continues after this 

READ: LOOK: Photos of expired medicines ‘buried’ by DOH shown in hearing

“Nag-oorder sila ng gamot na alam nila hindi kailangan, at alam nila hindi magagamit and worst, paexpire na… Kailangan talaga maimbestigahan ito,” Tulfo stressed.

(They are ordering medicine that they know they don’t need, and they know they can’t use it and worst, it’s about to expire… This really needs to be investigated.)

In response, Sen. JV Ejercito, sponsor of DOH’s budget, quoted Sec. Edwin Mercado who said that the agency will cooperate in any inquiries on expired medicines.

Ejercito also explained that under Mercado’s leadership, DOH’s procurement process for medicines has become stricter.

World.title: Bucor: Thiamine deficiency possible culprit in deaths among PDLs
World.content:
INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) on Friday said it is reviewing the food allocation and its nutritional content of persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) in the Zamboanga prison facility following a sudden rise in deaths possibly linked to thiamine deficiency.

Based on initial findings submitted on Thursday to Director General Pio Catapang Jr., BuCor said that deaths among infirmary patients at the San Ramon Prison and Penal Farm rose from eight in September to 25 this month.

Among the symptoms reported were difficulty breathing and edema, or swelling caused by fluid buildup. BuCor said that these could be connected to thiamine deficiency, which can lead to beriberi, a disease that could be fatal if untreated.

Article continues after this 

The same report also found that 170 other PDLs experienced neuropathic pain, edema and symptoms linked to heart failure

READ: BuCor to help inmates form co-ops for livelihood after release

This prompted Catapang to order immediate investigation in the diet of PDLs to find out whether thiamine deficiency was indeed present and to assess the extent of a possible health crisis within the prison facility.

The BuCor chief also sought the urgent assistance of the Department of Health for medical services and needs, such as nutritional supplements, of PDLs. /ms

World.title: Makabayan hits CA decision vs Talaingod 13
World.content:
Gabriela Women’s Party Rep. Sarah Elago, Kabataan Party-list Rep. Renee Co and ACT Teachers Party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio after filing House Resolution No. 1512. (Photo by Makabayan/Viber)

MANILA, Philippines — The Makabayan bloc has called out the Court of Appeals for upholding the conviction for child abuse of the so-called Talaingod 13 — which includes former lawmakers from progressive groups — saying that the move only sends a message that rescuing children is a crime.

In a statement on Friday, Makabayan lawmakers ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio, Gabriela party-list Rep. Sarah Elago, and Kabataan party-list Rep. Renee Co said the denial of the Talaingod 13’s motion for reconsideration is a wrong decision since the activists only responded to children’s call for distress.

Former Bayan Muna Rep. Satur Ocampo, former ACT Teachers party-list Rep. France Castro, and 11 other volunteer school teachers were convicted by a Tagum court in 2024 over child abuse raps, as they allegedly forcefully evacuated students after the closure of a Lumad school in Talaingod, Davao del Norte, in 2018.

Article continues after this 

“These motions sought to overturn the unjust rulings of the Tagum Regional Trial Court and the Court of Appeals in the child abuse case stemming from the 2018 evacuation of Lumad students in Talaingod, Davao del Norte. With this denial, the appellate court effectively affirms the conviction of former lawmakers France Castro and Satur Ocampo, along with volunteer teachers and other advocates, in a case that treats an act of rescue and solidarity as a crime,” Makabayan said.

“The 2018 evacuation was not child abuse. It was a response to a desperate call for help from Lumad teachers and students whose lives were under threat from the militarization of their communities and from paramilitary forces. Children walked long distances through the dark to escape danger, and the Talaingod 13 helped bring them to safety,” they added.

Castro and Ocampo, along with 16 others, were arrested by police in November 2018 for allegedly holding 14 minors, reportedly to teach them revolutionary ideas against the government.

The group was on board five vans which were intercepted at a police and military checkpoint in Talaingod. The minors, who Castro and Ocampo said were being rescued, are students of a Salugpungan School in Talaingod.

LOOK: Mugshots of Satur Ocampo, France Castro

Article continues after this 

According to Makabayan, the children who were rescued walked a long way because they felt they were not safe in their communities, not because they were being kidnapped.

“How can rescuing children from danger be treated as abuse? How can the act of bringing children to safety become a crime, while the threats, intimidation, and militarization that drove them from their homes are brushed aside? The children walked through the night because their community was no longer safe,” the lawmakers said.

Article continues after this 

“Yet those who came to their aid are the ones being prosecuted and punished. This reverses justice, penalizing compassion and solidarity while the dangers the children fled go unexamined,” they added.

According to lawmakers, who are part of the Makabayan Coalition umbrella that counts Ocampo and Castro as their members, the Talaingod 13 will elevate their case to the Supreme Court.

“The Talaingod 13 will elevate their case to the Supreme Court. Makabayan stands in full solidarity with them and calls for justice and accountability. We also call for the protection of Lumad children, communities, teachers, and schools from militarization, harassment, and attacks,” they said.

“Rescuing children from danger is not a crime. Standing with the Lumad people is not a crime. Solidarity must never be criminalized,” they added.

Last July, on the second anniversary of the Talaingod 13’s conviction, a group composed of clergy, indigenous peoples, Moro leaders, church workers, educators, and human rights advocates called for the reversal of the Tagum court’s decision.

The host of the program, the UP Institute of Human Rights-College of Law (UP-IHR), maintains that the 13 individuals did not commit a crime, noting they were part of a humanitarian and solidarity mission intended to protect Lumad children and families displaced by conflict and militarization.

They said that the charges, which advocates describe as a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP), were filed during the Duterte administration and culminated in a conviction under the Marcos Jr. administration.

READ: Groups to demand reversal of Talaingod 13 conviction on 2nd anniversary

After her conviction, Castro — who has been a steady voice for the opposition — turned emotional as she claimed that she had been protecting children for decades as a teacher and a lawmaker, and not as the charges against her state.

World.content:
Vice President Sara Duterte press briefing October 6, 2026 via Facebook/Inday Sara Duterte

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday said she is planning to sell properties to pay the P5 million she owed to her friends and to cover expenses of her impeachment trial and the case of her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, in the International Criminal Court (ICC).

World.title: Virtual assistant nabbed for forcing ‘GFs’ in ‘sexual’ livestream
World.content:
A 22-year-old virtual assistant was arrested by the National Bureau of Investigation in Guiguinto, Bulacan on Thursday, Nov. 26, for allegedly forcing his “girlfriends” to conduct sexual themes in a livestream with foreigners as viewers. (Photo: Mary Joy Salcedo/INQUIRER)

MANILA, Philippines — A 22-year-old virtual assistant was arrested in Guiguinto, Bulacan, for allegedly forcing his “girlfriends” to conduct sexual acts in a livestreaming platform with foreign viewers, according to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).

Two supposed ex-girlfriends of the suspect filed the complaint before the NBI, leading operatives to conduct an entrapment operation and arrest him in his apartment in Guiguinto on Thursday, Nov. 26.

In an interview with one of the complainants, a 21-year-old college student from Quezon City, she said she had been in a relationship with the suspect for a year and four months.

Article continues after this 

She said the suspect introduced the livestream platform in September this year as a “source of money,” and she only agreed because she feared he would break up with her.

She said there came a time when the suspect introduced her to his “other girlfriend,” aged 19 from Guiguinto, who was also allegedly forced to appear in the livestream where foreigners were watching.

READ: NBI: Ashes in pet urns appear to be ‘sand’ or ‘cement’

According to the complainant, the suspect allegedly made them do certain things in the livestream for foreign viewers, who would then send money for the supposed show.

She said the online platform is “blocked” in the Philippines; thus, all their viewers were foreigners.

Article continues after this 

“Dahil nga napamahal kami, napilitan na lang kaming gawin yun. Hanggang sa mali na talaga siya. Kapag nagkamali kami, magagalit siya, magdadabog siya. Minsan namimisikal na siya,” the complainant said.

(Because we fell in love, we were forced to do that. Until we realized that it was really wrong. If we made a mistake, he would get angry; he would lash out. Sometimes he would even complain.)

Article continues after this 

In a separate interview with reporters, the suspect admitted the livestreaming of women was true but noted he was unaware it was wrong.

He also denied that he forced his “girlfriends” to enter what he described as “nothing seems illegal.”

“Ang sabi ko sa kanila, ‘I saw this opportunity to get money, and if you don’t want, okay lang. I’ll find someone else na baka gusto, i-offer ko sa kanila,’” he said.

(I told them, ‘I saw this opportunity to get money, and if you don’t want it, that’s okay. I’ll find someone else who might want it, I’ll offer it to them.’)

According to the suspect, they usually earned around P5,000 for a three-hour livestream with about 30 foreign viewers.

READ: NBI detains 3 Malaysians behind scam hub disguised as FBI office

“Ginagawa namin before school or after school. Kapag walang pasok,” he said.

(We do it before school or after school, when there is no school.)

The NBI said the suspect is facing charges of alleged violations of the Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2003, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Children Act of 2004, and the Anti-Rape Law of 1997.

World.title: Former Naga mayor welcomes probe over stalled convention center
World.content:
Presidential Anti-Corruption Czar (PACC0 personnel, together with the NBI and DPWH Camarines Sur 3rd District Engineering Office, inspect the stalled construction of the Naga City Convention Center in Barangay Carolina on Nov. 15, following complaints from concerned citizens. The inspection revealed rusting steel structures and vegetation covering the project site, prompting an investigation into the P97.9-million first-phase contract. (Photos courtesy of PACC)

MANILA, Philippines — Former Naga City Mayor and now 3rd District Rep. Nelson Legacion on Friday, Nov. 27, welcomed the filing of a complaint before the Office of the Ombudsman to probe the stalled Naga City Convention Center.

Legacion told the Inquirer that the land in Brgy. Carolina where the project is situated is owned by the Naga City government per deed of donation.

“Its private character ceased and it is now public, owned by LGU Naga, including the improvements thereon, such as the Phase 1 of the proposed Convention Center,” he said in a message.

Article continues after this 

He further emphasized that his term as Naga Mayor has ended on June 30, 2025, which means that “all properties, accountabilities and responsibilities were already turned-over to the new administration.”

“I signed the Deed of Donation in my capacity as then Mayor of Naga City,” he said.

His clarificatory remarks came after the Philippine Anti-Corruption Czar (PACC), a civil society watchdog, filed a complaint-affidavit before the Ombudsman on Thursday, Nov. 26, due to concerns over the condition of the unfinished convention center.

The group’s previous inspection showed rusting steel structures and vegetation covering the project site.

READ: Complaint filed, probe into stalled Naga City Convention Center pushed

Article continues after this 

The former mayor said that the nearly P100-million phase 1 of the project started on January 9, 2024.

The first part of the construction was for the structural foundation of the building, which was completed on April 7, 2025.

Article continues after this 

These include structural excavation, driving of precast concrete piles, construction of footing, and columns with reinforcing steel bars that were prepared for the next phase.

However, due to the error in the project’s geo tagging, the supposed start of phase 2 this year did not push through.

He said the resumption of construction was already issued under Sub-Allotment No. SR2026-06-017005 dated June 22, 2026.

“The project was supposed to be multi-year with DPWH as the implementing agency,” he said.

The convention center has a multi-year funding of approximately P600 million, with a P97,901,095 budget for the first phase.

Legacion asserted that the initial budget was not transferred to the Naga City government.

“The funds were coursed through the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), specifically to the DPWH Camarines Sur 3rd District Engineering Office (3rd DEO), as the implementing agency of the project,” he explained.

According to him, the arrangement gave the DPWH the responsibility over the implementation of the project, including its procurement process, contract administration, supervision of construction, processing of progress billings, and disbursement of payments to the contractors in accordance with government rules and regulations.

“The role of the LGU Naga was primarily to provide the project site through the Deed of Donation and facilitate the necessary coordination,” he stressed.

“The project funds were never placed under the custody or direct control of the City Government of Naga,” he added.

READ: Civil society watchdog probes stalled Naga City Convention Center

The convention was intended to be a multipurpose facility for exhibits, cultural events, trade fairs, conventions, and other events, which may accommodate up to 5,000 people.

He said that the matters concerning the implementation, release, procurement, and utilization of the P100-million initial budget were within the records of the agency, particularly the DPWH Third District Engineering Office.

The PACC filed a complaint against the Centerways Construction and Development Inc. and four DPWH Third District engineers.

World.title: More Multinationals Exit Myanmar as Economic Turmoil Deepens
World.content:
At least four more international brands announced their withdrawal from Myanmar this month, as deepening post-coup turmoil triggers a fresh exodus of foreign investment.

They joined a broader retreat of multinational businesses since the 2021 military takeover, driven by regime import and currency controls, soaring production costs, power outages, and international sanctions.

On Thursday, Singapore-based Pezzo Pizza announced it would close all branches in Myanmar starting today (Nov. 27), ending 10 years of operations. The company entered the market in 2016, operating five branches across Yangon and Mandalay.

The announcement came a day after The Manhattan Fish Market shuttered its last Yangon outlet, at Myanmar Plaza, ending the Malaysia-based seafood chain’s 12-year presence.

On Nov. 13, Japanese automaker Isuzu announced it had ended Myanmar repair and maintenance operations after liquidating its local service unit.

Meanwhile, British consumer goods giant Unilever will exit Myanmar after 16 years by selling its shares to Centig Holding, a subsidiary of local partner Europe and Asia Commercial (EAC), with the deal expected to close in 2027.

While the four companies gave no reason for their exit, the World Bank 2026 report notes that Myanmar’s private sector is operating in “a highly challenging and uncertain environment” driven by conflict, macroeconomic pressures, policy reversal and weakening state capacity. It adds that firms are facing “higher cost, greater compliance risks, [and] weaker incentives to invest, expand and innovate.”

According to a Myanmar Peace Monitor report released on Nov. 27, the post-coup flight of foreign investment encompasses nearly 40 multinational companies across 16 countries ranging from neighboring Thailand, Malaysia and India to the U.S., UK, Spain, Germany, Austria, Italy and Norway. It said the withdrawals were being driven by the spread of armed conflict and a collapsing business environment.

The departing businesses span major sectors such as oil and gas, mining, banking, telecommunications, real estate, and manufacturing, including 12 global clothing brands whose exit has dealt a severe blow to local garment workers.

“More companies are monitoring the situation and planning exit strategies,” a Myanmar policy analyst told The Irrawaddy, blaming currency controls and raw material shortages triggered by regime import controls.

“Foreign investors can’t endure these losses any longer,” he said, adding that he expects the situation to worsen amid rising unemployment, soaring inflation and shortages of basic goods.

World.title: Beijing Shields Myanmar Regime After Genocide Ruling, Naypyitaw Begs for Energy Investment, and More
World.content:
Myanmar seeks more Chinese energy investment at Belt and Road forum

Naypyitaw’s reliance on China for energy investment, fuel supplies and electricity infrastructure is deepening all the time, with Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin using his latest trip to China to seek yet more investment across the sector.

At the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministers’ Conference in Qingdao on Nov. 25-26, Ko Ko Lwin met officials from China’s National Energy Administration (NEA), urging them to help Myanmar meet its electricity and energy needs. Discussions covered new offshore gas exploration, hydropower projects, cross-border power lines, solar and wind projects, and energy storage batteries.

Much the same topics were on the agenda when Ko Ko Lwin traveled to Kunming and Beijing in April to secure lower rates for fuel imports from a number of Chinese firms. Myanmar relies on imports for 97 percent of its gasoline and diesel needs, a dependence that had already taken a serious toll on the cash-strapped regime before the Middle East crisis triggered shortages and price hikes.

Regime officials are also asking Chinese state enterprises to invest in refinery projects linked to the Myanmar–China oil pipeline network. In April the regime signed a deal with China’s North Petro-Chem to increase production at the Htaukshabin-Kanni oil field in Magwe Region’s Minbu.

It has also revived the Thanlyin No. 1 Oil Refinery near Yangon with Chinese assistance, potentially enabling it to bypass jet-fuel sanctions and sustain air operations. The facility’s expected output of up to 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually roughly matching Myanmar’s imports last year.

China defends Myanmar regime after ICJ genocide ruling

China has publicly defended Myanmar after the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s landmark ruling that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing “noted” the ruling but argued that the Rakhine issue should be handled cautiously given its “complex historical, ethnic and religious dimensions.” He urged the international community to avoid “complicating” the issue and reiterated China’s support for dialogue and the repatriation of displaced Rohingya.

China also raised concerns about what it called judicial “overreach” and questions of jurisdiction by international courts.

The ruling stems from a case brought by the Gambia over the Myanmar military’s 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighboring Bangladesh.

Guo also defended the Chinese judge on the ICJ, Xue Hanqin, who voted in Myanmar’s favor, saying she had “acted independently in her personal capacity.”

As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China has consistently pushed back against international pressure on Myanmar over the Rohingya crisis, arguing that it should be resolved through dialogue and cooperation between Myanmar and Bangladesh rather than external intervention.

However, the ruling, the first finding of state responsibility for genocide in the ICJ’s 81-year history, places China in an awkward position while it continues to shield Naypyitaw from international pressure and deepens ties with a military regime now found guilty of one of the world’s worst atrocities in recent decades.

China drawn deeper into Myanmar–Thai river pollution dispute

China has promised to dispatch experts to help investigate river pollution affecting Mekong tributaries in Thailand due to unregulated Chinese-invested mining across the border in Myanmar.

The announcement came after a meeting in Bangkok on Tuesday where Thailand urged China to help halt mining operations in Shan State for at least six months as the Kok, Sai, Ruak and Mekong rivers flowing into northern Thailand are contaminated, threatening human health and livelihoods.

Thailand’s Pollution Control Department has repeatedly found arsenic, lead, cadmium and other heavy metals above safety limits in the rivers, tracing the pollution to unregulated gold and rare-earth mines in Shan State. Most of them are run by Chinese people in areas controlled by China-linked armed groups like the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Thailand and Myanmar agreed to conduct their first joint testing of the Kok and Sai next month. But while pledging to participate in the investigation, Beijing stopped short of agreeing to the proposed shutdown and cautioned against drawing “premature conclusions.”

Instead, the Foreign Ministry spokesman claimed Chinese companies operating overseas are required to comply with local laws and environmental regulations—except that these are non-existent in the lawless borderlands of Myanmar.

Still, China seems to feel it can no longer completely dodge the issue as Thailand has brought it up at every high-level meeting, no matter how amiable, in recent weeks amid growing outrage and protests at home.

Chinese scammers move with the times

Shaken up by major crackdowns on Myanmar’s border scam hubs, online fraud networks now infest other parts of the country, from upscale condominiums in the commercial capital Yangon to remote corners of Shan State.

Since mid-November, the military regime has reported a series of raids that netted more than 570 suspected online scammers and gambling operators, over 400 of them Chinese.

In Yangon, the raids in Yankin, Mayangone and Thaketa townships resulted in nearly 230 arrests. Nearly half of them were Myanmar nationals who reportedly worked voluntarily for their Chinese bosses. In Thaketa, arrests included a Chinese ringleader wanted by China’s Public Security Ministry, but in Yankin the boss escaped, throwing his workers under the bus.

In southern Shan around the same time, some 330 Chinese scammers and around 20 Myanmar women were arrested in Kyethi and Mong Kung townships. In Kyethi, they were nabbed with a cache of rifles and pistols.

Now some major border scam centers have been dismantled under pressure from Beijing, operators appear to have dispersed across the country, running smaller, more mobile operations. But in Myawaddy near the Thai border, big compounds still thrive under the protection of regime-aligned ethnic militias.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Garment Sector Braces for EU Bombshell After Genocide Verdict
World.content:
International labor unions’ calls for the European Union to strip Myanmar of its duty-free trade privileges after the International Court of Justice’s genocide ruling have sent shockwaves through local export industry. Operators warn that withdrawing benefits would have severe impacts on the country’s garment industry and hundreds of thousands of workers.

In a Nov. 24 letter to EU leaders, IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union called on Brussels to withdraw Myanmar’s Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preferences and terminate the EU-funded MADE in Myanmar program.

IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union represent over 50 million industrial and garment workers in more than 140 countries. Both have pressed for stronger action against Myanmar’s military regime over labor rights abuses since the 2021 coup.

The EBA grants tariff-free entry to European markets for all exports — barring weapons and ammunition — from least-developed countries, including Myanmar. The scheme underpins Myanmar’s US$ 3-billion annual garment export trade with Europe. MADE in Myanmar, meanwhile, is an EU-backed initiative aimed at improving labor standards and working conditions in the country’s garment industry.

Local garment manufacturers said international labor groups have pushed for withdrawal of Myanmar’s EBA privileges for years, but warned the move could devastate an industry on which hundreds of thousands depend.

“If the EU decides to suspend the scheme, we will have to find alternative markets. We can no longer rely on a single export destination,” one garment operator told The Irrawaddy.

Labor organizations argue that EBA and MADE in Myanmar help channel revenue into the coffers of an illegitimate military regime and should therefore be withdrawn. The EU has yet to respond their calls.

Local factory owners, however, say the industry’s difficulties stem more from domestic challenges since the coup — including foreign-exchange controls, rising production costs, shortages of raw materials, and financial transaction difficulties after Myanmar’s inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist.

The garment industry targeted $5 billion in export earnings for the 2026-27 fiscal year ending March, but industry sources say that goal is increasingly out of reach.

“With just a few months left, we have barely achieved half the target ,” said a Yangon-based garment business owner in Yangon.

Myanmar’s garment sector employs 450,000 to 500,000 workers, mostly women, and relies heavily on the Cut-Make-Pack (CMP) model, under which foreign brands pay factories to process their raw materials. Most exports go to Japan and the EU.

Before the 2021 coup, more than 70 percent of Myanmar’s garment exports went to the EU. That share has since fallen to around 50 percent after manufacturers began shifting production to other countries.

Industry sources say more than 20 manufacturers, including suppliers for major international brands such as H&M, have either closed or plan to leave Myanmar this year.

The Myanmar Garment Manufacturers Association (MGMA) has urged the EU to consider the potential impact on workers before making any decision, warning that broader trade restrictions could further weaken the export sector and threaten jobs across the industry.

World.title: Thailand Tests Find High Lead, Arsenic in River Shellfish
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other species in rivers contaminated by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.

The findings, from nearly two years of testing, prompted authorities to urge residents to avoid eating 10 species including shellfish and river snails.

The warning came earlier this week, but with no details of the contamination levels found or the testing processes.

An official from Thailand’s Fisheries Department, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to talk to media, told AFP that over 500 samples were taken from five rivers, and 18 had heavy metals at levels over safety limits.

The details came as Thai officials held talks in Bangkok to try to address growing public fears about river contamination from mining operations in war-torn Myanmar.

Heavy metals including mercury, lead, cadmium and arsenic were found at levels exceeding safety standards in 10 species, the Fisheries Department official said.

In some, arsenic was detected at nearly four times the permitted limit and lead at nearly six times the limit.

The affected species include freshwater shrimp, river snails, freshwater mussels and horse mussels, as well as local fish that feed on them, the official said.

The official said the tests involved samples from the Mekong and Salween rivers, which flow through Thailand and Myanmar, and three other rivers in Thailand’s north, the Sai, Kok and Ruak.

No contamination was found in farmed aquatic species, the official added.

Local residents in Thailand’s north and northeast have for months complained about river contamination from mines in Myanmar, but the issue has gathered growing public attention in recent weeks.

Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times higher than safe limits.

Campaigners, experts and politicians trace the pollution back to mining in Myanmar, where the long-running civil war has led to unregulated exploitation of natural resources.

In a bid to spur action, residents this week prepared traditional dishes with locally caught food from affected areas and invited politicians, attempting to highlight the risks they now face.

There are fears contamination could spread further down the Mekong, which supports millions of people across several countries.

“Fish are harder to find and even if you find, people won’t buy it,” said Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Chiang Mai, who joined a protest in Bangkok this week.

World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.

“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.

Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair next year, attended the stakeholders’ dialogue as an observer. Delegations from both the Philippines and Singapore received the SCEF’s policy paper on Myanmar during the meeting.

Also in attendance were representatives from Chin resistance forces, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), elected lawmakers and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on the military situation, obstacles to delivery of humanitarian aid, implications of the Rohingya genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and the regime’s escalating airstrikes against civilians.

SCEF said last week’s genocide ruling should spur stronger efforts to enforce accountability for the regime’s past atrocities and ongoing crimes in Myanmar. It urged the international community not to shield military leaders from responsibility or enable further violence.

Then-military chief Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the 2017 “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine that the World Court said amounted to genocide.

The regime rejected the ICJ ruling as “unfair” and stated its repatriation of Rohingya refugees would continue on its own terms, ignoring UN calls to grant them citizenship rights.

The democratic opposition’s appeal comes amid growing debate over ASEAN’s approach to Myanmar. While the bloc continues to exclude Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership from top-level meetings, members including Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia have expanded bilateral engagement with the regime in recent months.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Kazakhstan Votes for Local Councils: What Maslikhat Elections are All About
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan votes on Nov. 29 to replace every local council in the country, more than a year ahead of schedule, marking the final step in rebuilding the political system from the ground up after this year’s constitutional overhaul.

Nearly 11,000 candidates are running for 3,447 seats in 228 maslikhats, the elected assemblies that work alongside regional, city and district governments. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dissolved the maslikhats on Oct. 12.

The maslikhats approve the budgets that pay for roads, heating, schools and water pipes, and they can vote no confidence in akims, the appointed governors and mayors. Whether Sunday produces livelier councils or simply relabels the old ones will shape how much say people have over that money.

What a maslikhat does

A maslikhat is the elected council of a region, city or district, and the main voice voters have in local government. While the akims run the administration, the maslikhats are the elected check on them.

There are three tiers: 20 regional councils, 38 city councils and 170 district councils.

Their core powers include approving local budgets, proposing amendments, approving plans for a region, city or district, which decide, for example, where schools are built and which roads and utility networks get fixed. In cases set by law, deputies can start a no-confidence vote against an akim.

How the vote works

Deputies are elected for five years by secret ballot. Vote for maslikhats in the capital, the regions and cities of national significance, which are Astana, Almaty and Shymkent, mix party lists with constituency races, while districts and towns elect only individual candidates.

Of the 3,447 seats, 334 will be filled from party lists and 3,113 in single-member districts.

“In 20 regions, 97 party slates have been registered for 334 seats. These slates include 1,160 candidates. Thus, there are an average of three to four candidates per seat,” said Azamat Aimanakumov, a member of the Central Election Commission, at a Nov. 27 briefing in Astana.

Candidates are nominated by parties, in some cases by public associations, or by themselves in single-member races.

Seven parties are on the ballot: Auyl, the National Social Democratic Party, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Respublica, Aq Jol, the Baytaq Green Party and Adilet. Each party may register only one list per region, and women and young people together must make up at least 30% of it.

In single-member districts, 9,422 candidates are on the ballot. Any citizen aged 20 or older can run, except people a court has declared legally incapable, those serving prison sentences, and those with a criminal record or a corruption conviction. No one may run in more than one district.

“The fiercest competition is in the Turkistan Region, where there are up to five candidates vying for a single seat. In another 121 districts, four candidates are running for each seat. This represents the highest level of competition,” said Aimanakumov. “There are also regions with the least competition, where two candidates are vying for a single seat. Specifically, in 11 regions across 44 districts, two people are vying for a single seat,” he added.

Overall, 12,679,459 people are on the voter list. On Nov. 29, 10,338 polling stations will open: 101 at 6 a.m. and the rest at 7 a.m. Voting ends at 8 p.m. People with no permanent registration who were never on a voter list can register on the day at 218 designated polling stations.

Alongside digital outreach, precinct commission members went door to door with personal invitations to vote, said Mukhtar Yerman, the CEC’s deputy chairman.

“We see the task not just as reaching people with information, but as creating conditions in which every voter can easily get what they need to know and exercise their constitutional right on Nov. 29,” he said.

Some 258 public associations and nonprofit groups have accredited observers, 13 with the CEC and 245 with territorial commissions. O

Why now?

The maslikhats elected in March 2023 were not due to face voters until 2028. Their early end follows a year of rapid change at the national level. In March, a referendum approved a new Constitution that replaced the two-chamber parliament, the Senate and Mazhilis, with a single chamber, the Kurultai. It took effect July 1.

In June, Amanat, the former Nur Otan party built by first president Nursultan Nazarbayev, voted to merge itself into Adilet, a pro-presidential party registered in June. In August, Adilet won 71.17% of the parliamentary vote and 110 of Kurultai’s 145 seats. Its leader Aibek Dadebay, a former head of the presidential administration, became the chamber’s chairman.

In October, after consulting Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Kurultai Chairman Aibek Dadebay, as the Constitution requires, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the decree ending all maslikhat mandates.

World.title: Kazakhstan Brings Together Global Sports Leaders to Strengthen Anti-Doping Efforts
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan hosted a meeting of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Foundation Board on Nov. 26 in Astana, bringing together representatives of more than 50 countries to discuss global anti-doping policies, athlete protection and international cooperation.

The meeting was attended by WADA President Witold Bańka, Director General Olivier Niggli, Kazakh Tourism and Sports Minister Yerbol Myrzabossynov, representatives of the International Olympic Committee and International Paralympic Committee, and heads of national anti-doping organizations, the ministry reported.

Discussions focused on implementing the World Anti-Doping Code, strengthening safeguards for clean sport, expanding educational and scientific programs, and improving international cooperation.

Kazakhstan highlights clean sport priorities

Addressing the meeting, Myrzabossynov said Kazakhstan views clean sport as a matter of fairness and equal opportunities, emphasizing that athletes should win through honest effort.

He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to strengthening its national anti-doping system, aligning it with international standards and promoting anti-doping awareness among young athletes.

“Every athlete should achieve victory through honest work. Our common goal is to protect athletes’ rights, create equal conditions for everyone and preserve trust in sport,” he said.

Expanding cooperation with WADA

Cooperation between Kazakhstan and WADA gained momentum following Bańka’s visit to Kazakhstan in October 2025.

Earlier this year, Myrzabossynov and Bańka signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation in anti-doping education, prevention of anti-doping rule violations, scientific research and international knowledge-sharing.

The WADA Foundation Board is the agency’s highest governing body, comprising representatives of the international sports movement and governments. It plays a central role in shaping global anti-doping policy.

World.title: Hong Kong Sees Kazakhstan as Promising Tourism Market Ahead of Direct Flight Launch
World.content:
ALMATY – Hong Kong is looking to strengthen tourism ties with Kazakhstan and expand its presence in Central Asia ahead of the launch of direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong in January 2027, Hong Kong Tourism Board (HKTB) Executive Director Anthony Lau said at the travel mission presentation in Almaty on Nov. 27.

“The future has never looked brighter for tourism between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan,” Lau said in his welcoming remarks at the event.

Cathay Pacific plans to launch direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong on Jan. 9, 2027 with flights departing every Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday from Almaty.

The new route is expected to facilitate not only leisure travel but business exchanges. Forty representatives from Hong Kong’s tourism industry traveled to Kazakhstan to discuss opportunities for cooperation with local companies and industries.

“This enhanced connectivity will bring our cities closer than ever before and open up exciting new opportunities for tourism exchange and business cooperation in the years ahead,” Lau told The Astana Times.

Lau said the HKTB seeks to build long-term partnerships in Central Asia as part of their strategy. Tourism is not an exchange of residence, it is about exchange of culture, and friendship, and long-term business partnerships.

The mission also included a meeting between Lau and Yerkebulan Abikhan, the head of the Almaty Tourism Department to strengthen tourism exchanges.

“The world has changed, and for us, those developed markets are developed,” Lau said.

“We are looking for new sources of tourism growth. Our next phase of growth will be very much along the Belt and Road countries. We are picking different Belt and Road countries which we believe have potential for tourism growth. One factor in facilitating tourism exchange between two destinations would be air connectivity. There is really no point if there is no connection between one place and another. We think it is the right time for us to come to Almaty, to come to Kazakhstan, to understand the market,” he explained.

One of the main benefits is that Hong Kong offers 14-day visa-free entry for Kazakhstan passport holders, making it easier to plan visits.

“As of this moment, it is only three flights a week. Hopefully, if the business comes along, the number of flights will expand to daily, or even twice daily. We are also looking at possible connections with Chinese airlines. For example, from Almaty to Guangzhou or Shenzhen, you can take a fast 45-minute train ride to Hong Kong. You can spend a couple of days in Guangzhou, come to Hong Kong, and then return to Almaty,” said Lau.

Lau highlighted Hong Kong’s combination of urban attractions, natural landscapes, gastronomy and cultural experiences as part of its appeal to visitors. Visitors can travel from the city’s iconic skyline to its beaches in around 20 minutes. Its culinary scene ranges from Michelin-starred restaurants to local specialties, alongside a growing selection of halal-certified dining options.

Lau described Hong Kong as both a destination and a gateway to wider journeys across mainland China.

Cathay Pacific offers a 10% discount on the base fare for bookings made by Dec. 31, 2026, for travel to Hong Kong by March 31, 2027, and other options available on the company’s website.

“As Cathay Pacific’s very first destination in Central Asia, we look forward to welcoming customers onboard our non-stop flights connecting Almaty and Hong Kong. Whether traveling for business or leisure, customers can enjoy our signature hospitality, from our award-winning cabin crew services and lounges, Asia Pacific’s largest inflight entertainment selection, to Hong Kong-inspired dining and international flavors,” said Cathay Chief Customer and Commercial Officer Lavinia Lau.

World.title: Enjoy Final Days of Fall With Music and More
World.content:
ASTANA – As November comes to a close, the cities offer plenty of ways to enjoy the weekend. From ballet and classical music to theater performance and concerts, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events to explore with friends and family.

Astana

“Golden Centaurs” excursion, Nov. 28

Discover the military traditions of the Golden Horde through a guided museum tour featuring historical weapons, armour and interactive displays. Visitors can learn about the equipment used by medieval warriors and explore the history of nomadic military art.

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; 54 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Freedom Festival, Nov. 29

The internationally renowned London City Ballet will perform as part of the Freedom Festival, bringing together dancers from leading ballet companies. The programme features works by celebrated choreographers, including John Neumeier, Kenneth MacMillan and Ashley Page, offering audiences an evening of classical and contemporary ballet.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Symphony concert, Nov. 28

South Korean violinist Lim Ji-young will perform a classical music program. Enjoy beautiful melodies and experience the magic of live music.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Musical Heritage of Western Kazakhstan” concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate the musical traditions of western Kazakhstan through an evening of traditional songs and kuis. The program features works by renowned Kazakh composers and performers, including Mukhit Meraliuly and Garifolla Kurmangaliyev, highlighting the region’s rich musical heritage.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Dürer. Metamorphoses of Alchemy” exhibition, Nov. 27 – Jan. 24

Explore the artistic and intellectual world of the Renaissance through an exhibition dedicated to German artist Albrecht Dürer. The collection brings together engravings, historical books, geometric studies and alchemical texts, offering a closer look at the connection between art, science and philosophy.

Venue: LM Lulanshi Art; 22A Amanzholov Street. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Oyu gala concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate five years of Oyu live with a concert bringing together popular performers. For the first time in the project’s history, familiar songs by artists including Sadraddin, Ayau, ALEM, Yenlik and dudeontheguitar will be performed with a symphony orchestra, offering a new interpretation of contemporary music.

Venue: Almaty Theater; 30 Al-Farabi Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Kanysh” performance, Nov. 28

The theatrical production tells the story of Kanysh Satpayev, one of Kazakhstan’s most prominent scientists and the founder of Kazakh geology. Through scenes from his life and scientific journey, the play explores his dedication to knowledge, his contribution to national science and his service to the country.

Venue: Alatau Theater; 6 Nurkent microdistrict. Tickets are available here.

Night at the Museum, Nov. 28

What happens when a museum comes to life after closing time? This ballet production follows a young guide who discovers that museum exhibits have come alive. Combining traditional Korean dances, historical characters, humour and modern K-pop rhythms, the performance takes audiences on a journey through Korean culture.

Venue: Korean Theater of Musical Academy; 158 Bogenbay Batyr. Tickets are available here.

Kaleo concert, Nov. 29

The anniversary tour celebrates 10 years since the release of the album A/B. Fans can enjoy live performances of the band’s popular songs, including “Way Down We Go,” “All the Pretty Girls” and “No Good.”

Venue: Baluan Sholak Arena; 44 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Baiterek Holding to Expand Investment Support for Kazakhstan’s Economy in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Baiterek National Investment Holding plans to provide 8 trillion tenge (US$17.5 billion) in economic support in 2027, focusing on boosting investment, expanding industrial capacity and supporting businesses, following a meeting of its Board of Directors chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on Nov. 27.

The board approved the holding’s annual budget and key performance indicators for its chairman and management board members for 2027, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The holding’s performance targets will reflect the country’s priorities, notably improving investment efficiency and developing the real sector of the economy. Key indicators will include fixed-capital investment, revenue generated by supported enterprises and their export sales.

Of the planned support, investments in fixed capital across manufacturing, infrastructure and the agro-industrial sector are expected to reach 1.17 trillion tenge (US$2.6 billion). With the holding’s participation, approximately 2.7 million square meters of housing are also expected to be commissioned in 2027.

To finance these projects, Baiterek will continue raising funds on the market. Non-government sources are projected to account for 54% of the holding’s total borrowing next year. The holding will also assess the participation of second-tier banks in business financing through state support instruments.

The plans are based on the holding’s updated Development Plan through 2033, which its Board of Directors approved in August. One priority is to expand financing opportunities for businesses launching new production facilities or increasing the capacity of existing ones. Baiterek plans to involve commercial banks and private investors in financing these projects.

Bektenov also emphasized the need to improve the effectiveness of the holding’s anti-corruption compliance, internal audit and procurement control services. He called for concrete measures to prevent corruption risks and urged the holding to move beyond formal approaches to its responsibilities, focusing instead on practical proposals to improve performance.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Economic Development, Strategic Partnerships and Digital Ambitions
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest explores the country’s efforts to strengthen economic resilience, improve digital connectivity, position Central Asia as an emerging technology hub and more.

Kazakhstan’s approach to openness, innovation and long-term stability

EU Reporter published an article on Nov. 21 focusing on Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen its long-term economic resilience through three key priorities: expanding international trade and transport connectivity, applying digital technologies to improve water resource management, and maintaining financial stability through sustainable public finances and pension reforms.

“Kazakhstan’s development priorities are linked by a common time horizon. Transport corridors can strengthen its participation in regional and global markets. Digital water management can help protect a resource on which economic activity and community life depend. Sound public finances and a sustainable pension system can support confidence across generations. These ambitions require capable institutions, consistent implementation and sustained investment. Kazakhstan is seeking to turn its geographic advantages, technological ambitions and financial resources into a more resilient foundation for the decades ahead,” the article reads.

Kazakhstan ranks seventh for mobile internet affordability in November

Kazakhstan ranked seventh among 55 countries with high-speed internet in terms of mobile data affordability in November, with an average monthly tariff of around $10, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said, Trend reported on Nov. 24.

The ranking was presented during a government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, where officials discussed mobile internet affordability and investment in telecommunications infrastructure.

Madiyev noted that the average monthly mobile internet tariff in Kazakhstan is almost three times lower than the global average of $27.

Build! Once again – build! Kazakhstan accelerates infrastructure development

EU Reporter released an article on Nov. 17 about Kazakhstan’s decision to allocate approximately $14 billion from the National Fund to its three-year People’s Construction program, presenting infrastructure investment in schools, hospitals, roads and other public facilities as a long-term strategy to convert oil wealth into sustainable economic growth and human capital development.

“By directing part of its national reserves toward infrastructure development, Kazakhstan is creating the foundation for long-term growth, leaving future generations, alongside financial savings, modern schools, kindergartens, stadiums, medical facilities, and a country with a decent level of comfort for living,” the article reads.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan launch Eurasia technology hub in UK

Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have officially opened the Eurasia Growth Hub in London, marking a new step in strengthening technology cooperation and supporting Central Asian start-ups seeking to enter the UK and European markets.

The hub was launched during the international Digital Eurasia event as a joint initiative of Kazakhstan’s Astana Hub and Uzbekistan’s IT Park, The Caspian Post reported on Nov. 23.

Why Kazakhstan deserves a visit from a U.S. sitting president

Georgetown Security Studies Review, Georgetown University, published an article on Nov. 22 arguing that the United States should strengthen its strategic partnership with Kazakhstan by arranging the first-ever U.S. presidential visit to Astana, highlighting Kazakhstan’s importance to energy security, trade and regional geopolitics amid growing Russian and Chinese influence in Central Asia.

“The United States acknowledges Kazakhstan as a strategically important ally, but has not communicated this effectively enough through action. Today, the United States has demonstrated its stake in Kazakhstan primarily through cooperation on uranium and oil. Even though the current C5+1 forums have been successful, engagement between the two countries dates all the way back to Kazakhstan’s independence over thirty years ago. This kind of record makes the absence of a presidential visit from the United States even more striking. Meanwhile, Russia, China, and various other state leaders have all visited Kazakhstan routinely over the last few decades, showcasing a commitment to diplomacy in the strategically critical region. A presidential visit to Astana would show that Washington values its partnership with Kazakhstan just as much as they do,” the article reads.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s 2027 Outlook Improves as Inflation Forecast Falls, Tenge Strengthens
World.content:
ASTANA – Analysts have revised their forecasts for Kazakhstan’s inflation, exchange rate and export revenues upward, while slightly lowering expectations for economic growth this year, according to the National Bank of Kazakhstan’s November macroeconomic survey released on Nov. 26.

The survey, conducted on Nov. 12-18 among 15 financial, rating and research organizations, suggests a more favorable near-term economic outlook, although longer-term risks remain.

Higher oil prices, slower economic growth

Analysts raised their 2026 average Brent crude oil price forecast from $88.4 to $93.3 per barrel, while maintaining projections of $80 in 2027 and $75 in 2028.

Despite higher oil price expectations, Kazakhstan’s 2026 economic growth forecast was lowered from 4.8% to 4.6%. The 2027 projection remained unchanged at 4.7%, while the 2028 estimate edged up from 4.4% to 4.5%.

The figures suggest that favorable oil prices may support export revenues without necessarily translating into faster economic growth.

Inflation expected to ease, Tenge outlook improves

The inflation forecast for 2026 was revised downward from 9.5% to 9.1%, while the 2027 projection declined from 8.3% to 8%. Inflation is expected to reach 7% in 2028, slightly above the previous estimate of 6.9%.

Analysts also anticipate a gradual reduction in the National Bank’s base rate, from an expected 15.8% at the end of 2026 to 13.4% in 2027 and 10.8% in 2028.

Meanwhile, exchange rate expectations improved across the entire forecast period. The average exchange rate is projected at 472 tenge per U.S. dollar in 2026, compared with the previous forecast of 479 tenge. The estimates for 2027 and 2028 were revised to 489.8 and 510.4 tenge per dollar, respectively, from 499.6 and 527.1.

Despite these upward revisions, analysts still expect the national currency to weaken gradually in nominal terms over the coming years.

Export growth faces longer-term challenges

The forecast for Kazakhstan’s exports of goods and services in 2026 increased from $96 billion to $101 billion, while the 2027 estimate rose from $93.9 billion to $100 billion.

However, the projected positive gap between exports and imports is expected to narrow significantly, from $17.2 billion in 2026 to $11.8 billion in 2027 and $5.6 billion in 2028. This trend suggests that declining oil prices and rising imports could gradually reduce the support that foreign trade provides to the tenge.

Expert highlights need for economic diversification

Commenting on the survey on his Tengenomika Telegram channel, economic analyst Ruslan Sultanov described the November results as presenting a relatively favorable near-term outlook.

However, he cautioned that declining oil prices, rising imports and gradually easing monetary conditions increase the importance of productivity, export diversification and domestic sources of economic growth.

Long-term expectations remain broadly stable, with potential economic growth projected at 4.5% and inflation at 5.1% over a five-year horizon. Nevertheless, wide ranges in medium-term forecasts indicate persistent economic uncertainty.

World.title: Dubai to Host GITEX GLOBAL 2026 With Tech Leaders From More Than 120 Countries
World.content:
ASTANA – Technology leaders, policymakers, investors and innovators from more than 120 countries are expected to gather in Dubai for GITEX GLOBAL 2026, which will feature more than 6,000 exhibitors and 10,000 technology brands across 46 halls.

The 46th edition of the technology exhibition will open with the inaugural GITEX SUMMIT on Dec. 7 at Dubai World Trade Center, before moving to Dubai Exhibition Center at Expo City Dubai, where GITEX GLOBAL will run from Dec. 8-11 and Expand North Star from Dec. 8-10.

The event will focus on artificial intelligence, AI sovereignty, regulation, responsible deployment and intelligent infrastructure, amid the rapid development of technologies reshaping economies and industries.

“AI is accelerating discovery and reshaping economies, while intensifying debates around trust, ethics, sovereignty, security, infrastructure and energy,” said Trixie LohMirmand, executive vice president of inD, the organizer of GITEX GLOBAL and Expand North Star.

“GITEX GLOBAL 2026 captures this defining moment, bringing together competing perspectives to challenge assumptions, examine the strategic choices ahead and advance a shared commitment to responsible progress,” she added.

GITEX SUMMIT to examine technology priorities for 2027

The inaugural GITEX SUMMIT, The Global Reset 2027 – Through a New Lens, will focus on business networking, industry intelligence and knowledge exchange. Discussions will cover the compute economy, capital flows and the race to superintelligence.

Speakers include Marc Ganzi, CEO of DigitalBridge; Nina Schick, generative AI expert and author of Deepfakes; Anne Neuberger, general partner and head of global affairs at Andreessen Horowitz and former White House cyber and emerging technology adviser; and Gary Marcus, emeritus professor at New York University, advocate of neurosymbolic AI and critic of AI hype.

The five-day program will feature more than 500 speakers, with sessions covering AI market shocks, the agentic economy, physical AI, longevity and biosciences.

Robotics, computing and emerging technologies

GITEX Robotics & Mobility will feature companies developing humanoid and other robots, including Unitree, Pudu Robotics and UBTECH. The showcase comes as global humanoid robot shipments increased nearly 300% year-on-year in the first half of 2026.

The Robotics & Mobility Park will present Joby Aviation’s electric air taxi, which is expected to launch in Dubai with the Roads and Transport Authority, as well as Mercedes-Benz’s Level 4 robotaxi trials.

GITEX Super Data Center will focus on data center infrastructure supporting the AI race. GITEX RetailX will explore the regional retail market, while LIVX by GITEX will focus on AI and longevity technologies.

Companies valued at a combined $76 billion will also be represented, including Sweden’s Legora, valued at $8.8 billion; VAST Data, which powers nine of the world’s top 10 frontier AI labs; and Switzerland’s Nexthink, whose technology supports 30 million endpoints across more than 1,300 enterprises worldwide.

Technology companies focus on AI and digital sovereignty

AWS, Etisalat, G42, Google, Huawei, IBM, Lenovo, Microsoft and Oracle are returning with expanded presences, focusing on commercial opportunities, project launches and cross-border cooperation.

Shukri Eid, general manager of IBM Gulf, Levant and Pakistan, said the company would focus on scaling AI while maintaining control over technology and ensuring operational resilience.

“At GITEX GLOBAL 2026, we will focus on a question facing every organisation: Can you scale technology including AI while remaining in control and keeping critical operations running when conditions change? That is what resilience means today. It goes beyond the ability to recover from disruption. It is the ability to adapt, preserve choice and avoid becoming dependent on any single technology, platform or provider,” he said.

International pavilions and cross-border partnerships

Exhibitors from across the world are expected to use Dubai as a platform for international business, investment partnerships and expansion into new markets. According to the organizers, exhibitors from 31 European countries will participate, with larger pavilions from Italy, Cyprus and Greece.

Canada will bring its first pavilion to Expand North Star, joining startups from Suriname, Thailand and Uzbekistan.

According to Dalibor Palus, director of trade fairs at AHK UAE, which organizes the German Pavilion, Dubai combines ambitious technology investment with an internationally connected business environment.

“GITEX GLOBAL creates opportunities for German companies to exchange expertise, establish partnerships and develop business relationships that extend well beyond the event,” he said.

Tatiana Riera, general manager of ApexBrasil’s Dubai office, which leads the Brazil Pavilion, added that Dubai is a gateway for taking Brazilian innovation global.

“Our priority is to turn international connections into business opportunities, partnerships and investment that strengthen ties between Brazil and the Gulf,” she said.

World.title: ‘The entire logic of how power operates needs to change’: views on electoral reform in Abkhazia
World.content:
Heated debate has erupted in Abkhazia over electoral reform ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027.

The reform would replace the majoritarian system with a mixed electoral system. Yet supporters of both approaches agree on one point: both systems are too vulnerable to offer much hope of significantly improving the “quality” of the elected parliament.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure and former MP Ilya Gunia proposes considering a model of governance in which the election of MPs and the president would be entirely independent of local or party interests.

What Ilya Gunia proposes

Abolishing territorial constituencies in parliamentary elections

“Parliament is a national legislative body, not a local self-government institution. Therefore, citizens across the republic should be able to vote for individual candidates, regardless of where they live.

Under a nationwide vote, the first 35 or 45 candidates who receive the most votes would win parliamentary seats,” Gunia believes.

In his view, this model would shift the focus from local election campaigns to nationwide competition. It would also give people with a public profile across the republic, rather than just in individual districts, a chance to enter parliament.

Changing the way the president is elected

As an alternative to direct presidential elections, Gunia proposes that parliament elect the president:

“This would reduce the financial and political burden on society, eliminate the need for a separate large-scale presidential election campaign, and make MPs responsible for choosing the head of state.”

He stresses that the president’s powers must be clearly defined. The country must also establish safeguards for parliamentary independence and mechanisms to oversee the executive branch.

Redistributing powers and establishing a system of checks and balances

“The most important thing is to review the current system of relations between the branches of government. The Constitution must clearly define their powers, establish mechanisms for mutual oversight and accountability, and provide safeguards against the concentration of power in one person’s hands,” Ilya Gunia believes.

In his view, the relationship between the branches of government must be legally synchronised. If the president becomes unable to perform his duties and resigns before the end of his term, parliament should automatically dissolve. This would force the legislative and executive branches to work closely together, share responsibility to the public and spare Abkhazia from an endless cycle of elections.

The former MP says his proposal aims to create a system in which no branch of government can shift responsibility onto another without facing consequences.

*“Abkhazia does not simply need a new electoral system. We need to change the very logic of how power operates, put an end to recurring political crises and build institutions that function regardless of who occupies the presidential office or which political forces hold seats in parliament.

In my view, this should be the main goal of genuine political reform,”* Ilya Gunia says.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian deputy foreign minister announces new restrictions on Georgian companies
World.content:
Meeting between Russian and Georgian diplomats

The first meeting as part of the resumed dialogue between Georgia and Russia did not result in the lifting of restrictions on Georgian beverage exports. Giorgi Zurabashvili, the Georgian prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia, said that, on the contrary, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin had announced plans to impose sanctions on two more Georgian wine producers during their meeting in Minsk on 19 November.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also confirmed the information, suggesting that a “deep state” might be behind Russia’s decision and could have bribed mid-level Russian officials.

What did Galuzin tell Zurabashvili?

Zurabashvili is Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister. Since October, he has also served as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia. On 19 November, he met the Russian deputy foreign minister in Minsk. It was his first meeting in this capacity.

Zurabashvili first disclosed details of the meeting on 25 November on pro-government Imedi TV. According to him, the Georgian side’s main objective was to restore Georgian wine producers’ access to the Russian market.

● Moscow and Tbilisi prepare to resume dialogue

● Russia signals new opportunities for closer ties with Georgia

● ‘Moscow is ready to restore diplomatic relations with Georgia’ — Russian Foreign Ministry

● Kremlin message to Tbilisi: diplomatic ties with Russia would bring greater economic benefits

In October, Russia restricted imports of products from seven Georgian producers. Four of them are wine producers: Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, Vineni and Askaneli Brothers. The list also included beer produced by Georgian Beer Company, as well as Coca-Cola beverages and Nabeghlavi mineral water bottled in Georgia.

According to Zurabashvili, Galuzin cited three reasons for imposing the restrictions: product quality, allegations that the companies were funding the war in Ukraine, and “anti-Russian rhetoric”. Zurabashvili rejected all three accusations. His hopes that the restrictions would be lifted immediately did not materialise, with new announcements following instead.

“Naturally, I was surprised and stunned by this news, since nothing of the sort is happening,” Zurabashvili said, adding that Galuzin had not provided a single fact to substantiate his claims. “Therefore, these are political assertions that have absolutely no basis.”

According to Zurabashvili, the Georgian side raised a number of technical issues, while the Russian side put forward around 10 proposals, predominantly of a humanitarian nature. As an example, he cited an initiative to establish a partnership between a university in Russia’s Don region and a Georgian state university.
