In Zurabashvili’s view, these proposals were aimed against the Georgian Dream government and sought to strengthen the opposition’s position. He did not mention any other topics.

Who warned Zurabashvili?

Mamuka Pipia, international secretary of the pro-Russian Solidarity for Peace party, claimed that Zurabashvili had been warned while still in Tbilisi that the Russian ban would be extended to two more companies. According to Pipia, the companies in question are Winiveria and Chateau Mukhrani. This information has not been corroborated by other sources.

Kobakhidze confirmed that Yury Balashov, head of the Russian-Georgian Business Council, had visited Tbilisi ahead of the meeting in Minsk. According to the prime minister, Balashov had promised that all companies would be removed from the list by the end of the year but subsequently changed his position. Kobakhidze noted that Galuzin had expressed the same position.

‘Deep state’ – now in Moscow too

Kobakhidze described Galuzin’s arguments as absurd, noting that Tbilisi had expected all existing restrictions to be lifted. He compared Russia’s actions to the behaviour of the European bureaucracy, which, he claimed, had been “bought” by a “deep state” and was acting against the interests of its own countries.

The prime minister did not name any specific individuals. He expressed hope that the issue would be discussed at the highest level of the Russian leadership and added that the dialogue should continue.

In Moscow, Tbilisi – or nowhere at all

Six days after the meeting, on 25 November, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov welcomed remarks made by Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili.

Bochorishvili had called for overcoming the fear of engaging in dialogue with Russia. Meanwhile, according to Russian state news agency TASS, Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov said the sides had made significant progress in building mutual trust and that the talks could be moved to their respective capitals.

Bochorishvili denied this, saying that no proposals had been made or decisions taken regarding meetings in Moscow or Tbilisi. She noted that Belarus was not a party to the negotiations and had no information about their outcome.

The following day, Kobakhidze suggested that meetings could be held alternately in Moscow and Tbilisi. The prime minister insisted that neither this nor the presence of national flags posed a threat to Georgia’s policy of non-recognition of the occupied territories.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the prime minister would decide when and where the meetings would take place. He added that seeing the Georgian flag in Russia would be a source of pride. Papuashvili also stressed that the issue of occupation must be part of the negotiations.

“Do you really think the special representative would attend a meeting, talk about wine and herbs, and not even touch upon the main problem in relations with Russia?” he asked.

In his interview with Imedi TV, Zurabashvili also noted that dialogue was necessary to discuss issues of sovereignty and de-occupation. The informal dialogue format between Georgia and Russia was established in 2012 and initially focused exclusively on trade, economic and humanitarian issues. It is known as the Zurab Abashidze-Grigory Karasin format. Before Zurabashvili’s appointment, the post of special representative for relations with Russia had been vacant since December 2025.

‘Communication failure’: Reactions

Former Foreign Minister Irakli Menagarishvili told Radio Liberty that although dialogue with Russia was necessary, he saw no grounds for optimism. He urged caution.

Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia for Georgia party, described the meeting as a “disaster”. According to him, Minsk cannot be regarded as a neutral venue. He questioned Zurabashvili’s competence and highlighted Galuzin’s diplomatic experience, including his tenure as ambassador to Japan.

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, told TV Pirveli that a Georgian official’s visit to Belarus contradicted the government’s own rhetoric about pursuing peace. “This is not about striving for peace but, on the contrary, about indirectly participating on Russia’s side,” he said. Gvaramia called on the government to inform the public about what had been discussed in Minsk.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, argued that moving the negotiations to Moscow would constitute a diplomatic disaster.

“It is important to understand that all this is happening behind closed doors,” she said. Dekanoidze suggested that Zurabashvili had agreed to a visit by Galuzin to Tbilisi, although this information has not been confirmed.

Grigol Gegelia, a leader of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, believes that the government is preparing a “new stage of capitulation”. According to him, Georgian Dream has increased the country’s economic dependence on Russia, effectively giving Moscow leverage to blackmail Georgia.

Imprisoned former President Mikheil Saakashvili wrote: “We have been left completely defenceless and vulnerable in the face of an enraged Russia – entirely deprived of support from America or Europe.”

Salome Zurabishvili’s meeting with EU ambassador

On 26 November, the European Parliament adopted a strongly critical resolution on Georgia.

According to TV Pirveli, 441 MEPs voted in favour of the document. The resolution calls for the immediate release of Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze and Paata Manjgaladze. It also calls for sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili, Irakli Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili, Kakha Kaladze and other officials.

On the same day, Salome Zurabishvili met EU Ambassador Pawel Herczynski. According to the Foreign Ministry, she described the resolution as an attempt to spread “false narratives” about the country. Zurabishvili also asked EU representatives to clarify whom exactly they considered to be arbitrarily detained.

Commenting on the meeting, Irakli Kobakhidze said: “In this case, the European Parliament has reached the point of absurdity.” Shalva Papuashvili, in turn, described the European Parliament as a “reincarnation” of the Soviet-era Congress of People’s Deputies.

World.title: Besiktas football match in Batumi sparks political tensions between Georgia and Turkey
World.content:
Besiktas match in Batumi

A Europa League match in Batumi between Turkish club Besiktas and Israeli club Hapoel Be’er Sheva has sparked political tensions between Georgia and Turkey. The Turkish authorities reacted strongly to clashes between Turkish football fans and Georgian police. Just hours after the clashes in the stands, three Turkish ministers contacted their Georgian counterparts. The actions of Georgian police were condemned by the Turkish presidential administration, the sports minister and the ruling party.

According to Georgia’s Interior Ministry, Besiktas fans instigated the disturbances. The ministry said three police officers had been injured and 16 people detained.

What happened?

Tensions arose even before the start of the match, on the city streets where Besiktas fans were holding a march. According to InterPressNews, participants failed to comply with police demands and began throwing various objects at law enforcement officers. Police responded by using pepper spray.

The match kicked off at Batumi Arena at 21:45. Footage from Turkish TV channel TRT Spor, cited by Radio Liberty, shows police officers approaching two fans holding a Palestinian flag in the stands and confiscating it. A scuffle ensued.

Fans began breaking seats in the stands. Police again used pepper spray, and the clashes spilled onto the pitch. The match was suspended for about half an hour during the first half and resumed at 22:45.

How did Ankara respond?

According to Turkish media reports, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held a telephone conversation with his Georgian counterpart, Maka Bochorishvili. The Anadolu news agency, citing diplomatic sources, reported that representatives of the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate-general in Batumi were present at the stadium.

Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci contacted his Georgian counterpart, Sulkhan Tamazashvili. According to the Turkish side, Ciftci expressed dissatisfaction over the use of disproportionate force against Turkish fans and demanded that their safe return to Turkey be ensured.

Turkish Justice Minister Yilmaz Tunc, following a conversation with Georgian Justice Minister Paata Salia, said he expected the detained Turkish citizens to be released immediately. He also called for those responsible for the incident to be held accountable.

The strongest condemnation came from the administration of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Presidential communications director Burhanettin Duran said:

“I strongly condemn the disproportionate police intervention targeting our fans during the match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva in Batumi.”

According to Duran, peaceful expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people cannot justify violence or the use of force.

● “President Erdogan’s leadership is an example for all of us,” – Georgia PM

● “Batumi flag-bearer” Temur Katamadze deported from Georgia to Turkey

Youth and Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak condemned the “disproportionate actions” of security forces. Omer Celik, spokesman for the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), said the use of force against fans for displaying a banner and flag in support of Palestine was unacceptable. Celik also accused the Israeli team of “simulation” (feigning injury) on the pitch.

In a statement, Besiktas said it had contacted the Turkish consulate-general in Batumi and Uefa over the incident. According to the club, President Erdogan informed Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali that he was closely monitoring the situation. The Anadolu news agency reported that six other Turkish clubs, including Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor, had expressed solidarity with Besiktas.

Georgian Interior Ministry: Clashes began before flag incident

According to Georgia’s Interior Ministry, some Turkish fans had already displayed aggressive behaviour during their march from Europe Square to Batumi Arena.

The ministry said they had disturbed public order by shouting obscenities and throwing various objects, refused to comply with police demands and engaged in physical clashes with law enforcement officers.

At the stadium, fans broke seats and threw them at police officers. Police used special means to bring the situation under control.

The ministry denied foreign media reports that force had been used because of the display of flags and banners in support of Palestine.

According to the ministry, aggressive behaviour and clashes with police began during the march, well before these symbols were displayed. The ministry also stressed that Georgian law applied to everyone, regardless of citizenship or nationality.

Footage from Turkish TV channel TRT Spor, cited by Radio Liberty, shows police officers approaching two fans holding a Palestinian flag in the stands and confiscating it.

A scuffle broke out immediately afterwards. According to the Turkish Interior Ministry, Tamazashvili told Ciftci that the flags had been confiscated by Uefa representatives rather than Georgian government officials. He also said he had dispatched his deputy to the stadium. The Georgian side has not released its own account of the conversation.

Match results and detentions

The match was suspended for approximately half an hour during the first half and resumed at 22:45. Besiktas secured a 2-1 victory.

According to Turkish media reports, almost all detained Turkish citizens were released following the intervention of the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi. The same sources reported that two fans who had been hospitalised were discharged in the presence of consular officials. The Georgian side has yet to confirm the release of those detained.

Why was the match played in Batumi?

The match was originally scheduled to take place in Istanbul, but the Turkish authorities informed Uefa that this was not possible due to security concerns. On 30 October, Uefa announced that the match would be played in Batumi with spectators in attendance.

Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply over the war in the Gaza Strip. In November 2024, a match between Besiktas and Maccabi Tel Aviv was moved to Hungary and played behind closed doors.

World.title: Why Temu’s low prices are seen as a violation in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Investigation into Temu in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan’s State Agency for Antimonopoly Control and Consumer Market Supervision under the president has completed its investigation into the Chinese online shopping platform Temu. According to information released by the agency on 25 November, signs of violations of Azerbaijan‘s competition legislation were identified in the operations of PDD Holdings, which owns the platform. A special commission has been established to decide whether to initiate proceedings.

However, the nature of the allegations is unusual for antimonopoly investigations. The agency suspects Temu not of inflating prices but of selling goods at excessively low prices, including below cost. This raises the following question:

Whose interests is the state protecting by taking action against low prices: those of consumers or local retailers?

When do low prices become a violation of the law?

The agency announced the launch of its investigation in mid-July. At the time, it said the investigation had been prompted by a complaint it had received. It did not disclose who had submitted the complaint.

The agency cited three provisions of the Competition Code, each concerning the abuse of a dominant market position:

16.2.1: setting monopolistically low or high prices;

setting monopolistically low or high prices; 16.2.7: setting low prices that restrict competition or prices that prevent competitors from maintaining sustainable profitability;

setting low prices that restrict competition or prices that prevent competitors from maintaining sustainable profitability; 16.2.8: selling goods below cost without economic or technological justification.

For these provisions to apply, it must also be established that Temu holds a dominant position in the Azerbaijani market. According to guidance published on the agency’s website, a company may be deemed to hold a dominant position if its share of the relevant market exceeds 35%. However, the agency has not specified which market segment is concerned or what share Temu holds in it.

If the violations are confirmed, the company could face significant sanctions. According to the Axar.az news website, citing the Competition Code, the commission could order the company to change its pricing policy, impose a fine equivalent to 10% of its annual turnover in Azerbaijan or impose a financial penalty amounting to half of its unlawfully obtained revenue.

Who is complaining and who is concerned?

Although it remains unclear who filed the complaint, dissatisfaction with Temu’s operations emerged long before the investigation was completed. In July, Haqqin.az reported that local entrepreneurs had been complaining on social media about declining sales and a drop in the number of shops operating in shopping centres. They proposed introducing taxes or restrictions on purchases made through the platform, or even blocking the app in Azerbaijan.

However, several economists who commented on the situation in the media took a different view. Former MP and economist Vahid Ahmadov told Haqqin.az that Temu offered an alternative to well-known brand stores for middle- and low-income consumers. In his view, the antimonopoly watchdog should combat monopolies rather than restrict access to affordable goods. Complaints about product quality, meanwhile, fall within the remit of other government agencies.

Economist Rauf Garayev suggested in the same article that the pressure on the platform came not from manufacturers but from retailers operating in shopping centres such as Bina and Sadarak. According to Garayev, unlike Turkey, Azerbaijan has virtually no domestic production of consumer goods. Imposing restrictions on foreign shopping platforms would therefore only limit consumer choice.

Meanwhile, one of Temu’s competitors had previously spoken in favour of competition. In October 2024, at the opening of Turkish online shopping platform Trendyol’s Baku office, the head of its Azerbaijani division, Irem Cagri Yilandil, said in response to a question about Temu: “Competition always benefits consumers.”

Consumers have also expressed concern. According to Axar.az, since the launch of the investigation, there has been an increase in social media posts reporting rising prices on Temu.

What happened at customs?

Temu has no official representative office in Azerbaijan. Orders are delivered from overseas warehouses through transport companies. This year, delays occurred in the customs clearance of parcels ordered through the platform.

State Customs Committee Chairman Shahin Bagirov explained the reasons for the delays on 29 April at a meeting of one of the committees of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani parliament). According to him, the volume of shipments from Temu had increased sharply, with goods arriving at the airport without customs authorities being notified electronically in advance. This resulted in delays of approximately two weeks. The State Customs Committee therefore required Temu to provide shipment details in advance.

At the same meeting, Bagirov said that more than one million people in the country shopped online and that the number of customs declarations submitted had reached 18 million. He noted that a revision of the $300 duty-free import threshold was not currently under consideration, but pointed out that similar exemptions had already been abolished in neighbouring countries. Since 2020, goods imported into Azerbaijan by an individual within a 30-day period by post or through transport companies have been exempt from customs duties, provided their total value does not exceed $300.

What measures have other countries taken against Temu?

In Turkey, which Bagirov cited as an example, the simplified customs clearance procedure for overseas parcels worth up to 30 euros was abolished on 1 February. Earlier, on 21 January, Turkey’s competition watchdog conducted an on-site inspection of the platform’s Istanbul office. In late January, Temu suspended deliveries of goods from abroad to Turkey.

Other countries have also taken measures against the platform, although on different grounds:

European Union. In May, the European Commission fined Temu 200m euros for failing to adequately assess the risks associated with the sale of dangerous and illegal products on the platform. The company disagreed with the decision.

In May, the European Commission fined Temu 200m euros for failing to adequately assess the risks associated with the sale of dangerous and illegal products on the platform. The company disagreed with the decision. Uzbekistan. In March 2025, access to the platform was restricted. The authorities cited non-compliance with legislation on e-commerce, consumer protection and personal data protection, as well as outstanding tax liabilities.

In March 2025, access to the platform was restricted. The authorities cited non-compliance with legislation on e-commerce, consumer protection and personal data protection, as well as outstanding tax liabilities. Vietnam. In December 2024, Temu’s operations in the country were suspended over its failure to complete mandatory registration.

In December 2024, Temu’s operations in the country were suspended over its failure to complete mandatory registration. Indonesia. In 2024, the government called for the app to be blocked to protect the interests of local small businesses.

In the EU, Uzbekistan and Vietnam, the main concerns regarding the platform centred on product safety, compliance with registration requirements and tax legislation. The situation in Indonesia most closely resembles that in Azerbaijan, with the Indonesian authorities justifying their actions by citing the need to protect local retailers.

What happens next?

The competition commission must now decide whether there are grounds for initiating proceedings. If no violation is established, the matter may be dropped.

Economist Khalid Karimli believes that the platform is unlikely to be blocked in the near future. According to him, initial measures could include issuing a warning, imposing a fine and giving the company a deadline to rectify the violation. The company could also challenge the commission’s decision in court. Karimli noted that stricter measures could only be taken if the company continued to violate the law and failed to comply with the authorities’ requirements.

It remains unclear how the commission’s decisions would be enforced against a company with no official representative office in Azerbaijan. Temu has yet to comment publicly on the investigation.

World.title: Flurry of diplomatic visits to Baku fuels speculation over Azerbaijan’s OSCE chairmanship bid
World.content:
Diplomatic visits to Baku and OSCE

Between 17 and 26 November, Azerbaijan received visits from the foreign ministers of Germany, Italy, Georgia and Lithuania, the prime minister of Montenegro and the US secretary of homeland security. Estonia’s foreign minister is also expected to visit Baku on 27 November.

According to official statements, the main topics of discussion were energy, the development of the Middle Corridor and the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

However, these visits coincided with a decisive stage in another diplomatic process. On 19 November, Azerbaijan announced in Vienna its readiness to chair the OSCE. The issue of the organisation’s chairmanship for 2027–2029 will be discussed at a meeting of the OSCE Ministerial Council, scheduled to take place on 3–4 December in the Swiss city of Lugano. This raises the following question:

What are the objectives of these numerous visits by foreign officials to Baku, and are they linked to Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship?

Who visited and why?

According to official statements, the main topics of the visits were as follows:

Germany, 17–18 November. During a meeting between President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, discussions focused on Azerbaijani gas supplies to Germany, which began this year, the development of the Middle Corridor and “cooperation within international organisations”. Wadephul travelled to Yerevan after visiting Baku.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin discussed the TRIPP transport route, which will pass through Armenian territory, during his meeting with Aliyev. The launch of the project’s implementation was announced the following day.

According to the Italian Foreign Ministry, Azerbaijan is the country’s second-largest oil supplier and third-largest gas supplier. The ministry stressed that, against the backdrop of the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, Azerbaijan was a “strategic and reliable partner” in ensuring Italy’s energy security. Lithuania, 25–26 November. Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said that once Lithuania assumed the presidency of the Council of the EU in January 2027, Vilnius intended to initiate the process of easing visa requirements for Azerbaijani citizens. During his meeting with Aliyev, Budrys also announced the forthcoming signing of a joint declaration on strategic partnership between the two countries.

None of the official statements issued by the parties mentioned Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship.

What is at stake at the OSCE?

Switzerland currently holds the OSCE chairmanship. On 19 November in Vienna, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis proposed adopting a single decision on which countries would chair the organisation over the next three years. Switzerland believes that such an approach would ensure continuity in the organisation’s work and regional balance. According to the OSCE, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Austria and Norway expressed their readiness to assume the chairmanship during the meeting. Cyprus and Georgia reaffirmed their candidacies, although consensus on either has yet to be reached.

The decision requires consensus among all 57 OSCE participating states. This means that any of them, including Armenia, can block any candidacy. No agreement has yet been reached on the chairmanship for 2027. The foreign minister of Georgia, whose candidacy has also failed to secure unanimous support among participating states, visited Baku that same week. However, neither side mentioned the OSCE chairmanship in its official statements.

Relations between Baku and the OSCE have been strained for many years. In 2015, the Azerbaijani government terminated its memorandum of understanding with the OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Baku and ended the operations of its office. The OSCE Minsk Process, which facilitated mediation efforts to resolve the Karabakh conflict, was terminated in September 2025 by a decision of the OSCE Ministerial Council following a joint request from Baku and Yerevan. Azerbaijan is now seeking the chairmanship of the organisation.

All countries whose representatives visited Baku are OSCE participating states. Some carry particular political weight in the context of the forthcoming decision: Italy and Germany are among the EU’s largest member states, Lithuania will assume the presidency of the Council of the EU in January, and the US is acting as a mediator in the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

Who opposes Azerbaijan’s bid?

Civil society representatives were the first to openly oppose Azerbaijan’s candidacy. A joint appeal published on 23 November on the website of the human rights organisation Human Rights House Foundation was signed by 46 organisations, including the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), the US-based Freedom Now, the Human Rights Centre of Azerbaijan and the Network of Independent Lawyers.

The signatories called on OSCE participating states not to support Azerbaijan’s bid to chair the organisation. They cited a report by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), published in May 2026, according to which Azerbaijan had 328 political prisoners, including 31 journalists. The appeal also noted that Azerbaijan was among the countries with the highest number of unimplemented judgments of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).

The Azerbaijani government has yet to make any public statements regarding either the appeal by human rights organisations or its bid for the OSCE chairmanship.

Possible pardons and other explanations

The increase in diplomatic visits to Baku caught the attention of Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of the REAL party and now a member of its political committee. In a Facebook post, he suggested that one of the reasons behind the intensified diplomatic contacts could be Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship:

“If this is the reason, then the possibility of releasing some political prisoners through presidential pardons at the end of the year is also being discussed, so that participating states can justify their support for Azerbaijan’s chairmanship to international human rights organisations.”

Mammadov did not rule out other explanations. In his view, if the visits were linked to rising tensions surrounding Iran, this would be accompanied by an increase in oil prices, which has not materialised. The politician argued that the prospect of rising gas prices better explained the geographical pattern of the visits, but did not provide a complete picture either.

There has been no official information about possible pardons so far. Mammadov himself presented this as just one of several possible scenarios.

What to expect from the Lugano meeting?

The final decision on the OSCE chairmanship is expected to be taken by consensus in Lugano. Switzerland said consultations would continue until the meeting of the organisation’s Ministerial Council.

However, Baku’s diplomatic agenda extends beyond this issue. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov believes that Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the EU, which begins in January, will provide a good opportunity to advance the visa liberalisation agenda in the first half of 2027. Bayramov stressed, however, that decisions on visa policy are taken at EU level.

Estonia’s foreign minister is expected to visit Baku on 27 November, with just a week to go before the OSCE Ministerial Council meeting in Lugano.

World.title: ‘Not tailored to one person’: Pashinyan on Armenia’s new Constitution and its controversial provisions
World.content:
Pashinyan proposed that the opposition vote to put the draft Constitution to a referendum. He promised to resign if voters rejected it and not to stand for prime minister in the next election if they approved it. The opposition factions Armenia and Strong Armenia rejected his proposal. The parliamentary opposition calls the new Constitution “Aliyev’s Constitution”. Opposition politicians claim that the government is amending the country’s fundamental law at Azerbaijan’s request. Azerbaijan refuses to sign a peace treaty until Armenia amends its Constitution. Baku considers the reference in the preamble to the Declaration of Independence problematic. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. The new draft removes this reference. Parliament must first approve the proposal to put the new Constitution to a referendum. Two-thirds of MPs must vote in favour. The ruling Civil Contract party does not have enough seats and needs six more votes.

According to Pashinyan, “institutional peace is now entirely achievable — indeed, it is already within arm’s reach; all we need to do is reach out and grasp it”. He believes that adopting a new Constitution is the way to achieve this.

“This is exclusively our domestic agenda, but it will clearly have regional and international consequences as well,” he said.

During the briefing, Pashinyan also discussed some of the changes to the draft Constitution. In particular, he addressed provisions on judicial reform and possible changes to the state symbols. He stressed that discussions on the draft had only just begun and that dialogue with the opposition and society would continue. He said the ruling party was ready to consider any facts and arguments: “Every issue is open for discussion. But that does not mean we will accept every proposal.”

The following sections contain the prime minister’s comments and explanations of the changes to the draft Constitution.

Changes to the judicial system are “fundamentally important”

The prime minister said that the proposed changes to the judicial system were fundamentally important.

“We face criticism both for the possibility of vetting judges and for the possibility of not doing so. We must decide which of these critical positions carries more weight for us. This is a political choice.”

According to Pashinyan, adopting a new Constitution should resolve the problem of public trust in the judicial system.

“The louder the judicial system protests against these changes, the stronger public consensus will become around the text of the new Constitution,” he said, commenting on a statement by the Union of Judges.

Under the draft Constitution, more than 300 Armenian judges will become acting judges. Authorities will then assess their professional competence, conduct and the legality of their income. The assessment will also cover their compliance with codes of conduct and conflict-of-interest rules over the five years following the Constitution’s entry into force.

A five-member commission, elected by MPs, will assess the judges. The commission will issue either a positive or a negative assessment. Judges who receive a negative assessment will not be reappointed.

Judges will have no right to challenge the commission’s assessments in court.

The Union of Judges issued a statement condemning the draft Constitution. The judges argued that official discussions and consideration of its provisions could undermine the independence and authority of the judiciary.

“Constitutional guarantees of judicial tenure and judicial independence must not become casualties of political expediency. Nor can the need for constitutional reform justify any restrictions on these guarantees,” the statement said.

The Union of Judges also called on the Supreme Judicial Council — the constitutional body that safeguards the independence of courts and judges — to demand the removal of the provisions concerning the judiciary from the draft Constitution.

According to the prime minister, problems in the judicial system require fundamental solutions, including a new Constitution and the introduction of jury trials.

One of the changes proposed in the draft Constitution is the introduction of jury trials. A separate law will determine the categories of cases in which citizens can serve as jurors, as well as the procedures governing their participation.

Speaking about the problems in the judicial system, Pashinyan cited the cases against former president Robert Kocharyan. In particular, he referred to the fact that Kocharyan remained free and put a question to journalists:

“Do you think Robert Kocharyan should be free? I believe he should not be free. I have said so openly. I made that statement in Republic Square in front of tens of thousands of people. And tens of thousands of people applauded this position.”

The prime minister is convinced that the people themselves should make decisions about all aspects of the “life of the state”.

New constitutional provision on revoking citizenship is “a preventive measure”

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether the new constitutional provisions allowing the authorities to revoke citizenship could become an instrument of political pressure.

The prime minister replied that the most reliable way to neutralise this risk was to have an independent judiciary that “would guarantee that this cannot happen”.

“As for other cases — for example, if a person with dual citizenship is convicted of espionage — why should we preserve and protect their citizenship and continue to grant them civil rights?”

According to Pashinyan, the state must protect itself, particularly given the existence of dual citizenship.

“Imagine a situation in which a person with dual citizenship is caught acting as an agent of a foreign intelligence service and is subsequently convicted. Why should we not empower a court to revoke that person’s citizenship? This would serve as an additional preventive measure against treason or espionage.”

Article 24 of the draft Constitution provides that a person may lose their citizenship by court order in certain circumstances, including crimes against the foundations of the constitutional order or state security. The current Constitution does not allow the authorities to revoke citizenship on these grounds. Moreover, it explicitly states that the Republic of Armenia cannot deprive a citizen of their citizenship.

Citizens should decide on changes to state symbols in a referendum

Addressing the absence of descriptions of Armenia’s state symbols in the draft Constitution, Pashinyan said that a law would define them and that voters would approve it in a referendum.

“We have no specific proposal. We are saying that this law will be adopted in a referendum. Citizens themselves must decide what they consider to be their flag, coat of arms and national anthem.”

The prime minister believes that the authorities must do everything possible to ensure that citizens feel an organic connection with the state and its symbols.

One journalist asked: “Are you going to say now that if we do not remove Mount Ararat from the coat of arms, war will break out?”

“No, I will not threaten anyone,” Nikol Pashinyan replied.

The current Constitution describes the colours of the Armenian flag and their order, as well as the main elements of the coat of arms. The draft Constitution contains no descriptions of the flag or coat of arms. It states that the symbols of the Republic of Armenia are its coat of arms, flag and national anthem. A law, which voters will approve in a referendum, will define their descriptions or lyrics.

World.title: Abkhazia introduces law to curb dumping by Russian tour operators
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to introduce an anti-dumping law aimed at protecting small hotels from organised price-cutting by large Russian tour operators.

Abkhazia’s parliament has already passed the bill, titled “On Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Republic of Abkhazia to Prevent the Monopolisation of the Tourist Accommodation Services Market”, in its first reading.

For several years, a trend has emerged in which large Russian tour operators buy up hotel rooms in Abkhazia at low prices ahead of the tourist season. They then sell them to tourists at even lower rates, offsetting the losses through other services.

The tour operators themselves describe this kind of dumping — offering a hotel room with three meals a day for 200 roubles ($2–3) — as a “special offer” designed to attract tourists to Abkhazia.

Small hotels suffer the most. They cannot afford to adopt such pricing policies and find themselves at a competitive disadvantage. As a result, they incur losses, and some even go bankrupt, selling their properties or renting them out to the same large tour operators.

Under the new bill:

Hotels will have to register contracts containing fixed room quotas with the Ministry of Tourism.

The register will record the number of rooms and the purchase price.

If a tour operator sells a room for more than 30% below its purchase price, the Ministry of Tourism will be able to issue a formal complaint.

If the violation is not rectified, sales may be suspended or the contract terminated.

The bill also introduces the concept of a “high season”, covering the period from 1 June to 1 September, during which all promotional discounts will be prohibited.

Abkhazia’s Tourism Minister Astamur Logua stressed that the aim was not to ban discounts, but to prevent dumping and market monopolisation.

If passed, the new rules could come into force on 1 January 2027.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan repeals 47 decrees by former leader: what decisions are affected?
World.content:
Azerbaijan: Decrees by former Nakhchivan leader repealed

Jabbar Musayev, prime minister of Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic, has repealed 47 decrees signed by Vasif Talibov during his time as chairman of the Supreme Assembly and amended several others.

The autonomous republic’s official newspaper, Sharq Gapisi, reported the decision on 25 November. The text of the decision has not been made public, and the authorities have not explained the reasons behind it. The newspaper published only a list of the repealed decrees.

The decision came 20 days after the authorities abolished Nakhchivan’s permanent representation in Baku. We previously reported on how control over the autonomous republic had gradually shifted to Baku over the past four years.

Now another question arises: what does the list of repealed decrees reveal about the separate system of governance that Talibov built over 27 years?

What is on the list?

Most of the repealed decrees concern the establishment of autonomous republic institutions, the approval of their organisational structures and regulations governing their activities. The documents can be grouped into several categories.

Security and customs. Decrees approving the regulations and structure of Nakhchivan’s Ministry of National Security, the structure of the autonomous republic’s State Customs Committee, and social protection measures for customs officials.

Finance and economy. Decrees approving regulations for the Ministry of Taxes and the Ministry of Economic Development, as well as documents governing the activities of the State Procurement Agency, the Entrepreneurship Support Fund, industrial parks, the State Social Protection Fund and the Main State Insurance Agency.

Infrastructure. Decrees concerning Nakhchivan International Airport, the state-owned Nahavtoyol company, the State Motor Transport Concern, the Nakhchivan Oil and Gas Supply Enterprise, and the ministries of transport and communications.

Law, media and religion. Decrees concerning the activities of the Nakhchivan ombudsman, the Television and Radio Council, the State Committee for Television and Radio Broadcasting, the Office for Religious Organisations and the Civil Service Commission under the chairman of the Supreme Assembly.

Honorary titles. The first two items on the list concern the establishment of honorary titles in the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic and the approval of regulations governing them.

The repealed decrees also include those approving the “new structure” of the autonomous republic’s Cabinet of Ministers, the organisational structures of several central executive bodies and the Ministry of Education, as well as regulations governing the Nakhchivan branch of the Azerbaijan National Academy of Sciences (ANAS).

The legal foundations of a “state within a state”

Talibov served as chairman of the Supreme Assembly from December 1995 to December 2022. During his tenure, the autonomous republic had its own Ministry of Taxes, Customs Committee, Ministry of National Security, ombudsman institution, Television and Radio Council, and Civil Service Commission.

The list of repealed decrees shows that all these bodies were established or operated under decrees issued by the chairman of the Supreme Assembly. In other words, Talibov headed the parliament while also creating the autonomous republic’s executive bodies through his own decrees.

Now, however, the Cabinet of Ministers’ head — rather than the Supreme Assembly — is repealing these decrees. This became possible following constitutional amendments that took effect in March 2026. Under a law passed by the Milli Majlis in February, the article establishing the position of “highest official of the autonomous republic” was removed from Nakhchivan’s Constitution.

The Cabinet of Ministers is no longer subordinate to the Supreme Assembly and is authorised, in coordination with the president, to establish and abolish central executive bodies. The Constitution of the autonomous republic now recognises the president’s authorised representation in Nakhchivan as an executive body.

Almost four years have passed since Talibov’s resignation, but a new chairman of the Supreme Assembly has yet to be elected.

What will happen to the agencies?

The Sharq Gapisi newspaper’s report mentions only the repeal of the decrees. It does not clarify whether the agencies themselves will be abolished or which central government bodies will take over their functions.

Some changes took place even before the decision. Nakhchivan’s branches of the State Security Service and the State Customs Committee were transferred to the direct control of Baku. Following Talibov’s resignation, many officials in the autonomous republic came under investigation on charges of embezzlement and other crimes.

The fate of honorary titles remains another unresolved issue. It is not yet clear whether people who received honorary titles from the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic during Talibov’s tenure will retain their status and the associated benefits.

The future of the autonomous republic’s ombudsman institution is also uncertain. It remains unclear whether Nakhchivan residents will have to turn exclusively to the ombudsman in Baku if their rights are violated.

What does Baku say?

In August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said in an interview with AzTV in Nakhchivan that the autonomous republic would retain its status, but its system of governance needed to be “improved”. He noted that the model of special presidential representatives already operating in Karabakh and Eastern Zangazur also applied to Nakhchivan:

“In this way, we are effectively bringing these three regions together from an administrative point of view as well.”

Experts see the repeal of the decrees as another step towards strengthening central government control over the autonomous republic. Nakhchivan’s authorities have yet to provide any further explanation of the decision.

World.title: TRACECA presents Middle Corridor development strategy at forum in China
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. TRACECA Secretary General Zhasurbek Choriyev presented the development strategy for the Europe-Caucasus-Asia transport corridor at the Trans-Caspian Corridor Industry & Investment Forum 2026, held in Zhengzhou, China.

According to TRACECA, the forum was held as part of the 23rd China International Transportation and Logistics Expo and Logistics Industry Week. It was organized by the China Communications and Transportation Association and Beijing Trans-Eurasia International Freight Forwarding Co., Ltd.

The event brought together representatives of government agencies, diplomatic missions, industry associations, and leading logistics, railway and technology companies from China and across Eurasia.

Choriyev delivered a presentation titled "A Unified Development Strategy for the Europe-Caucasus-Asia Corridor, Multilateral Transit Facilitation Mechanisms and Regional Connectivity Plans."

In his remarks, he noted that, amid the realignment of global supply chains, the Trans-Caspian route had evolved from an alternative transport option into a strategic necessity for Eurasian trade.

The secretary general also highlighted TRACECA's institutional status as an intergovernmental organization operating under the legally binding Basic Multilateral Agreement signed in 1998.

Particular attention was given to the Development Strategy for the Europe-Caucasus-Asia International Transport Corridor for 2027–2036, which is currently undergoing approval by member states.

The document envisages a shift in TRACECA's role from coordinating national efforts to actively managing corridor development through measurable performance indicators.

The strategy sets the following targets:

- Reduce border-crossing times to two hours or less by 2030;

- Cut overall cargo delivery times on selected routes by 30% by 2036;

- Digitize 80% of transport documents by 2032;

- Double the share of container traffic and increase the share of environmentally friendly transport to 20% by 2036.

To achieve these goals, TRACECA is introducing several tools, including a Corridor Performance Monitoring System, a Corridor Bottleneck and Capacity Matrix, and a Corridor Digital Ecosystem of Platforms.

The strategy also provides for mechanisms for attracting investment through the TRACECA Fund and TRACECA Business Council.

Other speakers at the forum included Trade Representative of the Azerbaijani Embassy in China Teymur Nadiroglu, Deputy Secretary General of the International Association of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route Saut Shynybayev, and executives of major Chinese corporations operating in multimodal transport, the TIR system, electric transport and intelligent logistics equipment.

A separate part of Choriyev's presentation focused on prospects for expanding cooperation with China, the largest origin and destination market for cargo transported along the Middle Corridor.

The secretary general outlined opportunities for technological cooperation in smart logistics, Chinese business participation in TRACECA's priority infrastructure projects for 2027–2030, and the possibility of formalizing dialogue by granting China observer status under the TRACECA Basic Multilateral Agreement.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Türkiye's Eksim Holding sign agreement on mining cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Uzbekistan and Turkish investment group Eksim Holding have signed a bilateral agreement to advance cooperation in the mining industry, following a meeting in Tashkent between the company's representatives and Uzbek Deputy Minister of Mining Industry and Geology Ural Yusupov on November 27.

According to Uzbekistan's Ministry of Mining Industry and Geology, the sides discussed the progress of ongoing joint projects, results achieved so far and opportunities to expand their cooperation.

Eksim Holding representatives provided an update on projects being implemented jointly with Uzbekistan and outlined the next stages of their development.

The meeting concluded with the signing of a bilateral agreement.

Founded in 1986, Eksim Holding is a Turkish investment group operating in renewable energy, electricity distribution, food production, technology and venture capital. The group has more than 20 subsidiaries and approximately 10,000 employees. Its energy business includes wind, solar and hydropower projects in Türkiye and international markets.

Uzbekistan and Türkiye have continued to expand their economic partnership, with bilateral trade reaching approximately $3 billion in 2025. Turkish investment in Uzbekistan has also grown, with 2,137 enterprises involving Turkish capital operating in the country as of January 2026, according to Uzbekistan's official data.

Mining and geology are among the priority areas for further cooperation. During an October 2026 meeting in Ankara, the two countries agreed to deepen industrial cooperation and work toward increasing bilateral trade to $5 billion. The first meeting of the Uzbek-Turkish High-Level Business Support Council in Tashkent on November 19 resulted in trade and investment agreements worth $11.2 billion.

World.title: Uzbekistan signs tourism infrastructure memorandums with China, Türkiye
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Uzbekistan has signed memorandums of cooperation with Chinese and Turkish partners to develop tourism infrastructure, prepare destination master plans and attract international investment at the CAEx Exhibition Center during the 31st Tashkent International Tourism Fair, "Tourism on the Silk Road" on November 27.

According to Uzbekistan's Tourism Commitee, the Uzbek side signed the documents with Zhang Xiaoli, vice president of the China Tourism Association, and Tülay Hatırnaz, a representative of Turkish branch of Arup company responsible for its operations in Asian countries.

The memorandums provide for cooperation in the integrated development of tourism destinations and the preparation of master plans in line with international standards.

Moreover, the parties plan to work together to attract international experts and investors, secure grant funding and obtain technical assistance for tourism infrastructure projects.

As part of the cooperation, Uzbek representatives are expected to make working visits to China and Türkiye to study tourism destinations and the work of project offices responsible for developing master plans.

The agreements also envisage professional training for specialists and the exchange of experience in tourism planning and infrastructure development.

The 31st Tashkent International Tourism Fair, held under the theme "Tourism on the Silk Road," brings together representatives of the tourism industry, government agencies, international organizations and businesses to discuss sector development, promote tourism products and establish new partnerships. The event also serves as a platform for presenting investment opportunities and expanding international cooperation in tourism.
