World.title: Kyrgyzstan commissions about 50 hydropower plants in five years – ministry
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Kyrgyzstan has commissioned around 50 small and medium-sized hydropower plants over the past five years, while approximately 50 more facilities are under construction, according to the press service of the Ministry of Energy of Kyrgyzstan.

Minister of Energy Altynbek Rysbekov announced the figures at the first meeting of the Steering Council of the Belt and Road Energy Partnership, held in Qingdao, China, on November 25–26, 2026, as part of the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministers' Conference.

In his address, Altynbek Rysbekov noted that Kyrgyzstan's GDP increased by 11.1% in 2025, one of the highest growth rates in Central Asia. He stressed the importance of strengthening the country's energy capacity amid economic growth.

The minister highlighted the completion of the modernization of all four generating units at the Toktogul Hydropower Plant, which increased the facility's installed capacity by 240 megawatts. He also presented the construction of the 1,860-megawatt Kambarata-1 Hydropower Plant as a strategic project.

During the meeting, members of the Steering Council reviewed documents outlining the partnership's priority areas, including the transition to green energy, modernization of electricity grid infrastructure, digitalization, and the introduction of artificial intelligence in the energy sector.

Kyrgyzstan's participation in the partnership is aimed at strengthening international cooperation, attracting investment and advanced technologies, and implementing joint energy projects.

World.title: Azerbaijan's AI, IP proposals praised at WIPO forum – IP Agency
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) has highly commended Azerbaijan's proposals on intellectual property and artificial intelligence (AI), the Intellectual Property Agency of the Republic of Azerbaijan said.

The Global Forum on Intellectual Property and Artificial Intelligence, organized by WIPO, was held in Geneva on November 9–10, 2026.

According to the agency, the forum brought together intellectual property and innovation leaders from various countries, prominent scholars and experts from leading universities worldwide, representatives of international civil society organizations, and senior executives of international technology companies at the forefront of AI development.

Chairman of the Board of the Intellectual Property Agency of Azerbaijan Kamran Imanov addressed the forum online on November 10.

At the outset, Imanov thanked WIPO for organizing this important international dialogue on the interaction between artificial intelligence and intellectual property.

In his remarks, Imanov stressed that AI development is one of Azerbaijan's strategic state policy priorities. He noted that the special attention paid to this area by President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev underpins the country's efforts to accelerate digital transformation, introduce advanced technologies and build an AI ecosystem.

In this context, he highlighted the adoption of Azerbaijan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy for 2025–2028 and the establishment of the Digital Development Council, chaired by First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva. These initiatives demonstrate the importance attached at the highest level to coordinating state policy on digital development and AI and strengthening the institutional mechanisms in this area.

The agency chairman also addressed key issues at the intersection of intellectual property and AI. He examined the impact of generative AI on the nature of creative activity and traditional legal concepts, the philosophical, legal and practical aspects of AI legal personality, and the legal protection of intellectual outputs generated by AI.

Imanov put forward proposals on the gradual determination of AI's legal personality; introducing a special 25–30-year legal protection regime for works autonomously generated by AI; ensuring fair compensation for copyright holders whose protected works are used to train AI systems; establishing a compulsory licensing mechanism designed to support human creativity; and developing a dedicated international protocol governing the legal status of AI-generated content.

He also stressed the importance of establishing new legal mechanisms in response to technological progress while maintaining human oversight of artificial intelligence. Further details of his address are available here.

It is particularly noteworthy that, although the forum regulations allocated three minutes for each speaker, the organizers granted Imanov 10 minutes to deliver his address at their invitation.

His speech on contemporary intellectual property and AI issues was closely followed and highly appreciated by forum participants.

In this regard, WIPO Director General Daren Tang sent a letter of appreciation to Imanov.

In the letter, Tang said he was particularly pleased with Azerbaijan's active participation in the discussions and its contribution of perspectives and practical proposals on the evolving relationship between AI and intellectual property.

"Such active engagement by our Member States is important as we work together to ensure that the international intellectual property system continues to respond effectively to rapid technological change," the letter said.

World.title: Azerbaijan to establish paper bag production facility worth over $23.5M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. A paper bag manufacturing facility totaling over 40 million manat ($23.5 million) will be established in Azerbaijan, Economic Zones Development Agency under the Ministry of Economy reported.

According to the report, the project for the production of kraft-paper bags with multi-layer valves will be implemented by Aztech Packing LLC, a new resident of Sumgayit Industrial Park, which is managed by the agency.

Within the framework of the project, the production of multi-ply valved kraft paper sacks will be established within the Industrial Park. The project aims for an annual production capacity of 110 million sacks.

Established by a decree signed by the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev on December 21, 2011, the Sumgayit Industrial Park aims to create favorable conditions for competitive industrial production based on innovative and high technologies, support entrepreneurship, promote the sustainable development of the non-oil sector, and increase employment in industry.

The industrial park currently covers 640 hectares and is the largest of its kind in the South Caucasus. It has 46 registered residents, who have invested more than 5.6 billion manat ($3.29 billion) in the park to date and created over 6,400 jobs.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan's foreign trade exceeds $12B in eight months
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. Kyrgyzstan's foreign trade turnover exceeded $12 billion in January–August 2026, increasing by 13.3% year on year, according to the press service of the Cabinet of Ministers.

Chairman of the Cabinet of Ministers and Head of the Presidential Administration Adylbek Kasymaliev announced the figure during a meeting with the business community at the "Investment Vector: Government and Business – Open Dialogue" forum in Bishkek on November 27.

Adylbek Kasymaliev said Kyrgyzstan's strategic goal was to become a regional manufacturing and logistics hub and integrate into global value chains. He urged investors to view the country as a production base for accessing larger regional markets rather than as a market with limited domestic demand.

He stressed that investors needed not only financing and infrastructure, but also qualified personnel, digital services, and reliable legal protection. In particular, he highlighted the importance of protecting private property, ensuring compliance with contractual obligations, and providing fair judicial safeguards.

The forum brought together representatives of the Supreme Court, the Prosecutor General's Office, ministries, tax and customs authorities, the National Investment Agency, the Agency for Land Resources, and local administrations, among others.

During the meeting, business representatives raised questions concerning land relations, taxation, contractual obligations, bank financing, and preferential financing.

Following the discussions, Adylbek Kasymaliev instructed government and local authorities to appoint officials responsible for attracting investment and assess their performance against specific key performance indicators (KPIs).

World.title: Victoria's election day arrives, as state appears poised to dump Labor
World.content:
Election day has finally arrived in Victoria after a campaign marked by Labor's plummeting polling and a controversial last-minute policy dump from the Coalition.

Around half the state's 4.7 million eligible voters have already cast their ballots via postal votes and at early voting centres.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: For all the latest news from the campaign trail, read our blog.

The remainder will head to polling booths today, in an election widely expected to bring about a change of government after 12 years of Labor.

The Coalition's campaign has not been without controversy, with Liberal leader Jess Wilson on the defensive after a last-minute reveal of planned privatisation and kinder cuts.

The Coalition's path to victory, which relies on picking up more than a dozen new seats, could also be complicated by the rise in popularity of One Nation.

Jess Wilson has been trying to clean up the Liberal Party's image after years of internal division. (ABC News: Antonia O'Flaherty)

The past four years have involved difficult chapters for both Labor and the Liberals, with three leadership changes each since Daniel Andrews and Matthew Guy led their parties to the 2022 election.

Andrews resigned from politics in 2023, handing Labor leadership and premier's job to Jacinta Allan.

Then as Labor's popularity plummeted amid Big Build corruption allegations and a controversial change to the emergency services levy, Ms Allan was backed into resigning this July.

Ben Carroll seized the premiership from Jacinta Allan amid concerns over Big Build corruption. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

After earlier denying he would challenge Allan, then-deputy premier Ben Carroll became the leader after what has been described as a chaotic party room meeting.

The Liberal Party has rolled out three leaders since the last election — Matthew Guy, Brad Battin and finally Jess Wilson.

But the Liberals' leadership challenges faded firmly into the past as the party surged ahead in the polls on the back of the spate of home invasions, car thefts, machete attacks and firebombings.

Labor MPs conduct 'pre-mortem' After three successive election victories, Victoria's Labor Party is sensing electoral failure for the first time in 16 years.

The Wilson-led opposition continued on a platform of law and order throughout the year, which played out as an extended election campaign, well in excess of the traditional six-week timeframes of the past.

Also straying from tradition, there was no leaders debate.

However Carroll, Wilson, One Nation's Warren Pickering and the Greens' Ellen Sandell did front a televised leaders forum, discussing questions from the audience.

One Nation and Greens expected to perform well

Labor is bracing for a devastating hit to the party's primary vote.

Despite calling a royal commission into the Big Build allegations, Carroll has also been weighed down by Victoria's soaring debt and two controversial leaders during Labor's years in government.

And while polling continues to suggest a Wilson-led Coalition will win today's election, the results are not expected to be all rosy.

They may enter government with an historically low primary vote.

Earlier predictions of One Nation's success have been tempered by more recent opinion polls that now have Pauline Hanson's party trailing the Coalition by some way.

Pauline Hanson and Warren Pickering ahead of the race to pick up seats in the Victorian election. (ABC News)

It has been a bumpy campaign for the party with one candidate dumped over social media posts that praised Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler.

Another stepped down after anti-Muslim rhetoric and for making highly sexualised remarks including that seeking consent was "cringe".

Victorian election analysis As Liberal leader Jess Wilson's political prospects firm, the chances of a One Nation wipeout in Victoria's lower house are receding. But pockets of opportunity remain for the resurgent party.

Anti-violence campaigners accused yet another of making misogynistic comments on a video featuring former AFL player Dustin Martin.

Even party leader Warren Pickering had to front the media in September, admitting to a history of drug use and drink driving when he was younger, after allegations were aired by a former partner.

Still, One Nation is expected to attract more than 20 per cent of the primary vote.

Progressive voters are looking elsewhere, which has created hope among the Victorian Greens.

Ellen Sandell (left) used colourful stunts to keep the Greens campaign focused on the party's traditional strengths of environmental advocacy and social justice. (ABC News)

The party is looking to retain its seats in Melbourne, Richmond and Brunswick, and is optimistic about taking back Northcote and Prahran.

The Greens also have their eyes on Footscray, Pascoe Vale, and possibly Preston and Albert Park.

The key policies on offer from parties in the 2026 Victorian state election Political parties are laying out their visions for the state's future, as voters prepare to head to the polls on November 28.

But Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the party was facing some tough hurdles.

"We know that Greens seats are actually always incredibly close," she said.

"This time, in particular, in order for the Greens to win a seat, we essentially have to get more votes than Labor, Liberal, One Nation combined because of the preference deals [they] have done with each other."

Where to tune in for the ABC's election night coverage

As Victoria votes, the ABC will have comprehensive coverage across our radio, television and online platforms.

Our live blog will keep you across all the latest developments throughout the day, with results analysis from state political reporter Rachel Eddie.

Election night coverage kicks off at 6pm on ABC TV, ABC News Channel, and streaming on iview.

The program will be simulcast on 774 ABC Melbourne and across all ABC Regional Victorian radio stations. Tune in online using the ABC Listen app.

Hosts David Speers and Patricia Karvelas will be joined by chief elections and data analyst Casey Briggs, state political reporter Richard Willingham and 774 ABC Melbourne Mornings presenter Raf Epstein to bring you fast, accurate and reliable analysis of the results.

Keep an eye on the ABC's social media platforms for highlights from the day's coverage, and explore more Victorian election news coverage and analysis on our website.

World.title: Zelenskyy says Trump's relationship with Putin like being friends with Hitler
World.content:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Donald Trump's relationship with Russia's Vladimir Putin is comparable to being friends with Adolf Hitler as Kyiv grows increasingly frustrated at how the US is handling peace negotiations.

In an interview with the BBC in Kyiv, Mr Zelenskyy said it was "strange" for the US president to call Mr Putin a friend and would be similar to making the same comment about Hitler during World War II.

"He's an aggressor … and a killer. He can't be a friend," he said.

"It's the same that somebody say about Hitler during the Second World War that he's a good friend. No, he's not a friend."

Donald Trump's relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin has been questioned by Kyiv. (AP: Matt Rourke/Alexei Nikolsky)

Mr Zelenskyy was speaking a week after Mr Trump had embraced the Russian president as a "friend" at a summit in China.

Days later Mr Trump posted a photo on his Truth Social platform of the pair shaking hands there and titled it "My Friend".

Mr Trump's relationship with Mr Zelenskyy has long been uneasy, most notably breaking down publicly in February 2025 when the US president confronted him in the Oval Office.

The pair have continued to clash more recently with the US president blaming Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for high energy costs and threatening to cut off intelligence support.

Mr Zelenskyy has said Mr Trump's position is encouraging Russia to continue attacking Ukraine.

Speaking with the BBC, Mr Zelenskyy complained the US was not doing enough to negotiate peace with Russia and called on "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve an outcome.

"They have to pressure on the situation. The situation is when Russia is aggressor," he said.

"It's not about comfortable talks. It's about strong country who can pressure because this country (US) has power and respect."

Kushner praises Putin's 'restraint'

It comes as US envoy Jared Kushner praised the Russian president "grandmaster of politics" and a "historic figure" who had "shown restraint" by agreeing to not use nuclear weapons against Ukraine.

Loading...

Mr Kushner, Trump's son-in-law who is mediating Russia-Ukraine talks with envoy Steve Witkoff, said that after talking at length with Putin, he believed Putin wanted peace almost five years after Moscow's invasion.

Mr Putin "has agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing, and he's reassured us that that's not his intention", Kushner said on a podcast by German media group Axel Springer Creators.

Trump urges Putin to end 'military aggression' US President Donald Trump describes the war in Ukraine as a complete bloodbath.

Mr Kushner added: "What (Putin) is saying is peace, but I think it's always peace on what terms" as the talks have hit "a little bit of a deadlock" over the fate of Ukrainian territory.

Mr Zelenskyy and European leaders have criticised Mr Putin for what they describe as Moscow's refusal to compromise and persistence to press on with an invasion which has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians.

According to Mr Kushner, the Kremlin wants a new relationship with Washington as Russia seeks to keep NATO away from its borders.

Mr Trump has said on social media he would like to see Putin "pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly".

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said the US was approaching peace talks with an understanding of the need to eliminate what Russia calls the "root causes" of the conflict, including "the creation of threats to Russia's security right on our borders".

Ukraine races to bolster air defences

Mr Zelenskyy has warned Ukraine's intelligence indicates that Moscow is "completing preparations for a new massive strike" which Kyiv says aims to deprive civilians of power and running water as the winter approaches.

Ukraine defends strikes in international waters Two Libyan army personnel have succumbed to wounds suffered in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russian ships in Benghazi.

Russian missile and drone attacks have battered Ukraine's power grid, killed civilians and choked the economy since the invasion.

"The Russians continue to target substations, overhead powerlines, and the entire power grid," Mr Zelenskyy said on social media.

Ukraine is pushing its allies to provide more air defence supplies as crews work to restore electricity in six Ukrainian regions after a Russian assault on Wednesday night involving ballistic missiles and 113 drones.

Ukraine has used its own long-range weapons to hit back at targets in Russia, and Russian vessels docked at a Libyan port in an attack which has caused alarm amongst some European leaders.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Australia 'have to be better,' humbled by England at rain-soaked Gabba
World.content:
England has taken a 2-1 series lead in its T20I series against Australia with another dominant victory on a rainy Friday evening at the Gabba.

Australia was bowled out for just 108 in 16.5 overs, its lowest ever T20I score on home soil when batting first.

The 23,536 Gabba fans may have feared whether, after three superb Sheffield Shield games went down to the wire this week, they would see a second lopsided white-ball contest in as many matches following England's dominant victory at Carrara on Tuesday.

And although Riley Meredith (3-30) and Billy Stanlake (0-46) provided some jeopardy with their own vicious pace, the result was never in doubt.

"A very disappointing night. We have to own that," Mitch Marsh said.

"Some of our [shot] selection was not to up to it tonight, but I said to to this young group at the start of the series I don't want them to fear making mistakes.

"Probably tonight we needed to be more calculated and understand the conditions we were playing in.

"That was a belting wicket - as good as the Gabba can get - so no excuses. We have to be better."

England comfortably chased down a revised target of 93 with 43 balls to spare, sealing a seven-wicket victory.

Jamie Overton was irresistible, bowling with pace and ferocity that Australian bowlers have terrorised Englishmen with for decades at this ground, taking a career-best 5-12.

Jordan Cox scored an unbeaten 33. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

England has traditionally been carved up by Australian quicks at the Gabba, but this time the shoe was on the other foot.

England won the toss and bowled first, with former Australia coach Darren Lehmann saying on ABC Radio that "Australia will be looking for 220, maybe more," and were on track early despite Mitch Marsh being caught at mid-on for 11 off Dawson's bowling.

Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper both hit out, smashing five sixes between them before both fell in consecutive overs; Harper for 26 off 14 balls and Fraser-McGurk becoming Overton's first victim after an 11-ball 22.

Nikhil Chaudhary, scorer of 66 and 45 in his last two innings for Australia, forwent the power displayed by his colleagues to deliver a range of delightful dabs with a delicacy and deftness at odds with the slogging shown elsewhere.

Overton wasn't having a bar of it, though.

The 32-year-old Devonian aimed a sharp bouncer that cracked into Chaudhary's helmet in one over, and thumped Tim David on the forearm with a 142km/h the next.

The next ball, David (6) was out, hooking a 145km/h snorter straight to Henry Crocombe at fine leg, with Overton claiming the wicket of Joel Davies (3) soon after.

Chaudhary literally hit back for Australia, smashing a fearsome drive straight back at Overton, who was smashed on the thumb in his follow-through.

Jamie Overton delivered some blows, and took one himself. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

After a short delay for treatment, Overton had Chaudhary (19) caught after he spooned a lofted drive straight down long-on's throat.

Overton still was not done. Ben Dwarshuis was beaten for pace and edged behind for a four-ball duck, a double-wicket maiden to finish, giving Overton the second-best figures by an England player in T20 international cricket.

Adam Zampa's dismissal was the first wicket Overton did not play a part in, when he edged Dawson behind for 3.

But Australia's malaise deepened when Mitchell Owen, Australia's last real batting hope, was catastrophically run out for 16 by Phil Salt trying to take a mad second run to cover.

Curran, who went for 16 in his first disastrous over, ended Australia's innings in his second, bowling Billy Stanlake for a duck as Australia were all out for 108.

England started well but lost Phil Salt (5), caught at cover off a rising Riley Meredith delivery, and Aneurin Donald, carrying on with his big-hitting ways by belting six boundaries in a 13-ball 32.

The first brief rain delay 3.5 overs into England's reply gave Australia time to regroup, with Stanlake underlining the hosts' renewed vigour by knocking Harry Brook off his feet with a spectacular bouncer first ball back.

Billy Stanlake felled Harry Brook with a brute of a bouncer after the first rain break. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Meredith then took two wickets in the next over as England stumbled from 1-45 to 3-49 in six deliveries.

After a further delay that wiped three overs from England's chase, a revised target of 98 set by DLS method, Meredith should have had another, Chaudhary dropping Jordan Cox when the wicketkeeper was on 1.

Dwarshuis then shelled a tough caught-and-bowled chance on Banton with the Englishman on 9.

Another rain delay, with England just seven runs short at that point, further reduced the target to 93 in 16 overs, with the tourists comfortably making it with 43 balls to spare as Jordan Cox (33) and Tom Banton (10) steered them home.

England is now two wins from two in T20 cricket at the Gabba, having beaten New Zealand by 20 runs en route to the 2022 T20 World Cup title.

Australia was beaten for just the second time in nine completed matches, its first T20I defeat since losing to the West Indies in 2013.

England can seal the five-match series on Sunday at the SCG, with the final game in Canberra on Wednesday.

World.title: Sony's 1999 robot dog toys rehomed in Japan hospitals to offer companionship
World.content:
The people at Sony don't use words like "product" when they talk about Aibo, the Japanese electronics company's robotic dog.

Aibo robots, which first went on sale in 1999, are all sold out and no longer in production.

But some owners who had to part with their Aibo have donated the robots to Tokyo-based Sony Group Corporation for an "adoption program", where they get treated to repairs and upgrades.

Those robot pets now have new homes in hospitals and other facilities.

Sony does not disclose the pricing or the number of Aibo robots that have been sold.

Packed with sensors and digital cameras, Aibo has been programmed to remember its name, the owner's face and its surroundings.

Sony official Yoshiyuki Katsuno oversees the Aibo robot dog "adoption" program. (AP: Yuri Kageyama)

Aibo robot dog 'like a child'

The robot barks, cocks its head, moves its ears, waddles toward you, acts happy when petted, and goes to "sleep".

"The owners feel as though they are sending off what has become to them like their own child," said Sony official Yoshiyuki Katsuno, who oversaw the program.

Aibo gets people talking to each other, and can offer tired souls a perk to pick themselves up and keep going, according to Mr Katsuno.

"We hope to spread the emotional healing and human interaction that Aibo has to offer," he said.

Tokyo businesses where humans operate robots Ory Yoshifuji's Tokyo business employs housebound individuals to operate robots as waitstaff at a cafe and as personal tour guides in the city.

Cuteness is seen as desirable in Japanese culture, where being "kawaii", or "cute", is not a sign of weakness or inferiority, but an endearing trait that encourages harmony and communication.

And so, if the need is for a soulmate, it's better to have that cute look, said Jerry Wang, executive chairman of FF EAI Robotics Ecosystem.

"If you want some emotional attachment, you want a cute shape," he said.

At a University on the outskirts of Tokyo, a nurse had to do some looking to find a wandering Aibo during a recent visit.

But Aibo has helped with the long waits for visiting patients and succeeded in persuading reluctant children to get examined, says doctor Manabu Komori.

That field involves diagnosing and treating sicknesses related to the ear, nose and throat, with many child patients.

"It helps motivate the kids," Dr Komori said.

"Going to a hospital is basically not very pleasant."

The hospital also uses real dogs to help patients feel better, though the animals require care and food and can be temperamental.

That means a robot dog offers some advantages, although Dr Komori was careful not to say they were better than real dogs.

World.title: International child abuse investigations lead to Far North Queensland arrests
World.content:
Two men have been charged, and a third is under investigation, after international child exploitation cases led police to separate arrests in Far North Queensland this week.

Australian Federal Police said the men — a 37-year-old from Mossman, a 48-year-old from Cairns and a 31-year-old from Goldsborough, south of Cairns — are linked to alleged child abuse in Ukraine, the Philippines, and the USA.

The Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation and Europol allege a woman in Ukraine provided 'sexually explicit material' of her eight-year-old daughter to a Mossman man.

AFP officers arrest a 37-year-old man in Mossman, Queensland, on child exploitation charges. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

He was arrested on Tuesday and charged with using a carriage service to possess child abuse material, and faces a maximum sentence of 15 years in jail.

He has been bailed to appear in Mossman Magistrates Court on December 16.

AFP officers forensically examine devices at a Mossman property in relation to the arrest of a 37-year-old man in relation to child exploitation investigations. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

The Cairns man was arrested on Wednesday after he allegedly transferred money to an alleged child exploitation "facilitator" in the Philippines "on multiple occasions".

He was not charged with child abuse, but the AFP said investigations are ongoing.

He was charged with drug offences, and will appear in Cairns Magistrates Court on December 3.

A 31-year-old man from Goldsborough was arrested on the side of the Bruce Highway at Mount Sheridan in relation to child exploitation investigations. He has not been charged but remains under investigation. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

The 31-year-old man was arrested near Gordonvale yesterday after a tip-off from the United States' National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children.

They allege he is connected to an upload of child abuse material through a messenger platform, but he has not been charged and was released "pending further enquiries".

AFP Detective Sergeant Paul Gurn said none of the cases are believed to be linked.

"The AFP works closely with partners in Australia and overseas to identify alleged offenders, safeguard children and prevent further victimisation," he said.

World.title: Man found 'likely involved' in cold-case murder
World.content:
A coronial inquest into the deaths of three tourists in outback Queensland has found the police investigation was "fatally flawed" and the man previously charged over the deaths was reasonably suspected of having "direct involvement".

Karen Edwards, 23, Timothy Thomson, 31, and Gordon Twaddle, 22, died in a fatal shooting about 10 kilometres north of Mount Isa in October 1978.

After a two-week inquest into their deaths in October 2025, Queensland Coroner David O'Connell delivered his findings on Friday, and determined, on the balance of probabilities, that Bruce Preston, a Mount Isa resident in 1978, had "direct involvement" in the deaths.

Gordon Twaddle, Karen Edwards and Tim Thomson were last seen at the Moondarra Caravan Park in Mount Isa on October 5, 1978. (Supplied: Queensland Police Service)

What police know happened to the trio October 2 — They leave Alice Springs, stop at Aileron before camping the night at Ti Tree

October 3 — They make stops, including at Devils Marbles, before meeting a male motorcyclist at Frewena and all camp at Barry Caves

October 4 — They travel with the man to Mount Isa but he doesn't check in at caravan park. That night the trio are joined by the man in the Landcruiser

October 5 — The friends are last seen alive leaving with the man in the Toyota Landcruiser. The man later returns alone looking for the dog

October 6 — The campsite is packed up and the dog is found at the Mount Isa dump

October 24/25 — The bodies are discovered in bushland at Spear Creek

November 13 — A local man, 23, is arrested after being found with of Tim Thomson's red BMW motorcycle

Their bodies were discovered in bushland at Spear Creek.

The trio had been on a motorcycle trip from Alice Springs to Melbourne, and their bodies were discovered by a couple who were exercising their greyhound dog.

In his findings on Friday, Coroner O'Connell found conclusions from the 1978-80 police investigation report, presented to the 1980 inquest, were "incorrect and fatally flawed".

Following a fresh cold case investigation in 2019, Mr Preston, who had previously admitted to stealing one of their motorbikes, was arrested over the triple homicide.

However, in 2023, after being committed to stand trial, the prosecution withdrew the case against the then 63-year-old.

Lawyers for Mr Preston have previously said he denies having any involvement in their deaths.

Today, Coroner O'Connell found Mr Preston deliberately lied regarding meeting the three people "out of conscious of guilt".

A 1977 BMW motorcycle belonging to Tim Thomson who was found shot dead north of Mount Isa in 1978. (Supplied: Queensland Police)

"Accordingly, I find that he told lies simply because of his knowledge of having a direct involvement in their deaths," he said.

"I hold the view that I reasonably suspect that Mr Bruce Preston was involved in an indictable offence in the deaths of the three persons.

"Accordingly, I shall refer him to the Director of Public Prosecutions for them to investigate."

He found there was no evidence to indicate anyone other than Mr Preston was directly involved in the deaths, but said the possibility of others present or participating could not be entirely ruled out.

World.title: Roos create AFLW history with three-peat after downing Dees in epic
World.content:
North Melbourne has become the first club to claim three straight AFLW premierships after downing Melbourne in a thrilling grand final.

The Kangaroos were pushed to the limit in wet conditions at Princes Park, but kicked the last three goals of the match inside the final five minutes to run out 6.8 (44) to 2.6 (18) winners.

Kangaroos skipper Jasmine Garner was named Best on Ground after finishing with 26 disposals and five clearances to go along with a goal.

North came out of the gates kicking the first three goals of the game, but were pegged back when the Dees kicked the next two to cut the margin to six points at half-time.

Tayla Harris was inspirational for Melbourne in the second quarter, kicking her team's first goal of the match after taking a towering contested mark inside 50.

With rain increasing after the main break, the second half turned into a dour slugfest as both teams held each other goalless in the third quarter.

The Kangaroos were forced to defend grimly for much of the final quarter as the Demons drew to within one goal with five minutes remaining, but proved to be too strong in the end, with Bella Eddey's final quarter goal proving to be the eventual backbreaker.

North forward Blaithin Bogue was the only multiple goalscorer of the match, kicking both of her goals in the final few minutes to seal the premiership win.

Follow the live blog below for a blow-by-blow recap of the AFLW grand final.

World.title: Matildas legend enters arena of greatness in milestone match
World.content:
It was almost imperceptible.

The slightest shake of her head as Steph Catley listened to Matildas coach Joe Montemurro describe her as one of the world's best footballers.

It was as if she disagreed with the label. But there is no disputing the veteran defender's standing in the game.

She is among the world's elite and one of Australia's greatest ever, as a player, leader, and humble champion.

Against Colombia in Canberra tomorrow night, she will become just the seventh Matilda to reach 150 caps; three other members of that club are in this squad.

"This team feels like my family. We've grown up together, and I'm honoured every single time I touch the pitch with these girls, and I wear that jersey," Catley said.

"So 150 times is massive, and I'm very, very proud of that."

Steph Catley says it's special to reach the milestone at home. (ABC News)

Catley has been at the heart of this generation that has driven women's football in Australia at full throttle, from the shadows into the spotlight.

"I think the work that the previous Matildas have put into this team and women's football has been incredible," she said.

"But this group has done so much for the game, for this team, for women's sport in general.

"There's still a long way to go, but what we've achieved so far has been incredible."

Catley is a fierce presence on the pitch, whether playing for the Matildas or Arsenal, and, at 32, is still very much in her prime.

Steph Catley has been a mainstay of the Matildas' defence for over a decade. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

But when she took the time to reflect on her career, the tears welled up in her eyes.

She said the emotion made it hard to talk about, but she regained her composure and did it anyway.

"I'll never take it for granted that I'm able to represent this team and play for my country," she said.

"And even representing Arsenal, it's everything that I dreamed of as a kid. It's everything I've worked my entire life for, and 150 caps is massive.

"And you do get to a point where every day gets a little bit harder on your body and mentally. But I think being around the girls and the fact that we are like a family … I want to be the best version of myself for them.

"That's what drives me, I think, and my family as well. They're all the way over here in Australia, and I've played overseas pretty much my entire adult life.

"So those sacrifices are big, and I think you want to make it worth it in the long run."

Steph Catley says her teammates and family drive her to keep going. (ABC News)

Montemurro has been a constant in the Catley journey, from coaching her in the A-League Women, to Arsenal, to the national side.

His affection for her as a player and person is clear.

"I've had the honour and the pleasure of working with what I think is one of the world's best footballers, but more importantly, as a person," he said.

"We should be proud as a country to have someone of the calibre of Steph Catley in our midst and growing up and hopefully still with us for a while.

"But what she's given on the field and off the field, I think, has been absolutely special and very unique in the world of football."

Steph Catley has captained the side for extended periods during Sam Kerr's various absences. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Catley, like so many members of this Matildas' golden generation, has achieved so much but is still missing a major international trophy.

Her tearful interview after losing the Women's Asian Cup final in March was filled with the feeling of a missed opportunity.

Time has helped reignite the fire to try again.

"We really could have won that tournament, so I think that was tough for us to take," she said.

"It just builds that hunger for the next chance that we get, another step to build towards what we want to achieve."

World.title: How words from Cathy Freeman inspired North Melbourne’s three-peat
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFLW How words from Cathy Freeman inspired North Melbourne’s three-peat Hannah Kennelly and Roy Ward November 28, 2026 — 12:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Standing shoulder to shoulder in torrential rain, North Melbourne lifted the premiership and roared as pyrotechnics and fireworks illuminated the stormy sky. The rampant rain-soaked Roos have cemented their dynasty, defeating the Melbourne Demons by 26 points in a grand final clash, etching themselves into history by becoming the first AFLW team to clinch a three-peat. The Roos celebrate their premiership win. AFL Photos As the rain lashed Ikon Park, devastated Demons fell to their knees while North players rushed to embrace each other in ecstasy. Darren Crocker’s side will now go down as the most accomplished team in AFLW history – a generational side alongside fellow hat-trick teams Hawthorn and Brisbane in the men’s league. In a post-match press conference, Crocker and skipper Jasmine Garner revealed it was inspiring words from Cathy Freeman, that motivated them pre-game.



Freeman spoke to the Roos players during a visit to the club earlier in the season and something she said stuck with the team. “One of the questions she was asked was how she felt before her 400 metres final at Sydney 2000,” Roos captain and best-on-ground medallist Garner said. “Obviously, she had all that pressure on her but all she said when she was lining up at that starting line was ‘just do what I know’. Devastated Demons fell to the ground when the siren sounded. via Getty Images “Croc [Crocker] used that pre-game and I feel like that really motivated the girls. We didn’t have to go out and do anything special tonight. We just go back to what we had done all year, play the North Melbourne way and if we did that we were pretty confident results would go our way.



With three medals around her neck – premiership, best-on-ground and captain’s – Garner said she felt speechless about the historic three-peat. “Just so glad to do it, and probably [it’s] one of the best. Melbourne were coming and coming in that last quarter, and for us to find a way, like we always do ... it’s unbelievable,” she said. Garner said Friday’s conditions – which thankfully did not feature a lightning delay – made the style of footy scrappy but simple. “It becomes really simple footy, all about territory,” she said. “Get the ball forward, you don’t want to overuse in these conditions.” The Demons put up a valiant effort but were unable to spoil the three-peat, with the Roos storming to victory in the last three minutes, led by Irishwoman Bláithín Bogue, winning 6.8 (44) to 2.6 (18).

WHAT A COP-OUT

Here’s my suggestion for the closing speech at COP26. “We, the leaders of the world, have decided that it’s better for millions of people in the future to suffer and die than for us to have to change the way we live.” Short and sweet . . . and oh so true.

Tom Orren, Wamberal Heights

Greta Thunberg was correct: more blah, blah, blah, and a very weak outcome. We, our children and their children face a very bleak future, if any future at all. For Australians, the last chance to change things will come next May. Sack this ineffective government, ignore the major parties and vote independents to produce a real democracy for once. Then, and only then, will we force change.

Shane Nunan, Finley

COP-OUT26.

Rowan Wigmore, Launceston (Tas)

A RED-LETTER DAY

I was stunned! I can’t believe it! To be published in the Herald letters is fame indeed. For the same letter to be quoted in full by Peter FitzSimons in the Fitz Files (November 13-14) is an honour beyond measure. Thank you, Sydney Morning Herald. Thank you, Peter. At 80, I retire, the envy of all.

William Turner, Port Macquarie

Ye who are without sin, bowl the first ball (“Legacy in ashes: Paine quits after sexting revelations”. November 20-21).

Peter Fleming, Northmead

Why, oh why, didn’t he use Snapchat?

Pam Cameron, Rozelle

World.title: Accelerated learning benefits the brightest
World.content:
Letters NationalNSWLetters Accelerated learning benefits the brightest November 28, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. The comments by Dr Alan Parsons on the acceleration of capable, talented students in HSC courses are insightful to those critical of the process (“Concerns accelerated courses add to HSC’s advantage imbalance”, November 22). Selecting students whose knowledge and skills in particular courses indicates readiness for more advanced study ensures those students’ continued engagement in learning. They learn how the HSC works at their first sitting and study fewer subjects per year. Acceleration is not for everyone, just as not every student will achieve a Band 6 result. Ensuring the right students for acceleration is key. Accelerating whole class groups for some perceived marketing advantage is perverse. At the same time, conflating equality of opportunity with equality of outcome to create a lockstep approach to the HSC will only serve to restrict ultra-bright students to a longer wait before they can show what they have already learnt.

Wayne Duncombe, Glebe Learning levels based on age and convenience can create boredom and frustration for many students. Catering for their interests can create enthusiasm. All successful schools constantly change programs and teaching methods to ensure all students capitalise on their talents and interests and retain the interest and enthusiasm for all that life holds for them, as they journey into the future. To overcome any perceived HSC imbalance, a few more interested and enthusiastic bureaucrats, those who make the rules, may be needed to balance the scales. Joy Cooksey, Harrington The HSC is an internationally recognised credential that has great inbuilt capacity for flexible delivery of courses and acceleration of student learning. While there may be concerns that “accelerated courses add to HSC’s advantage imbalance”, the real issue is perhaps why there is not more flexible packaging of HSC courses through innovative school structures and timetabling models. The HSC unfortunately remains a prisoner of many old-fashioned school structures and practices that need to be rethought to better meet present day student needs.

Rod Leonarder, Roseville All hail Callithump



Your correspondent made my day (Letters, November 22). I had a Catholic education in the 1950s and 60s, but when my father stated his religion was “callithumpian” I accepted it as fact. Joy Heads, Wollstonecraft Unjabbed impose Hobsons choice Let me understand. After December 15, if someone is unvaccinated in a public venue, I, as a vaccinated citizen, cannot know and have no legal right to know (“Calculating social risks faced by vaccinated with science”, November 22). Unvaccinated attendees at a public venue may have a greater risk of contracting a serious COVID-19 infection. But what if I have an underlying health issue? I also could become infected and suffer serious health consequences, or even die. This leaves me with a choice. I can choose not to attend and not to risk it, or I can play Russian roulette and attend. Some choice. Geoff Black, Caves Beach



The unvaccinated will be stopped from entering all public venues when the first lawsuit is filed by a fully vaccinated individual who catches COVID-19 from a known unvaccinated contact. Restaurants, shops and gyms et cetera will not want to take the risk.

Stephanie Edwards, Roseville Lunch with a punch I sympathise with your correspondents’ views regarding expensive power lunches (Letters, November 22) but I believe there is a bigger picture. These lunches are keeping the restaurants operating and staff employed. They have also allowed the owner to fit out the premises, which keeps skilled tradesmen and food merchants employed. The circle of moving money through the economy continues, which benefits us all. It is not the responsibility of the power lunch diners to look after the disadvantaged in society, although I’d hope that their contributions to charities are as generous as their lunch bills. What is obscene is the federal government failing to do much to get wealthy corporations to pay their fair share of tax. It is the loopholes in the tax system that need to be tightened up Paul Gray, Daylesford (Vic) Four wheels good; two legs bad



Transport NSW may well say safety is the highest priority (“Light rail operator admits it put performance before passenger safety”, November 22) yet at Cremorne Junction, a heavily pedestrianised shopping centre, median refuge strips, fencing and walk signal buttons were removed for a multimillion dollar tidal flow system, and compensatory red light speed cameras and variable speed limit signage were omitted. It was all about traffic speed, while pedestrian safety languished.

Graham Short, Cremorne Multi beats mono From my experience having lived in America, there is a distinct difference between how Americans and Australians identify themselves (Letters, November 22). The tertiary students I mixed with in America made connections to their ethnic origins in a way I found peculiar. While they saw themselves as Americans, they used statements such as “I’m fourth generation Irish” to declare their heritage. Here people refer to their Australianness with statements such as “I’m first generation Australian”. It’s important for people to celebrate their origins. Multiculturalism brings with it the rich traditions that are lacking in monoculturalism. Meg Pickup, Ballina Seeing is believing



When Peng Shuai plays her first match outside of China, the world might believe she is safe and free. Until then, serious doubt surrounds what is actually happening to this courageous woman (“Pressure on China must continue until Peng Shuai is verifiably safe”, November 22). Denis Suttling, Newport Beach What a shame that the Uighurs are not tennis stars. Mark Propper, Bondi

World.title: Berejiklian politicised ‘health advice’, sidelined Chant
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

So, the truth many suspected throughout the Sydney lockdown finally comes to light (“State was urged to not divide the city”, November 22). We were constantly told by then premier Gladys Berejiklian that all decisions were based on “health advice”. The real message from Chief Health Officer Dr Kerry Chant to the government was actually that decisions should be based on “all health advice”. The placement of one word made an immense difference in how the lockdown was managed.

Linda Holmes, Balmain

Gladys’ halo now sits where it rightfully belongs, on the head of Dr Chant. The emails obtained by the Upper House show that Berejiklian misused Chant’s position for political purposes. They explain the apparent squirming by Chant at press conferences whenever “health advice” was used to justify unpopular decisions.

Tony Re, Georges Hall

Dr Chant’s sage advice about imposing a curfew for its messaging effect was indeed accepted by the then premier, but not as intended. The “message” was that we impose long-term curfews on areas of least political significance regardless of any disparity in case numbers favouring those areas.

Fred Jansohn, Rose Bay

The harsh lockdown of Canterbury-Bankstown was just one of the ways this area has been targeted by the NSW government. It’s an easy target, too: a place of many cultures and lower incomes. The NSW government has fast-tracked development and privatisation of public transport in this corridor. Locals are locked out of the housing market and there has been no new public housing. People here feel forgotten and outraged by political dishonesty which has left us with low-quality, over-priced development, a relative lack of open space, only 15 per cent tree canopy cover, the most polluted river in Sydney and communities devastated by job losses and business closures.

World.title: How PM fits the world history of leadership
World.content:
Letters NationalNSWLetters How PM fits the world history of leadership November 28, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In a study of world history, it can often be concluded that individuals who have the best ability to obtain power often have the least ability to exercise it (“PM facing dissension in the ranks”, November 29). This criticism is particularly appropriate for Scott Morrison, whose lack of leadership is much to Australia’s detriment. It seems inevitable that Liberal Party members will be forced to act, perhaps if the early polls indicate electoral disaster, but certainly after an election defeat. So, who would best replace Morrison? Josh Frydenberg bears the huge cross of the JobKeeper fiasco and is totally unapologetic for the loss of taxpayers’ billions. The smart money is likely on Peter Dutton, who genuinely has some leadership qualifications.

Geoff Harding, Chatswood Let’s do better than hotels Omicron’s arrival highlights one major deficiency in the governmental response to COVID-19 infection control, namely the glaring deficiency of purpose-built quarantine facilities. With current knowledge of the importance of aerosol transmission of this virus, it is patently obvious that hotels built for tourists are not adequate for the task. We will again see people who are negative being sent there to quarantine and contracting the virus. The emergence of new variants such as Omicron in countries with low vaccination rates such as South Africa could easily have been foreseen and moves undertaken to plan for this. Louise Dolan, Birchgrove So, Omicron is easier to transmit than Delta and we’re thinking of reopening hotel quarantine again? Hotel quarantine that was very “leaky” with Delta? We still don’t have proper quarantine? How hard is it to build some accommodation away from major centres? We can pull down a perfectly good stadium and rebuild it, but we can’t erect a few cabins like Howard Springs? Welcome to our next lockdown.

Moya Gibb Smith, Paddington



Gladys Berejiklian showed real foresight when she ordered the new, unseaworthy Manly ferries. They will make excellent COVID-19 quarantine hulks, preferably anchored just off Kirribilli.

Sandy Thomas, Lilyfield What happens if the hotel I’ve already booked into becomes a quarantine hotel? Will I be told? I don’t want to stay in those virus-spreading joints. Name all quarantine hotels. Bob Hall, Wyoming Pokies rort demands inquiry A royal commission is needed to investigate evidence that NSW’s pokies are being used to launder hundreds of millions of dollars of dirty money (“More than $1b washed through pokies”, November 29). While clubs and pubs provide immense social benefits for our communities, Australians can never allow either big business or government to turn a blind eye to organised crime because they bank its proceeds. The Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission estimates the cost of organised crime to Australia is more than $36 billion a year. We know organised crime will exploit the weakest links to launder its rivers of gold. Doing nothing corrodes our democracy.



Michael Walton, Lambton Character, not charisma My memory goes immediately to 2007 (Letters, November 29), and the electorate’s concern about the ineptitude of the Howard government and it was ready to go with a new broom who wasn’t, or even pretended to be, a “rock star” like Bob Hawke, or a “messiah” like our current PM sees himself to be. To continually call for Anthony Albanese to step aside ignores the Westminster system of governance, that is consensus ruling by an elected majority party. Let’s leave the lectern blatherers and snake oil salesmen with so-called popular charisma appeal in the past and get a government that wants to do something for our long-term well-being.

John Kingsmill, Fairlight Sand and deliver Sandbags (Letters, November 29) are nearly always filled by volunteers, mainly the SES, then volunteer firies, with a minute percentage by public volunteers, but these usually at the last minute. “Hand” filling includes the use of a wide variety of machines assisting, from the old inverted traffic cones in a horizontal ladder, to large and expensive specialised machinery. We (I’m now retired SES, both NSW and Queensland) frequently hear the call for large stocks of ready-filled bags. The major arguments against such stores include degradation of the bags – natural fibre by rot, polypropylene by sunlight – the cost of storage, management thereof, access, et cetera. A benefit of on-the-spot filling is the opportunity to instruct the users of the correct use of the bags, including placing a layer of polyethylene film behind the bags to waterproof the installation. Our usual advice for less rush when needed was for the householders who had previously experienced water problems to store a quantity of unfilled bags at their home, out of the weather/wet/sun, plus a bulk quantity of sand, and fill and use them when needed.

Dave Williams, Port Macquarie



How to beat speed cameras I have been caught out by speed cameras on a number of occasions throughout my driving career and usually feel like kicking myself for my lack of attentiveness or for my stupidity (“Speed camera body to quiz ex-minister”, November 29). I don’t resent the process, as I was caught fair and square. For the good of the community and my own well-being, I accept the imposition on my freedom. So, I can’t understand the logic behind putting up signs to warn speeding drivers there is a camera up ahead. Equally, I can’t understand why is there an expensive inquiry into speed cameras. Speed kills and if you speed you are breaking the law. No inquiry will ever convince me otherwise.

Peter Hull, Hat Head

Demons coach Tom Wilson said he was bullish about his young side’s future and the experiences they will take from going so close to the premiership.

World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Driver sentenced to 10 years for crash that killed father, four-year-old son Josephine Shannon and Catherine Strohfeldt November 27, 2026 — 8:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A driver who did not realise he had hit and killed a father and his four-year-old along a suburban Logan street will face up to 10 years behind bars. Trevor Galbraith, 43, pleaded guilty to the August 2025 crash that killed 33-year-old Braiden Timmins and his young son Hendrix-hemi Te Rongomau King, while the pair were walking along Green Road Regents Park. Braiden Ashley Timmins and his young son Hendrix-hemi Te Rongomau King were killed when struck by a ute along Green Road, in Regents Park. Nine The little boy had been riding his balance bike as the pair made the trip to a local convenience store to buy ice-cream. On Friday, the Beenleigh District Court heard Galbraith was an alcoholic, and had begun drinking about 1pm the day before the crash, consuming 35 standard drinks.



The 43-year-old then woke up on August 17, continued drinking, and then got behind a wheel with a blood-alcohol content four times the legal limit. Related Article Tragedy ‘Our little buddy’: Tributes for father and four-year-old son killed by ute south of Brisbane Galbraith had been distracted by his phone while driving, the prosecution said, and had not realised he had collided with the father and son. Speaking to the court, Galbraith said he accepted full responsibility for his actions, pleading guilty to one count of dangerous operation of a vehicle causing death while adversely affected by an intoxicating substance. “I am sincerely sorry and will be for the rest of my life,” the 43-year-old told the courtroom.



He said he had also completed several courses to address his “alcohol problem”. Acting Judge Douglas Wilson sentenced the 43-year-old to 10 years behind bars, with a minimum sentence of eight years, and revoked Galbraith’s licence. Tributes for Braiden Timmins and his son, Hendrix-hemi Te Rongomau King, were laid at the crash site in the days following their deaths. Catherine Strohfeldt Timmins’ stepfather, Peter Geary, told media the day had been “really hard” for the family of the 33-year-old father and his four-year-old son. “[The] reality is that both of them lost their lives because somebody did the wrong thing,” Geary said.



“But, when you look at the picture, to us, it is justice done.” Galbraith’s 10-year-sentence would include the 467 days he already served in custody while awaiting sentencing, meaning he would be eligible for parole in 2033.

World.title: Liberals’ privatisation proposal draws flak
World.content:
Letters PoliticsVictoriaLetters Liberals’ privatisation proposal draws flak November 27, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Who do we trust?

Well, no wonder Jess Wilson left it to the 11th hour to release her party’s privatisation plans to get the budget billions dollar debt back down. It turns out she’s planning to be Jeff Kennett 2.0.

Yes, Victoria’s debt is too high but what most of us are furious about is how Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan got us into this situation, particularly the latter for allowing CFMEU to corruptly bludge off the state to the tune of billions of dollars, while also insisting on SRL East, at the chronic cost of continued neglect of those most in need. Yes, it’s time to just pause the level crossings removals until the ship of state is righted. Who do we trust to do that?

Bernadette George, Mildura Problems will flow on

Two days before elections, Jess Wilson has announced she will privatise Melbourne’s sewerage system. This was done in the UK in 1989, and what a success that has been. Citizens started paying more, maintenance was virtually scrapped to the point where sewage started flowing into the river systems with only around 15 per cent of rivers reported as in good health.

The only winners were the shareholders being paid billions of dollars in dividends. What other hidden policies do you have up your sleeve?

Jane Taylor, Newport Wavering no more

Oh here we go again; leasing out Melbourne’s sewerage system to the private sector for almost a century to come. There are always crappy results from privatisation of publicly owned facilities and services. Why do governments keep doing this? And for 90 years? Nobody can possibly visualise that far ahead in these rapidly changing times.

I’ve been wavering for a month about who to vote for, but with the Liberals preferencing One Nation, and now treating voters like idiots by releasing policies so close to election day, my mind is now made up.

Fiona White, Alfredton



Avoiding dependency

Waleed Aly notes One Nation policies include cuts to spending on climate action and Indigenous affairs (“Opportunity is knocking for Taylor”, 27/11).

Suddenly, I’m hoping for Jess Wilson to win at least 45 of the 88 electorates in the state election, so that she has no dependency on populist One Nation.

John Hughes, Mentone Leased by who?

Economics for beginners: struggling government service (two entities: government employees and customers) is sold or leased to private interests. Next, private interests (four entities: management, shareholders, employees and customers) decide the first three entities need to be paid, but not all. Next, to reduce costs, employee numbers are reduced (sacked) and maintenance is deferred. Finally, at some time in the future the taxpayer will be asked to finance the clean-up (in the case of sewage, this is quite literal) while management and shareholders realise their gains and move elsewhere.

Selling off or leasing public utilities has a track record of more unemployment, poorer services and higher costs (there are more at the trough of public monies). The real question for voters: who will lease our water utilities? Local businesses or foreign entities? If the Murray Darling Basin is any guide, we will have foreign interests owning some of Melbourne’s water utilities. Not my first choice.

David Kennedy, Balwyn North No magic fix

Jess Wilson’s team has done their best to focus on their plan for potholes. One pothole they cannot dodge is the lack of trust voters have in politics. Last-minute announcements to privatise essential services like water will do nothing to lower costs or build trust. Privatisation of essential services is not a magic fix, as someone else pays the price. Just look at the rising costs, poor quality and scandals in aged care and childcare.

Jenny Kashyap, Bentleigh Giant step backward

It has taken a decade of work between government, First Nations people and community to develop the Treaty. Returning to a model where Indigenous affairs policy is managed directly by a government department, as proposed by both Liberal and One Nation parties, is a giant step backward.

Sarah Russell, Mt Martha Catch 22

It is almost deceitful the way political parties release costings and policies at the last minute. They are there at early polling booths exhorting you to vote for them, yet haven’t got the courage to give you a full picture as to why.

All through the campaign, questions have been asked about how the Liberals would pay for what they intend to do. We now find out a lot of it will come from selling off and leasing government assets, despite promising not to. Such duplicity should not be rewarded. However to get legislative change so that policies and costings must be released at the opening of pre-polling, we need to rely on honest politicians with integrity at their core. Do such beings exist? Or will this Catch 22 paradox always be with us?

Greg Tuck, Warragul



Expensive disaster

Two days before the election, the Liberals have announced a 90-year lease on Melbourne’s sewerage asset for an estimated $9.2 billion, to help pay down debt.

In 1989, the Thatcher Conservative government privatised the water and sewerage industries in England and Wales, becoming the only country in the world to have fully privatised water and sewerage disposal systems. In 2023 UK’s major water companies discharged untreated sewage into rivers and coastal waters for 3.6 million hours.

Do we really want to go down a path already shown to be an expensive disaster with excess profits going to private companies, spills of untreated sewage and lack of accountability with serious potential health risks?

Carolyn Worth, Brighton East Not truly conservative

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s claim that Liberal defector Leah Blyth is a ″⁣true conservative″⁣ demonstrates yet again her tenuous grip on facts. True conservatives don’t go storming in and wrecking the joint, à la Trump’s MAGA movement. They preserve the traditions and institutions that underpin civilised society. When will Australians wake up and realise cults spouting slogans do not a political party make?

Leon Burgher, Stony Creek Focused on the now

Scrapping net zero and abolishing the Climate Change Authority won’t save any money, nor will it end global warming. Politicians are so focused on the here and now, they fail to recognise there is a future. But I suppose that’s for future government, no need for us to worry about it. It’s been proven that renewable energy is already saving us money. Is ideology so much more important than us?

David Jeffery, East Geelong What about the birds?

Jess Wilson’s plan to privatise Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants could have disastrous consequences for the many who call them home. The “poo ponds” at Werribee are an internationally recognised haven for waterbirds and Victoria’s most important drought refuge. We can’t afford to sacrifice nature in the cause of debt reduction.

Juliet Le Feuvre, Hawthorn Inadequate target

The article “Australia nears 2030 climate goal, not 2035” (27/11) needs to be put in context. In 2020, the federal government proposed a 2030 target of 43 per cent emissions reduction despite the scientific community specifying that 76 per cent was needed. The Greens got the target changed to “at least 43 per cent”. Australia falling slightly short of an inadequate target should not be hailed as a success. What could be recorded as successes are that South Australian and Victorian states have met more realistic targets.

Tom Maher, Aspendale



Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Election

Jess Wilson’s backflip on Melbourne Water asset privatisation (“Where affluent meets effluent”, 27/11) was a sneaky one after so many have voted, but with her lead in the polls it won’t be political “sewer side”.

Bruce Watson, Belgrave Jess Wilson’s 11th hour call to privatise our sewerage system has a nasty smell about it.

Phil Alexander, Eltham It’s 1992 all over again. Using a tired government’s loss to impose the Liberal Party agenda of privatisation of anything it can get its hands on.

Jenni King, Camberwell



Grand sale, grand sale, grand sale (sorry Franco Cozzo). Sounds reminiscent of the old Jeff days. Jess’ legacy can be Victoria’s new number plate, Victoria: the fire sale state.

Danny Van Vliet, Mount Eliza As we can see from the aftermath of the Kennett years, while we may see the Wilson government deliver privatisation pain for several years, the effects are felt for decades.

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills Every time I reach for the toilet roll I will think of how I am bankrolling Victoria’s major projects and wiping billions off our bottom line.

Kevan Porter, Alphington Looks like the Coalition is adopting an “excremental” approach to debt reduction.

Anthea Hyslop, Eltham What will happen when, inevitably, there’s a future cash crisis and no more public assets left to sell?

Joe Wilder, Caulfield North



At last it becomes clear. Jess Wilson is “Jess Kennett”!

Bill Shepherdson, Brunswick Furthermore

I cannot get out of my head the expression on Chris Bowen’s face following the collapse of talks at COP31. It is the same look I have every time the government approves a new coal mine or gas project.

Barry Lizmore, Ocean Grove Another politician defects to a different party, midterm. The decision is not theirs but the voters, they should be prepared to contest a byelection.

Geoff Oliver, East Malvern

World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaCrime Law banning bikie gangs from government worksites never used Kieran Rooney, Nick McKenzie and Rachael Ward November 27, 2026 — 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Not a single bikie gang or organised crime outfit member has been banned from government worksites 15 months after a law threatening to jail them for setting foot on public projects came into force. Since August 2025, the Victorian government has had the power to stop members of particular organisations from entering taxpayer-funded worksites. Bikie insignia is banned on government worksites but the power to ban gang members has not been used. Paul Rovere The laws were created to address community concerns about organised criminal infiltration on the Big Build exposed by The Age. The government touted the new offence as “helping to further stamp out the rotten culture influenced by outlaw motorcycle gangs and other criminal organisations” when it passed parliament.



Anyone caught breaking the rule would risk up to three years behind bars and be fined. But 15 months after the law took effect, these powers are yet to be used to single out any groups or projects. Former union health and safety representative Dave Hawkins. The revelation the new law is yet to be used to help clean up the construction sector comes after Victoria Police’s Taskforce Hawk charged a key member of the so-called Irish faction of the CFMEU. Former union health and safety representative Dave Hawkins was charged on Friday with procuring fake qualifications for workers on the Big Build. Hawkins was also charged with distributing naked photos of the partner of a former CFMEU official.



The charging of Hawkins comes after weeks of frenetic activity by Taskforce Hawk, including multiple arrests and raids targeting bikie gang members and CFMEU figures still operating in Victoria’s construction sector. The head of the Irish faction, ex-CFMEU vice president Joe Myles, has also emerged as a key target of the Kourakis royal commission into wrongdoing in the building sector. A fortnight ago, the commission aired allegations that Myles had abused his union power in 2022, with the backing of the office of then minister Jacinta Allan, to install a suspected corrupt labour hire company on a major rail project. Allegations of crime and corruption in the state’s building industry and on taxpayer-funded infrastructure projects have become a defining state election issue heading into Saturday’s poll. The emergence of the rolling Building Bad scandal in mid-2024 led the then-Allan government to introduce new laws giving authorities the power to ban bikies and other criminal gang members from government worksites under changes to the Criminal Organisations Control Amendment Act.



The government confirmed on Thursday the attorney-general had issued no bans in the 15 months since the power came into force but did not explain why. Related Article Big Build royal commission Paid without turning up, then came a $165,000 pay day: Bikie Joel Leavitt’s Big Build bounty under microscope The law allows bans on particular criminal organisations, in consultation with the Victoria Police chief commissioner, from specific worksites if it would substantially assist in the disruption or prevention of criminal activity and is reasonably necessary. The government has acted on another part of the law which came into effect at the same time. In May 2026, insignia from 13 identified outlaw motorcycle gangs were prohibited from being displayed. This masthead has detailed multiple allegations of criminal influence at Big Build sites since July 2024, including gangland figures and bikie bosses working as union delegates, company owners or industrial relations fixers.



When the new laws were announced in August 2024, then attorney-general Jaclyn Symes said she did not expect employers to hand over lists of staff who were organised crime members but had confidence in the ability of police. Related Investigation

Building Bad Building Bad Barrister Geoffrey Watson, SC, who authored a damning report into CFMEU misconduct, said banning bikies from public worksites in 2024 would have already been “too late”, but was necessary to try and fend off the influence of organised crime on public building sites. “These laws can be difficult to apply, they can be draconian in effect, but every now and then, it’s recognised that they’re necessary because of the seriousness of the problem, and obviously the government recognised the seriousness of the problem and went so far but didn’t go far enough,” he said. “The point is that something needs to be done to get the bikies and other organised crime figures out of public building projects.”



He encouraged whoever formed Victoria’s next government to seek advice from Commissioner Christopher Kourakis, who is overseeing the ongoing royal commission, about whether certain organisations should now be prescribed or wait for his recommendations. Editor's pick Analysis

Naked City Teaching old cops new tricks: The comeback veterans helping fight a modern crime wave Liberal spokesman Jame Newbury claimed Labor “allowed criminals to infest government worksites” and if elected a Coalition government would ban bikies and anyone with links to organised crime from state run projects. “We will set the toughest standards in Australia because we want clean worksites, oversee a proper royal commission, and find exactly how much taxpayers’ money was taken by crooks”.
