World.title: Islands, cruises and cultural exchanges: How the class of 2026 is celebrating schoolies
World.content:
NationalSchoolies Islands, cruises and cultural exchanges: How the class of 2026 is celebrating schoolies Sally Rawsthorne November 27, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Maya Lama’s group chat is going off. The Newtown High School of the Performing Arts graduate is packing for her teenage rite of passage but, unlike generations before her, she is not making the pilgrimage to the Gold Coast. Recently 18 and at the end of 13 years of schooling, Lama is among the wave of schoolies celebrating the beginning of adulthood in new ways. Charlotte Nicholls and Blayne Wagstaff, both 18, chose Fiji to celebrate the end of the schooling. “We’ve been trying to figure out what to wear. There are different theme nights – secrets of the sea, Baywatch, which is classic Pamela Anderson swimwear, there’s festival outfits,” Maya said ahead of her schoolies trip to Fiji. Trips to Tokyo or Bangkok, helicopter parents keeping an eye on their kids in Bali from a nearby hotel, cruising the Pacific, or a cross-cultural exchange in Samoa are all schoolies options for the class of 2026.



Not that you can call it that. School-leavers now refer to it as a “grad trip”. It may still be the well-trodden path to the Gold Coast or Byron Bay that their parents took, but increasingly it’s less booze-sodden and debauched than in years gone by. Speaking from Fiji, Blayne Wagstaff said that he and six friends eschewed the Gold Coast because they wanted to experience an overseas holiday. Forget a road trip to the Gold Coast. Schoolies are now taking chartered flights by travel companies specialising in end-of-year trips to countries like Fiji. Kate Geraghty “It’s been so fun to meet people and party with random people we don’t know and have the best time of our lives together in a foreign country,” the 18-year-old said. Red Frogs – the Christian youth charity named for the lollies they hand out to revellers – began in Queensland in 1997 and now supports school-leavers in 10 locations across Australia. The group has noticed a marked change in how teens are now celebrating the end of school.



“Schoolies is evolving. While the Gold Coast remains a major destination, young people are increasingly choosing to celebrate in different locations,” Red Frogs’ spokeswoman Kate Smith said. This year, Red Frogs crews have deployed to Bali, Fiji and Vanuatu. Youth charity Red Frogs has been a feature of schoolies on the Gold Coast for decades, handing out lollies to teens. Paul Harris “The stereotype of schoolies being one big week of chaos doesn’t reflect the experience of most young people,” Smith said. Data backs her up. Flight Centre’s top five schoolies destinations for the year are Brisbane, Tokyo, Melbourne, Bali and London.



“The idea of spending a week in one spot just to drink and party doesn’t really resonate with teenagers any more,” Flight Centre global managing director Andrew Stark said. Safer Schoolies, a Queensland government initiative that aims to rein in illicit behaviour, issued 11,927 wristbands this year, compared with 18,017 distributed in 2022, a spokesperson said. Although these are not compulsory, fewer wristbands indicates fewer schoolies The long-time party destination boasts safety initiatives, theme park days, beach parties, DJs and options for underage school-leavers to party side-by-side with their 18 plus mates. But the sheen is wearing off. “We had heard that the Gold Coast and Byron were kind of dying,” said Lama, who will, early next month, go with four girlfriends to Fiji for a week with schoolies-focused travel company Unleashed.



The company will this year send 8000 Australian teenagers to five resorts in the popular Pacific destination. Also in Fiji this week is western Sydney’s Charlotte Nicholls, a graduate of Magdalene Catholic College. “It has been awesome. It had heaps of theme party nights and activities as well as a good crew and safety on a private island away from the public. The rooms are good, the food is good as well and even if you’re a picky eater they have a pizza and burger station,” she said. Gen Z’s parents share their distaste for the glitter strip, although for different reasons. “I am so happy my girl isn’t going to the Gold Coast. I wouldn’t sleep – too worried about drink spiking,” said one north shore mother who asked to remain anonymous so as not to mortify her daughter.



Related Article Courts ‘Incredibly distressing’: Teen beaten on Gold Coast still critical, community rallies support These trips cost an eye-watering $3000 for the week, with several parents saying they were happy to partially fund what they perceived as a safer option. These concerns are not unfounded. An Ipswich 15-year-old is in an induced coma with a broken jaw, fractured skull and bleeding on the brain after being set upon by a gang of attackers outside a Surfers Paradise McDonald’s about 3am on Tuesday. Eleven teens aged 17 to 19 have been charged over the alleged assault, with the boy’s family on Thursday saying they were “overwhelmed by the kindness and generosity of the local community”. Anxious parents, therefore, are somewhat soothed by the offerings boasted by companies such as Unleashed and its competitors.



Parental information sessions across Sydney, booking out resorts for exclusive use for schoolies (including 17-year-olds, who can party with their 18-year-old friends according to Unleashed’s marketing material) and around the clock staff, including medical and security, go a long way towards easing minds. Gen Zs, too, are safety conscious. “I don’t feel doubt about my safety while I’m here partying. My parents are happy that I’m not going to Surfers [Paradise]. It’s so much more secure,” Wagstaff said. Red Frogs’ Smith said that Gen Zs are interested in different options and have a greater focus on both mental health and safety. “They still want to celebrate; they’re just redefining what that looks like.”



Unleashed’s bright Instagram page has packing lists, tips for managing airport angst and suggestions of where to shop for themed nights (Cotton On for Pamela Anderson-style swimwear, the Royal Lifesaving Shop for those wanting a lifeguard-style hat). World.title: Invasive clams spread outside Waikato River's controlled area
World.content:
Invasive freshwater clams have been detected at Atiamuri Hydro Station on the Waikato River, outside the existing controlled area.

Biosecurity New Zealand has confirmed the presence of Corbicula clams, likely C. fluminea, commonly known as 'gold clams', at the hydro station.

It is the first confirmed detection outside the controlled area upstream from Whakamaru Dam.

It is not known how the clams reached Atiamuri.

National Corbicula Programme Manager Lisa Hargegger said the discovery highlighted how easily the clams can spread.

"Juvenile clams can be smaller than a grain of sand. You don't necessarily have to see one to spread one."

Waikato Regional Council, Biosecurity New Zealand, Waikato River iwi and other partners are working to establish the extent of the spread.

Surveillance of high-risk waterways is also continuing this summer.

Waikato Regional Council integrated catchment management director Greg Ryan said the discovery was a reminder that there was no room for complacency when it came to protecting Aotearoa's lakes and rivers.

"We've all invested significant time and effort into slowing the spread of freshwater clams. Now more than ever, we need people to keep doing the small things that make a difference, including checking, cleaning and drying equipment before leaving the water," he said.

Waikato Regional Council said ballast tanks in boats were considered a particular risk because they could hold water containing microscopic juvenile clams.

Although there were currently no specific restrictions on ballasted boats in this part of the river, owners were being encouraged to avoid moving their vessels between waterways where possible.

Freshwater clams reproduce rapidly and can establish large populations in a short time.

Once established, they are extremely difficult to control and can threaten native species, water infrastructure and the economy.

It is illegal to knowingly move the clams or water containing them.

People should not collect or eat the clams, as they can accumulate harmful contaminants.

World.title: Nestlé recalls Alfamino Junior 1+ Years toddler milk due to cereulide toxin
World.content:
Nestlé is recalling a specialist milk product for toddlers with allergies and medical conditions due to the presence of the cereulide toxin.

The company said 103 cans of its Alfamino Junior 1+ Years (400g) with a use-by date of 10/12/2027 and batch number 53440017Y1 were affected by the recall.

Food Safety (NZFS) deputy director-general Vincent Arbuckle said the affected products were mainly available through pharmacies and had been removed from shelves.

"The problem with one batch of this specialist toddler milk is that it could contain cereulide, which is produced by the microorganism Bacillus cereus and can cause gastrointestinal illness. Fortunately, there have been no reports of associated illness," he said.

A new, unaffected batch would be available at stores in the coming week.

"In the meantime, if you have the affected specialist Alfamino toddler milk at home, do not feed it to your child and return it to the place of purchase," Arbuckle said.

"Should you urgently need an alternative before Monday, your pharmacy will have other products available. If you cannot access alternative products, please contact Healthline for advice."

Symptoms linked to cereulide could include vomiting, diarrhoea or unusual lethargy. They would typically appear between 30 minutes to 6 hours after exposure and usually resolve within 24 hours.

The imported product was manufactured in Switzerland.

"As is our usual practice, NZFS will work with Nestlé to understand how the contamination occurred and prevent its recurrence," Arbuckle said.

World.title: Elon Musk's 1 million 'Starmind' satellites a 'land grab', Auckland professor says
World.content:
An Auckland professor says US trillionaire Elon Musk's move to put one million satellites into space - newly dubbed 'Starmind' - is like a "land grab".

Another researcher said the data centre satellites with solar arrays would be so big and bright they'd change the night sky from the likes of Mount John Observatory near Tekapo forever.

Elon Musk has already launched over 11,000 satellites mostly for his Internet provider Starlink - far more than the US and Chinese governments combined.

Now the Trump administration has given his company SpaceX the okay to deploy a million more to run data centres on 24-hour sunlight.

Richard Easther from Auckland University's department of physics said it is at the limits of what's feasible to harvest energy and cool the computing.

"The best way to get heat out of something is to have something cold touch it. And so space is cold but the only way to get rid of heat is what we call radiation ... that's the only option you've got for getting rid of heat in space," said Easther on Friday.

The US Federal Communications Commission has approved the plan, calling it an ingenious step into a bold frontier for America's "booming super-intelligence economy".

"Super intelligence" was repurposed by Donald Trump as the White House's name for artificial intelligence recently.

Easther called it something else.

Richard Easther. University of Auckland

"My take on it is that in some ways it's a land grab.

"If you can launch a lot of satellites very quickly, then that kind of gives you at least an informal right to have that amount of material in space.

"[It's] very much an attempt to exploit the fact that there are no clear norms about this kind of behaviour ... like, you know, a rush to claim land on a gold field."

Unlike a neighbourhood in Auckland, say, there were no planning rules in space, Easther said.

All the way

Musk has his own rockets so no new launch business may come anyone else's way.

While one worry is that other countries' digital sovereignty may flow to him.

Lecturer in AI Dr Kerry McInerney said for both business and politics, this is a bad idea.

"There's a really strong argument against one person and one company having such outsized power over our digital infrastructure," she said on Friday.

"Right now Elon Musk's companies already operate the vast majority of satellites in space and this would continue to further expand the amount of control that they have.

"And this has real implications because right now we're already moving towards a world where two countries, the US and China, provide the world with so much of the digital infrastructure we use on a daily basis. And so that puts countries like Aotearoa in a tricky situation."

Already Starlink satellites fall out of the sky at a regular rate as they only last a few years.

But they are much much smaller than a data centre satellite that would also require terrific energy and fuel to launch.

All those processes, fuelling and falling en masse, are a prospect that is disturbing environmental researchers.

Professor Laura Revell of Canterbury University said a million satellites would be arguably the "largest experiment in atmospheric chemistry" the world has ever seen.

"That would mean launching about eight satellites per hour from now until their deadline to complete the authorised constellation of 25 November, 2040," she told the Science Media Centre.

"We already know that emissions from rocket launches can cause depletion of the protective ozone layer."

Depletion has so far been insignificant due to low launch rates, she said - but maybe not for long.

"They will be disposed - as we feared - by atmospheric re-entry, fundamentally turning the atmosphere into a crematorium for satellites," Revell said.

Astronomer Dr Preeti Cowan is also thinking about what tamariki might end up looking up at.

"They will never be in Earth's shadow. They're always going to be up there in the sky. So whatever time you're observing, they're going to be there."

She guessed maybe in skies above New Zealand there might be thousands, and a lot brighter than existing satellites.

"They're going to have to have these huge solar panels to catch the sunlight. They're going to have these huge heat shields."

World.title: Opportunity could have the biggest opportunity in coalition talks
World.content:
Analysis: "...And it's National by a nose."

If we resorted to that most tired of political clichés and called today's final election count as a horse race, National with 40 seats, four more than Labour, is at the front of the pack and is set to govern again. A blue ribbon for the blue party. But this is an election where that cliché is especially unhelpful.

Looked at another way, National has fallen 10 percent from its 2023 vote to 28.35 percent and came second to Labour, which is ahead on 29.88 percent.

Through another lens, Opportunity is the winner; a party that rewrote the rules of politics to even make it into Parliament yet is now, incredibly, the kingmaker, able to make the final decision about the shape of the next government.

Audio player for " The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics_election-2026/2834759%2Fopportunity-could-have-the-biggest-opportunity-in-coalition-talks

The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? Caucus Download MP3 40m

So, what might the next government look like? Who really has the power to decide in the coming weeks? That's debated in a special episode of RNZ's politics podcast, Caucus.

Much will depend on how the governing parties interpret what the public is telling them. Do they see this as a mandate for further and faster? As a reason to come together more tightly as a coalition or to work more across the aisle? Will they need to go into 'survival mode' just to make it through a three-year term?

As Political Editor Jo Moir says in the podcast, Christopher Luxon has been behaving like he's won a great victory and David Seymour is throwing his caretaker deputy prime ministerial weight around, while Winston Peters has shown renewed interest in Foreign Affairs, after seeming to back away from it earlier in the year. Negotiating tactics, much?

But perhaps the most pressure, and the biggest opportunity, sits with the new kids, Opportunity. While they are called kingmaker, they can actually only make variations of one choice. To paraphrase Henry Ford, they can choose any kind of government as long as it's blue.

National must establish a coalition deal with ACT, NZ First and Opportunity to form a government. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

One option for them is to negotiate a full coalition deal with a seat at the Cabinet table. That seems the most unlikely scenario. The disdain coming from NZF and ACT - and indeed, some of the criticisms from Opportunity thrown their way - would make constructive relationships in a tight coalition challenging.

Perhaps more importantly, Opportunity being closely tied to a very right-wing bloc would likely harm their electoral prospects in 2029 and give them less influence over the other three parties.

Opportunity could also do a New Zealand first (lower case f) and sit on the crossbenches, only giving the government a majority one vote at a time. That would give them immense power but would also come with immense risk. Who do you think would be blamed if the government was unstable, or even collapsed? And voters would be asking if six percent of the vote warrants that amount of power.

So perhaps the most likely option for Opportunity would be to offer the coalition confidence and supply and nothing more. In the podcast I've called Qiulae Wong the heir to Peter Dunne and she could well follow his approach in 2002. Dunne's United Future gave confidence and supply to Helen Clark's Labour-led government but then frequently voted against it on issue after issue.

ACT leader David Seymour has again hinted at his interest in being finance minister following the announcement of the final election results. RNZ/Nosiphi Mapukata

In Parliament in March 2002, there was a fascinating exchange between Dunne and Clark celebrating 965 days of stable government, "the longest period of stable government under MMP" to that point.

Clark praised Dunne for his support and Dunne, clearly in good humour, reminded her that United Future had voted against the government on 20 major pieces of legislation and with National 65 percent of the time. Yet Clark finished the exchange saying, "it is possible to have disagreements while maintaining strong, stable Government".

Opportunity has many difficult choices ahead, but whichever path it chooses, the public, by and large, will be hoping that, like United Future, it can proudly point to a record of strong, stable government over the coming years.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's steep climb to the Beehive's ninth floor
World.content:
Audio player for " The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics_election-2026/2833062%2Fchristopher-luxon-s-steep-climb-to-the-beehive-s-ninth-floor

The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? Caucus Download MP3 40m

Analysis: The final election result is in and while only one Chris will be prime minister, both are declaring victory.

Christopher Luxon says National has secured its place as the "largest party in Parliament", while Labour's Chris Hipkins says his party is officially the "most popular political party" in the country.

While both of these things are true, only one of these leaders has a path to power and the ninth-floor Beehive office within arm's reach.

There are many unanswered questions after Friday's final election result but whether Labour can cobble together the numbers to form a government is not one of them.

Ramming home the point that in some respects the result doesn't marry with the parties now able to embark on coalition talks, Hipkins stressed that "more New Zealanders voted for change at this election than voted for the status quo".

Leaning into his disappointment, Hipkins also blamed the coalition's electoral enrolment changes for the situation his party finds itself in.

"We worked hard to get people onto the electoral roll and to get them out to vote. But there is no question in my mind that the changes made by the coalition government have needlessly prevented tens of thousands of New Zealanders from participating in this election, that must be put right before New Zealand's next election."

Hipkins will go away and await the formation of the government and eventually a review will be done by the Labour Party into what went wrong during its election campaign.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins' future is now in limbo as he awaits the outcome of coalition talks. Samuel Rillstone

Then he must make a decision about his future leading the party.

There's nobody immediately nipping at his heels to take the job from him, but as the party and caucus moves from sadness and disappointment to pointing the finger it will increasingly become untenable for Hipkins to stay on.

On the other side of the political divide, there will be less champagne-popping and more sighs of relief that the coalition parties will remain in power, albeit with a new Opportunity-sized handbrake.

All the hard work starts now for Luxon as he turns his attention to forming a government of four parties with plenty of competing ideas.

While Luxon may have learned a lot from his last round of negotiations, so have David Seymour and Winston Peters.

National has sunk to 28 percent. Together Act and New Zealand First have 20 percent of the vote.

If there is no deal between National, ACT, NZ First and Opportunity, the country will have to return to the polls. RNZ/Giles Dexter

But none of that works on its own. It's Opportunity's 6 percent that's doing the heavy lifting here.

That puts Opportunity in a pretty cushy position, but it's not an ultimate kingmaker and can't look elsewhere if it can't make it work with National, ACT, and New Zealand First.

It's either do the deal with the coalition or go back to the polls, and that's not a serious road the party can consider, even with leader Qiulae Wong refusing to rule it out.

In that very same boat are ACT and New Zealand First - neither of those parties have a realistic alternative option other than to sign a deal with their respective partners and Opportunity.

That will give National some small comfort.

Any suggestion the coalition talks ahead will be straightforward is la-la-land stuff, as is wishful thinking of a government by Christmas.

World.title: Explainer: How long can coalition talks last for New Zealand's next government?
World.content:
Audio player for " The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics_election-2026/2821557%2Fexplainer-how-long-can-coalition-talks-last-for-new-zealand-s-next-government

The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? Caucus Download MP3 40m

Explainer - The final results are in - and Opportunity will be in the driver's seat for coalition talks. What happens in talks and how long can they take?

It's clear that coalition talks will likely determine the next government, whether it's right or left wing.

National, ACT and New Zealand First now have 65 MPs, exactly the same number as Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity combined.

The National-led coalition would need the Opportunity Party to break the deadlock and form a government.

In the past 30 years of MMP elections, coalition talks have ranged from as short as eight days to as long as 59 - nearly two months.

Parliament must meet again by 14 January, but there is no requirement that a new government actually has to be formed by then. We could continue on under a caretaker government for some time.

Surprisingly, there aren't really a lot of hard and fast rules for coalition talks themselves.

The main thing that matters is they get to a deal to form a government.

"How you put a government together is a political matter, and is only limited by our imagination and a politician's imagination," said Dean Knight, an expert in constitutional law at Te Herenga Waka Victoria University of Wellington.

Once a deal is decided, the parties that intend to form a government go to the governor-general announcing they will have a majority in Parliament.

"The governor-general, she'll sit back and let the parties come to their own resolution," Knight said.

The other alternative is a hung parliament, which nobody wants to see.

How long have coalition negotiations taken in the past?

It could be anything from just over a week before a government deal is announced to as long as two months.

The longest coalition talks were in the very first MMP election in 1996, which took 59 days. (We're looking at the time from the election to when a deal was announced, rather than when a government was sworn in.)

But 2023 was the second longest. Then, it took National, ACT and New Zealand First 41 days after voting day to sign their coalition agreements.

The same length of time this year would take us to 18 December - just one week before Christmas.

Several other elections saw talks settled in as little as eight or nine days, however.

Before election day, both Labour leader Chris Hipkins and National leader Chris Luxon refused to put any deadline on when a deal could be made.

"I'm hoping that we can get something put together before Christmas - would be ideal," Luxon said. "But frankly, it'll take as long as it takes."

Are there rules about how talks have to go?

Talks are inherently a political process, and there's no real roadmap for them, Knight said.

The party with the largest share of the vote doesn't automatically get to form a government - witness the 2017 election where National had the highest party vote but Labour formed a government with New Zealand First and the Green Party.

Constitutionally, the parties don't even have to wait for the special vote totals to be returned, Knight said. Initial reaching out can start as soon as the day after the election, although there could be some tweaks to any deal if the special vote changes results.

"There have been instances where governments have been formed quite quickly, and discussions have happened before special votes," he said.

"Politically, there might be tactical reasons why they want to wait, but constitutionally they don't."

But the goal of all talks is quite carefully spelled out, Knight said.

"There are very strong rules and conventions about the key judgements ... that's the quality and the quantity that the governor-general expects in terms of being able to demonstrate the proposed government can command the confidence of the House."

"So constitutionally if you like, the end point, the finish line, is very clear."

In 2023, National, New Zealand First and ACT formed a coalition. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

What kind of agreements can be made?

There are several ways a government deal can come together.

"You can mix and match and whatever's going to work with the politics of the time, because there's very few constitutional constraints on the shape of the agreements," Knight said.

Three types of deals that have been prominent in MMP are coalitions, confidence and supply, and cooperation agreements.

A coalition, the strongest kind of agreement, involves two or more parties forming a government together, as in 2023 when National, ACT and New Zealand First did. It pretty much requires ministers to support government decisions once they're made in Cabinet.

A confidence and supply agreement is where a smaller party promises to provide the parliamentary support necessary to form a government. We saw those in 2011 and 2014 when National formed such deals with parties like ACT and United Future. It can allow for more disagreement with government plans.

A cooperation agreement is even looser than the two kinds above, where two parties might agree to work together in certain policy areas. In 2020 after Labour's majority victory - the only single-party one since MMP began - Labour had a cooperation agreement with the Green Party, giving it two ministerial positions outside Cabinet.

Parties can release details of their agreements, as the National-led coalition did in 2023.

In 2020, Labour and leader Jacinda Ardern formed MMP's only majority victory. AFP

So what actually happens in the talks?

Coalition talks are usually kept quite secretive, with a bit of a clock-and-dagger feel as MPs and leaders meet to try and hash out a deal. The media may know about meetings, but what goes on is usually between the leaders.

"It was useful to get all three of us in a room on neutral territory," ACT leader David Seymour said in 2023 after he met with Luxon and Peters for the start of talks at an Auckland hotel.

There may be informal get-togethers or shared meals if the parties involved need to get to know each other better.

For instance, Opportunity party leader Qiulae Wong has met with both Luxon and Hipkins since the election.

Referring to the rise of Opportunity, who have become pivotal in the final count, Knight said that would change negotiations.

"We've got new players in the mix and different ways of seeing executive government as well," he said.

The news that Opportunity's rules allow just two board members the power to veto a future government negotiated by the caucus also muddied the waters a bit.

In an interview with Hāpai Public Events, Stu Wilson, a former long-time campaign staffer for ACT leader Seymour, said there are many factors involved in the talks.

Wilson had been involved in previous coalition negotiations with ACT including in 2023. He told Hāpai that the parties involved will have to pivot after the stress of a long campaign.

"Mentally and physically they're absolutely exhausted on election night ... so they're shattered, and now they're expected to go into a very important negotiation that will set out what their three years will look like," he said.

Those involved will typically include party leaders and deputies, staffers and party officials and possible other experts. A lot of the energy will go into establishing solid working relationships.

Both Knight and Wilson noted that these kinds of negotiations don't actually come up all that often in a politician's career, with elections every three years and the possible players changing all the time. (Winston Peters, of course, has probably been through the most MMP era talks.)

"For many, this is their first big negotiation they've ever done," Wilson said.

People in the talks "may be lifelong political enemies and now they are all forced to be in the same room and develop rapport," Wilson said.

"The first negotiating is how they're going to negotiate," he said.

Is there a deadline that has to be met?

No. The post-election period will last as long as it takes to form a government.

"These things will take as long as they take," Knight said.

After the election, we have what's known as a "caretaker" government in place. The current prime minister remains prime minister, but their powers are, by convention, a bit more constrained.

The "caretaker convention," which is now encoded in the Cabinet Manual, lays out how power ought to be managed between governments.

"The political executive doesn't take significant decisions unless they have to, and then if they have to, they have to basically either try and put into place holding arrangements or .. consult with parties across Parliament to be sure that whatever they do has majority support within the new parliament," Knight said.

The return of the writ, the formal document signed by the governor-general that kicks off election season, is scheduled to be on 3 December, and that formalises results.

Parliament is required to meet by no later than six weeks after the return of the writ, which would be 14 January 2027.

Now if you want to get truly wild, a stalemate could theoretically last even longer than that, Knight said.

That date is "a big constitutional milestone, but we don't even need to have the government settled by then," Knight said, and Parliament could convene without a new government yet being formed, he said.

New Zealand has to have a government, "so the incumbent government continues to hold office, and there are provisions made .. to recognise that we haven't yet gotten a new anointed government. And that stuff really fascinates the constitutional trainspotters.

"Our constitution is a marvellous thing, that it makes provisions for these types of contingencies and tries to ensure that whatever is done is done with democratic legitimacy, and that's a real virtue of our constitution - despite the fact it's unwritten and sort of recorded in speeches and cabinet manuals and through practices over time."

Still, the optics of drawn-out negotiations matter, too, and how voters may react to endless haggling.

"I don't think any party wants to be negotiating around Christmas mince pies and roast lamb," Knight said.

Belgium was notorious for having the world's longest time without an official government formed - it lasted 541 days under a caretaker government from 2010 to 2011.

Obviously, nobody wants New Zealand's election to end up like Belgium.

What if coalition talks totally fail?

It's never happened in New Zealand, but in the event of an utter stalemate a new election could be called by the governor-general on the prime minister's advice.

That would be an absolute last resort, pretty much everyone would agree.

The governor-general also has the reserve powers to dismiss a prime minister, to force a dissolution of Parliament and call new elections, to refuse a prime minister's request for an election, and to refuse assent to legislation.

"These powers to act without or even against ministerial advice are reserved for the most extreme situations and with the exception of the appointment of a prime minister following an election, no New Zealand Governor-General has ever needed to use them," the governor-general's office notes.

"The larger parties always have the option to say we can't form an agreement, we're going back to the voters," Wilson told Hāpai.

"And the general sort of thought is that's very bad for all concerned but particularly the smaller party that's held the country up to ransom."

World.title: National's Mike Butterick reacts after losing Wairarapa seat to Labour's Kieran McAnulty
World.content:
Audio player for " The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/politics_election-2026/2826526%2Fnational-s-mike-butterick-reacts-after-losing-wairarapa-seat-to-labour-s-kieran-mcanulty

The Specials are in: Hung Parliament or a Golden Opportunity? Caucus Download MP3 40m

Labour's Kieran McAnulty is celebrating a narrow victory that's flipped the marginal Wairarapa seat.

National's Mike Butterick was ahead by 139 votes on election night, but a swing in the specials has given Labour a buffer of 81.

McAnulty said he's confident his lead will hold, with 40 votes the historical margin where a recount could make a difference.

"One thing this election has shown us is there's no certainties in politics, but they've declared me the winner and I'm going to have a beer tonight to celebrate."

He said he's "real stoked" to be returning as an electorate MP where he feels his voice carries more weight.

"It's the job that I wanted in politics, this is why I got into politics, I wanted to be the local MP to do good things for the region, and I've done it.

"I'm just real happy."

McAnulty acknowledged Butterick, saying politics is a brutal game.

"The bloke's lost his job and he's a good guy. You know, we're opponents, but we're not enemies, so whatever he chooses to do next, I wish him well."

'Very disapointing'

It was been a "long old day" for ousted Wairarapa MP, Mike Butterick, who while disappointed, says he has no regrets.

The National Party candidate was unseated by fewer than 100 votes, losing to Labour's Kieran McAnulty.

As it stands, it means the first time politician, Butterick, is out of Parliament.

National's Mike Butterick. VNP / Phil Smith

"It's obviously very disappointing, but the voters have spoken and as they say, the voters are always right and it's sort of like, close but no cigar."

Butterick - a Masterton-based sheep and beef farmer - says he needed something to keep his mind occupied until the results went live at 2pm on Friday.

"I went and jumped on the tractor, which I haven't been on for the best part of three years, and went and did some topping on some paddocks."

He says dodging concrete troughs kept his thoughts from wandering too much.

The National candidate had been in front on election night by a lead of 139 votes.

But after counting just over 5000 special votes for the electorate, the result swung to Labour's candidate for a margin of 81, although National extended its party vote lead with 30.2 percent, compared to Labour's 28.6 percent.

It's not the first time McAnulty and Butterick have gone head-to-head.

In 2023, it was another two-horse race between the National and Labour candidates. McAnulty, who had the seat was unable to keep it, losing to first time MP Butterick as a blue wave swept the country.

Butterick, who has been Land Information Minister as well as the Associate Minister for Agriculture says he was still taking in the result, and that it's too soon to talk about recounts.

"It's probably way too early to, you know, to say anything regarding that.

"It'll be taken into consideration and it'll be a bit more hurry up and wait, I guess - perhaps."

He says either way, it's been "one hell of privilege".

"And I can say that very genuinely, to have the opportunity to advocate not only just for your electorate, but also New Zealanders as a whole is a pretty extraordinary privilege that very few people get.

"Absolutely no regrets whatsoever and really proud to have been part of that team and done the best that we possibly could."

Butterick says the Wairapapa electorate, which extends from Dannevirke to South Wairarapa, was a wonderful part of the country to live and run a business in.

He thanked his supporters and the volunteers who put in an "extraordinary" number of hours and congratulated his Labour rival.

"They ran a hard campaign."

McAnulty won 19,688 votes compared to Butterick's 19,607, while New Zealand First candidate Ron Mark came in third on exactly 4000 votes.

As number 16 on the party list, Mark, the former Defence Minister would not return to Parliament.

World.title: Sam Walker signs with PNG Chiefs for 2028 NRL season
World.content:
Premiership-winning halfback Sam Walker has signed with the Papua New Guinea Chiefs for the 2028 season.

Walker, whose relationship with the Sydney Roosters fell apart after the club's grand final victory, will head to Port Moresby on a two-year deal.

The Queenslander is coming off the best year of his career, making State of Origin and Australian Test debuts.

"Sam is undoubtedly a gifted footballer who has already shown that he has tremendous vision, an outstanding kicking game and an ability to create something out of nothing," PNG Chiefs coach Willie Peters said.

"He is also a very smart footballer who understands how to influence and control a game and has shown that he can perform on the biggest of stages across club, state and now international level.

"We're really excited about what he can bring to the team and his partnership alongside Jarome Luai allows us to have one of the game's most creative and influential halves combinations — something which I'm excited to see develop as we take to the field."

Walker made his Test and Origin debuts this season. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The 24-year old was the 2021 Dally M Rookie of the Year and has been the Tricolours starter ever since.

He also attracted interest from South Sydney and Canterbury.

PNG Chiefs General Manager of Football Michael Chammas said the team believed Walker's best football was still yet to come.

"Sam was someone we identified as a player who we believe could have a transformational impact on our team — both in how we play on the field but also on the way we build our side and the way other players excel around him," Chammas said.

"He is a premiership winner, an Origin star and a World Cup winner and he has shown that he can perform under pressure in the biggest moments of our game.

Walker is the latest star signing for the PNG Chiefs. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"He is also still young and we believe that his best years are ahead of him.

"We're thrilled that Sam has committed to what we are building and we look forward to seeing him play a key role in the bright future of the PNG Chiefs."

Walker is the latest star signing for the Chiefs, who have created shockwaves in the player market with their ability to offer tax-free contracts.

In the past week, they have signed Canberra and New South Wales backrower Hudson Young and North Queensland star Jeremiah Nanai.

Luai, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and Joseph Manu will also line up for the Chiefs in their inaugural season.

Walker is the ninth player they have signed with either Test or Origin experience.

World.title: Lyon's career in limbo as he faces Test axe
World.content:
Nathan Lyon is set to be axed from Australia's squad for the first Test in a move that raises questions over the 39-year-old's future in the team.

Australia will on Saturday name their squad for the December 9 series opener against New Zealand in Perth, but it is understood Lyon will not be included.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner when fit for more than 13 years, but selectors have shown a willingness to go without a specialist tweaker more often recently.

Selections and strategy in the spotlight After a disastrous series loss to South Africa, Australian cricket faces some tough decisions.

He has three times been left out of Australia's team over the past 18 months, with selectors picking four quicks in Tests against West Indies, England and South Africa.

But the spinner's omission from the squad is even more notable, given previous such calls have been made on seeing the final wicket closer to the toss.

Lyon has made no secret of his desire to continue playing, with legacy-defining tours of India and England in the next nine months.

The sixth-leading wicket-taker of all time with 577 scalps, Lyon worked around the clock to recover from a hamstring injury last summer and return to the Test side.

His push has included giving up alcohol and spending more time in the gym, having previously described how he is trying to squeeze every last bit out of his career, with 145 Tests already to his name.

Nathan Lyon struggled to make a breakthrough in the latter stages of the third Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Grant Pitcher)

Where that career goes from here is now in question.

Lyon took six wickets at 43.67 in Australia's most recent tour of South Africa, where he was overlooked for Scott Boland in a wet second Test in Gqeberha.

Included in that was Australia's inability to take wickets on the fourth day of the final Test in Cape Town, as South Africa recovered from a 100-run first-innings deficit.

South Africa spinner Simon Harmer then bagged 6-16 on the final day to bowl the Proteas to victory.

NSW draw against Queensland Thanks to a sporting declaration by Queensland and some exceptional bowling, the SCG was treated to one of the best Sheffield Shield finishes in years as New South Wales hung on for a draw.

Lyon has since taken seven Sheffield Shield wickets across two matches on return to Australia, but was out-bowled by Queensland leg spinner Mitchell Swepson in Sydney this week.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald had indicated after the loss in Cape Town that Lyon remained Australia's number one spinner, when asked if that would be reviewed.

"Review it?" McDonald responded at the time.

"I don't think it's something to review now. We'll sit back and we'll go through Shield cricket.

"Nathan will be preparing for the first Test match in Perth."

AAP

World.title: Results of independent Sandpapergate forum to be made public
World.content:
Cricket Australia's (CA) forum into the 2018 ball-tampering scandal will not determine responsibility or make adverse findings against any individual, according to its terms of reference published today.

The scandal reignited this month after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja said the whole team had known about the ball-tampering plot during the tour of South Africa, not just the three players found culpable by CA's integrity unit.

Justin Langer's spray An Australian player suggested tampering with the ball in the nation's first Test after Sandpapergate before the intervention of then-coach Justin Langer.

CA announced on November ‌18 it would open an independent forum for all the players and staff to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 without fear of sanction.

The six-week forum, to be overseen by Australian barrister Fiona ‌McLeod, will be an "information-gathering and listening process", rather than a disciplinary process, its terms of reference said.

It will not make "any adverse findings about, or determine the ‌responsibility of, any individual", nor revisit the sanctions previously imposed. There will ‌be no recommendations for retrospective punishment or legal action, and participation will be entirely voluntary.

"Its purpose is to support the welfare of those impacted and to provide Participants with an opportunity to be heard and to have their experience acknowledged and understood without fear of retribution ‌or disadvantage," the terms said.

Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann told ABC Sport he would be happy to take part in the voluntary process.

"I can't see why you wouldn't," Lehmann said on ABC Radio ahead of Australia's third T20I against England at the Gabba.

Darren Lehmann looks into the distance. (Jason McCawley - CA/Cricket Australia via Getty Images)

"The big thing for me is transparency, care, and safety of the players and their wellbeing.

"Some will go, some won't, that's totally up to the individual I suppose.

"This lady running it, Fiona McLeod, I'm sure she'll get to the bottom of what she needs to get to and get her answers and people will tell their story."

CA's investigation in 2018 found only three players culpable — former captain Steve Smith and opening batters David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

Smith and Warner were banned for 12 months, with Bancroft suspended for nine.

Khawaja's ‌former teammates Warner, Bancroft and Chadd ‌Sayers have supported his claims that the wider playing group and staff were aware of the ball-tampering.

However, ‌captain Pat Cummins and bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have flatly denied any prior knowledge.

CA backed Cummins to remain captain of the Test and one-day ‌international sides last week and rejected any suggestion his integrity had been compromised amid the renewed furore.

Lehmann admitted that he didn't know if the forum would be successful, but said it was important to give his side of the story.

"I suppose [I want to be a part of it] to answer any questions that Fiona might have and give my side … because otherwise it's just going to keep going for everyone isn't it?" Lehmann said.

"We're going to try and get some closure somewhere. It's not a great spot for the game."

The scope of CA's forum will include "ball-management practices" by the men's team during all four Tests of the South Africa tour and not just the Newlands test where Australia's ball-tampering was exposed.

It will also include the conduct and scope of CA's investigation in 2018.

CA said a report into the forum would be published ‌in full and ‌it would respond within 30 days.

"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn," CA chairman David Boon said in a statement.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Opinions split ahead of Supercars move to MotoGP track
World.content:
Every year Supercars teams count down the days to racing on the Adelaide Parklands Circuit, and some say this year's event is tinged with a touch of sadness.

Racing gets underway today with a 100-kilometre race, followed by 250-kilometre races on both Saturday and Sunday to crown this year's title winner.

Currently Matt Payne leads, with Brodie Kostecki, Broc Feeney and Chaz Mostert still in contention.

It is the last time the drivers will race around the street circuit, a shortened version of the track unveiled in 1985 to host the Formula 1 Australian Grand Prix, before the race was moved to Victoria in 1995.

This year's Adelaide Grand Final will be the last race on the current circuit before a major overhaul. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The track made a comeback in 1999 for the newly created Adelaide 500 event up until a brief COVID hiatus, and a 2022 revival brought on by the Malinauskas election win.

Spectators and drivers alike have said they love the current circuit, with its tight corners and compact walls which make for exciting racing.

But in 2027, the Supercars race, now known as the Adelaide Grand Final, will move to the soon-to-be-built and controversial MotoGP track in the eastern parklands — with both the events scheduled for November next year.

The new track has some teams worried, including Ryan Walkinshaw, director of Walkinshaw TWG Racing.

"Is it going to dilute the value that we currently have in this current event? That's entirely a possibility," he said.

"It is perfect for Supercars, so the fact that's going to change I do have some concerns about."

Drivers have been consulted about the design of the supercars track. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Tom Moore, team manager for Dick Johnson Racing said he also shared some of those concerns.

"This circuit in particular will lose some of its raw edge that makes Adelaide different to everyone, but there will be some advantages," he said.

Triple Eight Race Engineering Team Manager Mark Dutton had a more positive view.

"As much as we all love this track, change is awesome, we'll all come here next year and we'll all adapt," he said.

Drivers were consulted about the design of the Supercars track and Ryan Wood said he was ready to embrace it.

He said he could see the benefits of a track that would have greater flow with the race walls being further back.

"Probably a bit more flowing than what the track's like at the moment, but I tell you what, it's always exciting to have a new track on the calendar, hopefully the locals can get around it," he said.

The street circuit will look different next year to also accommodate for the MotoGP circuit. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

While racing over the next three days, the drivers will also spend some time reminiscing.

Current series leader Matt Payne said turn eight on the current track was not your average stretch of bitumen.

"I've lost the championship at turn eight and I've won one the next year in Supercar twos," he said.

Brodie Kostecki was more blunt when asked if he would miss the notorious spot.

"Not really," he said, with a chuckle.

World.title: The remarkable journey behind one of oldest Wallabies debutants
World.content:
James Ramm, the late-blooming, one-time gymnast who has finally made the international rugby grade at the age of 28, wants his long, battling journey to the top to inspire a new generation of wannabe Wallabies.

When winger Ramm takes the field at Twickenham against Ireland for his Australia debut on Friday night (Saturday AEDT), it will be the culmination of a road beset by injuries and false starts, one on which he switched sports and had to move to the other side of the world to reboot his career.

But now, when he thinks how the one-time gangly kid who couldn't even break into his first-team at Sydney's St Joseph's College is going to be one of the modern-day Wallabies' oldest wing debutants after years of perseverance, he declares: "I'm really proud of my journey."

James Ramm shot to stardom with Northampton Saints in England. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

"And all I hope from it is that other people who are in similar situations, playing seconds or thirds at school who want to pursue rugby, realise that school's not the be-all and end-all," he said.

"As soon as you leave school, you understand that, but when you're in it, it's quite hard to see. A couple of years ago, I went back to Joey's actually to talk to the second XV players at the school and explain my story and show that not everyone's journey is the same.

"If you really want it, you can get it from whatever position you're in at school."

So it was that Ramm's rugby adventure really only began after he'd given up on his promising gymnastics career, which had once dealt him dreams of being an Olympian.

Yet he couldn't crack the rugby hierarchy at "Joey's", unlike his schoolmate Tom Wright, with whom he'll now be working in the back three at Twickenham.

"Wrighty was sort of a superstar at school, and I'd love it if he ever talked to me," said Ramm, as he sat next to a chuckling Wright at the Wallabies' team hotel in London on Thursday.

Ramm did finally break through for Randwick and represented the Junior Wallabies.

He went on to a brief spell in Dave Rennie's Australia squad while with the Waratahs, but injury woes and lack of progress at home led him to head for England, his mother's home country.

There, he really blossomed with Northampton, scoring 32 tries and helping them win two English titles and reach the final of last year's Europe's Champions Cup Final, before also going on to impress while propelling Northland to the NPC final in New Zealand.

Now firmly back in the Australian fold having signed a two-year deal with Western Force, he's suddenly burst back into the picture under coach Les Kiss, admitting he was "overwhelmed" when he got the call to play this week after not even being in the 23 the previous weeks on the Nations Championship northern tour.

Beale back in Wallabies team The return of Kurtley Beale to the Wallabies team for cap number 96 after a five-year absence is a reward for his continuing excellence, coach Les Kiss insists.

He's going to make his debut at the home ground of the country that even sniffed around trying to sign him up as an England player.

Having not even settled back at his new home in Perth before being jetting back out to the UK with his Wallabies teammates, Ramm said: "I didn't think I'd sort of be touching down in Sydney and then a couple of days later be back over here in this beautiful weather as quickly as I have."

That "beautiful weather" will be a bone-chilling night at HQ, but it will all be worth it for Ramm, who calls Twickenham "a sick stadium", having got used to the ambience in big finals with Northampton. He reckons he's ready for anything.

"Age is definitely just a number. My rugby career started a bit later than probably what's usual, so I'm hoping that I can bank those years at the back end of my career," Ramm said.

"And for me, this validates every time you wanted to take an easy option, or thought 'I'm gonna have a day off or skip this' but didn't. It validates the fact that all that hard work pays off.

"It's tough sometimes, and you're in the dumps, but it really shows that if you persist with it and you keep on that line, it's all worth it."

AAP

World.title: Everything you need to know as Roos hunt historic AFLW three-peat
World.content:
The AFLW is on the cusp of history as an all-conquering North Melbourne side looks to claim its third consecutive premiership in this year's grand final.

Standing in the Kangaroos' way will be Melbourne, a team that has been one of the most consistent over the last couple of years.

Here is everything you need to know ahead of tonight's decider between the Roos and Dees.

What time is the AFLW grand final?

This year's AFLW grand final takes place on Friday, November 27. Here is the first bounce time according to which state or territory you are watching from:

7:45pm AEDT: Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania

Victoria, New South Wales, Tasmania 7:15pm ACDT: South Australia

South Australia 6:45pm AEST: Queensland

Queensland 6:15pm ACST: Northern Territory

Northern Territory 4:45pm AWST: Western Australia

Where is the AFLW grand final being played?

This year's grand final venue — Princes Park — hosted the first ever AFLW contest in 2017. (Getty Images: AFL Media/Adam Trafford)

This year's AFLW grand final will once again be hosted by Princes Park in Melbourne.

Princes Park hosted the last three AFLW grand finals and also the 2018 decider between the Western Bulldogs and Brisbane.

Where can I watch the AFLW grand final?

Fans can watch the game on free-to-air TV on Channel 7 as well as its streaming services.

Kayo Sports will also broadcast the grand final.

ABC Sport will run a live blog where you can follow all the action and analysis, while you can also listen to the match live on ABC Sport via the website, local radio or the Listen app.

What are the AFLW grand final team line-ups?

North Melbourne

No change FB: Libby Birch, Jasmine Ferguson HB: Eliza Shannon, Erika O'Shea, Emma Kearney C: Taylah Gatt, Eilish Sheerin, Tess Craven HF: Alice O'Loughlin, Bella Eddey, Blaithin Bogue FF: Tahlia Randall, Vikki Wall FOLL: Kim Rennie, Ash Riddell, Jasmine Garner INT: Nicole Bresnahan, Amy Gavin Mangan, Ruby Tripodi, Jenna Bruton, Kate Shierlaw

Melbourne

IN: Lauren Pearce OUT: Laela Ebert (omitted) FB: Tahlia Gillard, Sarah Lampard HB: Sinead Goldrick, Molly O'Hehir, Paxy Paxman C: Maeve Chaplin, Shelley Heath-Barker, Eliza McNamara HF: Ryleigh Wotherspoon, Alyssa Bannan, Maggie Mahony FF: Kate Hore, Tayla Harris FOLL: Georgia Campbell, Olivia Purcell, Tyla Hanks INT: Jordyn S. Allen, Lauren Pearce, Megan Fitzsimon, Aoife Horisk, Mia Austin

Who are the key players for each team?

Ash Riddell has led all AFLW players with 33.8 disposals per game this season. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

North Melbourne will once again rely on its star duo of captain Jasmine Garner and midfield maestro Ash Riddell.

Riddell led the league in disposals per game with 33.8, while Garner added 30.1 touches herself, with both players making 14 appearances this season.

Melbourne's back line will also have to be wary of Kangaroos forward Tahlia Randall, who has slammed home a team-high 27 goals this season, while Garner has also hit the scoreboard with 14 goals.

The Demons also have their own dynamic duo in the midfield, with Olivia Purcell's 30.8 touches per game good for fourth in the league, while Tyla Hanks has added 25.5 touches of her own.

Mia Austin is Melbourne's leading goalkicker this season with 17 goals in just eight appearances, while skipper Kate Hore has kicked 10 goals and averaged 19.1 touches per game.

Who are the coaches for the AFLW grand finalists

Darren Crocker (left) has led North Melbourne to its two premiership wins over the last two seasons. (Kelly Defina/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

North Melbourne is still coached by Darren Crocker, who has led the team to the last two AFLW premierships.

Crocker, who played 165 games for North Melbourne's men's team, has coached the women's side since 2021.

Before his AFLW coaching career, Crocker led the Kangaroos men's side as caretaker coach in 15 matches during three separate seasons.

Tom Wilson has led Melbourne to the AFLW grand final in his first season in charge. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

Melbourne is coached by Tom Wilson, who is in his first season in charge of the Demons after taking over from the club's inaugural AFLW coach Mick Stinear.

Wilson joined the Demons after spending two seasons with Collingwood as the club's midfield coach and head of development.

He played 176 games for the Northern Blues/Bullants and Collingwood's reserves team between 2011 and 2025.

What is the recent history between North and Melbourne?

The Kangaroos have had the wood over the Demons in the last five meetings, winning four.

Here is a look at how exactly these two teams have fared against each other of late:

Round 7, 2026: North Melbourne 10.5 (65) def. Melbourne 5.4 (34) @ Princes Park Preliminary Final, 2025: North Melbourne 6.10 (46) def. Melbourne 5.6 (36) @ Princes Park Round 3, 2024: North Melbourne 11.5 (71) def. Melbourne 3.3 (21) @ Casey Fields Qualifying Final, 2023: North Melbourne 7.8 (50) def. Melbourne 1.3 (9) @ Princes Park Round 8, 2023: Melbourne 5.7 (37) def. North Melbourne 2.2 (14) @ Princes Park

How many AFLW premierships have these teams won?

North Melbourne has won the AFLW premiership over the last two seasons. (Getty Images)

North Melbourne has won two premierships over the last two years and hopes to be the first team in AFLW history to claim three straight wins.

This grand final appearance is North Melbourne's fourth, with the previous three coming over the last three seasons.

Melbourne has won one AFLW premiership during S7 (2022).

The Demons were runners-up during S6 (2021) and are making their third grand final appearance.

Who is doing the pre-match entertainment?

The Jungle Giants will provide the half-time entertainment this year. (ABC)

The Jungle Giants, an indie rock band from Brisbane, will headline this year's AFLW grand final entertainment.

The group's four members are Sam Hales, Cesira Aitken, Andrew Dooris and Keelan Bijker.

Their opening act will be Super Disco Club, who will also play music during breaks in play.

Kate Miller-Heidke will sing the national anthem.

World.title: Aussie rugby sevens star driven to 'tick off' goal of Olympic gold
World.content:
Tia Hinds may only be 24, but she's already experienced much in her young rugby career.

Representing Australia, claiming world titles, travelling to almost every continent and even playing alongside her mum, Janine, in a Randwick club match.

"She played on the wing for one game," Hinds told ABC Sport with the hint of a giggle.

"We were short of numbers."

There's one experience, though, Hinds hopes she can reflect upon when the time comes to hang up the boots.

The goal of winning an Olympic gold medal burns brightly for the unassuming Sydneysider, as it does for her Australian women's rugby sevens teammates.

Following the historic 2016 Rio Olympics triumph, Australia didn't reach the podium at the Tokyo and Paris Games, finishing fifth and fourth respectively.

Tia Hinds made her Olympic debut in Tokyo. (Getty Images: Dan Mullan)

The Paris result was a particularly bitter pill to swallow, given Australia was reigning world series champions.

"We're such a high-performing team on the world series circuit, it's been a bit hard to deal with that," said Hinds, who was a member of Australia's Tokyo and Paris squads.

"We've fallen short two times now."

The Australians, who won last season's World Championship, are chasing automatic qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

To book their berth, they must finish inside the top four in the 2027 World Championship, which will be decided across three tournaments (Hong Kong, Valladolid and Bordeaux) in April and May.

The six-leg world series takes place before those events, beginning in Dubai on Saturday.

Tia Hinds is among Australia's major attacking threats. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Under the guidance of new coach Reg Tayler, Australia is expected to meet New Zealand in the final of the season-opening tournament on Monday morning, AEDT.

But ahead of any potential match-up with its trans-Tasman rival, Australia must advance from its round-robin pool, which includes the well-credentialed USA and France.

"It's definitely one match at a time, as the USA and France are two powerhouse teams," Hinds said.

"We would love to play in the final and of course it's usually against the Kiwis, so it would be naive not to have a look at how they're doing in their pool matches.

"But we definitely will focus on the pool stage first."

Hinds's pivotal role

A calf injury robbed Hinds of the chance to play in last season's World Championship-deciding tournament in Bordeaux.

But Australia wouldn't have been in a position to lift the silverware in France if it hadn't been for the talented playmaker.

At the preceding World Championship leg in Valladolid, she triggered Australia's comeback in its thrilling 28-26 semifinal win over New Zealand.

Tia Hinds played a key role in Australia's World Championship victory last season. (Getty Images: Caean Couto)

With Australia trailing 14-0 in the first half, Hinds's outstanding ability to read the game came to the fore when she took advantage of lazy defence to score a runaway try.

Hinds's goal kicking also proved crucial, perhaps the by-product of playing Australian rules as a junior with the Maroubra Saints, where Sydney Swans AFL star Errol Gulden was a teammate.

A loss to New Zealand in Valladolid would have effectively dashed Australia's hopes of clinching the World Championship.

Expressing modesty when speaking about her influence on the result, Hinds instead heaped praise on captain Bella Nasser for steering Australia home.

"We've got a really captain in Bella, who is really composed and got her head screwed on," said Hinds, who sustained her season-ending injury in the Valladolid semifinal victory.

Tia Hinds represented the Wallaroos this year. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Rugby sevens isn't the only international stage graced by Hinds, as she also represents Australia's national 15-a-side team, the Wallaroos.

Making the Wallaroos squad for the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup is among her ambitions, especially as the tournament will be held on home soil.

But before the dream of playing in her second World Cup can be realised, climbing the podium at the LA Olympics remains a major priority for Hinds.

"There's some unfinished business, to tick off that goal of hopefully medalling at an Olympic Games," Hinds said.

World.title: Returning Matildas star Cooney-Cross wants to make late mum 'proud'
World.content:
When Kyra Cooney-Cross returned to the pitch for Arsenal in the Women's Super League in September, she shared a moving message from her mum.

Its essence is one that so many parents would have relayed to their kids in one manner or another in their sporting careers, whether they were as decorated as a Matildas' linchpin, or finding their feet for the first time in the under 5s.

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it," the message read.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Amongst the pain of losing her mother Jess to terminal bile duct cancer in July, Cooney-Cross has taken the message to heart, and three months after returning to club football, she's back for the Matildas.

Kyra Cooney-Cross returned for her club side Arsenal in August. (Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

The 24-year-old is in the squad for friendlies against Colombia in Canberra and Geelong, in a key test just seven months out from the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

"It's bittersweet. It's my first time back with the national team since everything that's happened with my mum and our family," she told ABC News Breakfast.

"But playing for your country, this is the highest level I can play at, and it's the highest level I can make my mum proud.

"So I'm really looking forward to it and being back at home in Geelong in front of my family and friends and just being back with the team."

Cooney-Cross last played for the Matildas at the Women's Asian Cup in March. (Getty Images: Corbis/Steve Christo)

Cooney-Cross's last international appearance was in March's Women's Asian Cup, and after her breakthrough tournament at the now fabled 2023 World Cup, she's eager to recreate those highs.

"It's definitely flown by. I don't think a lot of us players had even the time to process the World Cup and what we had done in this country and for women's football in Australia," she said.

"We're just going to work really hard. Stick together and focus on these next two games.

"The World Cup is obviously really important and we want to get really far."

McKenna making moves

Cooney-Cross will play a pivotal part in Brazil next year but others on the fringe, like midfielder Leticia McKenna, hope for their own breakout moment.

Leticia McKenna made her Matildas debut earlier this year. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

McKenna, 24, made her international debut in April, and starred for Melbourne City before securing a move to Nottingham Forest in the second tier of English women's football.

She was also recently named PFA Young Footballer of the Year.

"It's been very surreal. It's been a really big year, something I'm extremely proud of," she said.

McKenna's UK move made waves, setting an A-League Women's record with her transfer fee.

"It was a very, very hard decision to leave. It came up at quite short notice as well and I was very happy at the position I was in with Melbourne City and I was looking forward to the upcoming season in that regard," she said.

"But it was something I felt I was ready for. It was always in the back of my mind to make that step and move overseas."

Having made the most of her opportunities with the national side so far, and with only a handful of games left in the lead up, McKenna is eyeing off a berth in that final World Cup squad.

"You always gotta have a goal and aspirations and it's always been a dream," she said.

"Super grateful to be here and it's just making me even hungrier to keep dreaming."
